units.la: AU LECTEUR SAGE, ET DESINTERESSE.
units.tr: TO THE WISE AND DISINTERESTED READER.

units.la: MON CHER LECTEUR, Je vous donne ces Remar-ques, pour vous faire voir, quelle est la dignité des deux Escholes de Medecine les plus celebres, & vous monstrer en mesme temps les auantages que la Faculté de Paris, a sur celle de Montpelier, comme sur toutes les autres du monde. Cét ouvrage fut conceu dans la chaleur d'un procés, que l'authorité d'un Arrest n'a pû terminer; & si Theophraste Renaudot se formalise de se voir meslé
units.tr: MY DEAR READER, I give you these Remarks so that you may see what the dignity is of the two most celebrated Schools of Medicine, and at the same time show you the advantages which the Faculty of Paris has over that of Montpellier, as over all the others in the world. This work was conceived in the heat of a lawsuit which the authority of a Decree could not bring to an end; and if Theophraste Renaudot takes offence at finding himself mixed up

units.la: AU LECTEUR.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: dans ce Discours,il doit confiderer que les escrits diffamatoires dont il à déchiré noftre Eschole , demeurent toûjours, & que ce n'est pas assez que le Parlement ait condamné ses iniustes entreprises , si on n'efface encore les traits de sa langue & de sa plume.
units.tr: in this Discourse, he must consider that the defamatory writings with which he has torn apart our School remain forever, and that it is not enough that the Parlement has condemned his unjust undertakings, unless the marks of his tongue and pen are also erased.

units.la: Res falsa & inanis nisi corrigatur, habet nonnunquam fidem, multique sunt homines iudicij parum firmi, qui nihil audiant, legantve, quod non credant, nisi refutatum sciant, disoit Senecque.
units.tr: A false and empty thing, unless it is corrected, sometimes has credibility, and there are many men of little firm judgment who hear or read nothing that they do not believe, unless they know it has been refuted, said Seneca.

units.la: La memoire du nom de Renaudot, & de ses temeraires desseins, nous sera à jamais odieuse ; il a voulu s'immortaliser en destruisat nostreEschole, comme voulut faire autresfois cét Erostrate, en bruslant le Temple de Diane en Ephefe. C'est certainement une grande temerité à un particulier , de choquer tout un corps, & un corps composé de tant de sçauans, estably depuis huict cens ans dans la Capitale du Royaume,& qui ne peut ce semble perir,qu'auec cette florissante Ville. Mais cette temerité ne doit pas demeurer impunie ,& la playe que Renaudot a faite à nostre Eschole saignant encore, il est bien raisonnable de la guerir , & de chastier celuy qui l'a faite. Le libelle diffamatoire que l'Eschole de Montpelier a fait contre l'Eschole de Paris, se lit tous les jours ; ces nouueaux establissemens de pretendus Medecins de Montpelier , sous le nom de Conseillers & de Medecins du Roy , font tous les jours quelque bleffure nouuelle , à l'honneur de nostre Faculté , & on ne peut ny parer ces coups , ny repousser ces injures ,sans nommer le veritable Autheur de tous ces desordres.
units.tr: The memory of the name of Renaudot, and of his rash designs, will be hateful to us forever; he wished to immortalise himself by destroying our School, as that Erostratus once wished to do by burning the Temple of Diana at Ephesus. It is certainly a great rashness for one private person to assail an entire body, and a body composed of so many learned men, established for eight hundred years in the capital of the Kingdom, and which, it seems, can perish only together with this flourishing city. But this rashness must not go unpunished, and since the wound that Renaudot has inflicted on our School is still bleeding, it is entirely reasonable to heal it and to punish the one who inflicted it. The defamatory libel that the School of Montpelier has written against the School of Paris is read every day; these new establishments of so-called physicians of Montpelier, under the name of Counsellors and Physicians of the King, deal some new blow every day to the honour of our Faculty, and one can neither parry these blows nor repel these injuries without naming the true author of all these disorders.

units.la: Renaudot , qui retient tousiours la qualité vaine, & sans fonction d'Intendant, & de Commissaire general des pauures de France , & qui espere de trouver enfin quelque coniōcture[?] fa-
units.tr: Renaudot, who still retains the empty title, without function, of Intendant and Commissioner General of the poor of France, and who hopes at last to find some opportunity [?] fa-

units.la: Av LECTEVR.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: uorable pour faire reüssir ses desseins, est la seule cause de tous les maux, dont nous nous plaignons, & que la confideration du public nous rend encore plus douloureux ; autresfois nous traitions auec luy, & les autres Medecins de Montpelier, auec beaucoup de moderation, & de retenuë; nous les souffrions dans Paris sans les rechercher, nous auons laissé dormir long-temps nos Statuts & nos Priuileges, de crainte de troubler la Paix, ou d'exciter du scandale; mais voyant que Renaudot affembloit toutes les semaines dans son Bureau d'Adresse des Medecins, qui se disoient Medecins de Montpelier; voyás que ces assemblées grossissoient de iour à autre, & s'en alloient remplir cette ville de Medecins estrangers: qu'il se formoit vne cabale contre la saine doctrine de nostre Eschole, nous auons esté contraints de nous armer contre des nouueautez également preiudiciables à nostre honneur, & à la vie, & à la santé de nos Concitoiens. C'est une chose bien estrange, de voir de jeunes gens, ou plutost de jeunes Escoliers, qui se qualifient Docteurs Medecins en l'Vniuersité de Montpelier, s'esleuer orgueilleusement contre la Faculté de Paris, & s'efforcer de renuerser toutes les anciennes maximes de nostre profession; mais comme ces petits Docteurs, se sont sentis trop foibles pour se maintenir, & que Renaudot estoit pour eux vn appuy fort mal asseuré, ils ont imploré le secours, & mandié l'interuention de l'Eschole de Montpelier; cela pourtant ne leur a de rien seruy, car par Arrest du premier jour de Mars 1644. defenses ont esté faites àces nouueaux Docteurs, & aux Professeurs mesmes, residans en la ville de Montpelier, de faire des assemblées, n'y d'exercer la Medecine dans la ville de Paris. C'est ainsi que la Cour de Parlement a restably l'ordre ancien, & nous pésions voir bien tost cette grande Ville purgée de cette mauuaise semence, quand ils ont trouué un expedient pour rendre inutile l'authorité des Arrests, & toute la préuoyance du Parlement. Cét expedient a esté d'obtenir des Lettres de Conseillers Medecins du Roy, pour s'establir dans Paris: Sous ce titre, ils se qualifient Medecins, tantost Hermetiques, tantost Emetiques de l'Eschole de Montpelier: ils se vantent de scauoir mille beaux secrets de Medecine, qu'ils vendent eux mesmes, & bien cherement aux malades, & en cette qualité chimerique de Conseillers & Medecins du Roy, ils ont trouué un Chef qui les maintient, & qui les esleue infiniment au dessus des Medecins de Paris, qui ne sont que des ignorans, à leur dire, & qui traittent les malades à la vieille mode d'Hippocrate, & de Galien. Ils disent que si ces grands
units.tr: It is the vain title, held without any office, of Renaudot, who keeps the title of Intendant and Commissioner General of the Poor of France, and who hopes at last to find some favourable conjuncture to bring his designs to success, that is the sole cause of all the evils of which we complain, and which the thought of the public makes all the more painful to us. Formerly we dealt with him, and with the other physicians of Montpellier, with great moderation and restraint; we tolerated them in Paris without seeking them out, and for a long time we let our Statutes and our Privileges lie dormant, for fear of disturbing the peace or giving rise to scandal. But seeing that Renaudot gathered every week in his Bureau d'Adresse physicians who called themselves physicians of Montpellier; seeing that these assemblies grew larger from day to day and were going to fill this city with foreign physicians; and that a faction was forming against the sound doctrine of our School, we were compelled to arm ourselves against novelties equally prejudicial to our honour, to the life and to the health of our fellow citizens. It is a very strange thing to see young men, or rather young students, who style themselves Doctors of Medicine in the University of Montpellier, rise up proudly against the Faculty of Paris and strive to overthrow all the ancient maxims of our profession. But since these little doctors felt too weak to maintain themselves, and since Renaudot was for them a very insecure support, they implored help and begged the intervention of the School of Montpellier. This, however, did them no good at all, for by the Arrest of the first day of March 1644, prohibitions were issued to these new doctors, and to the professors themselves residing in the city of Montpellier, against holding assemblies or practising medicine in the city of Paris. Thus the Court of Parlement restored the old order, and we could soon have hoped to see this great city purged of this bad seed, when they found an expedient to render the authority of the Arrests and all the foresight of the Parlement useless. This expedient was to obtain letters appointing them Counsellor-Physicians to the King, so as to establish themselves in Paris. Under this title they style themselves physicians, sometimes Hermetic, sometimes Emetic, of the School of Montpellier; they boast that they know a thousand fine secrets of medicine, which they sell themselves, and very dearly, to the sick; and in this chimerical capacity of Counsellors and Physicians to the King they have found a Chief who maintains them and raises them infinitely above the physicians of Paris, who, by their account, are only ignoramuses, and who treat the sick in the old-fashioned manner of Hippocrates and Galen. They say that if these great...

units.la: AV LECTEVR.
units.tr: THE READER.

units.la: Maistres de noftre art reuenoient au monde, ils feroient rauis de voir leurs nouueaux remedes, condamneroient sans doute leur propre doctrine. Mais parmy toutes ces choses, il n'y a rien de plus déplorable, que de voir quelques Medecins de Paris, pratiquer vne methode si pernicieuse, & s'efforcer de rendre noftre Eschole Hermetique, & Emetique.
units.tr: If the masters of our art came back into the world, they would be delighted to see their new remedies, and would without doubt condemn their own doctrine. But among all these things there is nothing more deplorable than to see some physicians of Paris practising such a pernicious method and striving to make our School Hermetic and Emetic.

units.la: Iunguntur iam Tigres, equis, annoque sequenti Cum canibus timidi venient ad pocula damae.
units.tr: Now tigers are yoked with horses, and in the following year the timid deer will come with the dogs to the water-bowls.

units.la: Apres cela demandez d'où vient le defordre dans la Medecine.
units.tr: After this, ask whence the disorder in medicine comes.

units.la: Perditio tua ex te Israel, o fortunati nimium sua si bona norint Agricolae.
units.tr: Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel; O far too fortunate farmers, if only they knew their own blessings.

units.la: Neantmoins il y a parmy nous des Medecins fçauans, genereux & vertueux, qui n'ont point adoré cét Idole Antimonial, que noftre Eschole a de tout temps condamné. Tobie dans l'Ef-
units.tr: Nevertheless, there are among us learned, generous and virtuous physicians, who have not worshipped that antimonial idol, which our School has always condemned. Tobias in the Ef-

units.la: AU LECTEUR.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: criture Saincte, est loüé pour n'avoir point flechy le genoüil devant les veaux d'or de Jeroboam, & si nous croyons les Chymistes, ce premier veau d'or, qui fut adoré dans le desert, estoit formé par les mysteres de leur art, & quand il fut converty en poudre, & jetté dans l'eau, les Israëlites en burent comme de l'or potable. Ce vin Emetique, qui avoit esté aboly pendant 40. ans dans Paris, a esté ressuscité par Quercetan, dit la Violette, & Mayerne, dit Turquet, Medecins Chymistes, apres la mort desquels ces dangereux remedes avoient esté mesprisez, jusques à ce que quelques Medecins, ne se sentans pas assez forts pour soustenir la reputation qu'ils avoient acquise, ont eu recours depuis dix ou douze ans au vin Emetique, & au Laudanum, qu'ils distribuét eux mesmes à leurs malades. Il est bien vray qu'un Medecin ignorant, & sans conscience, peut donner du vin Emetique, & hazarder ainsi la vie des hommes, qui ne se peut perdre qu'une fois. Mais ceux qui sont demeurez dans les bonnes, & les anciennes maximes de nostre profession, sont obligez de desabuser le peuple, qui par une credulité, souuent mortelle, confie sa vie à ces jeunes Docteurs de Montpelier, qui peut-estre ne furent jamais à Montpelier. Certes, c'est un grand aveuglement, de preferer de jeunes gens, sans estude, sans instruction des anciens Maistres, aux Medecins de Paris, & à des hommes d'une experience consommée. Il y a dequoy s'estonner, que de grands personnages qui se croyent fort éclairez, se laissent pour tant tromper à ces dangereux vendeurs de fumée, & prennent pour bonne, une monnoye si visiblement fausse, Nemo iustius assiduè discit quàm qui de humana salute tractauerint, disoit Cassio-dore. Il est certain que pour bien reüs-
units.tr: Scripture praises Tobias for not having bowed the knee before the golden calves of Jeroboam; and if we believe the Chymists, that first golden calf which was adored in the desert was formed by the mysteries of their art, and when it was reduced to powder and thrown into the water, the Israelites drank of it as potable gold. This emetic wine, which had been abolished for forty years in Paris, was revived by Quercetan, called la Violette and Mayerne, called Turquet, Chymist physicians; after whose death these dangerous remedies had been despised, until some physicians, not feeling strong enough to sustain the reputation they had acquired, have had recourse, these ten or twelve years, to emetic wine and Laudanum, which they distribute to their patients themselves. It is indeed true that an ignorant physician without conscience can give emetic wine and thus risk the lives of men, which can be lost only once. But those who have remained within the good and ancient maxims of our profession are obliged to undeceive the people, who through a credulity often fatal, entrust their lives to those young Doctors of Montpellier, who perhaps never were at Montpellier. Truly, it is a great blindness to prefer young men, without study and without instruction from the ancient masters, to the physicians of Paris and to men of consummate experience. It is cause for astonishment that great personages, who believe themselves very enlightened, let themselves be so deceived by these dangerous sellers of smoke, and take for good a coin so visibly counterfeit. Nemo iustius assiduè discit quàm qui de humana salute tractauerint, said Cassiodorus. It is certain that to be well ...

units.la: AU LECTEUR.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: sir[?] en la science, & en l'exercice de la Medecine, il faut beaucoup d'esprit, un long & un continuel estude, un grand jugement, beaucoup d'experience & bien raisonnée, la conference & l'instruction des sçauans Maistres. Toutes ces choses se trouvent pleinement dans les Medecins de l'Eschole de Paris, au lieu que ces pretendus Medecins de Montpelier, sont destituez de tous, ou de la pluspart de ces avantages. Ce pendant ce sont ces hommes qui nous décrient tous les jours, qui nous appellét & ignorans, & grossiers; ce sont ces hommes qui mesprisent tous les autres, & qui se mocquent insolément de l'experience, & de la raison de tant de siecles, comme si pour envoyer, ou passer peut estre à Montpelier, on remport-oit delà tout l'esprit, & toute la suffisance necessaire à un doête, & à un sage Medecin. Certainement je plains le malheur de ceux qui par foiblesse, ou
units.tr: In the science and in the practice of Medicine one needs a great deal of wit, long and continual study, sound judgment, much experience well reasoned, and the conference and instruction of learned masters. All these things are found in full among the physicians of the School of Paris, whereas those pretended physicians of Montpellier are lacking in all, or in most, of these advantages. Yet it is these men who decry us every day, who call us ignorant and crude; it is these men who despise all the others and insolently mock experience and the reason of so many centuries, as if by going to Montpellier, or perhaps by passing through it, one carried away from there all the wit and all the competence needed by a learned and wise physician. Certainly I pity the misfortune of those who, through weakness, or

units.la: AV LECTEVR.
units.tr: AV LECTEVR.

units.la: par indiscretion, se mettent entre les mains de ces Docteurs sans doctrine: mais au moins l'Eschole de Paris a cette satisfaction, qu'elle n'aura pas contribué par son silence à leur malheur. Ce n'est pas son interest, c'est celuy du public qui la fait parler, & qui la touche: mais quelque chose qui arrive, elle fera tousiours son devoir, elle assistera tousiours les malades avec autant de generosité, que de suffisance & de soin; & si le siecle est ingrat pour elle, elle sçait qu'il y a là-haut un Juge qu'on ne peut tromper, & qui garde aux gens de bien des recompenses immortelles.
units.tr: through indiscretion, put themselves into the hands of these teachers without learning. But at least the School of Paris has this satisfaction: that it will not have contributed by its silence to their misfortune. It is not its own interest that moves it to speak, but that of the public, which concerns and touches it. Whatever happens, however, it will always do its duty: it will always assist the sick with as much generosity as skill and care. And if the age is ungrateful to it, it knows that there is a Judge above whom no one can deceive, and who keeps immortal rewards for good people.

units.la: Extraict du Priuilege du Roy.
units.tr: Extract from the King's Privilege.

units.la: PAR Priuilege de sa Maiesté, il est permis au Sieur IEAN RIOLAN, Docteur en Medecine de la Faculté de Paris, & Professeur Royal, &c. de faire imprimer, par tel Imprimeur ou Libraire qu'il voudra, vn Liure qu'il a composé, intitulé, Curieuses Recherches sur les Escholes en Medecine de Paris, & de Montpelier, &c. en telle forme & charactere qu'il luy plaira, & ce pour le temps & espace de dix ans, à compter du iour qu'il sera acheué d'imprimer pour la premiere fois: Et defenses sont faites à toutes personnes, de quelque qualité & condition qu'ils soient, d'imprimer, vendre, ny contrefaire ledit Liure, sans le consentement de GASPAR METVRAS, Marchand Libraire à Paris, auquel ledit Sieur RIOLAN a cedé & transporté ledit Priuilege; à peine de confiscation des Exemplaires, & de tous despens, dommages, & interests, comme il est plus amplement porté par ledit Priuilege. Donné à Paris le 9.[?] Fevrier 1648.
units.tr: By the privilege of His Majesty, Sieur JEAN RIOLAN, Doctor of Medicine of the Faculty of Paris and Royal Professor, etc., is permitted to have printed, by whatever printer or bookseller he chooses, a book he has composed, entitled Curious Researches on the Schools of Medicine of Paris and of Montpellier, etc., in whatever form and type he pleases, for the term and space of ten years, to be reckoned from the day it is finished printing for the first time. And prohibitions are made to all persons, of whatever quality and condition they may be, against printing, selling, or counterfeiting the said book without the consent of GASPAR METURAS, bookseller in Paris, to whom the said Sieur RIOLAN has ceded and transferred the said privilege; under penalty of confiscation of the copies and of all costs, damages, and interest, as is more fully set out in the said privilege. Given at Paris, the 9.[?] February 1648.

units.la: CURIEUSES RECHERCHES SUR LES ESCHOLES EN MEDECINE, DE PARIS, ET DE MONTPELIER, Necessaires d'estre sçeuës, pour la conserv- ation de la vie.
units.tr: CURIOUS RESEARCHES ON THE SCHOOLS OF MEDICINE IN PARIS AND MONTPELLIER, Necessary to be known for the preservation of life.

units.la: EN fin Theophraste Renaudot a tant fait par ses poursuites, escritures, & chiquaneries, qu'il a fait reüssir son grand dessein & chef-d'œuvre, qui estoit d'attirer dans son party l'Eschole de Montpelier, & nous mettre aux mains les uns contre les autres, puis se retirer hors de la presse, pour voir iouer les coups d'escrime, se rire de nos querelles, & disputes tres-dangereuses pour le public, particulierement dans la ville de Paris, où il auoit entrepris de brouiller, & detruire totalement la vraye Medecine, pour y introduire celle de Theophraste Paracelse son bon Maistre, qu'il faisoit enseigner dans son Bureau d'Adresse, assisté d'vne troupe de ieunes gens, soy disans Medecins de Montpelier, qui declamoient par mesdisances, & calomnies contre les Medecins de Paris, particulierement par la plume de Theophraste Renaudot, leur chef & conducteur.
units.tr: At last Theophraste Renaudot has accomplished, by his pursuits, writings and chicanery, what he had long designed as his great masterpiece: he has drawn the School of Montpellier over to his side and set us at each other's throats; then he has withdrawn from the fray to watch the fencing bouts and laugh at our quarrels and disputes, which are very dangerous for the public, particularly in the city of Paris. There he undertook to confuse and totally destroy true Medicine, in order to introduce that of Theophrastus Paracelsus, his good master, which he had taught in his Bureau d'Adresse, assisted by a troop of young men, self-styled physicians of Montpellier, who declaimed with slanders and calumnies against the physicians of Paris, above all through the pen of Theophraste Renaudot, their leader and director.

units.la: Tout cela s'est fait au veu, & au sçeu de toute la ville de Paris, & de la France. Les Libelles diffamatoires ont esté imprimez & distribuez auec ses Gazettes, par tout le Royaume, iusques aux pays estrangers.
units.tr: All this was done in full view and knowledge of the whole city of Paris and of France. Defamatory libels were printed and distributed together with his Gazettes throughout the kingdom, even into foreign countries.

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris se voyans ainsi attaquez & deschirez, leur Eschole & leur Doctrine horriblement diffamée, n'ont pû se taire, ont reparty à toutes ces calomnies, & iniures atroces, pour reparer les brefches[?], qu'on vouloit faire à leur honneur, sans offenser l'Eschole de Montpelier, qu'ils ont toujours par leurs escrits respectée, & reconnu auoir produit de sçauans hommes en la Medecine, tant en la Theorie, qu'en la Pratique, selon le climat du païs.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris, seeing themselves thus attacked and torn to pieces, their School and their Doctrine horribly defamed, could not keep silent. They have replied to all these calumnies and atrocious insults, to repair the breaches that were being made in their honour, without offending the School of Montpellier, which they have always respected in their writings, and whose men of learning in Medicine, both in theory and in practice, according to the climate of the country, they have acknowledged.

units.la: Nous n'auons jamais pretendu leur prescrire la methode d'exercer la Medecine en leur pays: en cela, & en tout nostre procedé, nous auons esté plus equitables qu'eux, qui veulent dans nostre climat, nous forcer à suiure leur forme de pratiquer, mais cela n'est qu'un incident.
units.tr: We have never intended to prescribe to them the method of practising Medicine in their own country. In this, and in our whole conduct, we have been more equitable than they, who wish to force us in our climate to follow their way of practising. But that is only a side issue.

units.la: Nostre plus grand crime, c'est d'auoir empesché, que tous ces jeunes gens tout fraischement forgez Docteurs à Montpelier, ne demeurassent en nostre ville, & là, former Eschole contre la nostre, qui est dresser Autel contre Autel, à la ruine de la vie de nos concitoyens. Les Ordonnances de nos Rois, les Arrests de la Cour de Parlement, la coustume ancienne de plus de cinq cens ans, nous ont donné ces Privileges. Pourquoy donc endurerons nous que de jeunes gens, presomptueux, ignorans, malicieux nous viennent braver jusques dans nos maisons? qu'ils publient par tout que nous sommes des ignorans en Medecine, que nous faisons mourir les malades par la Saignée, & par nos Medecines puantes & horribles.
units.tr: Our greatest crime is to have prevented all those young men, freshly forged as Doctors at Montpellier, from staying in our city and there forming a school against ours, which would be to raise altar against altar, to the ruin of the lives of our fellow citizens. The Ordinances of our Kings, the Decrees of the Court of Parliament, and the ancient custom of more than five hundred years have granted us these privileges. Why then should we endure that young men, presumptuous, ignorant and malicious, come to defy us even in our own houses, proclaiming everywhere that we are ignorant in Medicine, that we kill the sick by bloodletting and by our foul and horrible medicines?

units.la: Pour se maintenir contre nous ils ont rencontré pour chef & protecteur Theophraste Renaudot, lequel s'attribuant la qualité de
units.tr: To maintain themselves against us, they have found as their leader and protector Theophraste Renaudot, who, assuming for himself the title of

units.la: Commissaire general des pauures par toute la France, par Lettres Patentes du Roy, a voulu establir dans Paris, vne Compagnie de Medecins en tel nombre qu'il eut desiré, laquelle s'estoit accreuë iusques à plusieurs Medecins, tels quels, pour l'assister au traitement des pauures, qu'il pretendoit faire charitablement; Tres-beau, & specieux pretexte, que plusieurs loüoient, & approuuoient.
units.tr: Commissary General of the poor throughout all France, by letters patent of the King, wished to establish in Paris a company of physicians of whatever number he desired, which had grown to several physicians of sorts, to assist him in treating the poor, which he claimed to do charitably. A very fine and specious pretext, which many praised and approved.

units.la: Prob superi! quantum mortalia pectora caeca Noctis habent, ipso solers molimine Thereus Creditur esse pius, laudemque à crimine sumit.
units.tr: Good heavens! How much blind mortal hearts hold of night! Theseus, clever in his very contrivance, is believed to be pious, and takes praise from crime.

units.la: Et de fait, il s'estoit mis en possession d'exercer cette fonction, qu'il esperoit rendre vniuerselle par toutes les villes de la France, selon son pouuoir general: par consequent il pouuoit enuoyer des Missionnaires de cette Compagnie de Medecine, dans les grandes villes comme ses Commissaires, pour exercer la Medecine pour les pauures, tenir Bureau, assemblées, tout de mesme qu'à Paris sous la direction du General Theophraste Renaudot leur Chef.
units.tr: And indeed, he had put himself in possession of exercising this function, which he hoped to make universal throughout all the cities of France, according to his general power. Consequently he could send missionaries of this company of medicine into the great cities as his commissaries, to practise medicine for the poor, to keep offices and assemblies, just as at Paris under the direction of the General Theophraste Renaudot, their chief.

units.la: Partant il les faisoit receuoir malgré les Reglemens des Colleges, qui veulent derechef examiner les nouueaux Docteurs de Montpelier, sans auoir esgard à leurs Lettres, pour voir s'ils sont capables d'estre aggrégez au College de la ville.
units.tr: Accordingly he had them received in spite of the regulations of the Colleges, which wish in turn to examine the new Doctors of Montpellier, without regard to their letters, to see whether they are capable of being admitted into the College of the city.

units.la: De forte que si cette Compagnie de Medecine eut esté tolerée à Paris, il falloit de necessité qu'elle fut admise par toute la France. Par consequent, ces Missionnaires ayans attestation & attache de ce beau Chef, Theophraste Renaudot, comme ils avoient esté receus en ladite Compagnie ou Confrarie, & servy les pauvres quelques années ; Ils devoient sans contredit estre receus par toute la France, pour exercer leur fonction comme ses Commissaires, qui est un pouvoir en la Medecine, que ledit Renaudot s'attribuoit par dessus toutes les Vniversitez, tout pareil à celuy du Protomedico du Roy d'Espagne, qui a ce pouvoir d'examiner les nouveaux Docteurs, & donner licence de pratiquer par toutes les villes du Royaume d'Espagne sans contredit, & aucun refus, pourveu qu'ils ayent leurs degrez bien & devëment acquis.
units.tr: So that if this company of medicine had been tolerated at Paris, it was necessarily bound to be admitted throughout all France. Consequently, these missionaries, having the attestation and backing of this fine chief, Theophraste Renaudot, since they had been received into the said company or fraternity and had served the poor for some years, ought undoubtedly to be received throughout France to exercise their function as his commissaries. This is a power in Medicine which the said Renaudot claimed for himself above all the Universities, exactly like that of the Protomedico of the King of Spain, who has the power to examine new Doctors and grant licence to practise in all the cities of the kingdom of Spain without objection or any refusal, provided they have properly and duly obtained their degrees.

units.la: De forte que l'authorité, que prenoit Theophraste Renaudot alloit à la ruine de l'Eschole de Paris, & de celle de Montpelier, qui sont les deux Escholes, qui gardent plus de rigueur à la reception de leurs Docteurs, cõbien neantmoins qu'il n'y ait nulle comparaison du temps & de la rigueur des Examens de Montpelier, avec ceux de Paris. Tellement qu'on se fust contenté de prendre promptement, & à bon marché, sans aucun refus, des Lettres en d'autres Universitez, où ils les distribuent volontiers, tant aux absens comme aux presens, pour estre receus en cette Confrairie de Medecine du Bureau d'adresse, sous le bon plaisir de Theophraste Renaudot, grand Gazettier de France.
units.tr: So the authority which Theophraste Renaudot was assuming would lead to the ruin of the School of Paris and of that of Montpellier, which are the two Schools that keep the greatest strictness in admitting their Doctors, although there is no comparison between the time and the rigour of the examinations at Montpellier and those at Paris. Thus one would be content to take, promptly and cheaply, without any refusal, letters from other Universities, where they distribute them willingly, both to the absent and to the present, in order to be received into this Confraternity of Medicine of the Bureau d'Adresse, at the good pleasure of Theophraste Renaudot, great Gazetteer of France.

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris prevoyans la ruine totale de la Medecine, la destruction des anciennes Escholes, comme Paris, & Montpelier, abandonnées & desertées d'Escholiers, & les homicides, qui en pouvoient arriver; se sont genereusement opposez à cette nouveauté, & vsurpation de Renaudot. Ce faisant ils ont rendu un signalé service à l'Eschole de Montpelier, qui ne l'a pas reconnu: mais au lieu de nous en sçavoir gré, s'est iettée à corps perdu dans le party de Renaudot, contre l'Eschole de Paris, & sans distinguer leur interest d'avec la passion d'un homme irrité contre nous, est intervenuë en cause, a mis Advocat pour maintenir Renaudot & ses associez, soy disans Docteurs de Montpelier.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris, foreseeing the total ruin of Medicine and the destruction of the ancient Schools, such as Paris and Montpellier, abandoned and deserted by students, and the homicides which might follow from it, nobly opposed this novelty and usurpation by Renaudot. In doing so they rendered a signal service to the School of Montpellier, which did not acknowledge it. But instead of being grateful to us, it threw itself headlong into the party of Renaudot against the School of Paris, and without distinguishing its own interest from the passion of a man enraged against us, it intervened in the case, and engaged an advocate to uphold Renaudot and his associates, who call themselves Doctors of Montpellier.

units.la: Elle pretendoit d'obtenir par son seul renom, ce qui n'a iamais esté demandé, ny accordé, depuis que la ville de Montpelier est devenuë Françoise, encore qu'elle ait eu des occasions & rencontres plus specieuses, que celle de Renaudot. Si l'Eschole de Montpelier pretend cela par son antiquité, les Escholes de Medecine, de Toulouse, & de Bordeaux, qui font plus anciennes, peuuent bien auoir d'autres pretensions.
units.tr: It claimed to obtain by its reputation alone what has never been asked for or granted since the city of Montpellier became French, although it has had occasions and opportunities more specious than that of Renaudot. If the School of Montpellier claims this by its antiquity, the Schools of Medicine at Toulouse and Bordeaux, which are older, may well have other pretensions.

units.la: Il y a 48. ans, que nous auons eu pareille querelle & procez contre le sieur Mayerne, dit Turquet, & ses associez, qui vouloit faire des leçons aux Apothiquaires, & Barbiers Compagnons; & de plus, faire des Anatomies publiques. Il se defend & veut plaider contre l'Eschole de Paris, fait imprimer vn escrit diffamatoire contre Nous, où il implore le secours de l'Eschole de Montpelier, sa bonne mere, pour estre protegé & maintenu dans ses pretensions.Il s'adresse à Monsieur du Laurens, Chancelier de l'Eschole de Montpelier, qui estoit pour lors premier Medecin de la Reine, & Ordinaire du Roy, grand & intime amy du premier Medecin du Roy le Sieur de la Riuiere, nostre ennemy. Mais ny le Sieur de la Riuiere, ny le Sieur du Laurens, ny l'Eschole de Montpelier, n'ont point assisté Mayerne, ne voulans pas d'vne querelle particuliere, en faire vne generale, ny mettre en compromis l'Eschole de Montpelier, ny soufmettre au hazard du iugement des hommes, la reputation de ladite Eschole, sachans bien que les Docteurs de Montpelier, n'ont aucun droict dans Paris, non plus que ceux de Paris dans la ville de Montpelier.
units.tr: Forty-eight years ago we had a similar quarrel and lawsuit against the sieur Mayerne, called Turquet, and his associates, who wanted to give lectures to apothecaries and barber-companions, and moreover to hold public anatomies. He defended himself and wished to plead against the Faculty of Paris; he had a defamatory writing printed against us, in which he implored the help of the Faculty of Montpellier, his good mother, to be protected and maintained in his pretensions. He addressed himself to Monsieur du Laurens, Chancellor of the Faculty of Montpellier, who was then first physician to the Queen and ordinary physician to the King, a great and intimate friend of the first physician of the King, the sieur de la Rivière, our enemy. But neither the sieur de la Rivière, nor the sieur du Laurens, nor the Faculty of Montpellier assisted Mayerne, not wishing to turn a private quarrel into a general one, nor to put the Faculty of Montpellier at risk, nor to subject the reputation of that Faculty to the uncertain judgment of men; they knew well that the Doctors of Montpellier have no rights in Paris, any more than those of Paris have in the city of Montpellier.

units.la: Le Sieur du Laurens estant Docteur d'Avignon, fut contraint pour demeurer à Montpelier, & y exercer vne lecture, de se faire derechef Docteur de l'Eschole de Montpelier, comme vn simple Novice.
units.tr: Sieur du Laurens, being a Doctor of Avignon, was obliged, in order to remain at Montpellier and hold a lectureship there, to become a Doctor of the Faculty of Montpellier again, like a simple novice.

units.la: De plus considerez, que l'Eschole de Paris ayant iugé par vn Decret solemnel, & imprimé, Mayerne ignorant, incapable d'exercer la Medecine par toute la terre, l'Eschole de Montpelier l'a abandonné, & ne l'a pas restably en sa bonne renommée, par vn autre Decret de ladite Eschole, cassant & annullant celuy de Paris.
units.tr: Moreover, consider that the Faculty of Paris, by a solemn decree, which was printed, judged Mayerne ignorant and incapable of practising medicine anywhere on earth; the Faculty of Montpellier abandoned him and did not restore his good name, by another decree of that Faculty, quashing and annulling the one from Paris.

units.la: Or afin que l'on sache, que ie n'allegue point faux, ie produiray la Requeste de Mayerne en ses propres termes, & la response de l'Eschole contre son escrit. Adeste celeberrimae totius Europae Academiae, in quibus colitur à sacris, & puris Asclepiadis ὑγιὰς[?] fanum, non profanum: Tuque dulcissima mater Monspeliensis, cui caeterarum pace primae debentur, & ex cuius fecundissimo sinu tanquam ex equo Troiano tot prodeunt Medicinae Proceres, Adeste inquam, & quasi agmine facto concurrite, ad coercendam istorum hominum arrogantiam, vestros foetus vt nothos con-
units.tr: Now, so that it may be known that I allege nothing false, I will produce Mayerne's petition in its own words, and the Faculty's reply against his writing. Attend, you most celebrated Academies of all Europe, in which the temple of Asclepius is worshipped, sacred and pure, not profane, of health [?]: and you, most sweet mother of Montpellier, to whom, peace of the others, the first place is owed, and from whose most fruitful bosom, as from the Trojan horse, so many leaders of medicine come forth: attend, I say, and, as if forming a battle line, run together to curb the arrogance of those men, who wish your offspring to be treated as bastards.

units.la: culcant isti, quos obscurissimos extra propriam urbem, imò in urbe sua vix cognitos, nulla vestrum pro legitimis velit sine pudore admittere. Tu verò antiquissima & purissima Divæ Antistes & Cancellarie Laurenti Doctissime, & Excellentissime apud Regem nostrum, Matris communis causam age, & ut teneris, Defensor animosus, propugnator strenuus, & Patronus vigilans adveni. Hoc abs te illa poscit, hoc poscimus omnes, quod nec eius precibus, nec ei, quam in tam Augusta sustines Academia, dignitati possis denegare, &c.
units.tr: Those men trample them, whom, most obscure outside their own city, and scarcely known even in their own city, none of you would without shame wish to admit as legitimate. But you, most ancient and purest priestess of the goddess, and most learned Chancellor Laurent, and most excellent at our King's court, take up the cause of the common Mother, and come as a bold defender, a vigorous champion, and a watchful patron, as you are bound to do. This she asks of you, this we all ask, which you could not refuse to her prayers nor to the dignity you bear in so august an Academy, etc.

units.la: Voicy les termes de la Censure de l'Eschole de Medecine de Paris contre ce Mayerne Turquet. Collegium Medicorum in Academia Parisiensi legitimè congregatum, audita renunciatione censorum, quibus demandata erat provincia examinandi Apologiam sub nomine Mayerni Turqueti editam, ipsam unanimi consensu damnat, tanquam famosum libellum, mendacibus convitiis, & impudentibus calumniis refertum, quæ non nisi ab homine imperito, impudente, temulento & furioso proficisci potuerunt: Ipsum Turquetum indignum iudicat, qui usquam Medicinam faciat, propter temeritatem, impudentiam, & veram Medicinæ ignorationem: Omnes verò Medicos, qui ubique gentium & locorum Medicinam exercent, hortatur, ut ipsum Turquetum, similiáque hominum & opinionum portenta, à se suisque finibus arceant; & in Hippocratis ac Galeni Doctrina constanter permaneant; & prohibet nequis ex hoc Medicorum Parisiensium ordine cum Turqueto, eique similibus, medica consilia ineat: qui secus fecerit, Scholae ornamentis, honoribus, emolumentis, & Academiae privilegiis privabitur, & de Regentium numero expungetur. Datum Lutetiae in Scholis superioribus die 5. Decembris, anno salutis 1603.
units.tr: Here are the terms of the Censure of the Faculty of Medicine of Paris against this Mayerne Turquet. The College of Physicians, lawfully assembled in the University of Paris, having heard the report of the censors to whom the task of examining the Apology published under the name of Mayerne Turquet had been entrusted, condemns it with unanimous consent as a defamatory libel, filled with lying abuse and shameless calumnies, which could only have come from an unskilled, shameless, drunken and furious man. It judges Turquet himself unworthy to practise medicine anywhere, on account of his rashness, impudence and true ignorance of medicine. It urges all physicians who practise medicine everywhere and in every place to keep Turquet and similar portents of men and opinions far from themselves and their territories, and to remain steadfast in the doctrine of Hippocrates and Galen; and it forbids anyone of this order of Parisian physicians to take medical counsel with Turquet or with those like him. Whoever does otherwise will be deprived of the ornaments, honours, emoluments and privileges of the Academy, and will be struck from the number of the Regents. Given at Paris in the upper schools, on the 5th of December, in the year of salvation 1603.

units.la: Il a fallu proposer à l'Eschole de Montpelier un puissant motif, pour l'attirer dans le procez du Gazettier, mais il est facile de le def[?]couvrir. C'est leur avarice, qui en est cause, ayant fait entendre, que leur adjonction seroit le gain de sa cause, & que cela feroit valoir leur Eschole par toute la France, & dans Paris, quand leurs jeunes Docteurs auroient pouvoir de pratiquer, hic & ubique terrarum, & que les Escholiers de toutes parts, viendroient prendre leurs Degrez en leur Eschole.
units.tr: It was necessary to offer the Faculty of Montpellier a powerful motive to draw it into the lawsuit of the gazetteer, but it is easy to discover. Their avarice is the cause, since it was made known that their joining in would be the gain of his cause, and that this would enhance their Faculty throughout France and in Paris, when their young Doctors had the power to practise here and everywhere on earth, and scholars from all parts would come to take their degrees in their Faculty.

units.la: Quid non mortalia pectora cogis
units.tr: What do you not compel mortal hearts to do,

units.la: Auri sacra fames?
units.tr: accursed hunger for gold?

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris voyans que l'Eschole de Montpelier intervenoit au procez de Renaudot, qui deschiroit par des libelles diffamatoires, l'honneur de nostre Eschole, pour rendre celle de Montpelier plus glorieuse d'Ancienneté, plus riche en Doctrine, & en Medecine, plus sçauante ; desquels le plus ieune estoit plus docte, que le plus Ancien de Paris: Nous auons esté contraints par la bouche de nostre Aduocat, & du Doyen de nostre Faculté, de nous defendre, pour la conseruation de nos droicts. Quoy: l'Eschole de Mōtpelier sera cette teste de Medufe, qui rendra les personnes muettes: & la voyant paroistre dās ce procez, nous deuiōs tout abandonner, & acquiescer à sa demāde, qui estoit que tous les Medecins de Mōtpelier monstrans leurs Lettres testimoniales de Doctorat, au Gazettier Renaudot, fussent receus dans Paris à pratiquer la Medecine également aux Medecins de Paris? Tres-beau Priuilege, qu'ils acquerroient à bien meilleur prix, que les Docteurs de Paris. Ne vous estonnez donc pas, si nous nous sommes oppofez, & auons parlé contre cette violence. Le fils de Cresus, qui estoit muet dés sa naissance, quand il vit un meurtrier, qui vouloit massacrer son pere, l'effort de la cholere luy deslia la langue, & le fit crier contre le meurtrier. Les Medecins de Montpelier doiuent sçauoir les loix & coustumes des procez, que chacun est tenu de defendre la Iustice de sa cause, & employer tous les moyes pour ne point succomber. Tellement que ie trouue fort estrange, que l'Eschole de Montpelier se plaigne, par la plume & la bouche de son Doyen Courtaut, qu'on luy a fait grande iniustice au Parlement de Paris, & là dessus en a prononcé, & fait imprimer sa plainte, par une declamation satyrique Latine, la plus scandaleuse, & iniurieuse, qui aye jamais esté faite contre des hommes de mesme profession.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris, seeing that the Faculty of Montpellier was intervening in the lawsuit of Renaudot, who tore the honour of our Faculty apart with defamatory libels, in order to make the Faculty of Montpellier more glorious in antiquity, richer in doctrine and in medicine, and more learned, of whom the youngest was more learned than the oldest in Paris: we have been obliged, through the mouth of our advocate and of the Dean of our Faculty, to defend ourselves for the preservation of our rights. What! Shall the Faculty of Montpellier be that head of Medusa, which renders people mute? And seeing it appear in this lawsuit, should we abandon everything and consent to its demand, which was that all the physicians of Montpellier, showing their letters testimonial of doctorate to the gazetteer Renaudot, be received in Paris to practise medicine equally with the physicians of Paris? A very fine privilege, which they would acquire at a much better price than the Doctors of Paris. Do not be surprised, then, if we have opposed and spoken against this violence. The son of Croesus, who had been mute from birth, when he saw a murderer who wanted to slaughter his father, the force of anger loosened his tongue and made him cry out against the murderer. The physicians of Montpellier ought to know the laws and customs of lawsuits: that each person is bound to defend the justice of his cause and to employ every means not to succumb. So I find it very strange that the Faculty of Montpellier complains, through the pen and mouth of its Dean Courtaut, that great injustice was done to it in the Parliament of Paris, and on that ground has pronounced and printed its complaint in a Latin satirical declamation, the most scandalous and injurious ever made against men of the same profession.

units.la: Sans mentir, c'est grandement offencer le Roy, de vouloir diffamer, & deshonnorer l'Université de Paris, qui doit estre l'ornement de son Royaume, & la regle des autres Universitez. Toutes ces iniures & calomnies proferées contre l'Eschole de Paris, vont directement au mespris & deshonneur de l'Université, & de la France, si elle n'a dans un recoin du Royaume, que la seule Eschole de Montpelier sçauante, composée anciennement de quatre Medecins Professeurs jusques à l'année 1593. Maintenant de sept ou huict Medecins. Que dans Paris, la Capitale ville du Royaume, qui vaut en richesses, en bastimens, multitude de peuples, & nombre de sçauants hommes, plus que vingt Montpeliers, il y ait une Eschole, composée de six vingt Medecins tous ignorans. Partant la France estoit bien miserable, & malheureuse, avant qu'elle eut acquis la ville de Montpelier, d'où luy vient tout le secours qu'elle reçoit dans ses maladies, par les Medecins de Montpelier, qui estoient en la naissance de l'Eschole, Arabes, Mahometans, Iuifs: Puis sont deuenus Arragonnois, Espagnols, & ont continué longtemps apres la reduction de la ville à l'obeïssance du Roy, à posseder & gouuerner l'Eschole de Medecine, & pour cela, ces Medecins se vantent d'estre les premiers du monde d'origine, & en doctrine, qu'ils estoient mesmes auant Hippocrate, puisque ce petit vaisseau nommé le Soleil, (c'est Nauicula Solis de Courtaut,) estoit Montpelier, qui portoit Hippocrate en Abdere, pour visiter Democrite. Et tous les Medecins qui ont sceu quelque chose en la Medecine, l'ont appris de Montpelier; Mesme les Medecins de Paris ne sont sçauans que par la Doctrine de Montpelier; Tellement que leur gloire vient de cette Eschole, à laquelle appartient pour ces considerations la primogeniture, & principauté en la Medecine, consequemment à ses nourrissons, qu'elle a formez pour exercer la Medecine par toute la terre habitable.
units.tr: Truly, it is a great offence to the King to wish to defame and dishonour the University of Paris, which ought to be the ornament of his Kingdom and the rule of the other universities. All these insults and calumnies uttered against the Faculty of Paris go directly to the contempt and dishonour of the University and of France, if it has, in one corner of the Kingdom, only the one learned Faculty of Montpellier, formerly composed of four professor-physicians until the year 1593, and now of seven or eight physicians. That in Paris, the capital city of the Kingdom, which surpasses twenty Montpelliers in riches, buildings, multitude of people and number of learned men, there should be a Faculty composed of one hundred and twenty physicians, all ignorant! Therefore France was very wretched and unfortunate before it acquired the city of Montpellier, from which comes all the help it receives in its illnesses, through the physicians of Montpellier, who at the Faculty's beginning were Arabs, Mahometans, Jews; then became Aragonese, Spaniards, and continued for a long time after the city's reduction to the obedience of the King to possess and govern the Faculty of Medicine. For this reason these physicians boast of being the first in the world in origin and in doctrine, and that they were even before Hippocrates, since that little vessel called the Sun (that is Nauicula Solis of Courtaut) was Montpellier, which carried Hippocrates to Abdera to visit Democritus. And all the physicians who have known anything of medicine learned it from Montpellier; even the physicians of Paris are learned only through the doctrine of Montpellier; so that their glory comes from that Faculty, to which, for these reasons, belong the primogeniture and principate in medicine, and consequently over its nurslings, whom it has trained to practise medicine throughout the whole habitable earth.

units.la: Voila les resueries, & folies d'vn homme insensé, qui merite plustost d'estre estrillé en chien Courtaut, tourne-broche d'vne cuisine, que d'estre admonesté de sa folie, dautant qu'il n'a pas le jugement ny la raison de comprendre la repartie qu'on luy pourroit faire.
units.tr: These are the ravings and follies of a senseless man, who deserves rather to be curried like a short-tailed dog or a kitchen spit-turner than to be admonished of his folly, since he has neither the judgement nor the reason to understand the reply that might be made to him.

units.la: Ces injures scandaleuses demandent reparation d'honneur en bonne Justice, avec punition exemplaire pour cette temerité, qui va au detriment du public, seduit, & abusé, & au deshonneur du Roy & de son Royaume.
units.tr: These scandalous insults call for reparation of honour in good justice, with an exemplary punishment for this rashness, which works to the detriment of the public, which is seduced and deceived, and to the dishonour of the King and of his kingdom.

units.la: Si les cinq Professeurs de l'Eschole de Montpelier les approuvent, & protegent cét insolent, nous avons sujet de nous plaindre d'eux. Si ce Courtaut eust eu de l'esprit, & de la conduitte dans la Medecine, son Oncle maternelle Sieur Heroard, premier Medecin du Roy Louys XIII. eut tasché de l'installer en la Cour, pour estre son successeur en sa Charge: Mais luy faisant honte, a esté contraint de le renvoyer à Montpelier, sa ville natale, & le bannir de la Cour pour jamais; luy faisant vendre sa Charge de Medecin par quartier, qu'il luy avoit donnée, afin de luy oster l'occasion de revenir à Paris; Et pour l'obliger de demeurer à Montpelier avec quelque honneur, luy fit avoir la Lecture en Medecine, qu'il possede, bien qu'il en fut indigne & incapable.
units.tr: If the five Professors of the School of Montpellier approve of and protect this insolent fellow, we have cause to complain of them. If this Courtaut had any wit or good conduct in medicine, his maternal uncle, Sieur Héroard, first physician to King Louis XIII, would have tried to establish him at Court, to be his successor in his office. But, ashamed of him, Héroard was forced to send him back to Montpellier, his native town, and to banish him from the Court for ever, having him sell the office of quarterly physician that he had given him, so as to take away from him any occasion of returning to Paris. And to oblige him to remain at Montpellier with some honour, he procured for him the lectureship in medicine that he holds, although he was unworthy of it and incapable of it.

units.la: Les Medecins Professeurs ont sujet de chastier l'insolence de Courtaut, pour avoir injurié Messieurs de la Chambre des Comptes, seante à Montpelier, qui est l'ornement de la ville, dautant que dans la Lettre de Charles VII. par gaufferie il escrit, Delicto & fideli nostro Episcopo Laudunensi, Camera Computorum nostrorum Praesidenti, Comme s'ils estoient des yurognes & pourceaux du Roy. Cela merite un traict de plume, pour casser leurs gages.
units.tr: The Professors of medicine have cause to punish the insolence of Courtaut, for having abused the Messieurs of the Chamber of Accounts, sitting at Montpellier, who are the ornament of the town, since in the letter of Charles VII he writes in a mocking way, Delicto & fideli nostro Episcopo Laudunensi, Camera Computorum nostrorum Praesidenti, as if they were drunkards and pigs of the King. This deserves a stroke of the pen to cancel their salaries.

units.la: Pour desabuser les Françoys [?] du bruit qui court de ces grands Medecins de Montpelier, residans à Paris, qui font des miracles; Mon intention est en ce discours de faire connoistre quels sont les vrais Medecins de Montpelier, si ces nouveaux Docteurs tous frais esmoulus, sont de pareille valeur & doctrine, que ceux qui ont demeuré dix ou douze ans à Montpelier, enseignans & professans la Medecine; Et si ces deux especes de Medecins venans à Paris sont mieux instruits en la Pratique, pour traitter les malades en nostre climat, que les Medecins de l'Eschole de Paris. Ensuite, combien est prejudiciable pour la vie des Parisiens, d'assembler tels Medecins avec ceux de Paris pour consulter, mesme de leur permettre d'y pratiquer la Medecine à leur mode.
units.tr: To undeceive the French [?] of the rumour going about concerning these great physicians of Montpellier, residing in Paris, who work miracles: my intention in this discourse is to make known who the true physicians of Montpellier are, whether these new doctors, fresh from the whetstone, are of equal worth and learning to those who have lived ten or twelve years at Montpellier, teaching and practising medicine; and whether these two kinds of physicians, coming to Paris, are better instructed in practice for treating the sick in our climate than the physicians of the School of Paris. Next, how harmful it is to the lives of the Parisians to bring such physicians together with those of Paris to consult, or even to allow them to practise medicine there in their own fashion.

units.la: Apres avoir prouvé tout cela, je viendray à l'examen de la declamation de Courtaut, sans injures nouvellement forgées contre l'Eschole de Montpelier, encore que la Loy du Talion nous le permette : L'Escriture Sainte nous recommande, qu'on soit soigneux de conseruer sa bonne renommée ; qui ne se defend pas d'une injure notable, qui offence sa reputation, il est aussi criminel, que s'il abandonnoit sa Patrie, & ses parens à ses ennemis.
units.tr: Having proved all this, I shall come to the examination of Courtaut's declamation, without newly invented insults against the School of Montpellier, although the law of retaliation would allow it. Holy Scripture recommends that we take care to preserve our good name; he who does not defend himself against a notable injury that offends his reputation is as guilty as if he abandoned his country and his relatives to their enemies.

units.la: Il y a beaucoup de personnes qui croyent estre veritable ce qui n'est point refuté & convaincu de fausseté, le silence est pris souvent pour une tacite confession, lors qu'on n'ose éventer son ordure. Je n'allegueray que les authoritez irreprochables depuis cinq cens ans, de siecle en siecle, des Medecins & sçauans hommes, qui ont accusé l'Eschole de Montpelier, d'ignorance & de maluersation en la Medecine, & produiront les pieces justificatiues de leur condamnation. On verra si l'Eschole de Montpelier, Nauis[?] careat, nec illius pudenda, cùm pudendum nil habeat, vllus mortalium reuelare aufit. Je voudrois n'auoir point esté obligé de mettre en evidence les defauts & imperfections de l'Eschole de Montpelier, que nous avons toujours tenus cachez jusquesà present, pour l'honneur de la Medecine : Mais maintenant que nous sommes si furieusement, & fauffement attaquez par le Doyen de l'Eschole de Montpelier,
units.tr: There are many people who believe to be true what is not refuted and convicted of falsehood; silence is often taken for tacit confession, when one does not dare to expose his filth. I shall allege only the unimpeachable authorities, from five hundred years back, century by century, of physicians and learned men who have accused the School of Montpellier of ignorance and malpractice in medicine, and they will produce the documentary proofs of their condemnation. We shall see whether the School of Montpellier, Nauis[?] careat, nec illius pudenda, cùm pudendum nil habeat, vllus mortalium reuelare aufit. I would have wished not to have been obliged to bring to light the defects and imperfections of the School of Montpellier, which we have always kept hidden until now, for the honour of medicine. But now that we are so furiously and falsely attacked by the Dean of the School of Montpellier,

units.la: Fas odisse viros, atque omnia ferre sub auras Si qua tegunt.
units.tr: It is right to hate men, and to bring into the light all the things that they hide.

units.la: Quand Turquet fit de son chef pour sa defense, une invectiue satyrique contre l'Eschole de Paris, pour l'abaisser tant qu'il a pû, en eleuant celle de Montpelier, Nous avons mespris é ces injures sans ȳ repartir, entant qu'il n'estoit point Professeur de Montpelier, & sans adveu, fōdé sur le cōseil de Platon, qui dit, que les jeunes gens qui pensent sçavoir quelque chose, sont fort insolens, & ressemblent à ces petits chiens esveillez, qui jappent continuellement, deschirent à belles dents la robbe de leurs Maistres, se jettent sans discretion sur le Corps des grands chiens, les mordent par les oreilles, lesquels s'ils voulooient user de leurs forces, d'un coup de patte estoufferoient ces petits chiens, mais ils endurent cesfolies sans s'esmouvoir.
units.tr: When Turquet, on his own account, for his defence, published a satirical invective against the School of Paris, to lower it as far as he could while raising that of Montpellier, we despised these insults without replying to them, inasmuch as he was not a Professor of Montpellier and had no authority; founded on the counsel of Plato, who says that young people who think they know something are very insolent, and resemble those little wakeful dogs which bark continually, tear at their masters' gowns with their teeth, throw themselves without discretion upon the bodies of large dogs, and bite them by the ears; whereas, if the large dogs wished to use their strength, they would stifle these little dogs with one blow of a paw, but they endure such follies without being moved.

units.la: Neantmoins le Livre imprimé de Turquet, a donné matiere à Renaudot, pour bastir ses Libelles diffamatoires; & de là Courtaut a tout dérobé, & tourné en Latin, n'ayant pas l'esprit d'inventer de nouuelles injures, & médisances, ou croyant ne pouuoir mieux faire. Je ne sçay si c'est par ignorance, ou pour nous brauer dauantage, qu'il nous a si murié[?] avec tant de solecismes, & barbarismes, que cela nous offense dauantage, que les iniures, voyant que le Libelle diffamatoire est imprimé à Montpelier, & que ces grands Docteurs, & Professeurs ont laissé ces ordures. Ie voy qu'apres l'Arrest donné contre la Riuiere, dit Roch le Baillif, l'Eschole de Paris, fit connoistre en langage François, au peuple de Paris, l'équité du iugement de Nosseigneurs de la Cour de Parlement, contre ledit la Riuiere & ses associez.
units.tr: Nevertheless, Turquet's printed book has provided matter to Renaudot for building his defamatory libels; and from there Courtaut has stolen everything and turned it into Latin, lacking the wit to invent new insults and slanders, or believing he could do no better. I do not know whether it is through ignorance, or to brave us the more, that he has so mangled it with so many solecisms and barbarisms that this offends us more than the insults do, seeing that the defamatory libel is printed at Montpellier, and that these great doctors and Professors have let such filth stand. I see that after the judgement given against La Rivière, called Roch the Bailiff, the School of Paris made known in the French language, to the people of Paris, the equity of the judgement of our Lords of the Parliament Court against the said La Rivière and his associates.

units.la: C'est ce que i'ay entrepris en ce Discours François, pour faire connoistre aux Apothiquaires & Chirurgiens de Paris, & de toute la France, & à tout le Peuple, la difference de l'Eschole de Paris, d'auec celle de Montpelier, & des Medecins de l'vne & de l'autre Eschole.
units.tr: This is what I have undertaken in this French Discourse, to make known to the apothecaries and surgeons of Paris, and of all France, and to all the people, the difference between the School of Paris and that of Montpellier, and between the physicians of the one and of the other School.

units.la: Il est important de desabuser ces pauures Escholiers qui vont à Montpelier, prendre leurs degrez de Docteur, de la fourberie des Medecins de Montpelier par cette Declamation, sans doute ils la donneront auec leurs Bulles pour les asseurer, qu'ils sont les premiers Medecins de la terre habitable, & sous cette asseurance, s'en iroient effrontément exercer la Medecine. l'espere que ce discours les retiendra dans la modestie, & ne seront plus doresnauant si glorieux & infolens, qu'ils ont esté. Suivant donc mon dessein, je demonstreray quels sont les vrais Medecins de Montpelier.
units.tr: It is important to undeceive those poor scholars who go to Montpellier to take their doctoral degrees, concerning the trickery of the physicians of Montpellier, by this declamation; no doubt they will give it out along with their bulls to assure them that they are the first physicians of the inhabited earth, and under this assurance would go shamelessly to practise medicine. I hope this discourse will keep them in modesty, and that they will no longer be as vain and insolent as they have been. Following, then, my plan, I shall demonstrate who the true physicians of Montpellier are.

units.la: Quand on parle d'eux pour sçavoir leur capacité & doctrine, il faut distinguer ceux qui demeurent dans la ville de Montpelier, exerçans la Medecine, & qui tous enseignent, d'avec ceux qui y demeurent seulement six mois, pour estre instruits jusques au Doctorat obtenu, qui sont fort rares; ou estans instruits ailleurs, n'y demeurent que trois ou quatre mois, & souvent encore moins, pour obtenir leurs degrez. Les premiers Docteurs demeurans dans la ville, peuvent estre sçauans, pour l'exercice continuel qu'ils font de la Medecine, enseignans & pratiquans, qui sont les deux moyens pour devenir sçauant. Les autres nouveaux Docteurs, qui s'en retournent tous frais esmoulus en leur ville, ou autres lieux, ne sçavent pas la pratique de Montpelier, si ce n'est par Liures ou leçons des Professeurs de la dite Eschole, qu'ils auront leu, ou par les receptes de Medecins, qu'ils tirent des Apothiquaires. Cela n'est pas sçavoir la pratique de Montpelier, d'autant qu'en l'un & en l'autre aspirant au Doctorat, le temps est trop bref pour apprendre la Medecine, pour n'auoir veu penser, traiter & medicamenter les malades l'espace de trois ou quatre ans, à la suite des Docteurs.
units.tr: When people are discussed to establish their ability and learning, one must distinguish between those who live in the city of Montpelier, practising medicine, and who all teach, and those who stay there only six months to be instructed up to the obtaining of the doctorate, which is very rare; or who, having been instructed elsewhere, stay only three or four months there, and often even less, to obtain their degrees. The first, the doctors who live in the city, may be learned, through the continual exercise they make of medicine, teaching and practising, which are the two means of becoming learned. The other new doctors, who return all fresh and proud to their town or other places, do not know the practice of Montpelier, except from books or the lectures of the professors of that school, which they have read, or from the prescriptions of physicians, which they obtain from the apothecaries. That is not knowing the practice of Montpelier, since in either case, for one aspiring to the doctorate, the time is too short to learn medicine, not having seen the sick attended, treated and medicated for three or four years in the train of the doctors.

units.la: Que si on me dit, qu'il y en a qui demeurent tout ce temps là en la ville de Montpelier, ie maintiens qu'ils sont rares, & s'y morfondent, n'estans point aggregez, n'ayans aucun droit, ny emolument, n'estans point appellez dans leurs assemblées ; mesme leurs presences estans ennuyeuses aux Docteurs Professeurs, ils sont contraints de se retirer promptement, ioint que le nombre de 4. ou cinq Medecins est par Arrest dudit Parlement de Toulouse limité pour demeurer dans la ville ; Tellement que ces nouveaux Docteurs ne sont que passeuolans, oiseaux passagers, qu'ils renuoyent bufquer fortune ailleurs, (ubique terrarum) selon la teneur de leurs lettres. Tels Medecins sont aussi peu versez en la pratique de Montpelier, que ceux qui ont pris le Doctorat à Rheims, à Caën, à Bourges, à Valence, à Angers, à Cahors, à Toulouse, à Bordeaux, à Aix, en Auignon, à Orange, ou en Allemagne, ou en Italie. Ils sont semblables à ces ieunesEscholiers fraischement venus des estudes des Loix, ignorans la pratique du Palais : Neantmoins estans receus Aduocats, s'en vont pour estre Iuges, Baillifs dans des villes tous seuls : tels Aduocats ne sont nullement à comparer à ceux qui sont assiduement dans l'employ des affaires, escritures, consultations, arbitrages en plein Parlement ; de mesme est il des Medecins de Paris auec ces nouueaux Medecins de Montpelier, qui viennent à Paris fort ignorans. Ie confesse neantmoins, que s'ils ont de l'esprit, ils se forment en la pratique par la conuersation, qu'ils ont auec nous par nostre bonté & tolerance, qui sont neantmoins au public & à nostre Eschole preiudiciables : In qua conditione infidiosissima, authoritatem pessimis boni faciunt, ce dit Pline, lib. 29. cap. 1.
units.tr: But if someone tells me that there are some who stay in the city of Montpelier all that time, I maintain that they are rare, and that they pine away there, not being admitted to the college, having no right or emolument, and not being summoned to their assemblies; indeed, their presence being tedious to the doctor-professors, they are compelled to withdraw promptly. Besides, the number of four or five physicians is limited by decree of the said Parlement of Toulouse to remain in the city. So these new doctors are only passing guests, birds of passage, whom they send to seek their fortune elsewhere (ubique terrarum), according to the terms of their letters. Such physicians are as little versed in the practice of Montpelier as those who have taken the doctorate at Rheims, Caen, Bourges, Valence, Angers, Cahors, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Aix, Avignon, Orange, or in Germany or Italy. They are like those young scholars freshly come from the study of the laws, ignorant of the practice of the courts: nevertheless, once received as advocates, they go off to become judges or bailiffs in towns entirely on their own. Such advocates are in no way to be compared with those who are constantly employed in affairs, writings, consultations and arbitrations in full Parlement. So it is with the physicians of Paris and these new physicians of Montpelier, who come to Paris quite ignorant. I confess, however, that if they have wit, they form themselves in practice through the conversation they have with us, through our kindness and tolerance, which is nonetheless harmful to the public and to our school: In qua conditione infidiosissima, authoritatem pessimis boni faciunt, says Pliny, lib. 29. cap. 1.

units.la: I'aduoüe aussi, que dans des petites villes, ils s'en peut trouuer de sçauans, qui estudient fortement, prennent plaisir à leur vacation, & par l'estude peuuent monter dans vne plus grande perfection de science. Mais faute de conference, d'emulation, & grand exercice, qui ne se trouuent que dans les grandes villes, ils ne sont pas à comparer aux Medecins de Montpelier, residans dans la ville, encore moins aux Medecins de Paris, ny à ceux des grandes villes, comme Lyon, Roüen, Toulouze, Bourdeaux, Aix, & autres, qui tiennent College.
units.tr: I also admit that in small towns there may be learned men who study hard, take pleasure in their calling, and by study can rise to a greater perfection of knowledge. But for want of conference, emulation and great practice, which are found only in the large cities, they are not to be compared with the physicians of Montpelier who reside in the city, still less with the physicians of Paris, or with those of the great cities such as Lyon, Rouen, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Aix, and others, which keep a college.

units.la: Y a-il apparence que l'Escholle de Montpelier, composée autresfois de quatre Medecins seulement, & depuis cinquante ans, de six ou sept Docteurs, soit à preferer à l'Escholle de Paris, composée de six vingt Docteurs, entre lesquels il s'en trouuera plus que les deux tiers, presentement plus capables, que les six Professeurs de Montpelier, en attendant que les autres se meurissent & perfectionnent dans l'estude & l'exercice, escriuans, enseignans, disputans, & monstrans la Medecine, formans, & dressans tous les Escholiers non seulement de toute la France, mais de toute l'Europe: dautant qu'auant les guerres, il venoit des Allemans en quantité, des Anglois, Escosseis, Flamans, Polonois, Italiens, estudier à Paris: Et on ne voudra pas que de nostre Escholle vienne la bonne Doctrine, mais de ces six Professeurs de Montpelier.
units.tr: Is it plausible that the school of Montpelier, once composed of only four physicians, and for fifty years of six or seven doctors, should be preferred to the school of Paris, composed of one hundred and twenty doctors, of whom more than two-thirds are at present more capable than the six professors of Montpelier, while waiting for the others to ripen and perfect themselves in study and practice, writing, teaching, disputing and demonstrating medicine, forming and training all the students not only of the whole of France but of all Europe? For before the wars, many Germans, English, Scots, Flemings, Poles and Italians came in numbers to study at Paris. And will it be said that good doctrine comes not from our school, but from these six professors of Montpelier?

units.la: Quant au nombre des Docteurs residans dans la ville de Montpelier; il y a des Universitez & villes de la France, qui ont dauantage de Medecins, comme Poitiers, Tours, Angers, Lyon, Tolouze, Aix, Bourdeaux, Rouen, Orleans, Amiens: Les Medecins de Montpelier ne manqueront pas de dire, comme a publié Courtaut, qu'en ce petit nombre ils sont les plus sçauans non seulement de la France, mais de toute l'Europe, dautant qu'ils demeurent à Montpelier, qui rend les Medecins sçauans, à cause de la pureté de l'Air, & du lieu tout Medicinal. Ainsi Minerue voulant bastir une ville de sagesse, choisit un lieu propre pour bastir Athenes. Joint que In ore duorum vel trium stat omne verbum.
units.tr: As to the number of doctors residing in the city of Montpelier, there are universities and towns in France which have more physicians, such as Poitiers, Tours, Angers, Lyon, Toulouse, Aix, Bordeaux, Rouen, Orléans, Amiens. The physicians of Montpelier will not fail to say, as Courtaut has published, that in this small number they are the most learned not only in France but in all Europe, because they live at Montpelier, which makes physicians learned, because of the purity of the air and the wholly medicinal situation of the place. Thus Minerva, wishing to build a city of wisdom, chose a suitable place to build Athens. Besides, In ore duorum vel trium stat omne verbum.

units.la: Depuis quatre cens ans, l'Eschole de Paris n'a pas eu moins de Docteurs que trente & quarante, comme nous voyons par nos Registres: Et Montpelier n'a jamais eu tant de Docteurs residàs, que depuis Henry le Grand, qui a augmenté les Lecteurs de deux, auparauant ils n'estoient que quatre, selon la premiere creation. Ils ont demãdé ces deux Lecteurs pour faire le nombre de six, & auec deux qu'ils ont aggregé, ils composent une Eschole de huict, afin que le nombre fut complet de sept Docteurs, qui est requis à une fameuse Academie, pour faire des Docteurs, ce qui n'estoit point il y a 50. ans. Partant il ne faut appeller Medecins de Montpelier que ceux qui sont residens en la ville, pratiquans & enseignans la Medecine: Les autres sont Medecins graduez par lettres, tous semblables à ceux qui se nomment Medecins du Roy, respandus par toute la France, qui ont fait serment entre les mains du premier Medecin, & qui ont lettres signées de luy, & d'un Secretaire d'Estat: Et pour tout cela ne sont pas les vrais Medecins de la Maison du Roy, & ne laissent pas de payer la Taille, combien mesme qu'à cette intention ils ayent eu soin de faire enregistrer leurs Patentes en la Cour des Aides, en la Chambre des Comptes, & au Bureau de la Maison du Roy.
units.tr: For four hundred years the school of Paris has never had fewer than thirty or forty doctors, as we see from our registers. And Montpelier has never had so many resident doctors as since Henry the Great, who increased the readers by two; before that there were only four, according to the first establishment. They asked for these two readers to make up the number of six, and with the two they have admitted they make up a school of eight, so that the number was complete at seven doctors, which is required for a famous Academy to make doctors; this was not so fifty years ago. Therefore one should call physicians of Montpelier only those who reside in the city, practising and teaching medicine. The others are physicians graduated by letters, all like those who are called physicians of the King, scattered throughout France, who have taken the oath in the hands of the first physician and who have letters signed by him and by a Secretary of State. And for all that they are not the true physicians of the King's Household, and they still pay the taille; even though, to this end, they have taken care to have their patents registered in the Court of Aids, the Chamber of Accounts and the Office of the King's Household.

units.la: Quant aux Medecins Docteurs par lettres de Montpelier, habituez à Paris, ou suivans la Cour, ou dispersez par la France, quand ils viennent à estre premiers Medecins du Roy, on ne peut dire d'eux que le Roy aye choisi & preferé un Medecin de Montpelier aux Medecins de Paris, non plus que Henry le Grand aye preferé le Sieur d'Aliboux, & de la Riniere, Medecins de Basle, aux Medecins de Montpelier, & de Paris; mais estans François & habituez en France, le Roy les a pris d'un tel lieu, d'une telle ville, comme a fait le mesme Henry IV. du Sieur Petit, qu'il a pris de la ville de Gien, du Sieur Milon de la ville de Poitiers, pour estre ses premiers Medecins. Si le Roy envoyoit querir un Medecin Professeur de la ville de Montpelier, on pourroit dire qu'il l'a tiré & choisi de cette ville, mais depuis que la ville de Montpelier est Françoise, Il ne se trouve point que les Roys,ayent pris, choisi, & envoyé querir un Medecin Professeur de la ville de Montpelier & resident sur le lieu. Monsieur du Laurens estant venu à la Cour par degrez, est parvenu à cette charge. De mesme le Sieur Heroard, les autres par de grands artifices, suivans la Cour vingt & trente ans avant que d'y parvenir.
units.tr: As for doctors of medicine who graduated by letters from Montpellier, who settle in Paris, follow the Court, or are scattered through France: when they come to be first physicians to the King, one cannot say that the King chose and preferred a physician of Montpellier over the physicians of Paris, any more than that Henry the Great preferred the Sieur d'Aliboux and de la Rinière, physicians of Basle, to the physicians of Montpellier and of Paris. Rather, being Frenchmen and settled in France, they were taken by the King from such and such a place, from such and such a town, just as the same Henry IV took the Sieur Petit from the town of Gien and the Sieur Milon from the town of Poitiers to be his first physicians. If the King were to send for a professor of medicine from the city of Montpellier, one could say that he had drawn and chosen him from that city; but since Montpellier became French, it is not found that the kings have taken, chosen and sent for a professor of medicine from Montpellier who was resident there. Monsieur du Laurens, having come to the Court by degrees, rose to this office. Likewise the Sieur Héroard, and others, by great artifices, followed the Court twenty or thirty years before attaining it.

units.la: Prouvons maintenant la consequence dangereuse, d'assembler ces Medecins de Montpelier vieux & nouveaux, avec les Medecins de Paris, & de les laisser dans la ville pratiquer à leur mode. Ces jeunes Medecins, par l'instruction qu'on leur donne à Montpelier, conçoivent une haine,soit vraye, ou simulée contre les Medecins de Paris, croyans par cét artifice s'introduire dans nostre ville, & se mettre en credit en medisant des Medecins de Paris, & blasmant leur methode de pratiquer la Medecine. Les lieux communs d'où ils tirent leur medisance, sont de la Saignée, & de nos purgations, qu'ils qualifient puantes & horribles, & du mespris que nous faisons des remedes que les pipeurs & les souffleurs appellent Cardiaques. S'ils trouvent de leurs camarades nouvellement sortis de Montpelier, ou desia establis à Paris, ils s'unissent ensemble, comme voleurs en foires, font ligues offensives & defensives, puis vont battre les buissons courans deça & delà par toute la ville pour faire venir les bestes dans leurs filets.
units.tr: Let us now prove the dangerous consequence of gathering these physicians of Montpellier, old and new, together with the physicians of Paris, and of letting them practise in the city in their own fashion. These young physicians, from the instruction given them at Montpellier, conceive a hatred, whether true or feigned, against the physicians of Paris, believing that by this artifice they will insinuate themselves into our city and win credit by slandering the physicians of Paris and blaming our method of practising medicine.
