They obtain by petition permission to have a dead body in order to make and show anatomy to the students of medicine. This was granted to them at Pamplona in the year 1377. Charles V granted them letters patent for the preservation of their privileges, having requested them by petition in order to be exempted from tallies and contributions. Charles VI confirmed their privileges. Charles VII did the same in 1446. I cannot approve that under the same date there was published in the Aragonese language the proclamation forbidding the practice of medicine at Montpelier unless one is a physician of the said University, nor the apothecaries receiving the prescriptions of foreign physicians. You make it clear that you were not good Frenchmen in those times. From Louis XI they produce only a confirmation of the election of the Chancellor in Medicine. I believe it false because of the contradictions found in it concerning the words of the University and the Royal Statutes, since it is the Pope who, as they claim, created the Chancellor, whereas statutes ought to be made by the Bishop. Charles VIII confirms all the privileges at the request of Jean Martin, his first physician, and wishes them all to be the same as those of the Regent Masters, Doctors, Scholars and Officers of his dear daughter, the University of Paris, etc. This letter is false, and the conformity of privileges identical to those of the University of Paris is granted only to the whole University as a corporate body. The letter of royal foundation, of which they boast above the school of Paris, is shameful. They represented to King Charles VIII and King Louis XII the poverty of their school, and that they had expended much of their own to restore it and put it in good order, which had for some years been without Doctors and destitute, and was on the way to falling into ruin and discontinuing its teaching; which could happen again hereafter if the said foundation and ordinance were not maintained. Therefore they ask for provision, so that they may have the means to support themselves honourably, and to have and wear the gowns and decent robes belonging to the status and degree of Doctor.

units.la: Pour cét effet, lesdits Rois ont donné à quatre Docteurs, la somme de cinq cens liures, c'est à sçauoir pour chacun desdits Docteurs cent liures, & pour la reparation des Escholes cent liures, par chacun an.
units.tr: For this purpose, the said Kings have given four Doctors the sum of five hundred livres: that is, a hundred livres for each of the said Doctors, and a hundred livres for the repair of the Schools, every year.

units.la: Considerez la gueuserie de cette superbe Eschole, composée de quatre Docteurs, qui estoit preste d'estre submergée, si elle n'eust esté releuée & soustenuë par cette somme annuelle de cinq cens liures. Or il est porté dans les lettres, qu'auenant la mort de l'vn des quatre, ou de tous, lesdites lectures ne pourrôt estre remplies d'autres que de Medecins Regens en ladite Vniuersité. Ce qui exclud tous les autres Medecins, s'ils ne sont du Corps de ladite Vniuersité, enseignans & demeurans dans la ville, & par consequent, ils en sont dispensateurs quand ils en aggregent deux, qui sont dans l'expectatiue, & par là frustrent tous les autres Docteurs, qui viendroient disputer la lecture vaquante, comme ils ont fait paroistre en la dispute que fit le Docteur Scharpe, pour vne lecture vaquante, qu'il obtint malgré les Professeurs, qui vouloient l'adiuger à vn Aggregé beaucoup inferieur en doctrine. Ce qui eut esté fait sans l'opposition de Monsieur l'Euesque de Fenoüillet.
units.tr: Consider the beggary of this proud School, made up of four Doctors, which was ready to be submerged unless it had been raised up and sustained by this yearly sum of five hundred livres. Now the letters state that, should one of the four die, or all of them, the said lectureships may not be filled by anyone other than Regent Physicians of the said University. This excludes all other physicians, unless they belong to the body of the said University, teaching and residing in the city; and consequently they are the dispensers of it when they admit two who are in expectation, and by this means they thwart all the other Doctors who would come to contest the vacant lectureship, as they showed in the dispute that Doctor Scharpe had over a vacant lectureship, which he obtained against the wishes of the Professors, who wanted to award it to an Associate far inferior in learning. This would have been done had it not been for the opposition of the Lord Bishop of Fenouillet.

units.la: Les poursuites qu'ont fait les Medecins de Montpelier contre Maistre Honorat Picquet, soy disant Maistre en Medecine, pour empescher qu'il enseignât la Medecine, & ne conferât les degrez du Doctorat en la ville d'Oranges, sont honteuses, & font paroistre leur auarice. Car Oranges est du reffort du Dauphiné, les Universitez de Valence & de Toulouse, voisines, avoient plus juste raison de s'opposer à l'usurpation dudit Honorat Picquet, & toutesfois ne l'ont pas fait.
units.tr: The proceedings that the physicians of Montpellier have brought against Master Honorat Picquet, self-styled Master in Medicine, to prevent him from teaching medicine and conferring the degrees of Doctorate in the city of Orange, are shameful and reveal their avarice. For Orange falls within the jurisdiction of the Dauphiné, and the neighbouring Universities of Valence and Toulouse had a more just reason to oppose the usurpation of the said Honorat Picquet, and yet they have not done so.

units.la: Les Medecins de Montpelier, en leur Requeste, disent qu'ils tenoient les Escholes de Grammaire, & ayant obtenu contre luy des defenses pour l'empescher de faire aucun acte de Scholarité, craignant qu'il ne s'allât retirer dās quelque autre Université voisine, pour destourner les pigeons du colombier, l'ont attiré en leur College, luy ont donné la qualité de Docteur ; & l'ont fait un des premiers Professeurs de la Medecine. Le Sieur Ranchin, en ses descriptions, luy donne ces belles qualitez. Honoratus Picquetus, Philosophorum & Medicorum sua tempestate facile Princeps. C'est depuis qu'il a esté Docteur de Montpelier, auparavant il n'estoit pas Medecin, en prenoit la qualité faussement, & tenoit seulement Escholé de Grammaire à Oranges. Cecy soit dit en passant pour monstrer l'inconstance des Medecins de Montpelier.
units.tr: The physicians of Montpellier, in their Petition, say that they held the schools of Grammar, and, having obtained against him prohibitions to prevent him from performing any act of scholarship, fearing that he would withdraw to some other neighbouring University and lure the pigeons away from the dovecote, they drew him into their College, gave him the title of Doctor, and made him one of the first Professors of Medicine. Sieur Ranchin, in his descriptions, gives him these fine qualities: "Honoratus Picquetus, Philosophorum & Medicorum sua tempestate facile Princeps." It was only after this that he became a Doctor of Montpellier; before that he was not a physician, falsely assumed the title, and only kept a grammar school at Orange. I say this in passing, to show the inconstancy of the physicians of Montpellier.

units.la: Revenons aux lettres de nos Rois pour descouurir les faussetez, qu'ils y ont fait Louÿs XII. leur accorde tous leurs Priuileges[?]. ges anciens conformes à ceux de l'Université de Paris, sa Chere fille, defend expressement qu'aucun se mesle de la Medecine en la ville de Montpelier, s'il n'est examiné & approuvé par lesdits Docteurs. Le mesme Roy Louis XII. donne aux Medecins de Montpelier, sauvegarde pour les exempter du logement des soldats & gens de guerre, attendu qu'ils ne sont pas en grand nombre, lequel par la lettre Patente de Mõsieur le Marescal de Danuille, est reduit aux quatre Docteurs Regens en la Faculté de Medecine de l'Université de Montpelier. Partant ils n'estoient en l'an 1575. que quatre, autrement ils devoient demander ledit Privilege pour six, s'ils estoient autant.
units.tr: Let us return to the letters of our Kings, to uncover the falsehoods they contain. Louis XII grants them all their ancient privileges, conforming to those of the University of Paris, his dear daughter; he expressly forbids anyone to meddle in medicine in the city of Montpellier unless he has been examined and approved by the said Doctors. The same King Louis XII grants the physicians of Montpellier a safeguard to exempt them from billeting soldiers and men of war, since they are not in great number; which number, by the letters patent of Monsieur the Marshal de Danville, is reduced to the four Doctors Regent in the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Montpellier. Therefore in the year 1575 there were only four of them; otherwise they would have had to request the said Privilege for six, if there had been that many.

units.la: Depuis le Roy Louis XII. ils ont eu confirmation de tous les Rois ses successeurs, de François I. qui leur a donné du Sel; Henry II. a confirmé leurs gages, & leurs Privileges, Charle IX. en a fait de mesme, & a augmêté les gages de 300. liures à chacun. Ils n'ont rien demandé à Henry III. Ils ont eu confirmation de leurs Privileges en general par Henry IIII. Le mesme a eri-gé la cinquiesme regence Anatomique & Botanique ; Puis la sixiesme, pour la Chirurgie & Pharmacie. Il a augmenté les gages des Professeurs, iusques à la somme de six cens liures pour chaque Professeur. De plus il a erigé la charge d'un Dissecteur Anatomiste Royal, sous un faux aduis qu'il auoit esté obmis, comme il s'en trouue en toutes les Universitez celebres des Royaumes & Prouinces estrangeres, ce qui est faux.
units.tr: After King Louis XII they received confirmation from all the Kings his successors: from Francis I, who gave them salt; Henry II confirmed their salaries and their privileges; Charles IX did the same, and increased the salaries by 300 livres to each. They asked nothing of Henry III. They received confirmation of their privileges in general from Henry IV. The same King erected the fifth regency, in Anatomy and Botany; then the sixth, for Surgery and Pharmacy. He increased the salaries of the Professors up to the sum of six hundred livres for each Professor. Moreover he erected the office of a Royal Anatomist and Dissector, under the false impression that it had been omitted, as is found in all the celebrated Universities of the kingdoms and foreign provinces, which is false.

units.la: Le Roy Louis XIII. confirme tous les Priuileges. A quoy tendent toutes ces confirmations demandées aux Rois successiuement, sinon pour euiter la reuocation de leurs Priuileges, & gages, tant ils ont eu peur de les perdre. C'est dequoy les Medecins de Paris ne se sont point souciez, d'autant qu'on ne peut oster leurs Priuileges, qu'on ne les oste aux trois autres Facultez, en Theologie, Droict Canon, & des Arts, ioüissans toutes des mesmes Priuileges octroyez à l'Université en corps, nuls en particulier.
units.tr: King Louis XIII confirms all the privileges. To what end do all these confirmations, successively requested from the Kings, tend, except to avoid the revocation of their privileges and salaries? So much did they fear losing them. This is what the physicians of Paris have never troubled themselves about, since their privileges cannot be removed without removing them from the three other Faculties, of Theology, Canon Law and Arts, all of which enjoy the same privileges granted to the University as a body, none individually.

units.la: De sorte (Messieurs les Medecins de Montpellier) que j'ay grād suiet de soubçoner toutes vos lettres de fausseté. Vous estiez dés ce temps-là joints au Corps de l'Université. Il n'y a que 60.ans, ou plus, que vous en estes separez par l'instigation des Religionnaires, qui en estoient les maistres. Il n'y a point d'apparence que les Papes & les Rois ayent fait vne Universite pour quatre Medecins. Vostre Bulle du Pape Nicolas IV. compose l'Universite de quatre Facultez, leur donne pouvoir à chacune d'examiner & conferer le tiltre seulement de Maistres, en estans capables: Partant vous n'estiez pas Docteurs en l'an 1289. que la Bulle fut octroyée, & l'extrait de la Bulle de Conrard, Cardinal, qui appelle les Maistres, Docteurs, est fausse.
units.tr: So (Gentlemen physicians of Montpellier), I have great reason to suspect all your letters of forgery. You were at that time joined to the body of the University. It is only some 60 years, or more, since you were separated from it through the instigation of the Religionists, who were its masters. There is no likelihood that the Popes and Kings made a University for four physicians. Your Bull of Pope Nicholas IV composes the University of four Faculties, and gives each the power to examine and confer only the title of Master, being capable of it. Therefore you were not Doctors in the year 1289, when the Bull was granted; and the extract of the Bull of Cardinal Conrard, which calls the Masters Doctors, is false.

units.la: En lisant vos Lettres Patentes des Rois de France, Ie remarque beaucoup de choses, qui font contre vos pretensions. Les Rois ne vous ont rien donné au prejudice desautres Universitez, puis qu'ils ont inseré à la fin de leurs lettres, sauf nostre droict, & celuy d'autruy. Vous dites que vos Privileges sont reglez sur ceux de l'Universite de Paris. Ie voy neantmoins que vostre Eschole est si miserable & chetiue, qu'elle n'a pû subsister sans les gages donnez par les Rois de France. L'Eschole de Paris subsiste de soy-mesme, a esté fondée par les Medecins de Paris, entretenuë iusques auiourd'huy à leurs despens. Les Medecins, l'vnde la Reine Blanche, mere de Sainct Louys, a fondé la Sorbonne. Maistre Gernaus le College, qui porte son nom. Un autre le College de Cornoüaille, pour entretenir des Escholiers estudians en Medecine. Ie ne remarque point dans les Bulles des Papes ny des Rois de France, que vostre Eschole de Medecine soit Universite de fondation Royale. Ie n'y vois point le pouvoir que les Rois d'Arragon & de France, vous ont donné de pratiquer la Medecine par toutes les villes du monde, & particulierement de la France. Ce que les Papes ne vous ont point accordé, les Rois ne l'ont pas voulu faire. Ils vous permettent de chasser de vostre territoire, tous les Medecins qui ne sont pas licentiez & approuvez par les Docteurs de la ville de Montpelier. Partant vous n'avez aucun droit de mettre dans les lettres que vous donnez à ceux que vous avez fait Docteurs, Authoritate Apostolica do tibi licentiam legendi, examinandi, corrigendi, glossandi, practicandi, caterosque omnes actus Magistrales exercendi, hic & ubique terrarum. Notez qu'ils n'osent mettre Regia authoritate, & neantmoins se disent Commissaires du Roy en cette partie. Tous ces mots ont esté pris des lettres que donnent les Universitez Lutheriennes en Allemagne : Les Catholiques n'en usent pas de la sorte. Ce qui ne vous est point attribué par les Papes, ny par les Rois d'Arragon, ny de France: Nous avons sujet de nous plaindre de cette usurpation &attentat, qui va au détriment du public, qui est abusé par vos lettres, & au mespris de Monsieur l'Evesque de Montpelier: C'est à luy seul qu'appartient de conferer aux Bacheliers, la Licence de pratiquer la Medecine apres vostre examen & approbation. La Licence estant conferée par Monsieur l'Evesque, vous pouvez luy donner le bonnet solemnellement pour le former Docteur, & adopter en vostre Compagnie; de plus, luy donner lettre de son Acte Doctoral, celebré en tel iour & telle année. Cela suppose qu'il a esté trouvé capable. Je crois que si cet abus estoit bien consideré, & representé par Monsieur l'Evesque au Conseil du Roy, qu'il vous seroit defendu par Justice, dorefnavant d'en user de la sorte.
units.tr: In reading your Letters Patent of the Kings of France, I notice many things which tell against your claims. The Kings have granted you nothing to the prejudice of other Universities, since they inserted at the end of their letters, "saving our right, and that of others." You say that your privileges are regulated on those of the University of Paris. Yet I see that your School is so miserable and wretched that it could not subsist without the salaries given by the Kings of France. The School of Paris subsists of itself; it was founded by the physicians of Paris and has been maintained to this day at their own expense. The physicians... (the Queen Blanche, mother of Saint Louis, founded the Sorbonne; Master Gervais the College which bears his name; another the College of Cornouailles, to maintain scholars studying medicine). I do not remark in the Bulls of the Popes or of the Kings of France that your School of Medicine is a University of royal foundation. I do not see there the power which the Kings of Aragon and of France gave you to practise medicine in all the cities of the world, and particularly in France. What the Popes never granted you, the Kings have not wished to do either. They permit you to drive out of your territory all physicians who are not licensed and approved by the Doctors of the city of Montpellier. Therefore you have no right to put into the letters you give to those whom you have made Doctors: "By apostolic authority I give you licence to read, examine, correct, gloss, practise, and to exercise all the other Magisterial acts, here and everywhere on earth." Note that they do not dare to put "by royal authority," and yet they call themselves Commissioners of the King in this matter. All these words have been taken from the letters given by the Lutheran Universities in Germany; Catholics do not use them in this way. This is not attributed to you by the Popes, nor by the Kings of Aragon or of France. We have reason to complain of this usurpation and outrage, which works to the detriment of the public, who are deceived by your letters, and to the contempt of the Lord Bishop of Montpellier. It belongs to him alone to confer on Bachelors the licence to practise medicine, after your examination and approval. Once the licence has been conferred by the Lord Bishop, you may solemnly give him the cap to make him a Doctor and adopt him into your company; moreover, give him a letter of his Doctoral Act, celebrated on such a day and in such a year. This presupposes that he has been found capable. I believe that if this abuse were well considered, and represented by the Lord Bishop to the King's Council, you would be forbidden by Justice from using it in this way from now on.

units.la: Bien que tous ces Privileges des Rois de France,ne facent rien pour prouver le pouvoir que vous avez, de pratiquer la Medecine par toute la France, neantmoins je decouvre vostre dessein: Vous pretendez par la parole des Rois en vos lettres, monstrer la celebrité de vostre Eschole, l'estime qu'ils en ont fait, ayant tiré de là, de grands personnages pour servir leurs personnes, leurs femmes & leurs enfans. Le premier Roy qui a parlé de la sorte, c'est le Roy de Navarre, Seigneur de Montpelier. Le second Roy est de France, Charles VI. repetant les mesmes paroles contenuës en la Lettre Patente de Charles, Roy de Navarre, & adioustant de plus, que ses deuanciers ont pris des Medecins de Montpelier pour s'en servir.
units.tr: Although none of these privileges of the Kings of France proves the power you have to practise medicine throughout France, I nevertheless see your purpose. By the words of the Kings in your letters, you mean to show how famous your School is, and the esteem in which they held it, since from there they drew great men to serve their persons, their wives and their children. The first king to speak in this way was the King of Navarre, Lord of Montpellier. The second king is of France, Charles VI, repeating the same words contained in the letters patent of Charles, King of Navarre, and adding besides that his predecessors had taken physicians from Montpellier to serve them.

units.la: Examinons sommairement ce discours. Ceux qui sçauent le styl de la Chancelerie, aduoüeront que lors qu'on demande au Roy par requeste, on baille les Priuileges precedens, on propose tout ce que l'on croit seruir à la recommandation de son affaire, & on le fait inserer dans les lettres, comme motifs de l'octroy & graces que le Roy a fait. Presques en toutes les lettres que les Medecins de Montpelier ont obtenuës des Rois d'Arragon, & de France, il y a, à la supplication des Medecins de Montpelier, & les mesmes louanges y sont inserées, durant qu'ils rapportent les premieres lettres des Rois pour en auoir confirmation, en chasque mutation de regne.
units.tr: Let us briefly examine this claim. Those who know the style of the Chancery will admit that when one asks the King for a favour by petition, one submits the earlier privileges and sets out everything that is thought to help recommend the matter, and has it inserted in the letters as the grounds for the grant and the favours the King has bestowed. In nearly all the letters the physicians of Montpellier have obtained from the Kings of Aragon and of France, there is "at the supplication of the physicians of Montpellier", and the same praises are inserted there, while they bring forward the first letters of the Kings to obtain confirmation of them at each change of reign.

units.la: Quant à la lettre de Charles VI. où vous auez adiousté, que le Roy & ses predecesseurs, ont pris des Medecins pour leur conseruation de l'Eschole de Montpelier, c'est vne suppositiõ tres-manifeste: auant ledit Roy Philippe, la ville de Montpelier estoit sous la domination des Arragonois, anciens ennemis de la France. Est-il croyable, que les Rois deuanciers de Philippe, ayent pris des Medecins de Montpelier pour s'en seruir? C'est tout de mesme, si le Roy de France prenoit des Medecins Espagnols, des Vniuersitez d'Espagne, pour en estre secouru en ses maladies. Dans la vie de Charles VI. iene [?] trouue point de Medecins de Montpelier, mais vn Medecin Harseley, Chanoine de Laon, qui le mit en meilleure santé. Vous ne sçauriez produire ny monstrer vn Medecin de l'Eschole de Montpelier, plus ancien que Adam Fumée, qui seruoit le Roy Charles VII. Et bien que ce Medecin ait esté fait Maistre des Requestes par Louys XI. neantmoins ce qu'en dit de luy Bellefores, & d'autres apres luy, ne vous est pas honorable. Le Roy l'auoit mis prisonnier, le soubçonnant de l'auoir voulu empoisonner, gagné & suscité par Louys XI. son fils. Il est croyable qu'il ait pris Adam Fumée, lors que la ville de Paris estoit possedée par les Anglois, & le Roy refugié au delà de la riuiere de Loire.
units.tr: As for the letter of Charles VI, where you have added that the King and his predecessors took physicians for their preservation from the School of Montpellier, this is a very manifest supposition. Before the said King Philip, the town of Montpellier was under the rule of the Aragonese, old enemies of France. Is it credible that the predecessors of Philip took physicians of Montpellier to serve them? It would be just the same if the King of France took Spanish physicians from the universities of Spain to be treated in his illnesses. In the life of Charles VI I find no physicians of Montpellier, but a physician Harseley, Canon of Laon, who restored him to better health. You could not produce or point to a physician of the School of Montpellier older than Adam Fumée, who served King Charles VII. And although this physician was made Master of Requests by Louis XI, nevertheless what Bellefores and others after him say of him is not honourable to you. The King had imprisoned him, suspecting that he had tried to poison him, having been won over and incited by Louis XI, his son. It is believable that he took Adam Fumée at the time when the town of Paris was held by the English and the King had taken refuge beyond the river Loire.

units.la: C'est vne grande béveuë de vouloir faire Docteur de Montpelier Ferragius, Juif, Medecin pretendu de Charlemagne ; alors la ville de Montpelier n'estoit qu'vne bourgade, & ne s'est accrue, qu'en l'an millenaire, par la destruction de Maguelone. Sckenchius en sa Bibliotheque Medicinale, a donné sujet à cette resverie. l'apprend que Ferragius estoit Docteur de Salerne : Medecin de Charles, Roy de Naples & de Sicile, Il l'envoya à Tunis, pour auoir le Continens de Rhasis, que ledit Ferragius a tourné d'Arabe en Latin: & à la fin du 25. liure, il met ses qualitez que ie viens de dire, & en parle en sa Preface. Si on veut verifier cela, il faut prendre le Continens de Rhasis de Brixianus, d'autant qu'en la seconde edition, Surianus a tout reuersé [?], & peut-estre tout corrompu.
units.tr: It is a great blunder to want to make Ferragius, a Jew, a supposed physician of Charlemagne, a Doctor of Montpellier; at that time the town of Montpellier was nothing but a village, and it did not grow until the millennial year, through the destruction of Maguelone. Sckenchius in his Bibliotheca Medicinalis gave occasion for this fancy. I learn that Ferragius was a Doctor of Salerno, physician to Charles, King of Naples and Sicily, who sent him to Tunis to obtain the Continens of Rhazes, which the said Ferragius translated from Arabic into Latin; and at the end of the 25th book he sets down the qualities I have just mentioned, and speaks of them in his Preface. If one wishes to verify this, one must take the Continens of Rhazes of Brixianus, since in the second edition Surianus has overturned everything [?], and perhaps corrupted it all.

units.la: Vn chiquaneur comme Courtant, nous demandera des Bulles des Papes en faueur de noftre Efchole, des Priuileges des Rois de France, furquoy Courtaut nous donne vn cartel de deffy : Tu sanctiora & augustiora promitto Priuilegia Schola tua, quæ ne quidem nomen Facultatis ferre potest.
units.tr: A quibbler such as Courtaut will demand from us Bulls of the Popes in favour of our School, and the privileges of the Kings of France, on which Courtaut throws down a challenge: "I promise you privileges more sacred and more august than your school, which cannot even bear the name of Faculty."

units.la: Nous luy produirons les Bulles des Papes,[?] & les Priuileges des Rois de France donnez à l'Université de Paris, de laquelle l'Eschole de Medecine en compose la plus saine & meilleure partie apres la Sorbonne, qui enseigne la plus sainte Theologie. Ces Bulles & Priuileges sont communs & egaux à toutes les quatre Facultez de ladite Université; comme il a esté ordonné par ladite Université, toutes les Facultez assemblées, il y a prés de cinq cens ans; si l'Université de Montpelier auoit les mesmes Priuileges, que Nicolas III. a donné à l'Université de Paris, ils les feroient bien valoir auec arrogance: il donne Priuilege aux Docteurs de Paris, qu'ils pourront par toute la terre lire, regenter, & estre receus Docteurs par toutes les Universitez sans contredit, sur peine d'xcommunication.
units.tr: We will produce for him the Bulls of the Popes and the privileges of the Kings of France granted to the University of Paris, of which the School of Medicine forms the soundest and best part, after the Sorbonne, which teaches the most holy Theology. These Bulls and privileges are common and equal to all four Faculties of the said University, as was ordained by the said University, all the Faculties assembled, nearly five hundred years ago. If the University of Montpellier had the same privileges that Nicholas III gave to the University of Paris, they would make good use of them with arrogance: he grants the Doctors of Paris the privilege that they may read, teach and be received as Doctors in all Universities throughout the whole earth without contradiction, on pain of excommunication.

units.la: De plus, si les Medecins de Montpelier auoient seulement le mesme Priuilege concedé à l'Université de Toulouse, ils auroient sujet de se glorifier, & preualoir par dessus les autres Universitez. Gregoire IX. l'an 1233. par sa Bulle de fondation, ordonne que la dite Université iouïra des mesmes Priuileges que celle de Paris: & de plus, Quicumque magister ibi examinatus & approbatus fuerit in qualibet Facultate, vbique sine alia examinatione, regendi liberam habeat potestatem. Que les Medecins de Montpelier monstrent un pareil Privilege.
units.tr: Moreover, if the physicians of Montpellier had only the same privilege conceded to the University of Toulouse, they would have cause to glory and to prevail above the other universities. Gregory IX, in the year 1233, by his Bull of foundation, ordains that the said University shall enjoy the same privileges as that of Paris; and besides, "whatever master has been examined and approved there in any Faculty, may have the free power of teaching everywhere without any other examination." Let the physicians of Montpellier show a similar privilege.

units.la: Nos Privileges sont depuis Charlemagne, Fondateur des Universitez, lequel l'a estably de son authorité Royale & Imperiale, plus de 400. ans auant que les Papes eussent concedé leurs Bulles. Si vous desirez sçavoir nos Privileges que nos Rois nous ont donné, vous en trouverez une partie exprimée dans le livre de Rebuffus, Jurisconsulte Professeur de Montpelier: Vous y remarquerez deux Privileges de Louys IX. l'an 1229. & l'an 1311. de Philippe le Bel, l'an 1293. de Philippe VI. deux, dont l'un est de l'an 1340, l'autre l'an 1345. du Roy Jean, l'an 1360. de Charles V. plusieurs, l'an 1365. l'an 1368. de Charles VI. l'an 1383. de Charles VII. l'an 1473. de Louys XI. l'an 1478. Depuis ce temps-là nous en avons eu d'autres des Rois successeurs, selon l'occurrence des affaires, & en nostre particulier pour les affaires de nostre Communauté. Du Roy Jean, de Louys XI. de Louys XII. du Roy François I. du Roy Henry II. qui tous nous ont tousiours traité favorablement & exempté de subsides, impofts, gardes des ortes, & emprunts.
units.tr: Our privileges date from Charlemagne, founder of the universities, who established them by his royal and imperial authority more than 400 years before the Popes granted their Bulls. If you wish to know the privileges which our Kings have given us, you will find a part of them set out in the book of Rebuffus, a jurisconsult and professor at Montpellier. There you will note two privileges of Louis IX, in the year 1229 and in 1311; of Philip the Fair, in 1293; of Philip VI, two, one dated 1340 and the other 1345; of King John, in 1360; of Charles V, several, in 1365, in 1368; of Charles VI, in 1383; of Charles VII, in 1473; of Louis XI, in 1478. Since that time we have had others from the successor Kings, according to the occurrence of affairs, and in particular for the affairs of our Community: from King John, from Louis XI, from Louis XII, from King Francis I, from King Henry II, who all have always treated us favourably and exempted us from subsidies, taxes, guards of the gates, and loans.

units.la: Un chicaneur nous reprochera, que nos Privileges sont nuls, dautant que nous n'avons pas eu la confirmation des Rois. C'est la verité que nostre Université n'ayant aucun revenu des Roys, & particulierement nostre Eschole, nous n'avons pas sollicité la confirmation de nos Privileges en chaque mutation de Regne, dautant que l'Vniversité de Paris estant la premiere de l'Europe, & la plus ancienne de la France, on ne peut la casser & destruire sans faire tort à la ville de Paris, & à l'honneur des Roys tant anciens que modernes, qui s'en sont tousiours servy utilement, pour la conservation de leurs droicts, anthoritez, & libertez de l'Eglise Gallicane, contre les usurpations & attentats faits par les Papes sur la personne de nos Rois, & de leurs Estats; en quels cas la Sorbonne ne fait rien seule, sans l'assemblée du Recteur & des trois autres Facultez par deputation; tellement que Ramus recommandant au Roy Charles IX. d'aimer l'Vniversité de Paris, le Palladium du Royaume & de la ville, il finit sa Harangue par ces termes.
units.tr: A pettifogger will object that our privileges are void, since we never obtained the confirmation of the kings. It is true that our University, having no revenue from the kings, and our School in particular, has not sought confirmation of our privileges at each change of reign. The University of Paris, being the first in Europe and the most ancient in France, cannot be overthrown or destroyed without doing wrong to the city of Paris and to the honour of the kings, both ancient and modern, who have always made use of it to good effect for the preservation of their rights, authorities and liberties, and those of the Gallican Church, against the usurpations and assaults made by the Popes upon the person of our kings and their realms. In such cases the Sorbonne does nothing alone, without the assembly of the Rector and the three other Faculties by deputation. So much so that Ramus, when he urged King Charles IX to love the University of Paris, the Palladium of the kingdom and of the city, ended his harangue with these words.

units.la: Ætheream servate Deam, servabitis urbem,Imperium secum transferet illa loci,
units.tr: Preserve the ethereal goddess, and you will preserve the city; she will carry the empire with her, that power of place.

units.la: Ceux qui comparent l'Eschole de Montpelier auec celle de Paris, ne sont-ils pas ridicules, voulans mettre en parallele la ville de Montpelier, avec celle de Paris; Ils ressemblent à mon jugement à ce pauvre berger Tityrus, en la premiere Eclogue de Virgile, qui croyoit que son village estoit semblable à la ville de Rome,
units.tr: Do not those who compare the School of Montpelier with that of Paris look ridiculous, wanting to set the city of Montpelier in parallel with Paris? In my judgement they resemble that poor shepherd Tityrus in the first Eclogue of Virgil, who believed that his village was like the city of Rome,

units.la: Urbem quam dicunt Romam Melibœe putaui Stultus ego, huic nostra similem, quò sæpe solebant Pastores ovium teneros depellere fœtus: Sic canibus catulos similes, sic matribus hœdos Noram, sic paruis componere magna solebam, Verum hæc tantum alias inter caput extulit Urbes, Quantum lenta solent inter viburna cupressi.
units.tr: The city they call Rome, I once thought, O Melibœus, was like ours (foolish that I was), where shepherds were accustomed to drive away the tender young of their flocks. Thus I used to compare small things with great, as puppies with dogs and kids with their mothers. But this city has raised its head above other cities as much as the slender cypress usually rises above the pliant viburnum.

units.la: Ie puis asseurer sans mentir qu'il n'y a point d'Université au monde, où la Medecine soit mieux enseignée & pratiquée, qu'en la ville de Paris: cùm -----
units.tr: I can assure you without lying that there is no university in the world where medicine is better taught and practised than in the city of Paris: cùm -----

units.la: Nullus sit lucus, quo plus se jactet Apollo.
units.tr: Nullus sit lucus, quo plus se jactet Apollo.

units.la: Si ie suis suspect en nostre cause, ie m'en rapporteray au tesmoignage des estrangers.
units.tr: If I am suspected in our cause, I will refer to the testimony of foreigners.

units.la: Symphorianus Campegius recite vne Epistre de son Neveu Joannes Campegius, Medecin, où la reuommée des Medecins de Paris pour la langue Grecque, & pour la science de Medecine, est fort hautement louée en l'année 1532. Nusquam eloquentia clarior, nusquam Philosophia castior, ornatiorque quàm in Academia Parisiensi, toto orbe celebratissima, nusquam Medicina manifestior quàm illic. Quamprimùm in germanam linguam ac pristinum splendorem restituta est, quot illic, bone Deus Philosophi, Medicique praestantissimi, in utraque litteratura, in doctrina recondita. En suite il rapporte les louanges des Sieurs Martinus Akakia, de Joannes Vassæus, de Guarinus, de Sylvius, de Guinterius, de Guillelmus Copus, & de Ruellius.
units.tr: Symphorianus Campegius recites a letter from his nephew Joannes Campegius, a physician, in which the reputation of the physicians of Paris, for the Greek language and for the science of medicine, is praised very highly, in the year 1532. "Nowhere is eloquence more brilliant, nowhere philosophy purer and more adorned than in the University of Paris, most celebrated throughout the whole world; nowhere is medicine more evident than there. As soon as it was restored to its native language and former splendour, how many philosophers and most excellent physicians there were, good God, in both literatures, in recondite learning." Then he gives the praises of the gentlemen Martinus Akakia, Joannes Vassæus, Guarinus, Sylvius, Guinterius, Guillelmus Copus, and Ruellius.

units.la: Guillelmus Cafanatus l'an 1551. sçauant Medecin Escossois, escrivant à Cardan, de la Capitale ville d'Escosse, qui est Edimbourg. Jam vero Lutetiam omnium Disciplinarum genere, ac maximè Medicina Civitatem florentissimam profectus est Archiepiscopus, totam sanitati operam ibidem navaturus. Valetius, Medecin de Bordeaux, en la Préface sur la pratique de Hollier, dit des merueilles des Medecins de Paris, comme a fait Turnebus in Adversariis, lib. 17. cap. 18. Laurens Joubert, Medecin de Montpelier, donnant le bonnet Doctoral, loüe Daniel Galarsius, de ce qu'il a estudié en Medecine à Paris, soubs de grands, & sçauans Medecins. Idque Lutetiae Parisiorum, urbe totius Europae compendio.
units.tr: Guillelmus Cafanatus, in the year 1551, a learned Scottish physician, writing to Cardan from the capital city of Scotland, which is Edinburgh: Jam vero Lutetiam omnium Disciplinarum genere, ac maximè Medicina Civitatem florentissimam profectus est Archiepiscopus, totam sanitati operam ibidem navaturus. Valetius, a physician of Bordeaux, in the preface to Hollier's practice, speaks wonders of the physicians of Paris, as Turnebus has done in the Adversaria, book 17, chapter 18. Laurens Joubert, a physician of Montpelier, conferring the doctoral bonnet, praises Daniel Galarsius for having studied medicine at Paris under great and learned physicians. Idque Lutetiae Parisiorum, urbe totius Europae compendio.

units.la: Ie m'estonne grandement de l'ignorance des Medecins de Montpelier dans l'histoire de leur Eschole, ne pouvans prouver l'anciennete & excellence, que par les Bulles des Papes, & Lettres Patentes des Rois ; ce quia esté mandié par les Medecins , fabriqué & donné en leur faveur par les Secretaires des Papes , & des Royes, si elles sont veritables. Le sieur Ranchin dit sans preuue, qu'il y a 600. ans que la ville de Montpelier est consacrée & destinée pour la Medecine. Courtaut asseure & veut qu'on le croye sur sa parole, que l'Eschole de Montpelier est d'un temps immemorial, la premiere de l'Europe, & diroit volontiers ce qui est prophetizé dans Virgile, de la ville de Rome.
units.tr: I am greatly astonished at the ignorance of the physicians of Montpelier concerning the history of their School, since they can prove its antiquity and excellence only by the Bulls of the Popes and the Letters Patent of the Kings; and these, if they are genuine, were requested by the physicians, fabricated and granted in their favour by the secretaries of the Popes and the Kings. Sieur Ranchin says without proof that for 600 years the city of Montpelier has been consecrated and destined for medicine. Courtaut asserts, and wants us to believe on his word, that the School of Montpelier is of immemorial time, the first in Europe, and he would willingly say what is prophesied in Virgil of the city of Rome.

units.la: Huic ego nec metas rerum, nec tempora pono, Imperium sine fine dedi ---------
units.tr: To this city I set no limits of things or of time: I have given it empire without end ---------

units.la: Il proteste & pretend qu'elle est, Medicorum, tum Pontificum, tum Imperantium, tum societatis humana plusquam tritania & octauia; qu'elle est plus que trois fois grand-Mere, & Octayeule des Medecins, des Pontifes, des Rois, & de la societe humaine. Il a oublié de nous donner la genealogie, & le Liure de la generation, à la mode des Iuifs leurs anciens Maistres.
units.tr: He protests and claims that it is Medicorum, tum Pontificum, tum Imperantium, tum societatis humana plusquam tritania & octauia: that it is more than three times grandmother, and great-great-grandmother, of physicians, pontiffs, kings and human society. He has forgotten to give us the genealogy, and the Book of the Generation, after the manner of the Jews, their ancient masters.

units.la: C'est une pure resverie de dire que Marilef, Medecin de Gontrand, de la premiere race de nos Rois, estoit Arabe, venu de l'Eschole de Montpelier. Le Sieur Ranchin asseure qu'ils n'ont fleury en la Medecine qu'en l'an 1149. & n'ont esté chassez de Portugal, Castille, Arragon, Navarre, qu'en l'an 1230. auquel temps ils se sont refugiez à Montpelier. Si nous croyons les Medecins de ladite Eschole sans aucune preuve, il y a environ onze cens ans que Marilef vivoit, la damnable secte de Mahomet n'a paru au monde qu'en l'an 632. partant les Sarrazins Mahometans, n'estans pas encore venus en Espagne, Marilef n'a pû estre Medecin de Montpelier ; & ne sçauriez aussi montrer, que ledit Marilef ait esté Medecin de Meroüée, & de Childeric, Rois, pere, & fils, ny que Bengezlaus ait esté Medecin de CharleMagne, ny Ferragius, tous deux Juifs. Cét Empereur estoit trop pieux pour se servir de telles gens, ennemis de Chrestiens, qui ont entre eux conspiré la ruïne de la Chrestienté, croyans faire sacrifice à Dieu en faisant mourir clandestinement les Chrestiens, ce qu'ils peuvent executer aisément sous le voile & pretexte de la Medecine.
units.tr: It is pure fantasy to say that Marilef, physician to Gontran, of the first race of our kings, was an Arab who came from the School of Montpelier. Sieur Ranchin asserts that they flourished in medicine only in the year 1149, and were not driven from Portugal, Castile, Aragon and Navarre until the year 1230, at which time they took refuge at Montpelier. If we believe the physicians of that School without any proof, Marilef lived about eleven hundred years ago, and the damnable sect of Mahomet did not appear in the world until the year 632. Therefore the Saracen Mahometans, not yet having come into Spain, Marilef could not have been a physician of Montpelier. Nor can you show that the said Marilef was physician to Merovech and Childeric, kings, father and son, nor that Bengezlaus was physician to Charlemagne, nor Ferragius; both were Jews. That Emperor was too pious to make use of such people, enemies of Christians, who have conspired together for the ruin of Christendom, believing they are offering sacrifice to God by secretly putting Christians to death, which they can easily carry out under the veil and pretext of medicine.

units.la: I'ay montrè cy-dessus la resverie & fausfete de Ferragius, Iuif, Medecin pretendu de Charlemagne, ce qui m'exemptera d'en parler dauantage.
units.tr: I have shown above the fantasy and falsehood of Ferragius, the Jew, the supposed physician of Charlemagne, which will spare me from speaking of it further.

units.la: Voyant que les Medecins de Montpelier n'ont aucune preuue ny authorité valable pour prouuer l'anciennete, & l'excellence de leur Eschole, ie les veux assister, & fauoriser charitablement. Il est certain qu'il y a cinq cens ans qu'il y auoit des Medecins dans la ville de Montpelier, quand elle fut bastie apres la destruction de Maguelone, & que d'vne bourgade on en a fait vne grande ville, mais ils estoient sans Eschole & discipline reguliere, ils enseignoient grossierement la Medecine. Le Sieur Ranchin m'en a donné cette premiere lumiere, citant l'Ep.307.de S.Bernard, qui escriuoit Domino Hostiesi[?], qui estoit le Cardinal Hugo: en voicy le texte fort remarquable. De Domino Lugdunensi audite quod verum est, & quod certum sit vobis. Virile aggressus est iter, & venit cum tribus vel quatuor ministris, cum turba promiscua peregrinorum, tanquam unus ex illis peruenit ad sanctum Egidium, cumque infirmaretur, pertransiit usque ad Montem Pessulanum, ibi aliquandiu commoratus, cum Medicis expendit & quod habebat, & quod non habebat. Vous voyez que ce bon Archeuefque de Lyon alloit en pelerinage par devo-tion à saint Gilles, de son propre mouvement. Durant son voyage il devint malade, il va à la plus prochaine ville, qui étoit Montpelier, où les Medecins luy firent dépendre tout son argent, & l'obligerent à d'autres dépenses, qui est en bon François, luy couper la bourse, selon la doctrine des Arabes, leurs anciens Maistres. Il n'est point enoncé qu'il allât expressément à Montpelier pour se faire traiter, & qu'il fut guery de sa maladie, ce qu'adioufte de son crû le Sieur Ranchin. Sainct Bernard, Autheur de cette Epistre, l'escrivoit l'an 1113. presque au mesme temps 1140. florissoit Joannes Sarisberiensis, Evesque de Chartre, qui avoit voyagé presque par toute la France, & avoit esté plusieurs fois à Rome pour les affaires de l'Eglise: il parle des Medecins de Salerne & de Montpelier, Metalogici lib. 1. c. 4. qui enfeignoient la Medecine: Ils les depeint de leurs vives couleurs, & tels que nous les reconnoissons aujourd'huy.
units.tr: Seeing that the physicians of Montpellier have no proof or valid authority to demonstrate the antiquity and excellence of their school, I wish to assist and charitably favour them. It is certain that five hundred years ago there were physicians in the town of Montpellier, when it was built after the destruction of Maguelone, and from a village it became a great city; but they were without a school and regular discipline, and they taught medicine in a crude manner. Sieur Ranchin gave me this first light, citing Epistle 307 of St Bernard, which was written to "Domino Hostiesi" [?], who was Cardinal Hugo; here is the very remarkable text: "Hear about the Lord of Lyon what is true and what is certain for you. He undertook the journey like a man, and came with three or four ministers, with a mixed crowd of pilgrims; like one of them he arrived at St Giles, and when he fell ill, he passed on as far as Montpellier, where, staying there for some time, he spent with the physicians both what he had and what he did not have." You see that this good Archbishop of Lyon was going on pilgrimage out of devotion to St Giles, of his own accord. During his journey he became ill; he went to the nearest town, which was Montpellier, where the physicians made him spend all his money and obliged him to other expenses, which in good French means to cut his purse, according to the doctrine of the Arabs, their ancient masters. It is not stated that he went expressly to Montpellier to be treated, and that he was cured of his illness; Sieur Ranchin adds this on his own account. St Bernard, author of this epistle, wrote it in the year 1113. At almost the same time, around 1140, flourished Joannes Sarisberiensis, Bishop of Chartres, who had travelled through almost all of France and had been several times to Rome on the affairs of the Church. He speaks of the physicians of Salerno and of Montpellier, who taught medicine (Metalogicus, book 1, chapter 4), and he depicts them in their lively colours, as we recognise them today.

units.la: Aly autem suum in Philosophia intuentes defectum, Salernum vel ad Montem Pessulanum profecti facti sunt Clientuli Medicorum, & repente quales fuerant Philosophi, tales in momento Medici cruperunt; Fallacibus enim referti experimentis, in breui redeunt, sedulo exercentes quod didicerunt. Hippocratem ostentant, aut Galenum, verba proferunt inaudita, ad omnia suos loquuntur Aphorismos, & mentes humanas velut afflatas tonitruis sic percellunt nominibus inauditis, creduntur omnia posse, quia omnia iactitant, omnia pollicentur. Duo tamen deprehendi eos fideliori tenuisse memoria, & frequentius in eorum operatione versari. Alterum quidem Hippocratis est, (sed ibi vergit ad alium intellectum) ubi inquit indigentia, non oportet laborare, & reuera inopportunum & inofficiosum opinantes dare operam indigentibus, & eis qui nolunt, aut nequeunt; vel solis verbis eorum plenè gratiam referre mercedis. Alterum profecto est, non quod meminerim Hippocratis, sed diligentium adiecto medicorum; dum dolet accipe. Occasio siquidem exigendi maximè opportuna est, cum dolor excruciat agrotantem, sibique cooperantur languentis exulceratio, & anaritia medentis. Si convalescit aeger operam danti Medico adscribatur si deficit, eius inualescat auctoritas, qui hoc antea familiaribus suis reuelauit. Siquidem impossibile est non euenire quod de industria praenaticinatus est, cum huic sospitalem, isti sinistrum exitum pronunciauit agrotantis, si euasurus est aeger, curatur facile, nisi quatenus incolumitatem eius medicus praepedit imperitus. Sim[?] autem non ut Sollius Sidonius ait, occiditur officiosissime. Quidni ? nunquid enim natura secretos, latentesque cuniculos deprehendit, homo totius Philosophiæ ignarus, & qui nec recte loqui nouit, nec recte intelligit quæ scripta sunt, aut quæ dicuntur, cum fere quot disciplinæ sunt, tot sint linguæ, & in ipsis plerumque auctoribus non sit maior in corporali compositione diuersitas facierum, quam in usu varietas linguarum. Tout ce beau discours merite d'estre traduit en François, pour ceux qui n'entendent pas le Latin.
units.tr: Others, however, seeing their own lack of knowledge in philosophy, go off to Salerno or to Montpellier and become the little clients of the physicians; and at once, as they had been philosophers, in a moment they begin to be doctors. For, filled with deceptive experiments, they soon return, diligently practising what they have learned. They display Hippocrates, or Galen; they utter unheard-of words; they speak in aphorisms on every subject, and they strike men's minds, as if struck by thunderbolts, with names never heard before. They are believed able to do everything, because they boast of everything and promise everything. Yet I have found that they hold firmly to two things in their memory, and are more often engaged in them in their practice. The first is a saying of Hippocrates (but there it has a different sense): "where there is want, one must not labour"; and truly they think it an inopportune and unbecoming thing to attend the needy, who are unwilling or unable to repay the service fully, or at least with mere words of thanks. The second is certainly not something I recall from Hippocrates, but added by the diligent physicians of later times: "while the patient suffers, take." For there is no more opportune occasion for demanding payment than when pain racks the sick man, and the wretchedness of the illness and the greed of the physician work together. If the patient recovers, the credit is given to the physician who attended him; if he dies, the authority of the one who had earlier foretold this to his friends is strengthened. For it is impossible that what he foretold deliberately should not come to pass: he pronounced a favourable outcome for one patient and a grim one for another. If the patient is going to escape, he is easily cured, unless the unskilled physician hinders his recovery. But, as Sollius Sidonius says, he is not killed out of excessive zeal. Why not? For nature does not uncover hidden and secret passages, when a man ignorant of all philosophy, who knows neither how to speak correctly nor how to understand correctly what is written or what is said, is involved; since there are about as many disciplines as there are languages, and among the authors themselves there is usually no greater diversity in the make-up of bodies than there is variety in the use of languages. All this fine discourse deserves to be translated into French, for those who do not understand Latin.

units.la: Ceux qui connoissent leur propre ignorance en Philosophie, s'en vont à Salerne ou à Montpelier, & là se rendent esclaves des Medecins, pour devenir en un instant aussi sçauans Medecins comme ils estoient Philosophes. Ayans amassé des receptes trompeuses, & dangereuses, ils s'en retournent incontinent, pour pratiquer soigneusement ce qu'ils ont appris. Ils font parade d'Hippocrate & de Galien, iargonnent des mots inouïs. A tous propos ils alleguent leurs Aphorismes, & avec des paroles estranges, ils estourdissent tellement les esprits, comme s'ils estoient soufflez du Tonnerre. On croit qu'ils peuvent tout, parce qu'ils se vantent de tout faire, & promettent toutes choses: J'ay remarqué qu'ils ont fort bien retenu deux choses, qu'ils pratiquent souvent, l'une est un texte d'Hippocrate, qu'ils accommodent à leurs sens, où il y a de l'indigence & famine, il ne faut point travailler. À la verité, ils croyent que c'est une chose importune & mal gracieuse d'assister les pauvres, qui ne veulent, & ne peuvent satisfaire, à tout le moins avec belles paroles les remercier, & témoigner leurs obligations. L'autre Aphorisme n'est point tiré d'Hippocrate, mais les Medecins diligens & ardens au gain, s'en servent, Cependant que le malade pâtit; prenez. Il n'y a point de plus belle occasion d'exiger, que lors que la douleur bourelle le malade, & que l'avarice du Medecin, & la cruauté du mal cooperent ensemble, l'un pour donner, & l'autre pour escroquer. Le texte Latin est encore plus long, mais je me contenteray d'avoir representé les belles qualitez des Medecins de Mon-pelier, il y a cinq cens ans qu'ils n'estoient que des ignorans en Philosophie & en Medecine. Ils faisoient en un moment des Medecins, qui s'en retournoient avec des receptes dangereuses, pour abuser le peuple, & le faire mourir. Ils n'estoient nullement charitables, mais de vrais Arabes, qui tiroient des riches & des pauures pendant leurs maladies tout leur argent. Neft-cepas confirmer le texte de faincł[?] Bernard, que les Medecins de Montpelier couperent la bourse à l'Archeuesque de Lyon. Ie ne trouve point de plus anciens Autheurs, qui ayent parlé plus authentiquement des Medecins de Montpelier, que ces deux grands perfonnages ; qu'on ne peut iustement accuser d'imposture. Presque du mesme temps, un sçauant homme, Cesarius, en son Liure des Miracles, dit, qu'à Montpelier il y avoit une Image de la Vierge Marie, qui faisoit des Miracles pour la guerison des maladies, en despit des Medecins du lieu, lesquels par derision refusoient de donner conseil aux pauures, qui n'avoient point d'argent, les renvoyans à l'Image de la Vierge ; qui les guerissoit. Ie tire une quatriesme preuve de l'ancienneté de l'Academie de Montpelier, du Glossateur Accarse, qui a enseigné le droict Civil dans Montpelier, où il est decedé l'an 1192. enterré dans le Cimeriere de sainct Barthelemy, au rapport du Sieur Ca-tel, en son Histoire du Languedoc: Tellement qu'on enseignoit il y a cinq cens ans le Droit & la Medecine dans Montpelier: l'apprens par les vers de Petrus Egidius, Corboliensis, Chanoine de Paris, & Medecin du Roy Philippe second, que l'Eschole de Montpelier enseignoit la Medecine enuiron l'an 1220. mais tres-mal. Voila comme il le decrit à la fin de son poëme de Vrinis, imprimé ; Monsieur Mentel nostre Confrere, tressçauant Medecin, en a le Manuscript en sa riche Bibliotheque.
units.tr: Those who know their own ignorance in philosophy go off to Salerno or to Montpellier, and there make themselves slaves of the physicians, so as to become, in an instant, as learned physicians as they were philosophers. Having gathered deceptive and dangerous prescriptions, they straightway return home to practise carefully what they have learned. They make a show of Hippocrates and Galen, they jabber unheard-of words, and on every occasion they cite their aphorisms; with strange words they so stun men's minds, as if they had been struck by thunder. People believe they can do everything, because they boast that they can do everything and promise all things. I have noticed that they have very well retained two things, which they often practise: one is a text of Hippocrates, which they adapt to their own purposes, "where there is want and famine, one must not labour." In truth, they believe that it is an unseemly and ungracious thing to assist the poor, who are unwilling or unable to satisfy them, or at least to thank them and show their gratitude with fine words. The other aphorism is not taken from Hippocrates, but the diligent physicians, keen for gain, use it: "while the patient suffers, take." There is no finer occasion for demanding payment than when pain tortures the sick man, and the avarice of the physician and the cruelty of the disease work together, the one to give and the other to fleece. The Latin text is even longer, but I will content myself with having set out the fine qualities of the physicians of Montpellier. Five hundred years ago they were nothing but men ignorant of philosophy and medicine. In an instant they made physicians, who went home with dangerous prescriptions, to deceive the people and make them die. They were in no way charitable, but true Arabs, who drew all their money from rich and poor during their illnesses. Does this not confirm the text of Saint Bernard, that the physicians of Montpellier cut the purse of the Archbishop of Lyons? I find no older authors who have spoken more reliably of the physicians of Montpellier than these two great personages, who cannot justly be accused of imposture. At almost the same time, a learned man, Caesarius, in his Book of Miracles, says that at Montpellier there was an image of the Virgin Mary which worked miracles for the healing of diseases, in spite of the physicians of the place, who, by way of derision, refused to give advice to the poor who had no money, sending them off to the image of the Virgin, which cured them. I draw a fourth proof of the antiquity of the Academy of Montpellier from the glossator Accursius, who taught civil law at Montpellier, where he died in the year 1192, and was buried in the cemetery of Saint Bartholomew, according to Sieur Catel in his History of Languedoc. So it was that five hundred years ago law and medicine were taught at Montpellier. I learn from the verses of Petrus Aegidius of Corbeil, canon of Paris and physician to King Philip II, that the School of Montpellier taught medicine around the year 1220, but very badly. Thus he describes it at the end of his poem On Urines, printed; Monsieur Mentel, our colleague, a most learned physician, has the manuscript in his rich library.

units.la: Nec tecum moueat contraria secta duellum, Dyscholus & mordax, vehemens, clamosus, inanis, Quem sterili lolio pascit farragine cruda, Inflat, & infatuat Mons pessulanicus error.
units.tr: Let not the contrary sect move you to strife: the dyscholus, the biting, the vehement, the noisy, the empty one, whom the Montpellier error feeds with crude farrago of sterile darnel, and puffs up and infatuates.

units.la: Par là vous voyez l'ignorance & l'arroance des Medecins de Montpelier dés ce [?]emps là. Cy apres ie la feray connoistre de ecle en siecle.
units.tr: By this you see the ignorance and arrogance of the physicians of Montpellier from that time on. Hereafter I will make it known century by century.

units.la: Nous auons assez curieusement recherché l'ancienneté de l'Eschole de Montpelier; voyons si l'Eschole de Paris peut montrer & verifier son ancienneté de plus haut. Personne ne peut reuoquer en doute que l'Vniuersité de Paris ne soit la premiere de Europe, depuis le Christianisme.
units.tr: We have investigated fairly carefully the antiquity of the School of Montpellier; let us see whether the School of Paris can show and verify its antiquity from further back. No one can doubt that the University of Paris is the first in Europe since the coming of Christianity.

units.la: Iustus Lipsius, en son Liure de Louanio, asseure que l'Vniuersité de Paris, est la mere de [?]outes les Escholes, encore que celle de
units.tr: Justus Lipsius, in his Book on Louvain, assures us that the University of Paris is the mother of all schools, although that of

units.la: Sur les Efcholes en Medecine.
units.tr: On the Schools of Medicine.

units.la: Boulogne fe vante d'eftre la premiere, fur des faux tiltres. Alciate fouftient que l'Efchole de Boulogne, n'eft point du temps de Theodofe fecond, dautant que du temps d'Otho premier, Empereur dans toute l'Italie, l'on ne parlcit point de cette Efchole, comme rapporte Sigonius lib. 7. de regno Italiæ, & lib. 3. de rebus Italicis. Partant la Chartre qu'ils alleguent eft fauffe. Lupoldus, Euefque de Bamberg, qui viuoit l'an 1353. auquel temps il fut sacré Euefque en Avignon, nous enfeigne au Liure de Zelo Christiana religionis veterum Principum Germanorum, que long-temps auant Charlemagne, les sciences eftoient enseignées à Paris, qu'il n'a fait que releuer & amplifier l'Etude de Theologie, il le prouue par Seuerinus Boëtius, qui viuoit du temps de Zeno l'Empereur l'an 475. Voila le commencement des eftudes à Paris, qui ont esté mieux cultiues & releués par le soin de l'Empereur Charlemagne.
units.tr: Bologna boasts of being the first, on false titles. Alciato maintains that the school of Bologna does not date from the time of Theodosius the Second, since in the time of Otho the First, Emperor over all Italy, that school was not spoken of, as Sigonius reports in book 7 of On the Kingdom of Italy, and book 3 of On Italian Affairs. Therefore the charter they allege is false. Lupoldus, Bishop of Bamberg, who lived in the year 1353, at which time he was consecrated bishop at Avignon, teaches us in his book On the Zeal for the Christian Religion of the Ancient German Princes that long before Charlemagne the sciences were taught at Paris, and that he did no more than raise up and enlarge the study of theology. He proves this from Severinus Boethius, who lived in the time of the Emperor Zeno, in the year 475. There is the beginning of studies at Paris, which were better cultivated and raised up through the care of the Emperor Charlemagne.

units.la: Pour vous faire connoiftre la grande renommée de l'Vniuersité de Paris, ie vous puis asseurer, qu'il y a plus de huiet censans qu'elle a esté estimée non seulement dans la France, mais par toute l'Europe pour la premiere & la plus excellente Academie. Les Rois & Princes estrangers la reconnoissans telle, y enuoyent leurs enfans pour y estre instruits dans les Lettres, & bonnes meurs. Je ne veux point m'arrester aux Rois de France de la premiere race, & grands Princes, qui ont donné leurs enfans aux doctes Professeurs de l'Academie, pour monstrer son anciennete : Je la prendray seulement du temps de Louys le Gros, qui donna ses deux fils aux Chanoines de Paris pour les instruire, & lesdits Chanoines presques tous professoient les Sciences auec d'autres associez dans le Cloistre & au paruis de Nostre-Dame entre l'Euesché, & l'Hostel-Dieu, où estoient les Sales publiques pour enseigner. Dans les Epistres de Stephanus Tornacensis, Abbé de sainte Geneuiefue à Paris, vous y remarquerez deux lettres consolatoires, l'vne au Roy de Hongrie, & l'autre à sa femme, sur la mort d'vn sien fils, qui estudioit en cette Maison Religieuse, & y a esté enterré. Il auoit auec luy deux ieunes Seigneurs Hongrois, qui y sont demeurez pour acheuer leurs estudes. L'Abbaye de sainte Geneuiefue estoit pour lors vne Academie, qui florissoit du temps du Roy Robert, où enseignoit auec celebrité vn Huboldus, que l'Euesque de Liege fit venir en sa[?] ville comme son sujet. En ce lieu Ioannes Sarisberiensis y auoit appris la Philosophie sous vn Peripateticien, Palatin, tres-sçauant Docteur, qui estoit le Chef de l'Academie. Albert le Grand en son petit liure de Metallicis, se qualifie, Docteur de l'Academie de Paris, & parle d'vne grande escaille gravée, qui fut trouvée dans le ventre d'vne Plye, que le Cuisinier du fils du Roy de Ca-stille, estudiant à Paru luy apporta, par le commandement de son Maistre. Nous trouuons qu'vn fils du Roy d'Arragon a esté fait Licentié à Parù, contre les Loix de l'Vniuersité: par les plaintes des Escholiers, le Chancelier de l'Vniuersité fut démis de sa charge. D'Allemagne sont venus quantité de Princes Souuerains estudier à Paru, comme Albert IV. Duc de Bauiere, & deuant que partir de Paris, prit publiquement les degrez de Maistre és Arts. Ian Duc Megapolstain, a estudié vingt ans à Paris, auec le Roy de Chypre. Non seulement les grands Princes estrangers sont venus estudier à Paris, mais de leur païs ils ont enuoyé des colonies, pour apprendre l'Eloquence, la Philosophie, & la Medecine. Alphonse, Roy d'Espagne, a enuoyé quantité d'Espagnols estudier à Paris en toute sorte de Sciences. Petrus Hispanus est venu d'Espagne, pour estudier en Philosophie & en Medecine, où il a enseigné ces deux Sciences. Du depuis fut fait Cardinal, à la recommandation de la Reine Blanche, mere de Sainct Louys, en suite Pape, & nommé Iean XX. auquel il dedie ses Commentaires sur les Politiques d'Aristote, ayant esté son disciple lors qu'il enseignoit la Medecine à Paris environ l'an 1300. André Lacuna, Espagnol, en a fait de mesme, & confesse avoir appris des Medecins de Paris, tout ce qu'il sçait en Medecine & Philosophie. Il dit des Medecins de Paris, Quot homines video ceu lumina, tot numina quaedam revereor. Les Rois de Portugal entretenoient cinquante Estudians dans le College de sainte Barbe. Et sachans que le Principal Goueanus estoit vn sçauant homme, ils le firent venir en Portugal, pour estre Precepteur du Roy Sebastien dernier. Les Universitez d'Angleterre se vantent d'estre fort anciennes, neantmoins Beda lib. 3. cap. 18. asseure qu'elles ont esté formées sur le modele de Paris. Philippe Abbé de Bonne esperance, appelle la ville de Paris, à cause de l'Academie, Cariat Sepher, civitatem litterarum. Au mesme temps, (il y a six cens ans) vivoit Philippus Blesensis, qui la nomme Abelam: Lanzius, très-sçauant homme, Alleman, parlant de l'Vniuersité de Paris, dit ces paroles. Non Gallia modo, sed totius orbis Regina, & omnium Europa Academiarum mater, virtutis & eruditionis officina, ita semper Innocentij III. Papa affectus possedit, vt ex ea vna omnes Christiani orbis Episcopos, & ad alias Ecclesiæ dignitates viros idoneos legerit, honestissimo eiusque elogio permanente, studium Parisiense esse fundamentum Ecclesiæ. Gregoire IX. l'appelle scientiarum Parentem. Guilhelmus Aremoricus,en ses Philippiques liure 1.la nomme la premiere du monde.
units.tr: To make you aware of the great renown of the University of Paris, I can assure you that for more than eight hundred years it has been esteemed not only in France but throughout all Europe as the first and most excellent academy. Kings and foreign princes, acknowledging it as such, send their children there to be instructed in letters and good morals. I do not wish to dwell on the kings of France of the first race and great princes who entrusted their children to the learned professors of the academy, in order to show its antiquity. I will take it only from the time of Louis the Fat, who gave his two sons to the canons of Paris to be instructed. Those canons nearly all taught the sciences, together with other associates, in the cloister and the parvis of Notre-Dame, between the episcopal palace and the Hôtel-Dieu, where the public halls for teaching were. In the Letters of Stephen of Tournai, Abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, you will find two letters of consolation, one to the King of Hungary and the other to his wife, on the death of a son of theirs who studied in that religious house and was buried there. He had with him two young Hungarian lords, who remained there to complete their studies. The abbey of Sainte-Geneviève was at that time an academy, which flourished in the time of King Robert, where a certain Huboldus taught with great renown, whom the Bishop of Liège had brought to his city as his subject. In this place John of Salisbury had learned philosophy under a Peripatetic, a Palatine, a most learned doctor, who was the head of the academy. Albert the Great, in his little book On Metals, styles himself a doctor of the academy of Paris, and speaks of a large engraved scale that was found in the belly of a pike, which a cook of the son of the King of Castile, studying at Paris, brought to him by his master's command. We find that a son of the King of Aragon was made licentiate at Paris, contrary to the laws of the University; upon the complaints of the scholars, the Chancellor of the University was removed from his office. From Germany have come many sovereign princes to study at Paris, such as Albert IV, Duke of Bavaria, who, before leaving Paris, publicly took the degrees of master of arts. John, Duke of Mecklenburg, studied for twenty years at Paris with the King of Cyprus. Not only have great foreign princes come to study at Paris, but from their own countries they have sent colonies to learn eloquence, philosophy and medicine. Alphonse, King of Spain, sent a great number of Spaniards to study at Paris in every kind of science. Petrus Hispanus came from Spain to study philosophy and medicine, and taught both sciences there. Afterwards he was made cardinal, on the recommendation of Queen Blanche, mother of Saint Louis, and then pope, named John XX, to whom he dedicates his commentaries on the Politics of Aristotle, having been his disciple when he taught medicine at Paris around the year 1300. Andrés Laguna, a Spaniard, did the same, and confesses that he learned from the physicians of Paris all that he knows of medicine and philosophy. He says of the physicians of Paris: As many men as I see as lights, so many divinities I revere. The Kings of Portugal maintained fifty students in the College of Sainte-Barbe. And knowing that the principal Goveanus was a learned man, they brought him to Portugal to be tutor to the last King Sebastian. The universities of England boast of being very ancient, nevertheless Bede, book 3, chapter 18, asserts that they were formed on the model of Paris. Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, calls the city of Paris, because of its academy, Kiriath-sepher, the city of letters. At the same time (six hundred years ago) lived Philip of Blois, who names it Abelam. Lanzius, a most learned German, speaking of the University of Paris, says these words: Not only the queen of France but of the whole world, and mother of all the academies of Europe, workshop of virtue and learning, has always been so regarded by Pope Innocent III, that from it alone he chose all the bishops of the Christian world, and men fit for other dignities of the Church, its most honourable reputation remaining, the Parisian study being the foundation of the Church. Gregory IX calls it the parent of the sciences. Guillaume le Breton, in his Philippics, book 1, names it the first in the world.

units.la: Quod caput est regni, quæ grandia germina regum Educat, & doctrix existit totius orbis, Quæ quamuis verè toti pelluceat orbi, Nullus in orbe locus similis.
units.tr: What is the head of the kingdom, what great offspring of kings it rears, and is the teacher of the whole world; which, although it truly shines for the whole world, no place in the world is like it.

units.la: Le Pape Celestin III. qui mourut l'an 1192. fait mention en sa Decretale, de l'Vniuersité de Paris, par consequent elle estoit dès ce temps-là celebre & florissante. Depuis la fondation &creation de l'Vniuersité de Paris, les Papes voulans eriger d'autres celebres Vniuersitez, comme Vienne, Prague, Louuain, Cologne, ils les ont par leurs Bulles formé sur le modele de Paris, & toutes se glorifient d'en estre filles. Pour conclusion de cét article, ie produiray le tesmoignage de Kirchnerus, Iurisconsulte Alleman tres-docte. Floruit illa vetustis seculis tanta laude, vt nemo quidquam scire, quidquam sapere credereretur, nisi qui Parisiis aliquandiu in studiorum sastris [?] meruisset. Omnis itaque eo olim ex omnibus nationibus confluebat Iuuentus, inuentique ex Germania principibus sunt, qui viginti annos ibidem consumpserint. Inuenti Regum Nepotes, Ducum & principum filij, qui litterarum honores, & gradus Doctorum, Magistrorumque ibidem assumpserint. Ideoque iure dicere possum de Academia Parisiensi, quod de Athenis olim dictum fuit ex Strabone, maximo fuisse opprobrio etiam Romanis, Athenas non vidisse.
units.tr: Pope Celestine III, who died in the year 1192, makes mention of the University of Paris in his Decretal; consequently it was already famous and flourishing at that time. Since the foundation and establishment of the University of Paris, the popes, wishing to erect other celebrated universities, such as Vienna, Prague, Louvain and Cologne, have formed them by their bulls on the model of Paris, and all of them glory in being its daughters. To conclude this article, I shall produce the testimony of Kirchner, a most learned German jurisconsult: That academy flourished in such ancient ages with such great praise that no one was believed to know anything or to have any wisdom unless he had spent some time at Paris in the pursuit of studies. Therefore young men from all nations once flocked there, and princes from Germany were found who spent twenty years there. Grandsons of kings, sons of dukes and princes were found there who took the honours of letters and the degrees of doctor and master. And so I can rightly say of the Parisian academy what was once said of Athens by Strabo, that it was the greatest disgrace even for the Romans not to have seen Athens.

units.la: Est-il croyable que durant le huictiesme & neufiesme siecle, l'Academie de Paris estant florissante, qu'il n'y eut point de Medecins de Paris, qui enseignassent la Medecine. C'est là où les Medecins de Montpelier m'arresteront, aduoüans l'antiquité & celebrité de l'Vniuersité de Paris; Mais ils me demanderont les commencemens de l'estude en Medecine à Paris. Ie les prens de Charlemagne, lors qu'il dit en son Capitulaire, qu'on enuoye les ieunes gens auxestudes de Medecine, infantes mittantur discere Medicinam; puis qu'il n'y auoit point d'estude alors à Montpelier, il s'ensuit que c'est de Paris qu'il entend.
units.tr: Is it credible that during the eighth and ninth centuries, when the Academy of Paris was flourishing, there were no physicians in Paris who taught medicine? Here the physicians of Montpelier will stop me, acknowledging the antiquity and renown of the University of Paris; but they will ask me for the beginnings of the study of medicine at Paris. I take them from Charlemagne, when in his Capitulary he says that young men are to be sent to learn medicine, infantes mittantur discere Medicinam; since there was no study of medicine at Montpelier at that time, it follows that it is Paris he means.

units.la: Depuis Charlemagne, monstrons la continuation de l'estude en Medecine, par la suite des premiers Medecins qui estoient de l'Eschole de Paris, iusqu'à l'establissement de l'Vniuersité par les Papes. Auparavant vous sçaurez que le docte Hemeraus, en son liure de Academia Parisiensi, prouue que les Medecins enseignoient au Paruis de Nostre Dame, en vne maison, où il y auoit eu des Estuues, entre l'Hostel-Dieu & la maison de l'Euesque.
units.tr: From Charlemagne onward, let us show the continuity of the study of medicine through the succession of the first physicians who belonged to the School of Paris, down to the establishment of the University by the Popes. Beforehand you should know that the learned Hemeraus, in his book On the Academy of Paris, proves that the physicians taught in the Parvis of Notre Dame, in a house where there had been baths, between the Hôtel-Dieu and the bishop's house.

units.la: Venons à la suite des Medecins de l'Eschole de Paris. Obizo a esté premier Medecin de Louis le Gros, en l'an 1110.
units.tr: Let us come to the succession of physicians of the School of Paris. Obizo was the first physician of Louis the Fat in the year 1110.

units.la: Ce qui se trouue par la Chronique de l'Abbaye de sainct Victor, faite par vn Religieux nommé de Thoulouse; son epitaphe se voit dans le cloistre, vis à vis du lauoir & la cloche pour appeller les Religieux au refectoire.
units.tr: This is found in the Chronicle of the Abbey of Saint Victor, written by a religious named of Toulouse; his epitaph can be seen in the cloister, opposite the lavabo and the bell used to summon the religious to the refectory.

units.la: Petrus Lombardus estoit premier Medecin de Louis VII. en l'an 1138. Cela se verifie par l'obitulaire de l'Eglise Cathedrale de Chartres, d'où il estoit Chanoine, il y a esté enterré, & y a fondé vn Obit perpetuel.
units.tr: Peter Lombard was the first physician of Louis VII in the year 1138. This is confirmed by the obituary of the cathedral church of Chartres, of which he was a canon; he was buried there and founded a perpetual obit.

units.la: Roger de Prunino estoit Medecin de Louis IX. & Chanoine de Paris: cela se prouue par le Chartulaire de l'Eglise Cathedrale de Paris.
units.tr: Roger de Prunino was physician to Louis IX and a canon of Paris; this is proved by the Cartulary of the Cathedral Church of Paris.

units.la: Robert de Duaco, Chanoine de Senlis, estoit premier Medecin de Marguerite de Prouence, femme de sainct Louis. Cela se prouue par son Testament admirable, où il a fait des legs pieux à beaucoup de maisons Religieuses, & aux Escholiers, particulierement a laissé quinze cens liures pour les Estudians en Theologie. Il a constitué executeur de son Testament Robert de Sorbonne, premier Aumosnier du Roy sainct Louis, lequel adioustant du sien auec le legs dudit Robert, a fondé cét ancien & Venerable College de Sorbonne, que le Cardinal de Richelieu a renuersé par terre, pour auoir l'honneur d'estre le Fondateur du superbe bastiment qu'il a fait faire.
units.tr: Robert de Douai, canon of Senlis, was first physician to Margaret of Provence, wife of Saint Louis. This is proved by his admirable will, in which he made pious bequests to many religious houses and to the scholars, and in particular left fifteen hundred books for the students of theology. He appointed as executor of his will Robert de Sorbonne, first almoner of King Saint Louis, who, adding his own funds to the legacy of the said Robert, founded that ancient and venerable College of Sorbonne, which Cardinal Richelieu razed to the ground, in order to have the honour of being the founder of the superb building he had constructed.

units.la: De plus, les Chirurgiens Iurez seant devant le Regne de sainct Louis. Ils estoient Disciples des Medecins, & deuoient faire leurs cours en Medecine, auant qu'exercer la Chirurgie, par la permission des Medecins. Cela se prouue par nos Registres.
units.tr: Moreover, the sworn surgeons, sitting before the reign of Saint Louis, were disciples of the physicians, and had to complete their courses in medicine before practising surgery, with the permission of the physicians. This is proved by our registers.

units.la: Petrus Egidius Corbolienfis, enuiron l'an 1120. estoit Chanoine de Paris, & premier Medecin de Philippe Auguste. Il a composé un liure de Urinis, un autre de Pulsibus, que Gordon approuve, & l'appelle dans ses liures Venerabilem Egidium, à cause de sa qualité Ecclesiastique. A la fin de son Poëme, il nomme trois Medecins de Paris, Urso, Maurus, & Musandinus. Arnaud de Villeneufue cite Urso, assez souvent: pourMau-rus, il est allegué par Vincentius Bellouacensis. Campanus estoit Medecin de Paris environ l'an 1190. Simon Januensis luy dedie son Liure, Clavis Curationum. Il avoit escrit en Medecine, dautant qu'Arnaud de Villeneufue la cite souvent. Je pourrois continuer la suite des premiers Medecins des Rois de France, sortis de l'Eschole de Paris, jusques à nostre temps; nous le ferons voir ailleurs. Cela suffira pour monstrer que depuis Charlemagne, l'Exercice de la Medecine, & l'estude ont esté fort celebres, & par addition vous sçaurez que Rigordus, premier Medecin de Philippe second en l'histoire de ce Roy, escrit, que l'an 1185.
