Gaufridus, Comte de Bretagne, & fils de Henry Roy d'Angleterre, estant malade à Paris, le Roy Philippe assembla tous les Medecins de Paris pour l'assister. Le mesme Rigordus dit qu'en ce temps, les Medecins de Paris enseignoient pleinement & parfaitement toute la Medecine. Si nous remontons encore plus haut, nous trouuerõs que dés l'an 1163. les Medecins enseignoient auec vn tel rauissement & contentement des auditeurs, que les Religieux fortoient de leurs Conuens pour venir entendre ces leçõs; Ce qui obligea le Pape Alexandre III. en vn Concile tenu à Tours, de commander aux Religieux, sur peine d'excommunication, de se retirer das leurs Monasteres, auec defense de ne plus aller aux leçonsdes Physiciens,ainsi appelloient-ils les Medecins. Cela se verifie par les Decretales. Lanfranc, excellent Medecin & Chirurgien, vint à Paris l'an 1295. pour enseigner la Chirurgie, qu'il auoit composée, ce qui luy fut permis par la Faculté de Medecine. Il dit qu'il auoit vne telle affluence d'Escholiers, plus qu'il ne meritoit. Ce n'est donc pas sans raison, qu'Egidius Corbolien[?], Medecin, loüe l'Eschole en Medecine de Paris par dessus toutes les autres de son temps.
units.tr: Petrus Egidius of Corbeil, around the year 1120, was a canon of Paris and first physician to Philip Augustus. He composed a book On Urines, and another On Pulses, which Gordon approves, and in his books he calls him Venerabilem Egidium, on account of his ecclesiastical status. At the end of his poem he names three physicians of Paris: Urso, Maurus, and Musandinus. Arnald of Villanova cites Urso quite often; Maurus is cited by Vincent of Beauvais. Campanus was a physician of Paris around the year 1190. Simon Januensis dedicated his book, Clavis Curationum, to him. He had written on medicine, since Arnald of Villanova cites him often. I could continue the succession of the first physicians of the Kings of France, who came out of the School of Paris, down to our own time; we shall show this elsewhere. This will suffice to show that from Charlemagne onward the practice and the study of medicine were very celebrated there. And by way of addition, you will know that Rigordus, first physician to Philip II, writes in his history of this King that in the year 1185 Geoffrey, Count of Brittany and son of Henry, King of England, being ill at Paris, King Philip assembled all the physicians of Paris to attend him. The same Rigordus says that at that time the physicians of Paris taught the whole of medicine fully and perfectly. If we go back even further, we find that as early as the year 1163 the physicians taught with such delight and satisfaction to their hearers that religious left their convents to come and hear these lectures; this obliged Pope Alexander III, in a council held at Tours, to command the religious, under pain of excommunication, to withdraw to their monasteries, forbidding them to attend any more the lectures of the Physicians, as they called the Medici. This is confirmed by the Decretals. Lanfranc, an excellent physician and surgeon, came to Paris in the year 1295 to teach the surgery he had composed, which was permitted him by the Faculty of Medicine. He says that he had such a crowd of scholars, more than he deserved. It is therefore not without reason that Giles of Corbeil, physician, praises the School of Medicine at Paris above all the others of his time.

units.la: Ipse nouo fauerat operi, nec Parisianas Æstimet indignum Physicam resonare Camenas, Nam logices vbi fons scaturit, vbi plenius artis
units.tr: He himself had favoured the new work, and does not think it unworthy that the Parisian Muses should resound with natural philosophy, for there, where the spring of logic gushes forth, where the reason of the art is cultivated more fully, physics sets its foot for itself and rejoices, and does not disdain to attend upon its handmaids.

units.la: Excolitur ratio, sibi Physica figere pedem / Gaudet, & ancillis non dedignatur adesse.
units.tr: Reason is cultivated; Physics delights to fix its foot on her own ground, and does not disdain to attend upon the handmaids.

units.la: Ce mesme Egidius peut auoir esté à Montpelier pour leur enseigner la Medecine, dautant que Balæus dit, qu'Egidius Medecin de Paris a esté enseigner la Medecine à Montpelier: ma preuue est tirée de ce qu'il loüe dans sa Poesie vn Medecin Renaudus, qui enseignoit assez bien la Medecine, les autres estans tout à fait ignorans.
units.tr: This same Giles may have been at Montpelier to teach them medicine, since Bale says that Giles, a physician of Paris, went to teach medicine at Montpelier; my proof is drawn from the fact that in his poetry he praises a physician Renaud, who taught medicine fairly well, the others being wholly ignorant.

units.la: Il y a apparence que Philippus Blesensis auoit estudié en la Medecine; qu'il auoit fort bien apprise à Paris, encore qu'il en ait quitté l'exercice, comme il appert par sa lettre 43. qui est tres-docte, donnant son aduis sur vne fievre hemitritée. Il viuoit l'an 1160. Stephanus Tornacensis, Abbé de sainte Geneuieve, à la fin du douzième siecle, parle des Medecins de Paris, disciples d'Hippocrate & de Galien, qui l'assisterent en vne longue maladie. Cela se trouue en son Epistre 47.l'an 1281. Vn Medecin de Paris, l'an 1281. ayant esté outragé, toutes les Facultez cesserent leurs leçons. On fut trouuer le Roy pour reparer l'offense, & luy promettre, qu'on recommenceroit les leçons, Si emenda medico laesa esset sufficienter praestita. Dans les Statuts du College de Sorbonne, il est ordonné par le testament de Robert de Sorbonne, que la charge de Prouiseur venant à vacquer par decez, on assemblera l'Archidiacre de Paris, le Chancelier de l'Université, les Doyens des Facultez de Theologie, Decret, & Medecine, pour en esllire un autre. Notez le Doyen de Medecine en ce temps-là qui est l'an 1269. Je vous puis prouver par Bartholomeus Cocles, en sa Physiognomie, que Petrus de Apono, appellé Conciliator, a esté Docteur de Paris: qu'il y a enseigné la Medecine: & à la fin de ses Commentaires sur les Problemes d'Aristote, il est escrit que l'œuvre a esté fait à Paris par l'Autheur, qui vivoit à la fin du siecle 1200.
units.tr: It is likely that Philip of Blois studied medicine; that he learned it very well at Paris, although he gave up its practice, as appears from his letter 43, which is very learned, giving his opinion on a hemitritaean fever. He lived in the year 1160. Stephen of Tournai, Abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, at the end of the twelfth century, speaks of the physicians of Paris, disciples of Hippocrates and Galen, who attended him in a long illness. This is found in his Epistle 47. In the year 1281, a physician of Paris having been insulted, all the Faculties suspended their lectures. They went to find the King to make reparation for the offence and to promise him that the lectures would be resumed, Si emenda medico laesa esset sufficienter praestita. In the Statutes of the College of Sorbonne, it is ordered by the will of Robert de Sorbonne that, should the office of Provisor fall vacant by death, the Archdeacon of Paris, the Chancellor of the University, and the Deans of the Faculties of Theology, Canon Law and Medicine shall be assembled to elect another. Note that the Dean of Medicine at that time was in the year 1269. I can prove to you, from Bartholomeus Cocles in his Physiognomy, that Peter of Abano, called Conciliator, was a Doctor of Paris, that he taught medicine there; and at the end of his Commentaries on the Problems of Aristotle it is written that the work was done at Paris by the author, who lived at the end of the thirteenth century.

units.la: Voila assez de preuves pour monstrer depuis Charlemagne jusques à la fin du treiziéme siecle, que les Papes ont donné la forme de l'Université de Paris, joignant ensemble les 4. Escholes ou Facultez en un Corps, & que l'Exercice & estude de la Medecine a fleury à Paris avec celebrité, depuis sept ou huict cent ans, par dessus les autres Escholes de Medecine de l'Europe.
units.tr: That is enough evidence to show that, from Charlemagne down to the end of the thirteenth century, the Popes gave shape to the University of Paris by joining the four schools or faculties into one body; and that the study and practice of medicine flourished at Paris with renown for seven or eight hundred years, above the other schools of medicine in Europe.

units.la: Maintenant examinons les grandes singularitez qui se remarquent en l'Eschole de Medecine de Montpelier. L'excellence de leur Eschole vient d'avoir receu la premiere la doctrine des Medecins Arabes, qui étoiet pour lors Mahometans, ou Iuifs, chassez d'Espagne, desquels ils se vantent d'auoir apris la pureté de la Medecine. Il est certain que lors qu'on bastissoit Montpelier, après le razement de Maguelone, durant les siecles neuf cens, mil, & onze cens, que les Arabes & les Iuifs se sont habituez dans cette nouuelle ville pour traffiquer: & Beniamin Iuif, en son voyage, enuiron l'an 1170: parlant de Montpelier, rapporte qu'il a veu en cette ville quantité de Iuifs & Mahometans trafiquans en ce lieu, fort frequenté de toutes les Nations, à cause de la mer Mediterranée: il ne dit point auoir veu des Medecins Iuifs: incontinent après, parlant de Lunel, qu'il y auoit vn grand nombre de Iuifs en cette ville, & vn Medecin nommé R. Iuda, fils de Salomon. S'il y eut eu des Medecins Arabes, & Iuifs à Montpelier, il les eut nommez en ce temps là que les Arabes possedoient seuls les Escholes de Montpelier. S'ils enseignoient en Arabe la Medecine, comment pouuoient-ils estre entendus par les Espagnols ou François? Ioint que saincte Bernard & Ioannes Sarisberiensis, qui étoient du mesme temps, ne disent rien des Medecins Arabes demeurans à Montpelier.
units.tr: Now let us examine the remarkable peculiarities of the School of Medicine at Montpellier. The excellence of their school comes from having been the first to receive the doctrine of the Arab physicians, who were at that time Mahometans, or Jews expelled from Spain, and from whom they boast of having learned the purity of medicine. It is certain that when Montpellier was being built, after the destruction of Maguelone, during the ninth, tenth and eleventh centuries, the Arabs and the Jews settled in this new town to trade. And Benjamin of Tudela, in his travels, around the year 1170, speaking of Montpellier, reports that he saw there a multitude of Jews and Mahometans trading in this place, which was much frequented by all nations because of the Mediterranean Sea; yet he does not say that he saw Jewish physicians. Immediately afterwards, speaking of Lunel, he says that there was a great number of Jews in that town, and a physician named R. Judah, son of Solomon. If there had been Arab and Jewish physicians at Montpellier, he would have named them at that time, when the Arabs supposedly held the schools of Montpellier alone. If they taught medicine in Arabic, how could they be understood by the Spaniards or the French? Moreover, Saint Bernard and John of Salisbury, who were of the same period, say nothing of Arab physicians living at Montpellier.

units.la: S'ils sont venus en ce lieu apres auoir esté chassez des Espagnes, ce seroit l'an 1230, auquel temps les Medecins estoient Chre-stiens, & auoient obtenu Bulle du Pape pour eriger Vniuersité.
units.tr: If they came to this place after being driven out of Spain, that would have been about the year 1230, at which time the physicians were Christians and had obtained a Bull from the Pope to erect a University.

units.la: Ie vous prie de ne vous point glorifier de vos anciens Maistres Arabes, Iuifs, & Mahometans, autrement ie vous reprocheray auec Campegius, que vostre Eschole est Mahometane, puis que vous voulez que ce soient eux qui l'ayent formée & fondée. Ledit Campegius par tous ses Liures declame contre les Medecins Arabes, Iuifs, Mahometans, ennemis des Chrestiens, qui d'Espagne s'estoient respandus dans les pays voisins: ie ne sçay s'il entend le pays de Montpelier, qu'il n'a pas osé blasmer estant de cette Eschole, escriuant à vn Medecin Alleman, de l'Vniuersité de Tubinge, il dit, Precor Deum ut Tubingam, tuam Academiam, more Parisiensium, ab omni Mahometensium Me-dicorum haeresi liberet ac praeseruet [?].
units.tr: I beg you not to glory in your former masters, Arabs, Jews and Mahometans; otherwise I will reproach you, with Campegius, that your school is Mahometan, since you want them to be the ones who formed and founded it. The said Campegius, throughout all his books, declaims against the Arab, Jewish and Mahometan physicians, enemies of the Christians, who had spread from Spain into the neighbouring countries. I do not know whether he means the region of Montpellier, which he did not dare to blame since he belonged to that school. Writing to a German physician of the University of Tübingen, he says: "I pray God that He may keep and preserve Tübingen, your academy, after the manner of the Parisians, free from every heresy of the Mahometan physicians." [?]

units.la: Si nous croyons Fernel, que vous aurez pour suspect, estant de nostre Compagnie, les Arabes ont corrompu nostre Medecine; ils ont plustost formé des Apotiquaires, ou Charlatans, que de vrais Medecins. Ils ont escrit la curation des maladies tout autrement que les Grecs, & ont tellement embroüillé les regles de la Medecine, pour les euacuations, qu'on ne sçait quels remedes on doit suiure. Ils nous ont laissé des compositions de medicaments si mal bastis, sans iugement & raison, que cela ressent plutost son Medecin Empirique que rationel : Ie puis dire qu'vn medicament de la Medecine Arabesque, selon le proverbe ancien, Arabice olet, c'est à dire qu'il est dangereux. Et ie puis rapporter à mon propos ce qu'a dit Pline de l'Arabie, Felix appellatur Arabia, falsa & ingrata cognominis, quæ hoc acceptum superis ferat, cùm plus ex eo inferis debeat : Heureuse Arabie pour depeupler le monde. Apres cela vantez-vous de la Medecine des Arabes, que vous poisedez absolument. Ie dy plus, qu'estant ennemis des Chrestiens, plutost par malice que par ignorance, ils nous ont gasté la Medecine, & l'ont tres-mal descrite, pour nous faire mourir: Si vous en voulez des preuues trescertaines, vous en trouuerez dans Sebastianus Montanus, en ses Opuscules, où il rapporte de Pierre Alphonse, Iuif conuerti, Libro de bello Dei: Medici Recutiti Marranique omnes, ex Thalmudica legis precepto, Christianos medicaminibus occidere debent, & le reste qu'il poursuit. Un Juif converty, il y a plus de cent cinquante ans, descouvre les mefchancetez qu'ils commettent en la Medecine: Ils se vantent de sçauoir mieux la Medecine qu'Hippocrate & Galien: avec cette effronterie ils s'introduisent dans les maisons des Grands, pour pratiquer leurs mefchancetez dans l'occasion. Je conseille de fuir telles personnes, & ne point user de leurs remedes. N'avons nous pas eu un Roy de France, Charles le Chauve, qui a esté empoisonné avec un Syrop par un Juif, son Medecin, nommé Zedechias. A Verone en Italie, il y avoit un Medecin Juif en grande reputation, qui faisoit mourir la pluspart des Chrestiens qui se confoient en luy. Il avoit un Valet Chrestien, lequel en mourant confessa que son Maistre en avoit fait mourir plus de six cens, par poisons subtils, soubs pretexte de la Medecine. Il en dit davantage en la page 45. de son Livre de Impesturis Judaeorum. Dauid de Pomis Medecin Juif, a voulu defendre par une Apologie, la probité & fidelité des Juifs Medecins, mais n'a pas respondu à cès deux citations, que j'ay produit, qui sont long-temps devant l'impression de son Livre. De nostre temps on ne prend pas garde, qu'il y a un Medcein Juif nommé Zacutus en Amsterdam, qui a escrit de Histria medica admirada in curationibus morborum , remply d'impostures tant pour le traitement des maladies, que pour les remedes ridicules, extravagans, & tres-dangereux. Ie puis dire de luy ce que Crato, premier Medecin de trois Empereurs , a prononcé d'Amates Lusitanus Iuif , que dans ses Histoires il y a plus de fausseté que de verité , & que les Iuifs sçauent mieux tromper les Chreftiens, que les guerir.
units.tr: If we believe Fernel, whom you will regard with suspicion since he belongs to our Company, the Arabs have corrupted our medicine; they have formed apothecaries or charlatans rather than true physicians. They have written the cure of diseases quite differently from the Greeks, and have so tangled the rules of medicine concerning evacuations that one does not know which remedies to follow. They have left us compositions of medicaments so badly constructed, without judgement and reason, that they smell more of the empirical than the rational physician. I can say that a medicament of Arabic medicine, according to the old proverb, "smells of Arabia" [Arabice olet], that is, it is dangerous. And I can apply to my purpose what Pliny said of Arabia: "Arabia is called happy, though falsely and ungratefully named, which ascribes this to the gods above, when it owes more to those below" [Felix appellatur Arabia...]. Happy Arabia, for depopulating the world! After that, do you boast of the medicine of the Arabs, which you possess entirely? I say more: being enemies of the Christians, more through malice than through ignorance, they have spoiled our medicine and described it very badly, in order to make us die. If you want very certain proofs of this, you will find them in Sebastian Münster [Sebastianus Montanus], in his Opuscula, where he reports from Peter Alphonsi, a converted Jew, in his book On the War of God: "All physicians who are circumcised and Marranos, by the precept of the Talmudic law, ought to kill Christians with medicines," and the rest, which he goes on to pursue. A Jew who was converted more than a hundred and fifty years ago uncovers the wickedness they commit in medicine. They boast of knowing medicine better than Hippocrates and Galen; with this effrontery they insinuate themselves into the houses of the great, to practise their wickedness when the occasion arises. I advise fleeing such people and not using their remedies. Did we not have a King of France, Charles the Bald, who was poisoned with a syrup by a Jew, his physician, named Zedechias? At Verona in Italy there was a Jewish physician of great reputation, who caused the death of most of the Christians who trusted in him. He had a Christian servant, who on his deathbed confessed that his master had killed more than six hundred by subtle poisons, under the pretext of medicine. He says more about this on page 45 of his book On the Impostures of the Jews. David de Pomis, a Jewish physician, wanted to defend by an Apology the probity and fidelity of Jewish physicians, but he has not answered these two citations which I have produced, which were long before the publication of his book. In our own time no one takes notice that there is a Jewish physician named Zacutus at Amsterdam, who has written a Historia medica admiranda in curationibus morborum, full of impostures both in the treatment of diseases and in ridiculous, extravagant and very dangerous remedies. I can say of him what Crato, first physician to three Emperors, pronounced of Amatus Lusitanus, a Jew: that his Histories contain more falsehood than truth, and that the Jews know better how to deceive Christians than how to cure them.

units.la: Si quelqu'vn respond qu'il ne faut plus rien craindre de ces Medecins Mahometans, & Iuifs, dautant que tous les Medecins de Montpelier sont bons Chreftiens, à la bonne heure ; mais s'ils ne sont bien transmuez & purifiez par cinq ou six generations, i'apprehenderois touiours Mali corui ouum peffimum. Vn Euesque de Montpelier a escrit, que la malediction a esté sur cette ville.
units.tr: If someone replies that there is no longer anything to fear from these Mahometan and Jewish physicians, since all the physicians of Montpellier are good Christians, well and good; but unless they have been thoroughly transformed and purified over five or six generations, I would always fear "a bad crow's egg, the worst" [Mali corvi ovum pessimum]. A Bishop of Montpellier has written that the curse fell upon this town.

units.la: Hic locus insignis, fuit urbs, habitata malignis Gentibus, unde ruit, quod scelerata fuit.
units.tr: This remarkable place was a city, inhabited by hostile peoples; hence it fell, because it was wicked.

units.la: l'apprend du plus grand imposteur de la terre, qui auoit frequenté tous les plus grands trompeurs, forciers & empoisonneurs du monde, nommé Helmont ; qu'il a reconnu que les Iuifs Medecins Christianisez, sont pires & plus à craindre que les vrais Iuifs Medecins. Ie m'en rapporte à sa deposition escrite dans ses abominables livres, qu'il a mis en lumiere avant que mourir de la pleuresie, en laquelle il n'a voulu estre faigné.
units.tr: I learn this from the greatest impostor on earth, who had frequented all the greatest cheats, sorcerers and poisoners in the world, named Helmont; he recognised that Christianised Jewish physicians are worse and more to be feared than the true Jewish physicians. I rely on his testimony, written in his abominable books, which he published before dying of pleurisy, in which he would not allow himself to be bled.

units.la: Non est lex iniquior ulla, Quàm necis artifices, arte perire sua.
units.tr: There is no law more unjust than that the makers of death should perish by their own art.

units.la: Quand la Reine Mere ayeule du Roy, estant à Bruxelle, par la persuasion & sollicitation de Fabroni Italien, a retiré ce meschant homme de la prison de l'Archevesque de Malines, où il devoit finir ses jours, elle ne pensoit pas que ce diable incarné, deust brouiller la Medecine de la sorte qu'il a fait. Je laisse la poursuitte & la vengeance aux Medecins de Louvain, qui sont obligez de censurer tels livres, aussi abominables, que ceux d'Agrippa, tous deux Medecins de Louvain, & Professeurs.
units.tr: When the Queen Mother, grandmother of the King, while at Brussels, by the persuasion and solicitation of the Italian Fabroni, withdrew this wicked man from the prison of the Archbishop of Mechelen, where he was to end his days, she did not think that this incarnate devil would throw medicine into confusion in the way he has done. I leave the prosecution and the vengeance to the physicians of Louvain, who are obliged to censure such books, as abominable as those of Agrippa, both physicians of Louvain and professors.

units.la: Une grande singularité de l'Eschole de Montpelier paroist, en ce qu'elle seule tient le nom d'Université, comme si elle estoit universelle pour toute la terre habitable, ou à cause que toutes les parties de la Medecine y sont enseignées. Par ces deux raisons, l'Eschole de Medecine de Paris pourroit estre appellée Université tout autrement mieux que celle de Montpelier. Mais, dira le Medecin de Montpelier, les Papes l'ont seule qualifiée de la forte: Ils ne peuvent prouver cela par leurs: Bulles, ny par les Lettres des Rois. Si cela estoit veritable, il y auroit dans la ville deux Universitez, l'une composée de trois Facultez, Theologie, Jurisprudence, & des Arts: L'Autre Université seroit de la Medecine. C'est grandement ignorer la signification du nom d'Université, & en quelle maniere il est pris & expliqué par les Jurisconsultes. Université est un Estude general, pour tous ceux qui viennent apprendre toutes les Sciences qui sont enseignées. Je sçay qu'un grand Jurisconsulte, Petrus Gregorius, Tolosanus, lib. 18. de Republica, c. 1 dit qu'il n'est pas de l'essence de l'Université, que toutes les Sciences soient enseignées en cette Eschole; il suffit que l'estude soit public & gratuit pour tous ceux qui voudront y estudier: Nam ge-neralitas non ad Universitatem scientiarum pertinet, sed ad publicam causam docendi. Cette raison ne favorise pas davantage l'Eschole de Montpelier, que celle de Paris, d'autant que nostre Eschole est publique, la Medecine y est enseignée gratuitement, sans argent du Roy en toutes ses parties. Laissons cette niaiserie. Si je voulois approfondir cette matiere, laissant Gregorius Tolosanus, je trouverois quantité de Jurisconsultes contraires à son aduis, qui sont Besoldus, Cottomannus, Iunius, Lansius, en leurs traitez de Academiis. C'est vne chose inouïe, que dans vne ville il y ait deux Vniuersitez , comme à Montpelier , ce que les Iurisconsultes n'ont point encore traité ny decidé.
units.tr: A great peculiarity of the School of Montpellier appears in that it alone holds the name of University, as if it were universal for the whole inhabited earth, or because all the parts of medicine are taught there. For these two reasons, the School of Medicine of Paris could be called a University far more fittingly than that of Montpellier. But, the physician of Montpellier will say, the Popes alone have given it that title by force: they cannot prove this by their bulls, nor by the letters of the Kings. Were that true, there would be two universities in the city, one composed of three faculties, theology, law and the arts; the other university would be of medicine. This is to be greatly ignorant of the meaning of the name University, and of how it is taken and explained by the jurists. A University is a general study, for all those who come to learn all the sciences that are taught. I know that a great jurist, Pietro Gregorio of Toulouse, book 18 of De Republica, chapter 1, says that it is not of the essence of a University that all the sciences be taught in that school; it is enough that the study be public and free for all who wish to study there: For generality does not pertain to the universality of the sciences, but to the public cause of teaching. This reason favours the School of Montpellier no more than that of Paris, since our school is public, and medicine is taught there free of charge, without money from the King, in all its parts. Let us leave this silliness. If I wished to go deeper into this matter, leaving aside Gregorio of Toulouse, I would find a host of jurists holding views contrary to his, namely Besold, Cottomann, Junius, Lansius, in their treatises on academies. It is an unheard-of thing that in one city there should be two universities, as at Montpellier, a point the jurists have not yet treated or decided.

units.la: Pour vous oster de l'esprit cette vanité & folie , que l'Eschole de Medecine soit Vniuersité , Ie vous prouueray par vos Chartes,& vos Lettres,que vous auez produit,tout le contraire. La Bulle d'érection ou fondation d'Vniuersité , donnée par Nicolas IV. 7. Kalendarum Nouembris anno eius Pontificatus 2. Christi 1289. l'appelle Studium generale, in quo magistri doceant,& scholares liberè studeant in quauis facultate : qu'ils puissent obtenir Lettres de Maistrise, & dumtaxat Magistri decorari titulo. Notez que cette Vniuersité est appellée Studium generale,& ceux qu'on appelle aujourd'huy Docteurs , ne deuoient seulement qu'estre appellez Maistres d'vne telle Facultez. C'est à quoy Courtaut n'a pas pris garde, en rapportant les Bulles des Papes , Legats , & les Lettres des Rois d'Arragon , & de France. Dans la Bulle de Conrad, ce mot de Docteur, est suffisant de la faire soubçonner de faux. Il n'y auoit point de Docteurs en ce tempslà,[?]& la Bulle de fondation defend de prendre autre tiltre que de Maistre. Il y a transposition en ces mots ou fausseté, Necnon Vniuersitatis Medicorum tam Doctorum, quàm Discipulorum. L'Eschole de Medecine seule n'a iamais esté qualifiée Vniuersité: il n'y a pas d'apparence qu'on aye pris le conseil des Escholiers pour faire les Statuts d'vne Vniuersité.
units.tr: To rid you of this vanity and folly, that the School of Medicine should be a University, I will prove to you from your charters and your letters, which you have produced, the very opposite. The bull of erection or foundation of the University, given by Nicholas IV, on the 7th of the Kalends of November, in the second year of his pontificate, in the year of Christ 1289, calls it a general study, in which masters teach and scholars study freely in every faculty; that they may obtain letters of mastership, and only be adorned with the title of Master. Note that this university is called studium generale, and those whom we today call Doctors were to be called only Masters of such a faculty. This is what Courtaut did not notice, in reporting the bulls of the Popes, Legates, and the letters of the Kings of Aragon and of France. In the bull of Conrad, the word Doctor is enough to make one suspect it of being false. There were no Doctors at that time, [?] and the foundation bull forbids taking any title other than Master. There is a transposition in these words, or forgery: Necnon Universitatis Medicorum tam Doctorum, quam Discipulorum. The School of Medicine alone has never been called a University; there is no likelihood that the advice of the scholars was taken in making the statutes of a University.

units.la: Le Pape Alexandre addresse sa Bulle aux Maistres & Estudians à Montpelier. Guido Legat addresse de mesme sa Bulle Magistris Monspeliensibus. I'oserois asseurer qu'en cette commission de Nicolas III. Pape, il n'est point fait mention de l'Vniuersité de Medecine de Montpelier, mais de la Faculté de Medecine en l'Vniuersité de Montpelier, comme toutes les Lettres des Rois le contiennent.
units.tr: Pope Alexander addresses his bull to the masters and students at Montpellier. The legate Guido likewise addresses his bull Magistris Monspeliensibus. I would venture to assert that in this commission of Pope Nicholas III there is no mention of the University of Medicine of Montpellier, but of the Faculty of Medicine in the University of Montpellier, as all the letters of the Kings contain.

units.la: Dans la Bulle de Clement VI. Studium Medicinæ, ne peut estre qualifié Vniuersité. Dautât que dâs tout le corps de la Bulle, quatre fois est repeté studiû Medicinæ. Ce mot d'Vniuer-sité a esté adioufté. Les Docteurs d'aujourd'huy sont appellez Maistres, dans l'autre Bulle de Clement, quatre fois l'Eschole de Medecine est appellée studium Medicinæ.
units.tr: In the bull of Clement VI, Studium Medicinae cannot be described as a University, since throughout the whole body of the bull studium Medicinae is repeated four times. The word University has been added. The Doctors of today are called Masters; in the other bull of Clement, four times the School of Medicine is called studium Medicinae.

units.la: Dans la Bulle du Pape Ieau XXII. le mot d'Universite est general, pour toute l'Université, où est comprise la Faculté de Medecine. Dans la Bulle du Cardinal Jean, est contenuë l'élection du Chancelier dans l'Estude de Montpelier, conformément à toutes ces Bulles. Les Anciens Docteurs de Montpelier, Joannes de Tornamira, Gordon, Valescus de Tarenta, Guido de Cauliac se qualifient seulement Medecins studij Monspeliensis, comme on remarquera à la fin de leurs livres, ou au commencement.
units.tr: In the bull of Pope John XXII the word University is used generally, for the whole University, which includes the Faculty of Medicine. In the bull of Cardinal John, the election of the Chancellor in the Studium of Montpellier is set out, in conformity with all these bulls. The ancient doctors of Montpellier, Johannes de Tornamira, Gordon, Valescus de Taranta, Guido de Cauliac, describe themselves only as physicians of the Montpellier study, as will be noted at the end or the beginning of their books.

units.la: Les paroles de la Bulle du Pape Urbain V. sont à la louange de l'Universite de Montpelier, qu'il appelle studium Universale, comme les autres Papes.
units.tr: The words of the bull of Pope Urban V are in praise of the University of Montpellier, which he calls studium universale, as the other Popes do.

units.la: Apres les Bulles des Papes parcourons les Lettres des Rois de France, pour voir si nous trouverons la qualité d'Universite donnée à l'Eschole de Medecine de Montpelier. Les Medecins en leur Requeste presentée au Roy de France Philippe VI. se qualifient Docteurs & Maistres en Medecine de l'Estude en la ville de Montpelier. Notez que ce sont les paroles de leur Requeste, sur laquelle est expediée la Lettre Patente, & les suiuantes des Rois, qui conviennent à la supplication des Medecins de Montpelier: Dans le Privilege ils ont fait une[?] transposition des mots : Ad supplicationem dilectorum nostrorū Vniversitatis Medicorum, il est croyable que Medicorum est devant Vniversitatis. Dans la Lettre de Louis Duc d'Anjou, Magistri studij generalis Ville Montis-pessulanæ, s'ils disent que studium generale se prend pour Vniversité, il y a en suite, seu alterius studij Medicina : & partant les autres Escholes de Medecine sont Vniversitez.
units.tr: After the bulls of the Popes let us run through the letters of the Kings of France, to see whether we find the title of University given to the School of Medicine of Montpellier. The physicians, in their petition presented to the King of France Philip VI, describe themselves as Doctors and Masters in Medicine of the study in the city of Montpellier. Note that these are the words of their petition, on which the letters patent and the following royal letters are issued, which accord with the supplication of the physicians of Montpellier: in the privilege they have made a [?] transposition of the words: Ad supplicationem dilectorum nostrorum Universitatis Medicorum; it is credible that Medicorum stands before Universitatis. In the letter of Louis Duke of Anjou, Magistri studii generalis Ville Montis-pessulanae, if they say that studium generale is taken to mean University, there follows, seu alterius studii Medicinae: and therefore the other schools of medicine are universities.

units.la: En la Requeste presentée au Roy de Navarre, ils s'appellent Magistri studij generalis Ville Montis-pessulanæ, & plusieurs fois l'Eschole de Montpelier, est appellée studium. Dans les Lettres de Charles V. pro parte Magistrorum & Scholarium Facultatis Medicinæ studij generalis Ville Montis-pessuli. La Lettre de Louis XI. est falsifiée, où il y a repetition d'Vniversité trop frequente, affectée, & supposée. En la Lettre de Charles VIII. les Maistres Docteurs en la Faculté de Medecine en l'Vniversité de Montpelier. Voila la Faculté de Medecine, qui est comprise dans l'Vniversité. En la Lettre de François premier, il y a tousiours, la Faculté de Medecine de l'Vniversité de Montpelier: & ledit Roy en sa seconde Lettre parle de la Faculté de Medecine en l'Vniversité de Montpelier. Charles IX. en sa Lettre, accordant aux Medecins de Montpelier leurs demandes, parle de mesme façon que le Roy François premier. En la lettre de Monsieur le Mareschal de Danville, il accorde exemption de soldats aux quatre Docteurs Regens en la Faculté de Medecine de l'Université de Montpelier. Par cette reveuë des Bulles des Papes, & Lettres des Rois, les anciens Medecins de Montpelier n'ont pas affecté cette qualité d'Université pour leur Faculté. Guillaume Rondelet, en toutes ses oeuures, se qualifie Professeur,& Chancelier de l'Eschole de Montpelier. Mais les Medecins Professeurs depuis soixante ans & plus, s'estans separez de la Jurisdiction de l'Evesque, ne voulans prendre de luy la licence, à cause de leur religion contraire, se sont sequestrez du Corps de l'Université, qui est Ecclesiastique, & ont voulu rendre leur Eschole Royale, dependante du Roy, & l'ont appellée eux-mesmes Université. Ces nouveaux Medecins de no-stre siecle, ambitieux d'honneur, pour fai-re valoir les Bulles de Doctorat, qu'ils donnent pour de l'argent à leurs Escholiers, se sont advisez, voyans la decadence de l'Université, & que les autres Facultez avoiët cessé de lire, de s'attribuer la qualité d'Université, je croy que s'ils n'euffent obtenu par l'entremise & assistance de Iacques Pon-ceau, Medecin de Paris, & à la sollicitation d'Honorat Picquet, les gages pour quatre, puis pour deux autres Professeurs, que la Faculté de Medecine seroit maintenant reduite au neant, dautant qu'ils eussent negligé d'enseigner, & faire les fonctions de Scholarité, ce qui eut deserté leur Eschole. I'ay esté contraint de faire ce long discours ennuyeux, touchant la qualité d'Vniversité, pour destruire cette vanité & presomption de l'Eschole de Montpelier.
units.tr: In the Request presented to the King of Navarre, they call themselves Magistri studij generalis Ville Montis-pessulanæ, and several times the School of Montpellier is called studium. In the Letters of Charles V. pro parte Magistrorum & Scholarium Facultatis Medicinæ studij generalis Ville Montis-pessuli. The Letter of Louis XI. is falsified, where the repetition of University is too frequent, affected, and supposed. In the Letter of Charles VIII. the Masters Doctors in the Faculty of Medicine in the University of Montpellier. There you have the Faculty of Medicine, which is included in the University. In the Letter of Francis I, there is always the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Montpellier; and the said King, in his second Letter, speaks of the Faculty of Medicine in the University of Montpellier. Charles IX., in his Letter granting the physicians of Montpellier their requests, speaks in the same way as King Francis I. In the letter of Monsieur the Marshal de Danville, he grants exemption from soldiers to the four Regent Doctors in the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Montpellier. From this review of the Bulls of the Popes and Letters of the Kings, it is clear that the ancient physicians of Montpellier did not claim this title of University for their Faculty. Guillaume Rondelet, in all his works, styles himself Professor and Chancellor of the School of Montpellier. But the physician-professors of the last sixty years and more, having separated themselves from the jurisdiction of the Bishop, not wishing to take their licence from him because of their contrary religion, have withdrawn from the body of the University, which is ecclesiastical, and have wished to make their School royal, dependent on the King, and have themselves called it University. These new physicians of our age, ambitious for honour, to give value to the Doctorate Bulls which they sell for money to their students, have, seeing the decline of the University and that the other Faculties had ceased to lecture, taken it upon themselves to assume the title of University. I believe that if they had not obtained, through the intercession and assistance of Jacques Ponceau, physician of Paris, and at the solicitation of Honorat Picquet, the salaries for four, then for two other Professors, the Faculty of Medicine would now be reduced to nothing, since they would have neglected to teach and to perform the duties of scholars, which would have deserted their School. I have been obliged to make this long, tedious discourse, concerning the title of University, to destroy this vanity and presumption of the School of Montpellier.

units.la: Allons aux autres singularitez. Ce qui recommande l'Eschole de Montpelier par dessus celle de Paris, c'est la dignité de Chancelier que possede vn Medecin de la Compagnie, esleu selon la forme prescrite par le Pape Clement V I. sa fonction est descrite par le Sieur Ranchin, jadis Chancelier de la dite Eschole. Je vous adverty que ce n'est pas le Chãcelier, qui donne la licence d'enseigner & pratiquer la Medecine, hic & ubique terrarum. Mais sur son rapport, Monsieur l'Evesque la doit donner de la part du Pape. Cette dignité qui se donnoit autrefois par election de Docteurs au plus digne, est maintenant par l'avarice des Medecins donnée par le Roy à celuy qui court le plus viste en Cour, & qui a plus de faueur. Puis vantez-vous, Statutorum sapiens constitutio & observatio, que vos Statuts sont inviolablement gardez, il en est de mesme des lectu-res. L'Eschole de Medecine de Paris a son Chancelier commun à toute l'Université, qui donne la licence de lire & pratiquer la Medecine, hinc & ubique terrarum. Il en donne attestatio par lettres, si on les veut prendre. De plus il est Conservateur des Privileges, que les Papes ont concedez à l'Université. Si l'Evesque refuse son visa aux Benefices, on a recours à luy, qui le peut donner. Il preside à la distribution des lieux, & donne sa voix quand on vient dans l'égalité des suffrages. Mais il n'a pas le pouvoir que Monsieur l'Evesque de Montpelier, lequel en l'Eschole de Medecine, Potest statuta novâ promulgare, & confirmare, au rapport de Ranchin. Nos Statuts sont faits & ordonnez par nous-mesmes, sans que personne s'en mesle.
units.tr: Let us come to the other peculiarities. What recommends the School of Montpellier above that of Paris is the dignity of Chancellor, held by a physician of the Company, elected according to the form prescribed by Pope Clement VI. Its function is described by Sieur Ranchin, formerly Chancellor of the said School. I warn you that it is not the Chancellor who gives the licence to teach and practise medicine, hic & ubique terrarum. Rather, on his report, Monsieur the Bishop must grant it on behalf of the Pope. This dignity, which was formerly conferred by election of the Doctors upon the most worthy, is now, through the avarice of the physicians, given by the King to whoever runs fastest to Court and has the most favour. Then you boast, Statutorum sapiens constitutio & observatio, that your Statutes are inviolably kept; it is the same with the lectures. The School of Medicine of Paris has its Chancellor common to the whole University, who gives the licence to lecture and practise medicine, hinc & ubique terrarum. He gives attestation of it by letters, if one wishes to take them. Moreover, he is Conservator of the Privileges which the Popes have granted to the University. If the Bishop refuses his visa to benefices, recourse is had to him, who can give it. He presides over the distribution of places, and gives his vote when the votes are equal. But he does not have the power which Monsieur the Bishop of Montpellier has, who, in the School of Medicine, Potest statuta novâ promulgare, & confirmare, according to the report of Ranchin. Our Statutes are made and ordained by ourselves, without anyone meddling in them.

units.la: Nous trouvons dans les Registres de l'Université, que les Chanceliers sont establis dés l'an 1030. Que les Escholiers l'an 1281. démirent un Chancelier de l'Université, Ioannes de Aurelianis, qui avoit fait licentié Fernand, fils du Roy d'Arragon, sans au[?]un examen, puis conferé le Doctorat, au mespris des Bulles de nos Sainćts Peres les Papes. Nous lisons dans nos Registres, depuis trois cens ans, l'ordre de la presentation des Bacheliers à Monsieur le Chancelier de l'Université, pour estre licentiez, tout de mesme qu'il se pratique aujourd'huy. Et le Paranymphe, qui est un Acte fort solemnel, se faisoit, lors que Sigismond Empereur estant à Paris, vint en nos Escholes pour entendre les belles harangues qu'il admira, & en sortit fort satisfait, au rapport de Scipion Dupleix, Historien de France, qui tient cela d'une vieille histoire manuscrite en son Histoire des Rois de France.
units.tr: We find in the Registers of the University that Chancellors have been established since the year 1030. That in the year 1281 the scholars deposed a Chancellor of the University, Ioannes de Aurelianis, who had licensed Fernand, son of the King of Aragon, without any examination, and then conferred the Doctorate, in contempt of the Bulls of our Holy Fathers the Popes. We read in our Registers, for three hundred years, the order of presenting the Bachelors to Monsieur the Chancellor of the University, to be licensed, just as it is practised today. And the Paranymph, which is a very solemn Act, was performed when Sigismund, Emperor, being in Paris, came to our Schools to hear the fine harangues, which he admired, and left very satisfied, according to the report of Scipion Dupleix, Historian of France, who has this from an old manuscript history in his History of the Kings of France.

units.la: Or comme les interests des quatre Facultez sont communs par une Bulle expresse, & par le Concordat des quatre Facultez, aussi le Chancelier de l'Université est commun à toutes les Facultez, en general & en particulier : & chaque Faculté peut dire auoir son Chancelier, auec un tiltre plus honorable que celuy de Montpelier, dautant que le Chancelier de l'Université est ordinairement un Venerable Chanoine de Nostre Dame, sçauant, & d'Authorité, le plus souvent Conseiller de la Cour de Parlement, & est nommé par Monsieur l'Evesque, maintenant Archevesque de Paris. Aujourdhuy cette charge de Chancelier de l'Université n'est pas en pires mains: celuy qui la possede & l'exerce dignement, est Monsieur Loisel, Docteur de la Maison de Sorbonne, Curé de sainct Jean en Grève, homme de grande erudition & de probité singuliere, & duquel ie puis dire avec toute verité, de quo mentiri fama veretur.
units.tr: Now, as the interests of the four Faculties are common by an express Bull and by the Concordat of the four Faculties, so the Chancellor of the University is common to all the Faculties, in general and in particular; and each Faculty may say it has its own Chancellor, with a more honourable title than that of Montpellier, since the Chancellor of the University is ordinarily a Venerable Canon of Notre Dame, learned and authoritative, most often Councillor of the Parliament Court, and is named by Monsieur the Bishop, now Archbishop of Paris. Today this office of Chancellor of the University is not in worse hands: the one who holds and worthily exercises it is Monsieur Loisel, Doctor of the House of the Sorbonne, Curé of Saint-Jean-en-Grève, a man of great erudition and singular probity, and of whom I can say with all truth, de quo mentiri fama veretur.

units.la: Une autre singularité de l'Eschole de Montpelier est, que les Privileges donnez aux Medecins par les Papes, eslevent tellement ladite Eschole par dessus les autres, qu'il n'y en a pas une seule au monde, qui en ait de pareils: les voila bien glorieux, & fort satisfaits des Papes. Les laisseray-ie dans leur contentement sans les troubler, leur en faisant voir des plus authentiques concedez à l'Eschole & à toute l'Université de Paris. Non, il faut abaisser leur orgueil & presomption, & desabuser le peuple qui les croioit. L'Université de Paris a deux Privileges des Papes, qui n'ont esté donnez à pas une des Universitez. Le premier est d'Urbain V. Il porte que les Docteurs des quatre Facultez, en Theologie, Decret, Medecine &, & les Arts, pourront en toutes les autres Universitez lire, pratiquer les fonctions de leur science ; mais quand ils ne le voudront point faire, ils pourront y demeurer, s'establir, & estre reputez Docteurs de ladite Université. De sorte qu'un Docteur Medecin de Paris, pourra aller à Rome, à Padoue, à Boulogne, lire & pratiquer la Medecine, & quand il ne le voudra pas faire, il pourra y demeurer, & sera reputé Docteur de ladite Faculté. Voila le Privilege descrit tout au long, que m'a communiqué Monsieur Mentel, tres-sçauant Medecin, & tres-affectionné à nostre Eschole, qui l'apris sur l'Original.
units.tr: Another peculiarity of the School of Montpellier is that the Privileges granted to the physicians by the Popes raise that School so far above the others that there is not a single one in the world which has similar ones: there they are, very glorious and quite satisfied with the Popes. Shall I leave them in their contentment without disturbing them, by showing them some of the most authentic ones granted to the School and to the whole University of Paris? No, it is necessary to lower their pride and presumption, and to undeceive the people who believed them. The University of Paris has two Privileges from the Popes which have not been given to any other University. The first is from Urban V. It provides that the Doctors of the four Faculties, in Theology, Canon Law, Medicine, and the Arts, may in all other Universities lecture and practise the functions of their science; but when they do not wish to do so, they may remain there, settle, and be regarded as Doctors of the said University. So that a Doctor of Medicine of Paris may go to Rome, to Padua, to Bologna, lecture and practise medicine, and when he does not wish to do so, he may remain there and be regarded as a Doctor of the said Faculty. Here is the Privilege described at full length, which Monsieur Mentel, a very learned physician, and very devoted to our School, communicated to me, having learned it from the original.

units.la: NICOLAVS Episcopus servus servorum Dei, dilectis filiis Universitatis Magistrorum & Scholarium Parisiensium, Salutem & Apostolicam Benedictionem.
units.tr: NICOLAUS, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the Masters and Scholars of the University of Paris, greeting and the Apostolic Benediction.

units.la: Dum attenta considerationis indagine perscrutamur quod per litterarum studia cooperante illo à quo omne datum optimum, omneque donum confluit & perfectum, viri efficiuntur scientiis eruditi, per quos litterarum veritas explicatur, eruditur rudes, provecti[?] ad altiora crescunt, & fides Catholica invalescit, libenter loco ubi pollent huiusmodi studia, & studentes in eis munimus, immunitatibus & libertatibus honoremus, cupientes itaque ut studentes in agro Lutetiæ, apud Civitatem Parisiensem ad Magisterij braium animentur, & in facultatibus in quibus cathedra decorari meruerint Magistrali, cunctos valeant erudire, præsentium tenore litterarum decernimus, ut quicumque ex Universitate vestra apud Civitatem prædictam, ab illis per quos consueuit licentiandis in dictis Facultatibus authoritate Apostolica regendi licentia elargiri, prout est ibi hactenus observatum, examinatus & approbatus fuerit, & ab eis huiusmodi licentiam obtinuerit in Theologia, vel Iuris Canonici, aut Medicinæ, seu liberalium Artium Facultatibus, ex tunc absque examinatione & approbatione publica vel privata, vel aliquo alio novo principio regendi, atque docendi ubique locorum extra Civitatem prædictam, liberam habeat Facultatem, nec à quoquam valeat prohiberi, non obstantibus aliquibus contrariis consuetudinibus vel statutis, & sive velit regere, sine non, in Facultatibus prælibatis, pro Doctore nihilominus habeatur. Nulli ergo hominum liceat hanc paginam nostræ constitutionis infringere, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem attentare præsumpserit, indignationem Omnipotentis Dei, & Beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum eius, se noverit incursurum. Datum Romæ apud sanctam Mariam Maiorem, x. Kalend. Aprilis, Pontificatus nostri anno quinto.
units.tr: Since we consider with careful inquiry that, through the study of letters, with the cooperation of him from whom every best gift and every perfect gift comes down, men are made learned in the sciences, through whom the truth of letters is explained, the unlearned are instructed, the advanced grow towards higher things, and the Catholic faith grows strong, we gladly honour with immunities and liberties the place where such studies flourish, and those who pursue them in it, desiring therefore that students in the field of Lutetia, in the city of Paris, may be encouraged to win the badge of the Master's degree, and may be able to instruct all in the faculties in which they have deserved to be adorned with the Master's chair, we decree by the tenor of these present letters that whoever from your University in the aforesaid city has been examined and approved by those through whom it is customary, by Apostolic authority, to grant the licence to teach in the said Faculties, as has hitherto been observed there, and has obtained from them such licence in Theology, or Canon Law, or the Faculties of Medicine or the liberal Arts, shall then, without public or private examination and approval, or any other new principle of teaching and lecturing, have the free faculty of teaching everywhere outside the aforesaid city, nor may he be prevented by anyone, notwithstanding any contrary customs or statutes; and whether he wishes to teach or not, in the aforesaid Faculties he shall nonetheless be held as a Doctor. Therefore let no one of mankind presume to infringe this page of our constitution, or to contradict it with rash daring. If anyone should presume to attempt it, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at Santa Maria Maggiore, the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

units.la: L'autre Privilege donné par le mesme Pape, est qu'un Docteur de l'Universite de Paris, estantaux autres Universitez, precedera les autres Docteurs de la Faculté du lieu, mesme où il sera: De sorte qu'un tres-sçauant Docteur & Professeur de Sorbonne, nommé Monsieur Hallier, s'estant trouvé à Rome au temps d'une dispute celebre, il demanda d'ouvrir la dispute, & disputer le premier; ce qui luy fut accordé en vertu de la Bulle. Ces deux Privileges doivent bien humilier les Docteurs de Montpelier, mesmes les Professeurs, s'ils ont de l'esprit, & de la modestie, pour comprendre l'excellence de ces deux Privileges en faveur des Docteurs de Paris. Je ne veux point m'arrester à deduire cent autres Privileges donnez à l'Universite en corps, composée des quatre Facultez, c'est assez de dire, qu'ils sont communs par une Bulle expresse du Pape, & par le Concordat des quatre Facultez, l'an 1281.
units.tr: The other privilege granted by the same Pope is that a Doctor of the University of Paris, when he is at other universities, takes precedence over the other Doctors of the faculty of the place where he is, wherever it may be. So it was that a very learned Doctor and Professor of the Sorbonne, named Monsieur Hallier, having found himself at Rome at the time of a famous disputation, asked to open the disputation and to dispute first; which was granted to him by virtue of the Bull. These two privileges ought well to humble the Doctors of Montpellier, even the Professors, if they have wit and modesty, to understand the excellence of these two privileges in favour of the Doctors of Paris. I do not wish to stop to list a hundred other privileges granted to the University as a body, composed of the four Faculties; it is enough to say that they are shared in common by an express Bull of the Pope, and by the Concordat of the four Faculties, in the year 1281.

units.la: Un autre singularité de l'Eschole de Montpelier est, qu'elle a un Privilege tres-signalé, donné par les Papes, confirmé par les Rois d'Aragon, & de France, qui est de chasserhors de son territoire tous les estrangers Medecins, qui ne sont point approuuez par les Medecins de Montpelier, lesquels traittent ignominieusement les Empiriques & les Charlatans, comme il est rapporté par Syluius en la Preface de sa Pharmacie: mesmes ils ont vne Bulle du Pape, qui excommunie ceux qui pratiqueront illicitement la Medecine dans le reffort de Montpelier.
units.tr: Another singularity of the School of Montpellier is that it has a very distinguished privilege, granted by the Popes and confirmed by the Kings of Aragon and of France, which is to drive out of its territory all foreign physicians who have not been approved by the physicians of Montpellier, who treat empirics and charlatans with contempt, as is reported by Sylvius in the preface to his Pharmacy. Indeed they also have a Bull of the Pope which excommunicates those who practise medicine unlawfully within the jurisdiction of Montpellier.

units.la: L'Eschole de Paris a le mesme Priuilege du Pape Clement VI. auec excommunication, tant pour ceux qui pratiqueront illicitement sans approbation des Medecins de Paris, que pour ceux qui se seruiront de tels Medecins. Le Roy d'Angleterre possedant la ville de Paris, a confirmé cette Bulle, & a adiousté defense à telles personnes de pratiquer la Medecine dans l'enclos de Paris. En la reformation de la ville de Paris quefist le Roy d'Angleterre, enregistrée dans le Liure noir de Monsieur le Procureur du Roy au Chastelet de Paris, il est defendu à tous les Medecins de Paris, de pratiquer dans Paris, ou aux enuirons auec aucun estrager s'il n'est licentié en la science, ou s'il n'est approuué suffisant par le Preuost de Paris, appellez avec soy les Medecins de Paris.
units.tr: The School of Paris has the same privilege from Pope Clement VI, with excommunication, both for those who practise unlawfully without the approval of the physicians of Paris, and for those who make use of such physicians. The King of England, while holding the city of Paris, confirmed this Bull and added a prohibition against such persons practising medicine within the precincts of Paris. In the reformation of the city of Paris made by the King of England, registered in the Black Book of the Procurator of the King at the Châtelet of Paris, it is forbidden to all physicians of Paris to practise in Paris or in its neighbourhood with any foreigner, unless he is licensed in the science, or unless he is approved as sufficient by the Provost of Paris, with the physicians of Paris called in with him.

units.la: HENRY par la grace de Dieu Roy de France & d'Angleterre; au Preuost de Paris, ou son Lieutenant, salut. Combien que pour obvier à plusieurs maux & inconveniens, qui au temps passé s'ensuivoient & commettoient en nostre ville de Paris, ou au pais d'enuiron, par la faute & ignorance d'aucunes personnes, eux s'entremettans en fait & science de Medecine, comme des abortissemens, sortileges & autrement, Nos predecesseurs Rois de France, par vertu de leurs Constitutions & Ordonnances Royaux, eussent fait defenses à toutes personnes, que dudit fait & science de Medecine ne s'entremissent en aucune maniere sur peine de prison, & autres grosses peines & amendes causées, au cas toufjours qu'icelles personnes n'auroient esté Maistrisez ou Licentiez en ladite science de Medeci-ne en l'Universite de nostredite ville de Paris, & approvées par icelle. Neantmoins il est venu à nostre connoissance, que plusieurs personnes, voire mesmes gens de Me-stiers & œuures mechaniques, se sont[?] entremis, & entremettent de jour en jour de faire & exercer iceluy fait, & science, & y pratiquer, jaçoit qu'ils soient en ce ignorans, & non instruits & aussi qu'ils n'ayent esté Maistrisez ou Licentiez audit fait & science de Medecine en nostredite Université de Paris, ou approuvez par icelle. Pourquoy semblablement s'ensuivent, & successivement se pourroient ensuivre les dits abortissemens, & autres maux & inconveniens dessusdits, si pourveu n'y estoit de remedes convenables. Pource est-il que Nous, qui au preiudice & contre le salut de la chose publique de nostredite ville de Paris, & du pais d'environ, ne voulans tels abus estre tolerez ny soufferts, & mesmement en ensuivant les traces & bonnes ordonnances de nosdits predecesseurs: Vous mandons, & enioignons expressément, en commettant, si mestier est, que ce par information ou autrement deuëment, il vous appert des choses dessusdites, Vous defendiez ou faites defendre de par Nous, à toutes personnes exerçans ledit fait & science de Medecine, & pratiquant en icelle en nostredite ville de Paris, & audit pais d'environ, que de cy en avant ne s'en entremettent en quelque maniere que ce soit, sur peine de detention de prison, d'en estre griefvement punis, & d'autres grosses peines & amendes à nous à appliquer, s'ils ne sont Maistres ou Licentiez en ladite Université, ou approuvez par icelle. Et si aucuns non Maistres ou Licentiez vouleient exercer ladite pratique en nostredite ville de Paris, eux se disans suffisans & bien renommez, nous ne voulons que aucunement soient par vous en ce receus, si de la suffisance ne vous appert, appellez avec vous des Maistres en ladite Faculté de Medecine, tels, & en tel nombre, qu'il vous semblera estre expedient & convenable, en faisant reclamer & publier ces presentes en nostre Chastelet de Paris, & autres lieux accoustumez à faire cris & publications en icelle nostre ville de Paris, afin qu'aucun n'en puisse pretendre ignorance, car ainsi Nous plaist estre fait, nonobstant quelconques Lettres subreptices au contraire. Donné en nostre dite ville de Paris le 4. jour de Septembre, l'an de grace 1423. & le premier de nostre Regne. Aussi signée, Par le Roy à la relation du Conseil, FLOVRY. Au dos desquelles estoit escrit ce qui ensuit. Publiées en jugement au Chastelet de Paris, le Lundy sixiesme jour de Septembre, 1423. Item publiées suffisamment aux lieux accoustumez à faire cris en la ville de Paris, par moy Jean Morel, Preneur & Crieur du Roy nostre Sire, le Lundy 6. jour de Septembre, 1423.
units.tr: HENRY, by the grace of God King of France and of England, to the Provost of Paris, or his Lieutenant, greeting. Although, in order to forestall many evils and inconveniences which in past times followed and were committed in our city of Paris, or in the surrounding country, through the fault and ignorance of certain persons who meddled in the act and science of medicine, such as abortions, sorcery and other things, our predecessors the Kings of France, by virtue of their royal constitutions and ordinances, had forbidden all persons to meddle in any way with the said act and science of medicine, under penalty of imprisonment, and other heavy penalties and fines, always provided that those persons had not been made Masters or licensed in the said science of medicine in the University of our said city of Paris, and approved by it. Nevertheless it has come to our knowledge that many persons, even people of trades and mechanical occupations, have meddled, and meddle more and more every day, in performing this act and science and practising it, although they are ignorant and untaught in it, and also that they have not been made Masters or licensed in the said act and science of medicine in our said University of Paris, nor approved by it. For which reason the said abortions and other evils and inconveniences mentioned above follow, and could continue to follow, unless suitable remedies were provided. Therefore We, who wish, to the prejudice and against the welfare of the public weal of our said city of Paris and of the surrounding country, that such abuses should not be tolerated or suffered, and especially following the footsteps and good ordinances of our said predecessors: We command you, and expressly enjoin you, appointing commissioners if need be, that, by inquiry or otherwise as is duly done, it shall appear to you concerning the matters above said, that you forbid, or cause to be forbidden on our behalf, all persons who exercise the said act and science of medicine, and practise in it in our said city of Paris and in the said surrounding country, that from now on they meddle with it in any manner whatsoever, under penalty of imprisonment, of being severely punished, and of other heavy penalties and fines to be applied to Us, if they are not Masters or licensed in the said University, or approved by it. And if any who are not Masters or licensed should wish to practise in our said city of Paris, claiming to be sufficient and of good repute, We do not wish that by you they should in any way be received in this, unless their sufficiency is shown to you, with Masters in the said Faculty of Medicine called in with you, of such number and of such kind as shall seem to you expedient and suitable; and that these present letters be proclaimed and published in our Châtelet of Paris and in other places accustomed to have proclamations and publications made in our said city of Paris, so that no one may plead ignorance of them, for thus it pleases Us to be done, notwithstanding any contrary surreptitious letters. Given in our said city of Paris on the 4th day of September, in the year of grace 1423, and the first of our reign. Likewise signed, By the King on the report of the Council, FLOVRY. On the back of which was written what follows. Published in court at the Châtelet of Paris, on Monday the sixth day of September, 1423. Likewise published sufficiently in the places accustomed to make proclamations in the city of Paris, by me Jean Morel, Taker and Crier of the King our Lord, on Monday the 6th day of September, 1423.

units.la: Depuis cent trente ans, la Cour de Parlement a donné plusieurs Arrests contre tous ceux qui pratiquent la Medecine à Paris, sans l'approbation des Docteurs en Medecine, auec peine pecuniaire & corporelle, s'il y eschet, aux contreuenans.
units.tr: For a hundred and thirty years, the Court of Parliament has issued several decrees against everyone who practises medicine in Paris without the approval of the Doctors of Medicine, with pecuniary penalties and, where it applies, bodily punishment for offenders.

units.la: Puis que les Medecins de Montpelier, ont ce pouuoir de chasser les Medecins estrangers, Empiriques, & Charlatans, qui pratiquent la Medecine dans l'estenduë & ressort du Presidial, pourquoy sont-ils si iniustes de ne pas permettre aux Medecins de Paris de se seruir de leurs Priuileges contre les estrangers. Ils veulent qu'on excepte leurs ieunes Docteurs frais esmoulus, pour le respect qu'on doit porter à leur Eschole, & à leurs enfans, lesquels en six mois d'estude qu'ils font à Montpelier, pour estre formez Docteurs, sont plus sçauans & capables d'exercer la Medecine, que ceux de Paris dans leurs estudes de six ans.
units.tr: Since the physicians of Montpelier have the power to drive out foreign physicians, empirics and charlatans who practise medicine within the bounds and jurisdiction of the Presidial court, why are they so unjust as not to allow the physicians of Paris to use their privileges against foreigners? They want their young doctors, fresh from their studies, excepted out of respect for their School and for their own children, who, after six months of study at Montpelier to be made doctors, are more learned and more capable of practising medicine than those of Paris after their six years of study.

units.la: Ie ne veux rien reprocher sur cét article que par tesmoins irreprochables. Nous auons desia monstré comme du temps de Ioannes Sarisberiensis, Euesque de Chartres, la Medecine estoit tres-mal enseignée à Montpelier: que les Medecins, qui en sortoient pour exercer la Medecine, n'estoient que des ignorans: Cent ans apres, Egidius Corbolienfis s'en plaint à la fin de son Poëme de Vrinis, & en vn autre Poëme il dit qu'on receuoit à Salerne, des enfans au Doctorat, comme l'on fait aujourd'huy à Montpelier, à dix-huict & dix-neuf ans. Il y a cent ans que Iulius Cesar Scaliger, grand & subtil Philosophe, aussi bien que tres-sçauant & tres-excellent Medecin, demeurant à Agen, ville de Guyenne, que vous auez appellé vous-mesme Praestantissimum litterarum heroa, se plaint de l'ignorance des nouueaux Docteurs de Montpelier : c'est en ses Poësies Latines, Epiderpidum lib. 3. Le titre de l'Epigramme est, Ignari Medici, aux Ignorans Medecins.
units.tr: I will not bring any reproach on this point except by unimpeachable witnesses. We have already shown how, in the time of John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres, medicine was very badly taught at Montpelier, and that the physicians who went out from there to practise were nothing but ignoramuses. A hundred years later, Giles of Corbeil complains of it at the end of his poem On Urines, and in another poem he says that at Salerno children were admitted to the doctorate at eighteen and nineteen years old, just as is done today at Montpelier. A hundred years ago Julius Caesar Scaliger, a great and subtle philosopher, as well as a very learned and most excellent physician, living at Agen, a town in Guyenne, whom you yourself have called "the most outstanding hero of letters," complained of the ignorance of the new doctors of Montpelier. This is in his Latin poems, Epidericon, book 3. The title of the epigram is "Ignari Medici", the ignorant physicians.

units.la: Mera colluuies scutica subsellia linquens Olida, puerorum calefacta sessione, Statim ubi tetigit vel pede Pessuli tabernas, Et duas modulo, & ordine formulas docentum Olfecit, ab his illico temeraria regnū, Sese in penetrale induit Æsculapiorum. Prauis in nouitatibus ergo deprehensi, Torum tumido gutture sic vociferantur, Quantum Pharicus Perfica iam castra sequutus Clamauit ad Istrum, neque Stentorive cedunt Marti, Diomedis manibusque vulnerato.
units.tr: A mere deluge of a bench, leaving the seats of the schoolroom foul, warmed by the sitting of boys, as soon as it touched with its foot the shops of Pessulum, and taught two formulas in measure and order, straightway from these a reckless rule took hold and clothed itself in the inner sanctum of the Aesculapians. Caught therefore in their wicked novelties, they cry out thus with swollen throats, as far as the Pharian, having followed the Persian camp, shouted to the Ister, nor do they yield to Stentor's Mars, wounded by Diomedes' hands.

units.la: Par vn autre Epigramme addressé à l'Eschole de Montpelier, il descrit la friponnerie d'vn Medecin de Montpelier, que l'Eschole souftenoit & approuoit pour sien. C'est en la page 639. ad Montem Pessulum d' Caluo.
units.tr: In another epigram addressed to the School of Montpelier, he describes the roguery of a physician of Montpelier, whom the School supported and approved as its own. It is on page 639, "ad Montem Pessulum de Caluo".

units.la: Iean Hucher, natif de Bonnieres prés de Beaunais en Picardie, Professeur Royal de Montpelier, qui a succedé à la lecture de Castellanus, en la Preface de son liure de Morbis mulierum, ne peut souffrir que de son temps on reçoiue au Baccalaureat, à la Licence, & Doctorat des ignorans, qui ne sçauent pas les Rudimens de la Medecine, & on leur permet l'exercice. Plerique protinus à Grammaticorum aut Physicorum Scholis egressi, ad Medicinæ studia conuolant, quorum etiam vix decursis Rudimentis, immaturam non intellectæ artis praxim, viatici causâ suscipiunt, ad eamque Baccalaurei, Licentiati, & Doctoris Encomia, sine accurata artis præceptione, nedum exercitatione. Qui est cause de ce desordre, & malheur pour le pauvre peuple? sinon les Professeurs de Montpelier, qui les font à la haste Docteurs pour leur argent, & leur donnent de belles Lettres bien enluminées, auec des Seaux à lacets de soye, portant pouvoir d'exercer la Medecine comme personnes tres-capables, hic & ubique terrarum.
units.tr: John Hucher, a native of Bonnieres near Beauvais in Picardy, royal professor at Montpelier, who succeeded to the reading chair of Castellanus, in the preface of his book on the diseases of women, cannot bear that in his time ignoramuses are admitted to the baccalaureate, the licentiate and the doctorate, men who do not know the rudiments of medicine, and that they are permitted to practise. Most of them, straight out of the schools of grammar or natural philosophy, rush to the studies of medicine, and when they have barely run through the rudiments, they undertake an immature practice of an art they do not understand, for the sake of their livelihood, and to this end they receive the praises of bachelor, licentiate and doctor without careful instruction in the art, let alone practice. Who is the cause of this disorder and misfortune for the poor people? None other than the professors of Montpelier, who make them doctors in haste for their money, and give them fine letters, well illuminated, with seals on silk cords, bearing the power to practise medicine as most capable persons, here and everywhere in the world.

units.la: Voyons ce qui se pratique aujourd'huy en la creation des Docteurs en Medecine à Montpelier. Je rapporteray les paroles des Medecins de Rouën, la pluspart[?] de Montpelier, én la response au Factum d'un Medecin de Montpelier, qui vouloit s'introduire dans la ville de Rouën, en monstrant sa Lettre de Docteur, sans receuoir examen, ny soustenir Theses. Voicy les paroles.
units.tr: Let us see what is done today in the creation of doctors of medicine at Montpelier. I will report the words of the physicians of Rouen, most of them from Montpelier, in the response to a memorandum of a physician of Montpelier, who wished to settle in the city of Rouen, showing his letter of doctorate without undergoing examination or defending theses. Here are the words.

units.la: Tout ce qui se fait à Mōtpelier maintenant, n'est que l'ombre de ce qui s'y faisoit iadis, c'est vne purepiperie, que la lecture de trois mois, que doit faire vn Bachelier, depuis le Baccalaureat iusques à la Licence. On les voit en effet en robbe & en bonnet entrer à la Salle au son de la cloche, mesme prendre la Chaire, mais ce n'est que par forme, pour s'y monstrer vne seule fois, & puis apres laisser couler trois mois de temps, au bout duquel on est obligé de prendre Lettre de lecture, qui est de grand profit au College, sans lequel ceste coustume inutile auroit esté abrogée. Ainsi les Professeurs voyent cét abus, & ils y connivent, & attestent à la relation de quelques-vns, que le pretendant a traité, qu'il a leu par ledit temps de trois mois. Se peut-il voir vne plus impie prevarication, voilée d'vn pretexte plus specieux? Nous ne l'accusons pas seulement, mais ce sont ceux qui y connivent.
units.tr: Everything that is done at Montpelier now is only the shadow of what was done there formerly; it is pure mockery, the reading of three months, which a bachelor must do between the baccalaureate and the licentiate. One sees them indeed enter the hall in gown and cap at the sound of the bell, even take the chair, but this is only for form, to show themselves just once, and then afterwards let three months of time slip by, at the end of which one is obliged to obtain a letter of reading, which brings great profit to the college, without which this useless custom would have been abolished. Thus the professors see this abuse, and they connive at it, and attest, on the report of some of those who sought the degree, that he has read for the said three months. Can one see a more impious prevarication, veiled under a more specious pretext? We do not accuse them alone, but those who connive at it.

units.la: Nous avons refusé justement l'aggregation à plusieurs, qui venoient de Montpelier, lesquels en leurs Requestes à cette fin en demie page de Latin, faisoient des solecismes qui eussent mérité le fouet à la troisième. Nous ne disons point cecy pour decrediter l'Université de Montpelier, mais pour l'aduertir de son deuoir, & de n'ennoyer pas, par toutes les bonnes villes de ce Royaume, sous pretexte de sa reputation & authorité, des ignorans, & gens mal conditionnez, pour disposer de la vie de ses suiets, pour la conservation de laquelle, la consideration & les soins du Prince ne peuvent estre plus legitimement employez. Les Professeurs Medecins de Montpelier pour s'excuser d'une si grande circonspection, qu'ils doivent avoir, disent que ce sont passeolans, qui ne demeurent point dans le pays, & qu'ils les envoyent occidere Caim, qui est par leur explication, prenant chaque lettre à part, Carmes, Augustins, Jacobins, Mineurs. Si tout ce discours estoit sorty de la bouche d'un Docteur de Paris, ceux de Montpelier s'inscriroient en faux, demanderoient reparation d'honneur, & l'appelleroient imposteur, ou calomniateur endiablé. Le Gazettier Renaudot mit l'an 1642. un de nos Compagnons en procez pour bien moindre chose, pretendant d'avoir esté appellé Nebulo & Blatero, termes pretendus par luy injurieux, & pour lesquels il demandoit reparation de lezeGazette: mais faute d'avoir bien sceu adiuster ce Patin à son pied, il perdit son procez tout au long, en belle & bonne compagnie, le Jeudy 14. d'Aoust 1642. aux Requestes de l'Hostel.
units.tr: We have justly refused admission to several who came from Montpelier, who, in their petitions to this end, written in half a page of Latin, made solecisms that would have deserved the whip by the third. We do not say this to discredit the University of Montpelier, but to remind it of its duty, and not to send out, through all the good towns of this Kingdom, under the pretext of its reputation and authority, ignoramuses and ill-conditioned men, to dispose of the lives of its subjects, for whose preservation the consideration and care of the Prince cannot be more legitimately employed. The professor-physicians of Montpelier, to excuse themselves for such great circumspection as they ought to have, say that these are passeolans, who do not remain in the country, and that they send them to "occidere Caim", which by their explanation, taking each letter separately, means Carmelites, Augustinians, Jacobins, Minorites. If all this discourse had come from the mouth of a Doctor of Paris, those of Montpelier would have denied it under oath, would have demanded reparation of honour, and would have called him an impostor or a devilish calumniator. The journalist Renaudot, in the year 1642, brought one of our Companions to law for much less, claiming to have been called Nebulo and Blatero, terms which he claimed were injurious to him, and for which he demanded reparation from the Gazette. But, not having known how to fit this Patin to his foot, he lost his suit entirely, in fine and good company, on Thursday 14 August 1642, before the Requests of the Hôtel.

units.la: Pour vous faire connoistre qu'on n'obseruoit pas il y a 60. ans tous les Statuts, en donnant les degrez pour estre Docteur: Je vous alleguera un extraict de Cragius, Danois, sçauant homme aux lettres humaines, comme il a fait paroistre par ses escrits. Il auoit pris ses degrez à Montpelier, en l'année 1595. & a fait imprimer Lauream Doctoralem Monspeliensem, où il remarque tout ce qui s'y obseruoit de son temps pour y obtenir le Doctorat. Je trouue en son Epistre Liminaire, que les Medecins obligent par serment tous les aspirans au Doctorat, d'estre reconnoissans enuers leur Eschole, de l'honneur qu'ils ont receu, d'où vient le grand zele de ceux qui sont Docteurs en cette Eschole, ce qui sert aussi à leur honneur. Academiæ Monspeliensi fidem & Jusiurandum gratitudinis dedi, quod sanctè ut seruem cura mihi est, & esse debet: Ce qu'il a fort bien executé, & que ie ne blâme pas. Il aduoüë que les Medecins de Montpelier luy ont permis de prendre tels points qu'il voudroit en la Medecine pour disputer. Liberum mihi fecerunt Monspelienses ex quauis sine delectu Medicinæ & Philosophiæ parte, quæ libuit elimanda problemata proferre.
units.tr: To show you that the statutes were not all observed sixty years ago in conferring the degrees of Doctor, I will cite an extract from Cragius, Danois, a man learned in the humane letters, as his writings make clear. He took his degrees at Montpellier in the year 1595, and he had printed Laurea Doctoralis Monspeliensis, in which he notes everything that was observed in his time for obtaining the doctorate there. In his prefatory epistle I find that the physicians bind every candidate for the doctorate by oath to be grateful to their School for the honour he has received, whence comes the great zeal of those who are Doctors in this School, which also serves their honour. I have given the faith and oath of gratitude to the Academy of Montpellier, which it is and ought to be a care to me to keep faithfully. This he carried out very well, and I do not blame him. He admits that the physicians of Montpellier allowed him to take whatever points he wished from medicine to dispute upon. The Montpellier men left it free to me to put forward, from any part of medicine and philosophy without distinction, whatever problems I pleased to elucidate.

units.la: Partant ce ne sont pas les Docteurs qu, donnent les points pour disputer & faire Theses.
