Il dit qu'on avoit de coustume en l'Eschole de Montpelier, estant receu Bachelier dedans trois mois, faire trois cours, qui sont leçons à trois reprises, pour connoistre la suffisance du Bachelier: mais ne pouvant rien faire qui peut égaler les Leçons des Professeurs, & qu'il n'avoit pas le loisir de demeurer si long-temps en ce lieu; il supplie pour trois mois, de luy donner trois jours pour faire quelque discours: en suite il y a un Examen pro intentione, pour estre Licentié, auquel on propose deux questions, puis une maladie pour en expliquer la curation. Apres cela vient l'examen rigoureux, qui est tel. Le Bachelier vestu d'une robbe rouge, accompagné des Bacheliers & Escholiers, le Bedeau marchant devant, va aux Maisons du Chancelier de l'Eschole, & des autres Docteurs, pour les prier de se trouver le jour suivant chez le Chancelier, pour assister à son Examen rigoureux, qui est qu'on luy donne le Livre pretendu de Galien, de Arte parua, fermé, & avec un stilet il l'ouvre, & là où il s'adresse, il prend le Chapitre, pour l'expliquer: le jour suivant on luy donne le Livre des Aphorismes d'Hippocrate fermé; pour trouver par hazard, en mettant le stilet dans les fueillets, l'Aphorisme qu'on rencontre, pour l'expliquer. Il est fort aisé d'introduire le stilet au commencement, ou à la fin du Livre pour rencontrer ce que l'on veut, & à quoy on est preparé.
units.tr: Therefore it is not the Doctors who give the points for disputation and the writing of theses. He says that it was the custom in the School of Montpellier, once a man had been received Bachelor, for him to give three courses within three months, that is, lectures on three occasions, so as to show the sufficiency of the Bachelor. But since he could not produce anything to equal the lectures of the Professors, and had no leisure to remain so long in that place, he begged that, for the three months, he be given three days to make some discourse. After that there is an examination pro intentione, for the licence, at which two questions are proposed, and then a disease whose cure he must explain. After this comes the rigorous examination, which is as follows. The Bachelor, dressed in a red robe and accompanied by the Bachelors and scholars, with the beadle walking in front, goes to the houses of the Chancellor of the School and of the other Doctors, to ask them to attend the following day at the Chancellor's house for his rigorous examination. In it they give him the book supposedly by Galen, De arte parva, closed, and with a stylus he opens it; wherever it falls open, he takes the chapter to explain. On the following day they give him the book of the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, closed; he must find by chance, by putting the stylus between the leaves, the aphorism that he comes upon, and explain it. It is very easy to insert the stylus at the beginning or the end of the book to find whatever one wants, and for which one has been prepared.

units.la: Apres que cet Examen rigoureux est achevé, intra priuatos parietes, auant que recevoir la Licence, Religiosus D. Vicarius, fait repeter les deux points sommairement, qui ont esté donnez à l'examen rigoureux, puis il donne la Licence, sans parler, de hic & ubique terrarum, ce que ie ne trouue point dans Cragius.
units.tr: After this rigorous examination is finished, within private walls, before receiving the licence, the Religiosus D. Vicarius has the two points given at the rigorous examination repeated briefly, and then gives the licence, without speaking de hic et ubique terrarum, which I do not find in Cragius.

units.la: En suite, on propose quatre questions pour obtenir le Doctorat, qu'on doit disputer contre les Docteurs, cum quovis Antagonista per triduum. Nous voila parvenu au Doctorat, où le Licentié donne une question au Promoteur à expliquer. C'étoit Saporta qui en eut la charge de la part de l'Eschole. En son oraison, il parla de l'Eschole de Montpelier de la sorte. Et quo fato quove consilio factum esse dicam, ut in his sacratissimis, augustissimisque sedibus, ac totius prope Imperij, & gloriæ Gallicæ domicilio, hoc est villa Monspeliensi, ars nostra obscurato pristina dignitatis splendore, deformatoque multas consenescens fasces submittat. Il feint que son Licentié respondra. Quid? Academica pramia, laboribus & vigiliis nostris debita in ea Civitate expectetur[?], in qua Carbonarÿ & sufflones, in Grammaticis rudes, in Dialecticis, Physicisque ignari, probis, eruditis, & iudicio maturis hominibus anteponuntur. Voyez quelles gens ils auoient & receuoient de son temps. Sa-porta en auoit honte, & s'en plaint en donnant le bonnet à Cragius. Il n'a point dit toutes les paroles, qu'ils mettent en leurs Lettres, & Cragius ne se glorifie point de pouuoir pratiquer la Medecine par toute la Terre, & estre le premier de toute la la Terre, estant Docteur de Montpelier.
units.tr: Next, four questions are proposed for obtaining the doctorate, which must be disputed against the Doctors, with any opponent for three days. Here we have come to the doctorate, where the licentiate gives a question to the Promoter to explain. It was Saporta who had this charge on behalf of the School. In his oration he spoke of the School of Montpellier in this way: And by what fate or by what design shall I say it came about that in these most sacred and most august seats, and almost the home of the whole empire and of French glory, that is, in the town of Montpellier, our art, its former splendour obscured and its form disfigured, grown old, submits to fasces? He pretends that his licentiate will reply: What? Shall academic prizes, owed to our labours and vigils, be looked for in that city in which charcoal-burners and bellows-men, untaught in grammar, ignorant of dialectic and physics, are preferred to upright, learned men mature in judgement? See what sort of people they had and admitted in his time. Saporta was ashamed of this and complains of it in handing the bonnet to Cragius. He did not say all the words which they put in their Letters, and Cragius does not glory in being able to practise medicine throughout the whole earth and to be the first in the whole earth by being a Doctor of Montpellier.

units.la: Par tout, son discours il appelle l'Eschole de Medecine, tantost Academiam Monspeliensium, tantost Scholam, iamais Université, titre que l'Eschole de Montpelier n'affectoit pas de ce temps là: dautant qu'il ne l'eust pas oublié, ny le pouuoir de pratiquer hic & ubique Terrarum. Les Allemans & estrangers estans fort curieux des honneurs & droits honorifiques, qu'ils reçoivent dans les Academies, je doute s'ils donnoient de ce temps-là, des Lettres semblables à celles d'aujourdhuy, dautant qu'il ne les a pas adjoustées à la fin deson Liure, Laurea DoDoctoralis[?] Monspeliensis; ce qu'il n'eust pas oublié s'il les eut eu de la sorte, qu'ils les donnent aujourdhuy. Mais ie crois qu'ils donnoient une simple attestation, comme il estoit Docteur de Montpelier, capable d'exercer la Medecine. La forme presente des Lettres est prise sur le modele des Lettres des Academies Luteriennes d'Allemagne.
units.tr: Throughout his discourse he calls the School of medicine sometimes Academia Monspeliensium, sometimes Schola, never Université, a title which the School of Montpellier did not then aim at: since he would not have forgotten it, nor the power of practising hic et ubique terrarum. The Germans and foreigners, being very keen on honours and honorary rights which they receive in academies, I doubt whether at that time they gave letters like those of today, since he did not add them at the end of his book, Laurea Doctoralis Monspeliensis; which he would not have forgotten if he had had them in the form in which they give them today. But I believe they gave a simple attestation, that he was a Doctor of Montpellier, capable of practising medicine. The present form of the Letters is taken on the model of the Letters of the Lutheran Academies of Germany.

units.la: Ce n'est pas seulement de ce temps-cy que les Professeurs Medecins de Montpelier ne se sont pas souciez de parler correctement Latin, mais ils ont affecté le barbarisme. Symphorianus Campegius me l'apprend pag.68. de son Liure de Phlebotomia. Sunt nostri Montispedenses Medici quidam, hac tempestate plurimum incompti, quibus satis est, imo ex industria eos delectat rudis sermo magis, quàm Latinorum vocabulorum obscuruantia, non satis aduertentes, tam immensam, tamque præclaram artem barbarie vitiari, flagitiosissimum esse ac penitus nobilissimam Facultatem infamare. Qu'on lise les escrits en Medecine des anciens Medecins de Montpelier, & particulierement ceux de De Tornamira, on ne trouvera que des barbarismes & solecismes: neantmoins comme le plus sçavant de la troupe, il en avoit esté le Chancelier. Iugez du reste des Professeurs.
units.tr: It is not only in our own time that the professor-physicians of Montpellier have not cared to speak Latin correctly; they have affected barbarism. Symphorianus Campegius teaches me this at p. 68 of his book on Phlebotomy. There are some of our Montpellier physicians, at this time very unpolished, who take so much pleasure, or rather deliberately take pleasure, in crude speech rather than in the obscurity of Latin words, not sufficiently noticing that so immense and so distinguished an art is corrupted by barbarism, and that it is most disgraceful and utterly brings into disrepute the most noble Faculty. If one reads the medical writings of the old physicians of Montpellier, and particularly those of De Tornamira, one will find nothing but barbarisms and solecisms; nevertheless, as the most learned of the company, he had been its Chancellor. Judge the rest of the Professors by this.

units.la: Pour excuser les barbarismes & solecismes de Courtaut, il ne falloit que produire Galien, qui defend de reprendre les Medecins faisans des solecismes, qu'vn Medecin est à preferer, qui in verbis solœcisat, non in moribus, & sur ce sujet il en auoit composé vn Liure, qu'il cite souuent. Les Medecins de Paris font curieux d'expliquer & d'enseigner, soit publiquement, soit en particulier, dans les consultations, la Medecine nettement, correctement,& elegamment. Partant l'Eschole de Monpelier receuant au Doctorat, des Ignorans, & des Enfans à 18.& dix-neufans, ne merite elle pas d'estre priuée de ses Priuileges?
units.tr: To excuse the barbarisms and solecisms of Courtaut, one had only to cite Galen, who forbids reproaching physicians who commit solecisms, and who holds that a physician is to be preferred who makes solecisms in words, not in morals; and on this subject he had composed a book, which he often cites. The physicians of Paris are keen to explain and to teach medicine, whether publicly or privately, in consultations, neatly, correctly and elegantly. Therefore, should not the School of Montpellier, which receives into the doctorate ignorant men and boys of eighteen and nineteen years, deserve to be deprived of its privileges?

units.la: Il est ordonné par le Concile de Constance, que ceux qui seront promeus au Doctorat, soient sçauans, & d'âge competant. Si les Vniuersitez font autrement, elles descherront de leurs Priuileges. Ily a plus de cent cinquante ans, que les Medecins habituez dans les grandes villes, se plaignent de ce desordre en la Medecine, quand ils voyent tels ignorans Docteurs venir auec leurs Bulles pour s'establir dans les villes. Trithemius le premier en ses Epistres en a formé sa plainte, parlant en general des Vniuersitez. sine scientia gradum, aut magnum cum parva eruditione vocabulum, sed Doctos Viros quaerimus, qui Doctores multos habemus. Scientia gradum commendat, non gradus scientiam; verecundia est nescire Magistrum, & eum qui scientiae signum publicè portat, necessariam non habere doctrinam. Quid Circulus ante domicilium expositus, ubi non venditur vinum? aut quid Regale Sceptrum in manibus stulti, absque signato signum tribuitur, quoties indoctus, & sine scientia homo in Doctorem sublimatur, & proh pudor, quàm frequens hodie in Scholis apud quosdam reperitur abusus, quo gradus Magisterij datur in signum, ubi sufficiens non invenitur signatum. Numquid tibi non verum dixisse videmur, cùm orbis Magistris scateat simul & Doctoribus, inter quos Docti pauciores, indocti plures occurrunt.
units.tr: It is ordained by the Council of Constance that those who are promoted to the Doctorate shall be learned and of suitable age. If the universities act otherwise, they shall forfeit their privileges. For more than a hundred and fifty years, physicians settled in the great cities have complained of this disorder in medicine, when they see such ignorant Doctors arrive with their Bulls to establish themselves in the towns. Trithemius was the first to voice this complaint in his Epistles, speaking in general of the universities: "We seek not a degree without knowledge, nor a great title with little learning, but learned men; we have many Doctors. Knowledge commends the degree; the degree does not commend knowledge. It is a shame not to know the Master, and for one who publicly bears the sign of knowledge not to have the necessary learning. What is a circle set out before a house where no wine is sold? Or what is a royal sceptre in the hands of a fool, when a sign is given without the thing signified? As often as an unlearned man, a man without knowledge, is raised up to be a Doctor, and, alas for shame, how frequent today is the abuse found in certain schools, by which the degree of Master is given as a sign where no sufficient thing is found to be signified. Do we not seem to have told you the truth, since the world swarms with Masters and Doctors at once, among whom there are fewer learned men and more unlearned ones?"

units.la: Particulierement pour la Medecine, Ianus Cornarius, sçauant Medecin, qui a tourné Hippocrate en Latin, se plaint que de son tēps on faisoit des Docteurs en Medecine fort ignorans, page 328. de son comment. sur le Liure de Galien, de composit. medicam. secundum locos. Nondum erant adhuc Galeni seculo studiorum larua, quibus hodie omnia litteraria Gymnasia sunt deformata, plures sunt Medici qui videri quàm esse Docti maluerunt. Sed longè infeliciores, qui hodie in Scholis, in urbibus ac Principum aulis regnant, illi vulgi tantum opinione sibi placebant, his etiam vniuersitatum vi vocant authoritas accedit, atque hominis facie tantum, alias Cumani Asini leonis pelle induuntur: ponitur enim mitra quae tegat Midae aures, atque annulus virtutis quondam insigne, bestiae traditur quae nullam rationalem artem attigit, ac neque primas quidem disciplinas gustauit. Laurentius Hofmannus, en sa Preface sur les Conseils de Brunnerus, fait vne grande plainte contre les Vniuersitez d'Allemagne, où cet abus s'est glissé. Sed quae causa tam foecunda insulsissimorum, rudissimorumque Medicorum transplantationis alia, quam modernorum quorundam Academiae Professorum execranda ac flagris castigan-da auaritia, inexplebilisq; accumulandarum opum auiditas, quae pessimo saepe exemplo dignum pariter atque indignum, modo is crumena nummis probe turgida accedat, ad summum Medicinae fastigium turpiter euehunt, Doctoremque clarissimum salutant quauis interdum eiusmodi nouum Doctorculus vix tria verba Latinè hiscere, aut vnam alteramque quam breuissimam periodum sine haesitatione aut balbutie ex adamato suo Paracelso aut alio simili scriptore recitare possit. Quid vero aliud illi Promotores publici faciunt, quam quod tam suâ quam candidatorum conscientiam nefariè polluât ac aggrauent, necnon densissimas imperita multitudinis oculis offucias offundant, eámque miserè technis suis circumueniant, dum scilicet hæc falsò opinatur, sibique persuadet stolidè nulli tutius, facilíusque concredi posse vitam, salutè, ac sanitatem corporis, atque illis, qui titulo Doctoris superbiunt, magnificéque se efferunt, necnon splendidissima suo ære emendicata testimonia superciliosè aliis ostentant. Quæ interdum ita sunt comparata, ut si ea perlegas, sanctè iurare ausis, te nullum unquam excellentiorem vidisse Doctorem. Cùm tamen non raro lateat anguis in herba, & detracta pelle leonina, demptisque hisce hyperbolicis encomiis, Asinus Cumanus in prospectum prodeat. Un Allemand tres-doctè se mocque de ces Docteurs bullez, Doctores bullati, siue Codicillares, par un Epigramme fort elegant,
units.tr: Particularly for medicine, Janus Cornarius, a learned physician who translated Hippocrates into Latin, complains that in his time there were made Doctors of Medicine who were very ignorant (page 328 of his commentary on the book of Galen, De compositione medicamentorum secundum locos): "Not yet in Galen's age had the mask of learning, by which all the literary schools are today disfigured, been put on; many physicians have preferred to seem learned rather than to be so. But far more unhappy are those who today reign in the schools, in the cities and at the courts of princes. Those others took pleasure only in the opinion of the common people; to these men the authority of the universities is added by their power, and they are clothed, in appearance only, as men, while underneath they are the Cumaean ass in the lion's skin. For a mitre is placed upon them to cover the ears of Midas, and the ring, once the mark of virtue, is handed to a beast that has touched no rational art and has not even tasted the first disciplines." Laurentius Hofmann, in his Preface to the Counsels of Brunnerus, makes a great complaint against the universities of Germany, where this abuse has crept in. "But what other cause so fruitful of the transplanting of the most foolish and crudest physicians is there, than the execrable and worthy-of-the-lash avarice of certain modern professors of the academies, and the insatiable greed for piling up wealth, which, by a very bad example, shamefully raises to the highest summit of medicine whoever, equally worthy and unworthy, comes with a purse well stuffed with coins, and sometimes salutes as a most distinguished Doctor any such new little Doctor who can scarcely utter three words of Latin, or recite one or another very brief period without hesitation or stammering from his beloved Paracelsus or some other similar writer? What, indeed, do those public promoters do, but defile and burden, shamefully, both their own conscience and that of the candidates, and throw the thickest deceptions before the eyes of the unskilled multitude, miserably deceiving them with their arts, while they foolishly suppose and persuade themselves that life, health and bodily soundness can be entrusted to no one more safely and easily, and that those who swell with the title of Doctor and boast grandly, and display with haughty airs the most splendid testimonials bought with their money, are such that, if you read them through, men who dare to swear in good faith would say you had never seen a more excellent Doctor; when yet not rarely the snake lies hidden in the grass, and, the lion's skin being stripped off and these hyperbolic praises removed, the Cumaean ass comes forth into view." A very learned German mocks these Doctors who are bulled, Doctores bullati, sive Codicillares, in a very elegant epigram:

units.la: Doctorem te bulla creat, tibi Bulla decori est, Bulla tibi vires, bulla parit titulos: Sed caveas ne forte nimis te bulla perennet, Bulla homo es, & Doctor, bulla quid ergo tumes?
units.tr: "A bull makes you a Doctor; the bull is your ornament, the bull your strength, the bull brings forth your titles. But take care lest the bull perhaps keep you too long; you are a bull, and a Doctor: why then do you swell up, bull?"

units.la: Examinons si le terme de fix m ois est suffisant pour estudier en Medecine, & former un Docteur pour aller pratiquer la Medecine, hic & ubique Terrarum. Ceux qui demeurent un an à Montpelier, sont fort rares. Il y en a plus qui ne demeurent que le temps qu'il faut aux petits oiseaux pour auoir des plumes & s'en voler, qui illic igna-rus accesserat, fere non moratur in Scholis vlterius quàm eo curriculo temporis quo auium pulli plu-mescunt & auolant ; voila comme en parle Ioannes Sarisberiensis. Hippocrate dit, que la science de la Medecine est fort longue à apprendre, & la vie fort courte pour la bien sçauoir. Encore qu'il fust fort âgé, & consommé dans l'exercice de la Medecine, il cõfesse n'en auoir pas acquis vne parfaite connoissance. Pour cette raison, on vous aduertit qu'vn Medecin doit sçauoir beaucoup de choses, auant qu'exercer la Medecine : & Petrus de Apono veut que celuy qui desire estudier en Medecine, soit Maistre dans les autres sciences. Hippocrate deplore le malheur de ceux qui tombent entre les mains des Medecins ignorans : Ce n'estoit pas assez, dit-il, pour faire mourir vn malade, que la violence du mal, si l'ignorance du Medecin ne le precipitoit dans son malheur. Cette science Medicinale, qui est requise à vn Medecin auant que pratiquer, se peut-elle apprendre dans l'Eschole de Montpelier en six mois, ou, enuiron ? Cette ville Agatha, arrousée du fleuve Lanus, rend-elle les apprentis si sçauans en si peu de temps ? L'air de Montpelier fe[?] roit-il fi bon, qu'il pût en peu de mois faire vn grand & intelligent Medecin ? Est-il de la Medecine comme de la Poësie, qu' ayant beu de la fontaine du Pegase, pour auoir sommeillé sur le Mont de Parnasse, on deuenoit incontinent Poëte, par vn certain Enthousiasme ? Ce n'est pas l'opinion de Perse.
units.tr: Let us examine whether the term of six months is sufficient to study medicine and form a Doctor to go and practise medicine, here and everywhere on earth. Those who stay a year at Montpellier are very rare. There are more who stay only the time it takes little birds to grow feathers and fly away: "He who came there ignorant hardly stays in the schools beyond that course of time in which the chicks of birds grow their feathers and fly away," so speaks John of Salisbury. Hippocrates says that the science of medicine is very long to learn and life very short to know it well. Although he was very old and accomplished in the practice of medicine, he confesses that he had not acquired a perfect knowledge of it. For this reason, it is warned that a physician must know many things before practising medicine; and Peter of Abano wants whoever desires to study medicine to be a master in the other sciences. Hippocrates laments the misfortune of those who fall into the hands of ignorant physicians: it was not enough, he says, to make a sick man die, that the violence of the disease should do so, if the ignorance of the physician did not hurl him into his misfortune. Can this medical science, which a physician needs before practising, be learned in the school of Montpellier in six months, or thereabouts? Does that town Agatha, watered by the river Lanus, make its apprentices so learned in so little time? Would the air of Montpellier be so good that in a few months it could make a great and intelligent physician? Is medicine like poetry, so that, having drunk from the fountain of Pegasus, or having slept on Mount Parnassus, one at once becomes a poet by a certain enthusiasm? That is not the opinion of Persius:

units.la: Nec fonte labra prolui-caballino, Nec in bicipiti somniasse Parnasso Memini, vt sic repente Poëta prodirem.
units.tr: "Nor did I ever wet my lips at the horse's fountain, nor did I dream on two-peaked Parnassus, that I should suddenly come forth thus a poet."

units.la: A Salamanque, Vniuersité d'Espagne, il faut estre quatre ans Auditeur, auant qu'estre Licentié, & deux ans à suiure les Docteurs en Medecine auant qu'estre Docteur, au rapport de Rodericus. à Castro in Medico politico. Ce qui est confirmé par Jacobus Mi:dendorpius in Academia Salamanticensi. A Paris pour estre Bachelier, il faut auoir quatre ans d'Estude, & l'âge de vingt-cinq ans. Du Baccalaureat à la licence, deux ans d'exercices, par les disputes & les pratiques sur les malades auec les Docteurs, pour estre par apres Docteur & adopté par la Regence. Rhafis Arabe est encore plus rigoureux, descriuant tout ce que doit sçauoir vn Medecin auant que pratiquer la Medecine, libello de iis quæ requiruntur in approbatione Medici. Il veut qu'un Medecin estudie iusques à quarante ans, & en cét âge, qu'il exerce la Medecine iusqu'à septante. Cassiodore recommande aux Medecins, ut libris delectetur antiquis, nemo iustius assiduè discit, quàm qui de humanâ salute tractauerit. Or auant qu'enseigner, il faut estre Docteur. Il faut auoir estudié long-temps, les sciences ne s'apprennent que par un trauail assidu : Multum temporis addisce, antequam doceas, disoit sainct Hierosme. Aristote nous apprend les degrez qu'il falloit auoir auant qu'estre Medecin parfait, & capable de pratiquer la Medecine. Il falloit estre [illegible, ~12 letters] apprentif de ieunesse : Soranus dit qu'à l'âge de douze ans on mettoit les Enfans à la Medecine, qui estoit παιδομαθ[?]ν, que desire Hippocrate, ayant veu iusques à dixsept ans leur Maistre pratiquer la Chirurgie, & la Pharmacie, qu'ils apprenoient comme les Rudimens de la Medecine ; ils deuenoient δημιουργοί[?], alors mettoient la main aux operations, & estoient hors d'apprentissage, puis ils deuenoient Architectonici, quand ils ordonnoient, estans Maistres parfaits en la Medecine, & auoient soubz eux des apprentifs. & autres ouuriers trauaillans soubz leur direction. Nous voyons la mesme chose se pratiquer parmy les Chirurgiens & Apothiquaires ; Il faut estre trois ans chez des Chirurgiens en apprentissage, puis quatre ans seruir les Maistres. En Pharmacie quatre ans apprenty, & quatre ans seruir les Maistres, auant que de pouuoir aspirer à la Maistrise. Mais les Estudians de Mont-pelier deuiennent en fix mois plus parfaits Medecins auec leur Doctorat acquis, que les Escholiers de Paris en fix ans : ils iouïssent de la bonne fortune du lieu, qui est nommée dans Stephanus, lib. de Vrbibus, ἀγαθὴ τύχη [?]. Ils peuuent prendre pour leur deuise, Virtute Duce, Comite Fortuna, dautant que la bonne fortune les accompagne : ils ne manqueront pas de dire qu'ils sont mieux instruits en 6. mois d'estude à Montpelier, pour deuenir sçauans Medecins que d'autres en sept ans d'estude, dans l'Eschole de Paris;
units.tr: At Salamanca, a university of Spain, one must be an auditor for four years before becoming a Licentiate, and two years following the Doctors of Medicine before becoming a Doctor, according to the report of Rodericus à Castro, in Medicus politicus. This is confirmed by Jacobus Midendorpius, in Academia Salamanticensi. At Paris, to be a Bachelor, one must have four years of study and be twenty-five years of age. From the Baccalaureate to the Licence, two years of exercises, by disputations and practice on the sick with the Doctors, so as to be afterwards a Doctor and admitted by the Regency. Rhazes the Arab is even more rigorous, describing all that a physician must know before practising medicine (in the little book on the things required for the approval of a physician). He wants a physician to study until forty years of age, and at that age to practise medicine until seventy. Cassiodorus recommends to physicians: "Let him delight in the ancient books; no one learns more diligently than he who has treated of human health." Now, before teaching, one must be a Doctor. One must have studied for a long time; the sciences are learned only by assiduous labour: "Spend much time learning before you teach," said St Jerome. Aristotle tells us the degrees one had to pass before becoming a perfect physician, capable of practising medicine. One had to be [illegible, ~12 letters] an apprentice from youth: Soranus says that at the age of twelve children were put to medicine, which was παιδομαθία [childhood learning], which Hippocrates desires; having watched their master practise surgery and pharmacy until the age of seventeen, which they learned as the rudiments of medicine, they became δημιουργοί [craftsmen], then they put their hand to operations and were out of apprenticeship; then they became architectonici [master-builders], when they gave orders, being perfect masters in medicine, and had under them apprentices and other workers labouring under their direction. We see the same thing practised among surgeons and apothecaries: one must be three years an apprentice with surgeons, then serve the masters four years. In pharmacy, four years as an apprentice, and four years serving the masters, before one can aspire to the mastership. But the students of Montpellier become more perfect physicians in six months, with their Doctorate obtained, than the scholars of Paris in six years: they enjoy the good fortune of the place, which is named in Stephanus, De urbibus, ἀγαθὴ τύχη [good fortune]. They may take for their device Virtute duce, comite fortuna [virtue as leader, fortune as companion], since good fortune accompanies them: they will not fail to say that they are better instructed in six months of study at Montpellier, to become learned physicians, than others in seven years of study in the school of Paris;

units.la: Ingenium sibi quod vacuas desumpsit Athenas, Et studijs annos septem dedit, insenuitque Libris, & curis, statuâ taciturnior exit, Plerumque & risu populum quatit.
units.tr: Having taken for himself Athens, which is said to be empty, and given seven years to his studies, and grown old among books and cares, he comes out more silent than a statue, and for the most part shakes the people with laughter.

units.la: Disons vn mot de cette bonne fortune, qu'on fait tant valoir en la Medecine. Pour terminer cét article,il semble aux vulgaires, & à quelques Medecins ignorans, que la Medecine soit un jeu de hazard, comme si on jouoit à trois dez la vie des hommes, souhaittant à nos malades bonne fortune, & bon succez de nos remedes. On voit quelquefois les plus temeraires & ignorans donner des remedes aussi dangereux que des poisons, par une violence faite à tout le corps, la nature se delivrer par haut & par bas des mauvaises humeurs, ce que n'eust pas osé entreprendre un Medecin prudent, qui ne hazarde rien. Mais ces gens-là en font plus mourir qu'ils n'en reschappent, Malefacta terra tegit, benefacta Sol aspicit. Les morts ne mordent plus, & ne ressuscitent pas pour se plaindre. Alors on peut dire, Sauve qui peut. Ubi ars non profuit, temeritas adiuvit, comme parle Celse. Aristote, au 2.de ses grandes Morales, dit, que la fortune est sans jugement & conduite, mais que l'art & la science sont gouvernez par la raison, sans fortune & hazard. Ce qu'il a pris de Platon in Gorgia, où il dit, que la fortune est ennemie de l'art& de la raisõ, & se recontre toujours dans l'ignorance. Hippocrate, au livre de Arte, nous enseigne que la fortune dans la curation des maladies, n'a point de lieu;
units.tr: Let us say a word about this good fortune, which is so much vaunted in medicine. To conclude this article: to common folk, and to some ignorant physicians, it seems that medicine is a game of chance, as if the lives of men were being thrown with three dice, and as if we wished our patients good fortune and good success from our remedies. One sometimes sees the most rash and ignorant men give remedies as dangerous as poisons, by inflicting violence on the whole body, so that nature delivers itself of bad humours upwards and downwards, something a prudent physician, who risks nothing, would not have dared to attempt. But such men kill more than they save: Malefacta terra tegit, benefacta Sol aspicit. The dead no longer bite, and they do not rise again to complain. Then one may say, Sauve qui peut. Ubi ars non profuit, temeritas adiuvit, as Celsus says. Aristotle, in the second book of his Great Ethics, says that fortune is without judgement and conduct, but that art and science are governed by reason, without fortune and chance. He took this from Plato in the Gorgias, where he says that fortune is the enemy of art and reason, and always meets with ignorance. Hippocrates, in the book De Arte, teaches us that fortune has no place in the cure of diseases;

units.la: que ceux qui s'y fient, hazardent la vie des malades. Quand Hippocrate a dit que la fortune peut quelque chose dans les maladies, selon l'explication de Mercurial, il entend ωφαξίαν [?] & ἀτυχίαν [?], qui se rencontrent dans la conduite d'un sçauant, & bien experimenté Medecin en la curation des maladies. Plutarque, au liure de la Fortune, demonstre par plusieurs raisons, que les heureux evenemens ne viennent pas de la fortune, mais d'un sage conseil & bonne conduite, qui donne de la hardiesse dans les affaires.
units.tr: that those who trust in it risk the lives of their patients. When Hippocrates said that fortune can do something in diseases, according to Mercurialis's explanation, he meant eupraxia [?] and atychia [?], which occur in the conduct of a learned and well-experienced physician in the cure of diseases. Plutarch, in his book On Fortune, demonstrates by several arguments that happy outcomes do not come from fortune but from wise counsel and good conduct, which gives boldness in affairs.

units.la: Caveat successibus opto
units.tr: Caveat successibus opto

units.la: Quisquis abeventu facta notanda putat.
units.tr: Quisquis abeventu facta notanda putat.

units.la: Nullum numen abest si sit prudentia, sed nos Te facimus Fortuna Deam, caeloque locamus.
units.tr: No godhead is absent if there is prudence, but we make Fortune a goddess and place her in heaven.

units.la: Tenons-nous au jugement d'Hippocrate, liu. 6. des Epid. Nihil contemnere, nihil temere, interdum quiescere, interdum agere. Partant on ne doit rien mesprisser, ny rien hazarder dans le traitement des maladies.
units.tr: Let us hold to the judgement of Hippocrates, Epidemics book 6: Nihil contemnere, nihil temere, interdum quiescere, interdum agere. Therefore one must despise nothing, risk nothing rashly in the treatment of diseases.

units.la: L'Eschole de Montpelier est douée d'une tresgrande singularité, c'est qu'elle a le pouvoir de donner à leurs jeunes Docteurs, la licence & la permission de lire, enseigner, & pratiquer la Medecine en tous les endroits de la terre habitable, particulierement en France, & mesmes à Paris ; ce que n'a pas l'Eschole de Paris, ny pas une autre.
units.tr: The School of Montpellier is endowed with a very great singularity: it has the power to give its young Doctors the licence and permission to read, teach and practise medicine in all places of the inhabited earth, particularly in France, and even in Paris; which the School of Paris does not have, nor any other.

units.la: Pour l'Eschole de Paris, voila comme en parle Cortaut[?]. Cuius ubique meteoricum, prae-textumque raptum non ratum, nullibi gentium existens, neque datum, sed in calamitosa ridiculæque suorum nuditatis paludamentum impotenter & illegitimè ad aliquod saltem paupertatis solatium effingitur. Voila un jargon estrange, qui fera peur aux Escholiers en Medecine. Ie ne trouve point dans les Bulles des Papes, & dans les Chartes des Rois de France, & d'Arragon, ce pouvoir exprimé, ny rien qui en approche. Leurs jeunes Docteurs n'ont pas le pouvoir de lire, enseigner & pratiquer la Medecine dans la ville de Monpellier, & ne sont point admis comme les autres Docteurs professans la Medecine, aux Disputes, Actes des Bacheliers, ne participent point aux émolumens, ils les renvoyēt ailleurs busquer fortune, aussi-tost qu'ils sont formez Docteurs. Ce qu'ils ne veulent pas leur octroyer dans leur ville, ils veulent que les autres villes & Universitez, par-ticulierement Paris, leur accordent en leur monstrant leurs Bulles. Encore que les Privleges[?] soient generaux, il faut s'accommoder aux Statuts des Universitez particulieres:
units.tr: As for the School of Paris, this is how Cortaut[?] speaks of it: "Its power is meteoric, a pretended usurpation, not ratified, nowhere existing among the nations, nor given, but fashioned, without authority and without legitimacy, into some kind of cloak for the wretched and ridiculous nakedness of its members, at least as a consolation for their poverty." Here is a strange jargon, enough to frighten the students of medicine. I find nothing in the Bulls of the Popes, nor in the charters of the Kings of France and of Aragon, that expresses this power, nor anything that comes near it. Their young doctors do not have the power to read, teach and practise medicine in the city of Montpellier, and they are not admitted, like the other doctors who profess medicine, to the disputations and the acts of the bachelors, and they do not share in the emoluments. They send them elsewhere to seek their fortune as soon as they have been made doctors. What they will not grant them in their own city, they want the other cities and universities, particularly Paris, to grant them when they show their Bulls. Although the privileges are general, one must conform to the statutes of the particular universities.

units.la: Nam Statuta sunt leges privatæ:
units.tr: Nam Statuta sunt leges privatae:

units.la: Si fueris Romæ Romano vivito more.
units.tr: Si fueris Romae Romano vivito more.

units.la: C'est la verité que le Pape Boniface VIII. a concedé ce Privilege general à toutes les Universitez de France, que leurs Docteurs pourront lire, enseigner leur profession ubique terrarum. Mais au temps de cette concession, qui estoit l'an 1290. la ville de Montpelier n'estoit pas sous la domination des Rois de France : & partant Montpelier n'a pû jouïr de ce Privilege. Mais on dira qu'il luy appartient dés lors, qu'elle est deuenuë Françoise, participant aux mesmes Droits, & Privileges, qu'ont les autres Universitez. Puis que les Rois ont donné à l'Univer-sité de Montpelier, les Privileges pareils à ceux de l'Université de Paris, si les Medecins sont separez du corps de l'Université de Montpelier, ils ne peuuent jouïr des Privileges que les Papes ont donné à toute l'Université. Joint qu'ils devoient avoir Bulle expresse pour cét article, & le faire specifier & declarer en leurs Lettres Patentes du Roy. Mais les bonnes gens du temps passé ne se soucioient pas de ce Privilege, n'estans pas si ambitieux que ceux d'aujourd'huy.
units.tr: It is true that Pope Boniface VIII granted this general privilege to all the universities of France, that their Doctors may read and teach their profession ubique terrarum. But at the time of this grant, which was the year 1290, the city of Montpellier was not under the rule of the Kings of France; therefore Montpellier could not enjoy this privilege. But it will be said that it belongs to her from that time, since she has become French, sharing in the same rights and privileges as the other universities. Since the Kings have given the University of Montpellier privileges like those of the University of Paris, if the physicians are separated from the body of the University of Montpellier, they cannot enjoy the privileges that the Popes have given to the whole university. Moreover, they ought to have an express Bull for this article, and to have it specified and declared in the Letters Patent of the King. But the good people of past times did not concern themselves with this privilege, not being so ambitious as those of today.

units.la: Courtaut se glorifie. Nostris Doctoribus nulla provincia decerni potest, illorum provincia mundus est, potestas nobis data, vobis denegata, omnia loca nobis late patent, quàm patebant Hippocrati: si licet Parisinis Doctoribus ubique mederi, ergo etiam Monspeliensibus, quia iisdem Privilegiis fruimur ex concessione Regum. Voyez les niaiseries de Courtaut. Les Medecins de Paris n'ont point cette Licence, s'ils l'ont, nous l'avons aussi. Hippocrate n'a pratiqué la Medecine que dans un petit canton de la Grece: contenez-vous dans l'estenduë du ressort de Montpelier, auquel vous a borné le Parlement de Toulouse, qui a verifié vos Lettres, sine prejudicio aliarum Facultatum: C'est ce que les Rois ont entendu quand ils ont mis à la fin de vos Lettres, Saluo iure nostro, & in omnibus alieno.
units.tr: Cortaut boasts: "No province can be assigned to our doctors; the world is their province. The power has been given to us and denied to you; all places lie open to us as widely as they lay open to Hippocrates. If it is lawful for the doctors of Paris to heal everywhere, then it is also lawful for the Montpellier doctors, since we enjoy the same privileges by the grant of the Kings." See the silly nonsense of Cortaut! The doctors of Paris do not have this licence; if they have it, we have it too. Hippocrates practised medicine only in a small corner of Greece. Keep yourselves within the extent of the jurisdiction of Montpellier, to which the Parlement of Toulouse, which verified your letters, has confined you, sine prejudicio aliarum Facultatum (without prejudice to the other faculties). This is what the Kings understood when they put at the end of your letters, Saluo iure nostro, & in omnibus alieno (saving our right, and in all things not belonging to others).

units.la: Courtaut adiouste, Ubique docendi, medendique potestas, tam latè se diffundit, quàm vivifica vis Solis se expandit. Partant vous pouvez aller aux Indes Orientales & Occidentales pratiquer la Medecine: Nous ne vous envierons pas ce bonheur. Il poursuit, assignatorum regnum, provinciam, civitatem, aulam, nostris ab avo non cognitam & imperviam. Je vous cotteray les Espagnes, l'Allemagne, la Cour de ces deux Rois Souverains. La Cour de Rome, la Seigneurie de Venize, la Flandre, la Hollande, le Dannemarck, la Suede, la Pologne, la Moscovie, la Chersonese Taurique, l'Empire du Grand Turc l'Afrique, la Perse, la Tartarie, l'Asie, les Indes orientales & Occidentales, la Chine, le Iapon.
units.tr: Cortaut adds: "The power of teaching and healing everywhere spreads as widely as the life-giving force of the sun expands." So you may go to the East and West Indies to practise medicine; we will not begrudge you that happiness. He goes on: "a kingdom, province, city, court assigned to us, unknown and unapproachable to our forefathers." I will list for you Spain, Germany, the court of those two sovereign kings, the Court of Rome, the Lordship of Venice, Flanders, Holland, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, Muscovy, the Tauric Chersonese, the empire of the Grand Turk, Africa, Persia, Tartary, Asia, the East and West Indies, China, Japan. There are plenty of countries here that I list for you, if you want to advise the Montpellier doctors to go there, and if they are simple enough to believe you.

units.la: Voila bien des païs que ie vous cotte pour enuoyer les Medecins de Montpelier, si vous leur voulez conseiller des'y en aller, & s'ils font assez simples pour vous croire.
units.tr: Here are many countries that I list, so that you may advise the physicians of Montpellier to go and practise there, if they are simple enough to believe you.

units.la: Mais ils aiment mieux demeurer à Paris qu'ailleurs. Les Medecins de Montpelier, hors les originaires du païs, ne sont point receus à pratiquer la Medecine dans les païs étrangers: Il a fallu que Monsieur de Primerose, sçauant Medecin, qui auoit pris ses degrez à Montpelier, pour demeurer à Londres, aye suby l'Examé, afin d'estre aggregé au corps de la Medecine, & auoir permission de la pratiquer; & auec tout cela, il s'est retiré ailleurs, ne faisant point estat des Medecins de Montpelier.
units.tr: But they prefer to stay in Paris rather than anywhere else. Physicians of Montpellier, apart from those native to the country, are not admitted to practise medicine in foreign lands. Monsieur de Primerose, a learned physician who had taken his degrees at Montpellier, had to undergo examination in order to be admitted into the body of physicians and to receive permission to practise, in order to remain in London; and even with all that, he withdrew elsewhere, making no account of the physicians of Montpellier.

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris, outre ce Priuilege general, commun à toutes les Vniuersitez, en ont deux tres-nobles, qui leur sont concedez priuatiuement à toutes les autres Vniuersitez de la terre habitable, qui vous ont esté rapportez cy-dessus.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris, besides the general privilege common to all universities, have two very noble ones, granted to them exclusively, which extend to every other university on the inhabited earth, as I have reported above.

units.la: Ie trouue que les Professeurs de Montpelier, en voulans donner cette licence de pratiquer la Medecine, hic & vbique terrarum, pechent en la forme & en la matiere.
units.tr: I find that the professors of Montpellier, in wishing to grant this licence to practise medicine hic & vbique terrarum (here and everywhere on earth), err both in form and in substance.

units.la: Ce n'est pas un Professeur, qui la doit donner en conferant le bonnet, mais l'Evefque seul, par la constitution de l'Universitė, au rapport de Ranchin : Ce n'est pas à l'heure du Doctorat, que cette Licence se donne, mais en un temps qui precede le Doctorat, sous l'attrestation des Professeurs, ou du Chancelier en Medecine. Le Bachelier pour estre capable de receuoir de l'Evefque cette Licence, doit estre Catholique, se mettre à genoux, pour receuoir de la part du Pape, la benediction, & la Licéce tout ensemble, autrement on ne la peut receuoir que dans des Universitez Ecclesiastiques: & quiconque ne la reçoit de la sorte, nela peut avoir legitimement.
units.tr: It is not a professor who ought to grant it by conferring the cap, but the bishop alone, by the constitution of the university, according to Ranchin. This licence is not given at the hour of the doctorate, but at a time that precedes the doctorate, under the attestation of the professors or of the chancellor in medicine. For the bachelor to be able to receive this licence from the bishop, he must be a Catholic, kneel down to receive the blessing and the licence together from the Pope; otherwise it can only be received in ecclesiastical universities, and whoever does not receive it in this way cannot legitimately have it.

units.la: Les Rois de France ne se sont pas encor attribué ce pouVoir, comme a esté contraint de faire l'Empereur aux Universitez Luthe-riennes, qui ne reconnoissent point le Pape. J'expliqueray cét article au long, pour l'instruction des Medecins de Montpelier, comme il se doit entendre, & pratiquer.
units.tr: The Kings of France have not yet claimed this power for themselves, as the Emperor was forced to do for the Lutheran universities, which do not acknowledge the Pope. I shall explain this point at length, for the instruction of the physicians of Montpellier, as it ought to be understood and practised.

units.la: Il est certain que les Sciences sont dons du S. Esprit, que nous devons continuellement demander à Dieu par nos prieres pour les avoir, & en bien user. Nostre S. Pere le Pape, estant Vicaire de Dieu en terre, & ayant pouvoir sur les amez, & sur tout le spirituel, a pris le soin par toute la Chrestienté, d'establir des Escholes, Academies ou Universitez, pour l'instruction des Sciences, depuis les petites Escholes, jusques aux plus grandes. Dans tous les Dioceses, il y a un Scholarque, Chanoine de la grande Eglise, qui a connoissance des petites Escholles. Un homme ou une femme ne peut tenir petites Escholes publiques sans sa permissiõ, afin qu'il connoisse de la vie, mœurs, & de la capacité de ceux & de celles qui se meslent d'enseigner. De mesme nostre S. Pere le Pape, establissant les Academies, il a constitué pour Directeurs & Censeurs, les Euesques des lieux, ou ceux qui tiennent les premieres dignitez Ecclesiastiques aux villes, où sont fondées les Academies. Si nous croyons Baronius en ses Annales, anno 60. num.15. sous l'Empire des Rois de France, les Euesques auoient le soin d'establir & gouuerner les Escholes, & eux-mesmes enseignoient jusques aux preceptes de Grammaire. Or pour conuier aux estudes, & exciter les Estudians aux Lettres, mesmes pour donner courage & emulation aux Professeurs de bien faire leur deuoir, ils ont conferé des Priuileges aux Estudians, & aux Professeurs : ils ont aussi estably des degrez d'honneur dans les Vniuersitez, pour honorer & qualifier le trauail & progrez des Estudes. De sorte que pour les Lettres humaines, par où l'on commence, l'ont aierigé[?] le degré de Maistre aux Arts. Ceux qui en sont venus là, peuuent estudier en telle science qu'ils voudront, en Theologie, Iurisprudence, Droit Canon, ou Medecine. En toutes ces sciences, on a erigé des degrez d'honneur, selon l'auancement aux estudes, qui sont le Baccalaureat, la Licence, & le Doctorat, qui est l'ancienne façon de proceder au Doctorat. Maintenant en Allemagne & autres Academies d'Italie, ils donnent tout à la fois ces trois degrez pour exempter du temps d'estudé, & pour auoir tant plustost de l'argent des aspirans : Ce que blasme fort Cothmannus, Iurisconsulte, qui approuue d'aller par degrez auec interualles de temps, examinant à chaque degré si l'on a profité dans l'estude : & ainsi ces interualles ont esté appellez degrez.
units.tr: It is certain that the sciences are gifts of the Holy Spirit, which we must continually ask of God by our prayers, both to obtain them and to use them well. Our Holy Father the Pope, being the Vicar of God on earth, and having authority over souls and over everything spiritual, has taken care throughout Christendom to establish schools, academies or universities for the instruction of the sciences, from the small schools up to the greatest. In every diocese there is a scholarch, a canon of the cathedral church, who has oversight of the small schools. No man or woman may keep a public small school without his permission, so that he may know the life, morals and capacity of those who undertake to teach. Likewise, our Holy Father the Pope, in establishing the academies, has appointed as directors and censors the bishops of the places, or those who hold the first ecclesiastical dignities in the cities where the academies are founded. If we believe Baronius in his Annals, year 60, number 15, under the rule of the Kings of France, the bishops had the care of establishing and governing the schools, and they themselves taught even the rules of grammar. Now, to invite people to study, and to stir students to letters, and even to give courage and emulation to professors to do their duty well, they have conferred privileges on students and professors; they have also established degrees of honour in the universities, to honour and mark the labour and progress of studies. Thus, for the humane letters, with which one begins, the degree of Master of Arts was instituted. Those who have reached this point may study whatever science they wish: theology, jurisprudence, canon law, or medicine. In all these sciences, degrees of honour have been set up according to advancement in study, which are the baccalaureate, the licence, and the doctorate, which is the ancient manner of proceeding to the doctorate. Now in Germany and other academies of Italy, they grant all three degrees at once, to save the time of study and to obtain money from the candidates sooner; this Cothmannus, a jurist, strongly blames, approving of going through the degrees by steps with intervals of time, examining at each degree whether one has profited in study; and so these intervals have been called degrees.

units.la: Les Papes non contans d'auoir accordé cette dignité à ceux qui font profession des Sciences, ils ont à quelques Academies les plus celebres donné certains Priuileges pour les rendre plus recommandables. Les Papes Urbain IIII. Clement VI. & Eugenius III. ont donné des Bulles à l'Université de Padoüe, qui sont descrites tout au long par Riccobonus, Libro de Gymnasio Patauino, où se voit la forme de faire des Docteurs à Padoüe. Le pouvoir est attribué à l'Euesque, les Professeurs luy ayans donné fidelle attestation de la capacité de l'aspirant au Doctorat, qu'ils ont prealablement examiné.
units.tr: The Popes, not content to have granted this dignity to those who profess the sciences, have given certain privileges to some of the most celebrated academies to make them more esteemed. Popes Urban IV, Clement VI and Eugenius III have issued Bulls to the University of Padua, which are described at length by Riccobonus in Libro de Gymnasio Patauino, where the form of creating doctors at Padua is seen. The power is attributed to the bishop, the professors having given him a faithful attestation of the capacity of the candidate for the doctorate, whom they have previously examined.

units.la: Horstius en ses disputes qu'il a fait aux promotions des Doctorats, explique la façon dont on se fert en l'Academie de Girssen, qui appartient au Landgraue de Hessen, qui est toute pareille à celle des autres Vniversitez d'Allemagne. Ego pro auctoritate Cæsarea, & Principali mihi concessa à Cancellario, ex Decreto totius Academiæ, & in primis Collegij Medici, te creo & renuncio, & proclamo Doctorem, atque potestatem docendæ & exercendæ Medicinæ unà cum Privilegijs, & immunitatibus Doctoribus Medicis concessis tibi tribuo, in nomine Sanctissimæ Trinitatis, Dei Patris, Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. Je dis bien davantage, que les Empereurs n'ont jamais voulu accorder aux Calvinistes des Privileges de leurs Academies ; & par le Traitté de Passavv, ne peuvent faire un Docteur, ny donner licence, d'autant qu'ils sont plus éloignez de la Religion Catholique que les Lutheriens ; & delà inferent les Jurisconsultes Allemans, que les Academies Lutheriennes & Catholiques, si elles deviennent Calvinistes, perdent leurs Privileges.
units.tr: Horstius, in his disputations held at the conferring of doctorates, explains the procedure used at the University of Giessen, which belongs to the Landgrave of Hesse and is exactly like that of the other universities of Germany. "By the authority granted to me by Caesar and by the Prince, and by the decree of the whole university, and above all of the Medical College, I create you, nominate, proclaim and declare you Doctor, and I grant you the power of teaching and practising medicine, together with the privileges and immunities granted to medical doctors, in the name of the most holy Trinity, God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit." I say more than this: the Emperors have never wished to grant the Calvinists privileges for their academies, and by the Treaty of Passau they cannot make a doctor or give a licence, inasmuch as they are further removed from the Catholic religion than the Lutherans. From this the German jurists infer that Lutheran and Catholic academies, if they become Calvinist, lose their privileges.

units.la: En toutes les Academies de la France, il y a un Ecclesiastique honorable, le plus souvent Chanoine de la grande Eglise Cathedrale, qui est commis par l'Evesque pour tenir la place de Chancelier de l'Université, lequel, authoritate Apostolica, sive Pontificia, confere la licence en Theologie, Jurisprudence, & Medecine, & les Lettres de licence sont données par ledit Chancelier. Les Docteurs des Academies de France conferent seulement la dignité de Docteur, en la Faculté dont ils sont. Les Bacheliers de Paris prennent cette licence du Pape par les mains du Chancelier de l'Université. Nous trouvons en nos Registres qu'il y a plus de quatre cens ans, que les Bacheliers estans presentez au Chancelier, par le Doyen assisté de tous les Docteurs dans la grande Sale Episcopale, pour recevoir la licence de lire, enseigner, & pratiquer, hic & ubi-que Terrarum, avec la benediction que don[?] ne le Chancelier de la part de nostre saint Pere le Pape, aux Licentiez, estans à genoux devant luy; ce qui se pratique aujourdhuy de la mesme façon. Il se trouve vne Bulle dans les Archives de l'Vniversité de Paris, de l'an 1230. par laquelle le Pape ordonne, que les Licences n'auront lieu & pouvoir, si elles ne sont conferées par le Chancelier de l'Vniversité, qui doit estre Ecclesiastique. Il y a plus de mil ans que les Euesques de la part des Papes, ont eu l'intendance & le pouuoir sur les Academies de la Chrestienté.
units.tr: In all the academies of France there is an honourable ecclesiastic, most often a canon of the great cathedral church, who is commissioned by the bishop to hold the place of Chancellor of the University. He, "by apostolic or papal authority", confers the licence in theology, law and medicine, and the letters of licence are given by the said Chancellor. The doctors of the French academies confer only the dignity of doctor, in the faculty to which they belong. The bachelors of Paris receive this licence from the Pope through the hands of the Chancellor of the University. We find in our registers that for more than four hundred years the bachelors, presented to the Chancellor by the Dean, assisted by all the doctors, in the great Episcopal hall, have received the licence to read, teach and practise "here and everywhere on earth", with the blessing that the Chancellor gives on behalf of our Holy Father the Pope to the licentiates kneeling before him; and this is still practised today in the same way. In the archives of the University of Paris there is a bull of the year 1230, by which the Pope orders that licences shall have no force or validity unless they are conferred by the Chancellor of the University, who must be an ecclesiastic. For more than a thousand years the bishops, on behalf of the Popes, have had the oversight and authority over the academies of Christendom.

units.la: Nous lisons dans Eusebe, que les Euesques sont appellez Alexandrini Gymnasii moderatores, ceryphæique Professorum. Aux Academies de Louuain & Cologne, qui sont deux filles de l'Academie de Paris, & qui se glorifient d'estre telles, dautant qu'elles ont esté erigées par l'ordonnance des Papes sur le modele de celle de Paris, le Chancelier qui est Ecclesiastique, donne la licence, Authoritate Apostolicâ, & la font receuoir à genoux auec humilité; & donnant la benediction, il prononce ces paroles citées par Vernuleu, en son Liure de Academia Louaniensi, Authoritate Apostolicâ damus licentiam & Facultatem legendi, docendi, disputandi, resoluendi, & quoslibet actus scholasticos ad Facultatem Medicam spectantes, hic & vbique locorum exercendi.
units.tr: We read in Eusebius that bishops are called "overseers of the Alexandrian gymnasium and the chiefs of the professors". In the academies of Louvain and Cologne, which are two daughters of the Academy of Paris and which glory in being so, since they were founded by papal ordinance on the model of that of Paris, the Chancellor, who is an ecclesiastic, gives the licence "by apostolic authority" and has it received kneeling with humility; and giving the blessing, he pronounces these words, quoted by Vernulaeus in his book On the Academy of Louvain: "By apostolic authority we grant licence and faculty to read, teach, dispute, resolve, and to exercise any scholastic acts pertaining to the Faculty of Medicine, here and in every place."

units.la: Le President de l'acte, ou Promoteur aux Academies, qui reconnoissent le Pape, ne repetent point au Doctorat en donnant le bonnet, les paroles, que le Chancelier de l'Vniuersité a prononcées, mais seulement, Te creo & pronuncio Doctorem, & omnibus ornamentis insignio, In nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. De sorte, voyant que les Medecins Professeurs de Montpelier, n'ont aucun droict de donner la licence d'exercer la Medecine par toute la terre, en donnant le Doctorat, encore moins de l'exprimer dans les Lettres qu'ils donnent à leurs ieunes Docteurs, & que ce droict ne leur est point attribué par les Bulles des Papes, ny par les Lettres Patentes des Rois d'Arragon, & de France; nous avons sujet de nous plaindre de cette vsurpation, & attentat, qui va à la ruine du public, & au mespris de Mr l'Evesque de Montpelier à qui seul appartient le droict & le pouuoir de conferer; Authoritate Apostolica, la licence, legendi & exercendi Medicinam, hic & vbique terrarum. Apres votre examen & approbation de la capacité du Bachelier, vous pouuez de furabondant, luy donner le bonnet pour le faire Do-cteur, qui est l'adopter & l'aggregerà vostre compagnie, pour ioüir des droits & emolumens, qui appartiennent aux Docteurs également. S'il s'en va ailleurs demeurer, vous pouuez luy donner Lettre de son Doctorat en tel iour, & telle année. Mais de luy conceder toutes les autres Facultez, que vous inferez dans les Lettres, vous ne pouuez, ny deuez le faire, & en bonne Iustice, dorefnauant cette forme deLettres vous deuroit estre interdite. L'Eschole de Paris donne Lettres du Doctorat seulement à ceux qui les demandent : s'ils veulent auoir Lettres de Licence, on les renuoye à Monsieur le Chancelier de l'Vniuersité. I'aduoüe que la licence de lire & enseigner, & en suite la dignité du Doctorat, ont esté fort prudemment instituez, pour recompeser les trauaux des Estudians dans les sciences: Mais quand on a veu que les abus & les corruptions se sont glissez dans les Academies: que ces dignitez, qui ne se conferoient auciennement qu'à des hommes sçauans, dignes, & d'âge, se donnoient à des ignorās,& à des enfans; les Medecins des grandes villes qui forment College, n'ont plus voulu receuoir dans leurs villes à pratiquer la Medecine auec eux, telles personnes, encore qu'ils monstrassent leurs Lettres de Doctorat, portans pouvoir de faire la Medecine, hic & vbique Terrarum: Ils ont voulu auparavant que les admettre, connoistre leur suffisance & capacité. Celas'observe par tous les Roiaumes, en toutes les grandes villes & Republiques qui n'ont pas mesmes Université: ils ne reçoivent dans leur ville, un seul Medecin portant & monstrant sa Lettre Doctorale, s'il n'est prealablement interrogé par un acte probatoire, pour voir s'il est veritablement docte; non pas Docteur en apparence par Bulle. Fort à propos le Pape Gregoire XIII. demandoit à un certain Docteur, qui postuloit un benefice, se voulant prevaloir de son charactere de Docteur, Siete voi Dottore guero siate addottorato?
units.tr: The president of the act, or promoter, in the academies which acknowledge the Pope, does not repeat, at the conferring of the doctorate when giving the cap, the words which the Chancellor of the University has pronounced, but only: "I create and pronounce you Doctor, and I invest you with all the insignia, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Accordingly, seeing that the professor physicians of Montpellier have no right to give the licence to practise medicine throughout the whole earth in conferring the doctorate, still less to express it in the letters which they give to their young doctors, and that this right is not attributed to them either by the bulls of the Popes or by the letters patent of the Kings of Aragon and of France, we have cause to complain of this usurpation and attempt, which tends to the ruin of the public and to the contempt of the Bishop of Montpellier, to whom alone belongs the right and power to confer, by apostolic authority, the licence "to read and practise medicine here and everywhere on earth". After your examination and approval of the bachelor's capacity, you may, over and above this, give him the cap to make him Doctor, which is to adopt him and admit him into your company, to enjoy the rights and emoluments which belong equally to the doctors. If he goes to live elsewhere, you may give him a letter of his doctorate on such a day and in such a year. But to grant him all the other faculties which you insert in the letters, you cannot, nor ought you to do so, and in good justice this form of letters should henceforth be forbidden to you. The School of Paris gives letters of the doctorate only to those who ask for them; if they wish to have letters of licence, they are sent on to the Chancellor of the University. I admit that the licence to read and teach, and afterwards the dignity of doctor, were instituted very prudently, to reward the labours of students in the sciences; but when it was seen that abuses and corruptions had crept into the academies, and that these dignities, which in former times were conferred only on learned, worthy and mature men, were given to the ignorant and to children, the physicians of the great cities who form a college no longer wished to admit into their cities such persons to practise medicine with them, even though they showed their letters of doctorate, carrying power to practise medicine "here and everywhere on earth". They wished, before admitting them, to know their sufficiency and capacity. This is observed throughout all kingdoms, in all the great cities and republics which do not even have a university: they admit into their city no single physician carrying and showing his doctoral letter unless he has first been examined by a probationary act, to see whether he is truly learned, and not a doctor merely in appearance by bull. Very aptly Pope Gregory XIII once asked a certain doctor, who was seeking a benefice and wished to avail himself of his character as doctor: "Are you a doctor, if you are not learned?" (Siete voi Dottore, guero siate addottorato?)

units.la: Je puis prouver par exemple, que cela se pratiquoit anciennement du temps d'Hippocrate en la Grece, du temps des Cesars à Ro-me, & s'observe encore tres-exactement aujourd'huy en Italie, Espagne, Allemagne, Angleterre & en France, par toutes les grandes villes & Acdemies, excepté la ville de Paris. Verifions cette bonne coustume du temps d'Hippocrate. Avant qu'il vint au monde,la Medecine eftoit entretenuë dans de certaines familles, & fe communiquoit seulement par traditiue aux defcendans des familles, qui prenoient origine d'Efculape. Ces Medecins fe difoient Afclepiadæ, fortis d'Afclepius, qui eft le mefme que Efculape. De forte qu'vn Medecin pour eftre reputé fçauant, il falloit qu'il fuft de cette famille, & les fçauans Medecins s'appel-loient [?]παῖδες ἰατρῶν[?], filij Medicorum. Hippo-crate, qui tenoit Efchole pour inftruire plufieurs Medecins, comme il eft rapporté dans le Decret des Atheniens, en fa loüange, les vns eftoient [?]συγγεγραμμένοι[?], immatriculez ou enroolez, qui fe donnoient à luy fous fa difcipline. De ceux-là il en menoit les plus aduancez en la Medecine chez les malades, & en laiffoit quelqu'vn pour les affifter: quand ils eftoient inftruits, & façonnez en la Medecine, il leur donnoit la licence de pratiquer comme il a fait en la pefte des Illyriens, où il enuoya quelquesvns de fes difciples. Or auant que d'obtenir cette licence, il leur faifoit iurer les Statuts qu'il auoit eftablis. Ces Medecins eftoient nommez [?]ὁρκομόσιοι νόμῳ ἐπιτεχνῷ[?], Medici Iurati. Outre ces Medecins qui eftoient inftruits par luy, & dans les Efcholes de la Grece, Rhodia, Coa, & Cnidia, il y auoit des Coureurs & Charlatans, qui se mesloient de la Medecine. Hippocrate, au liure de decenti ornatu, nous aduertit que les Medecins les chassoient de leurs villes. Ils venoient ( dit-il ) auec une arrogance & presomption, paroissoient en habits & cageolerie, n'ayans ny estude, ny science en Medecine. Ce qui confirme ce que dit Hippocrate au liure de Natura humana, que dans les disputes, celuy qui a la langue & le discours coulât paroist habile homme au vulgaire. C'est assez qu'ils usent de quelques termes & paroles de Medecine, pour se faire valoir Medecins, comme rapporte le mesme Hippocrate, liure 1. de la diette des maladies aiguës. Voyez en l'Epistre derniere d'Hippocrate, comme son fils Thessalus, par son Deputé, represente aux Atheniens, les seruices que luy, & son pere ont rendu à la ville d'Athenes, tant par la Medecine que par les armes, tant par mer que par terre. Pour recompense, il demande le droit de Bourgeoisie pour demeurer dans la ville d'Athenes. Dans les Epistres de Pline le jeune, liu. 10. Il y en a une qu'il addresse à son bon Maistre l'Empereur Traian, pour le prier de donner à trois Medecins, dont l'un estoit Abascantus, Medecin de Lyon, duquel fait mention Galien, in libris de compos. Medicam. secundum locos, & lib. 2. de Antidotis, c. 12. le droit de Bourgeoisie, pour demeurer à Rome, & y exercer la Medecine.
units.tr: I can prove by example that this was practised anciently, in the time of Hippocrates in Greece, in the time of the Caesars at Rome, and is still observed very exactly today in Italy, Spain, Germany, England and France, in all the great cities and academies, except the city of Paris. Let us verify this good custom in the time of Hippocrates. Before he came into the world, medicine was maintained within certain families and was passed on only by tradition to the descendants of the families which took their origin from Aesculapius. These physicians called themselves Asclepiadae, from Asclepius, who is the same as Aesculapius. So that for a physician to be reputed learned, he had to be of this family, and learned physicians were called "sons of physicians" (παῖδες ἰατρῶν, filii medicorum). Hippocrates, who kept a school to instruct several physicians, as is reported in the decree of the Athenians in his praise, had some who were enrolled (συγγεγραμμένοι, matriculated or registered), who gave themselves to him under his discipline. Of these he took the most advanced in medicine to the sick, and left some one of them to assist them; when they were instructed and formed in medicine, he gave them licence to practise, as he did in the plague of the Illyrians, to which he sent some of his disciples. Now before obtaining this licence, he had them swear to the statutes which he had established. These physicians were called "sworn physicians" (ὁρκομόσιοι νόμῳ ἐπιτεχνῷ, medici iurati). Besides these physicians who were instructed by him, and in the schools of Greece, Rhodes, Cos and Cnidus, there were runners and charlatans who meddled with medicine. Hippocrates, in the book On Decent Ornament, warns us that physicians drove them out of their cities. They came, he says, with arrogance and presumption, appeared in showy clothes and flattery, having neither study nor science in medicine. This confirms what Hippocrates says in the book On the Nature of Man, that in disputes, he who has a fluent tongue and discourse appears a capable man to the common people. It is enough for them to use some terms and phrases of medicine to make themselves pass for physicians, as the same Hippocrates reports, in the first book On the Diet in Acute Diseases. See in Hippocrates' last Epistle how his son Thessalus, through his deputy, sets before the Athenians the services which he and his father have rendered to the city of Athens, both by medicine and by arms, both by sea and by land. In return he asks the right of citizenship to live in the city of Athens. In the Epistles of Pliny the Younger, book 10, there is one which he addresses to his good master, the Emperor Trajan, to beg him to grant to three physicians, one of whom was Abascantus, a physician of Lyon, whom Galen mentions in his books On the Compound Medicines according to Places, and book 2 On Antidotes, chapter 12, the right of citizenship, to live at Rome and practise medicine there.

units.la: Vous voyez par ce discours qu'il n'estoit pas permis à tous les Medecins de s'establir à Athenes, & à Rome. Faisons maintenant vne reueuë sur tous les Royaumes de l'Europe, où la Medecine est enseignée & exercée, & aux Academies, pour voir s'ils receuoient dans les villes tous ceux qui se disent Medecins graduez ouDocteurs. En Italie ils ne reçoiuent personne à pratiquer dans les grandes villes, qu'il n'ait esté par les Medecins du lieu au prealable examiné. Il y a prés de deux cens ans qu'vn Medecin nommé Iean Vochs, natif de Cologne, demeurant à Magdebourg, en son traité de la peste, se plaint que les Italiens donnoient indifferemment à tous venans la Licence de Doctorat en Medecine pour de l'argent, & receuoient toute sorte de personnes, doctes ou ignorans; que pour euiter ce desordre & grands abus, les Rois de Sicile, Alphonse, & Ferdinand, auoient ordonné, que nul ne seroit receu à pratiquer la Medecine dans leur Royaume, s'il n'auoit esté examiné par les Medecins deputez par le Roy. Ce qui s'obseruoit du temps de Philippe Ingrassias, qui en fait mention en la Preface de son Commentaire sur le liure de Galien, de Ossibus: Et luy-mesme en auoit la commission de la part du Roy d'Espagne: mesmes ils veulent que les Medecins de leurs païs apprennent la Medecine dans leur païs, pour estre formez à la pratique de leur climat. Les Venitiens ont ordonné l'an 1458. Que ceux qui estudieroient, ou prendroient leurs degrez en Medecine en d'autres Vniuersitez que celles de la Republique, ne ioüiroient dans l'estenduë de leur Terre, des Priuileges des Docteurs: Federic premier, dit Barberousse, Empereur, & Roy de Naples, a estably cette loy, que personne ne fut admis aux dignitez des Academies, qu'il n'eust estudié dans l'Academie de Naples, & y eust pris ses degrez, sur peine de prison d'vn an, & confiscation des biens. Ce qui auoit esté auparauant ordonné par le Roy de Sicile, & Prince de Salerne Rogerius, qui est la loy dix-huit. De probabili experientia Medicorum.
units.tr: You see from this discussion that not every physician was permitted to settle in Athens and Rome. Let us now review all the kingdoms of Europe where medicine is taught and practised, and their academies, to see whether they admit into their cities everyone who calls himself a graduate or Doctor of medicine. In Italy they admit no one to practise in the large cities until he has first been examined by the physicians of the place. Nearly two hundred years ago a physician named John Vochs, a native of Cologne living at Magdeburg, complained in his treatise on the plague that the Italians granted the licence of doctorate in medicine indiscriminately to all comers for money, and admitted every sort of person, learned or ignorant. To prevent this disorder and great abuse, the Kings of Sicily, Alfonso and Ferdinand, had ordered that no one should be admitted to practise medicine in their kingdom unless he had first been examined by physicians appointed by the King. This was observed in the time of Philip Ingrassias, who mentions it in the preface to his commentary on Galen's book On the Bones; and he himself held the commission for this from the King of Spain. Moreover, they want the physicians of their country to learn medicine in their own country, so as to be trained in the practice suited to their climate. In the year 1458 the Venetians ordered that those who studied, or took their degrees in medicine, at universities other than those of the Republic, should not enjoy the privileges of Doctors within the extent of their territory. Frederick the First, called Barbarossa, Emperor and King of Naples, established the law that no one should be admitted to the dignities of the academies unless he had studied at the academy of Naples and taken his degrees there, on pain of a year's imprisonment and confiscation of goods. This had previously been ordained by Roger, King of Sicily and Prince of Salerno, which is law eighteen, On the probable experience of physicians.

units.la: Hippolytus Marsilius, Iurisconsulte, rapporte qu'vn Euesque de Capoüe, de son temps, faisoit interroger de nouueau tous les Docteurs, qui venoient s'habituer en son Euefché, & s'il les trouuoit ignorans, il les privoit du Doctorat. Il est loüé par ce Iurifconsulte, qui souhaitte que cela se pratique aujourd'huy.
units.tr: Hippolytus Marsilius, a jurist, reports that a Bishop of Capua in his time had all the Doctors who came to settle in his diocese examined afresh, and if he found them ignorant, he deprived them of the doctorate. This jurist praises him and wishes that this practice were followed today.

units.la: En Espagne, Philippe second a ordonné, que nul ne se mesle de pratiquer la Medecine, qu'il n'aye fait son cours en Medecine l'espace de quatre ans, & n'ait esté Bachelier deux ans pour estudier en pratique: puis ayant esté examiné pour le Doctorat, l'ayant receu legitimement, il faut qu'il soit derechef examiné par le premier Medecin, ou ses commis, avant que pratiquer la Medecine.
units.tr: In Spain, Philip the Second ordained that no one should take up the practice of medicine unless he had completed his course in medicine over a period of four years, and had been a Bachelor for two years to study in practice; then, having been examined for the doctorate and legitimately received, he must be examined again by the first physician, or his deputies, before practising medicine.

units.la: En Allemagne, les Statuts des Vniversitez & des Republiques font formelles pour la seureté de leur vie, chassant tous ceux, qui ne font pas Docteurs de l'Vniversité, ou qui ne font aggregez par examen & disputes. Charles-Quint, Cap. 134. Institutionum criminalium, ordonne l'an 1532. Prohibendi sunt ȳ[?] profiteri, vel facere Medicinam, qui non per statuta tempora Medicinæ eruditioni inhesse noscuntur, ne Medicorum consortio socientur. Il veut de plus, que l'enqueste & informations des crimes & maluersations des Medecins, soit faite par le College, ou l'Vniversité, qui en fera son rapport au Magistrat, pour ordonner du supplice, ou de l'amende, ou de la vie. Les Statuts du College de Nuremberg, portent que nul ne pourra pratiquer la Medecine, s'il n'est approuué par les Medecins & Magistrat, auec defenfe aux habitans & hosteliers de loger les Medecins estrangers sans en aduertir le Magistrat, sur peine de dix florins. A Cologne, les defenses sont expresses dans les Statuts, de receuoir les Medecins estrangers, s'il ne sont approuuez par le College. Dans l'estenduë des terres du Duc de Wirtèberg, personne ne peut pratiquer la Medecine, s'il n'est approuué par les Docteurs de l'Eschole de Tubinge. Les mesmes defenses sont en la Republique d'Ausbourg. Thomas Forsterus Norman, natif d'Auranche, qui auoit beaucoup voyagé en Flandre, en Angleterre, & plusieurs autres Royaumes, enfin estant reuenu à Rouën, où il a composé & fait imprimer l'année 1480. son Liure de peste & tenesmone, se plaint qu'on chasse des Vniuersitez, les autres Medecins graduez, qui viennent pour s'y establir & traiter les pauures. Son dessein estoit tout semblable à celuy du Gazetier Theophraste Renaudot, qui se plaint qu'on l'a voulu empescher de pratiquer la Medeci-ne à Paris, estant Docteur de Montpelier, charitablement pour les pauvres, accompagné de sept ou huict Medecins, qui avoient aussi bonne volonté que luy de penser les pauvres, afin, sous ce pretexte, de pouvoir demeurer à Paris. Le Sieur de Primerose, sçauant Medecin, Docteur de Montpelier, ayant son pere en grande reputation dans Londres, pour sa Doctrine, qui estoit premier Ministre de l'Eglise Françoise; n'a neantmoins pû estre receu à pratiquer la Medecine dans Londres, qu'il n'aye esté interrogé, & soustenu Theses, pour estre Aggregé audit College de Londres. Ils ont en Angleterre deux Universitez fameuses, Oxfort & Cantebrige. Les Docteurs des deux Efcholes sont encore de nouveau examinez, avant que pouvoir demeurer en la ville de Londres. Là dessus, ledit de Primerose fait un fort beau discours, que ie rapporteray en abregé. Il y a beaucoup de personnes, qui veulent paroistre sçauans, bien qu'ils soient ignorans, par un titre d'honneur, qui est le Doctorat; qu'on donne maintenant à tous venans pour de l'argent. C'est pourquoy en Italie & en France, ils ne font pas grand estat d'un Docteur venant des Universitez avec leurs Lettres. Quand ils viennent aux grandes villes, ils veulent derechef les examiner, pour voir s'ils sont capables d'exercer la Medecine, & d'estre Aggregé geʒ[?] à leurs corps. Il n'est pas permis à vn Docteur d'aller à vne autre Academie s'installer, & y exercer la Medecine, s'il n'est Medecin de la dite Academie. Il n'est pas permis à vn Docteur, de quelque Academie qu'il soit, de s'y habituer, s'il n'est derechef examiné & approuvé, voyant les abus qui se commettent en conferant le bonnet Doctoral.
