Il seroit expedient d'establir cette loy, que les Originaires n'iroient plus hors de leurs païs chercher le degré Doctoral, afin que[?] dans le païs on les connoisse, & qu'on soit asseuré de leur suffisance, & de la verité de leurs Lettres. André du Laurens, ce grand Anatomiste, ayant obtenu vne Lecture Royale à Montpelier, il fut contraint derechef de prendre le Doctorat par tous les degrez. De mesme les Medecins de Bordeaux, ne voulurent receuoir dans leur ville, Iulius Cæsar Scaliger, qu'il n'eust suby l'examen; ce que n'ayant voulu accepter, pour ne point hazarder sa reputation à vne dispute quodlibetaire, il se retira à Agen. Primerose adiouste. J'ay veu les Lettres de Scaliger, & de Maniald, Medecin de Bordeaux, qui sont entre les mains de son fils, sur ce suiet.
units.tr: In Germany, the statutes of the universities and of the commonwealths are explicit for the safety of life, expelling all those who are not Doctors of the university, or who are not admitted by examination and disputations. Charles V, chapter 134 of the Institutiones criminales, ordained in 1532: Those who are not known to have devoted the prescribed time to the study of medicine are to be forbidden to profess or practise medicine, lest they be joined to the fellowship of physicians. He further wills that the inquiry and information concerning the crimes and misdeeds of physicians be made by the College or the University, which shall report to the magistrate, so that punishment, or a fine, or life itself may be decreed. The statutes of the College of Nuremberg provide that no one may practise medicine unless he is approved by the physicians and the magistrate, with a prohibition on residents and innkeepers lodging foreign physicians without informing the magistrate, on pain of ten florins. In Cologne the statutes expressly forbid receiving foreign physicians unless they have been approved by the College. Within the lands of the Duke of Württemberg, no one may practise medicine unless he has been approved by the Doctors of the school of Tübingen. The same prohibitions hold in the Republic of Augsburg. Thomas Forster, Norman, a native of Avranches, who had travelled much in Flanders, in England, and in several other kingdoms, and finally returned to Rouen, where in 1480 he composed and published his book On the plague and tenesmus, complains that graduate physicians who come to settle in the universities and treat the poor are driven out. His aim was entirely similar to that of the gazetteer Theophraste Renaudot, who complains that attempts were made to prevent him from practising medicine in Paris, though he was a Doctor of Montpellier, and who worked charitably for the poor, accompanied by seven or eight physicians who were just as willing as he was to care for the poor, so that under this pretext they might remain in Paris. Monsieur de Primerose, a learned physician, Doctor of Montpellier, whose father enjoyed great reputation in London for his learning, and who was first minister of the French Church, could nevertheless not be received to practise medicine in London until he had been questioned and had defended theses, in order to be admitted as a member of the said College of London. In England they have two famous universities, Oxford and Cambridge. The Doctors of both schools are examined again before they may settle in the city of London. On this subject the said de Primerose makes a very fine discourse, which I shall report in summary. There are many persons who wish to appear learned though they are ignorant, by means of a title of honour, which is the doctorate, now given to all comers for money. That is why in Italy and France they do not set much store by a Doctor coming from the universities with their letters. When they come to the great cities they wish to examine them again, to see whether they are capable of practising medicine, and of being admitted as members of their body. It is not permitted for a Doctor to go and settle in another academy and practise medicine there, unless he is a physician of that academy. It is not permitted for a Doctor, of whatever academy he may be, to settle there unless he is again examined and approved, seeing the abuses that are committed in conferring the doctoral cap. It would be expedient to establish this law, that natives should no longer go outside their country to seek the doctoral degree, so that in their own country they may be known, and their sufficiency and the truth of their letters may be assured. André du Laurens, that great anatomist, having obtained a royal lectureship at Montpellier, was obliged again to take the doctorate through all the degrees. Likewise the physicians of Bordeaux would not receive Julius Caesar Scaliger into their city unless he submitted to the examination; and as he would not accept this, not wishing to risk his reputation in a quodlibetical disputation, he withdrew to Agen. Primerose adds: I have seen the letters of Scaliger and of Maniald, physician of Bordeaux, which are in the hands of his son, on this subject.

units.la: Nous trouuons dans nos Registres, que l'an 1571. le 18. de May, la Faculté fut assemblée pour entendre vn Medecin de Valence, nommé Fauchet, lequel nous proposa[?] des articles que les Medecins de Valence auoient dreffez pour reformer la Medecine,en Dauphiné. Or afin d'obtenir plus aisément confirmation du Roy, ils demanderent nostre Approbation, laquelle leur fut accordée, apres auoir examiné lesdites propositions, qui furent signées par le Sieur Variquet, pour lors nostre Doyen: Entre autres articles est celuy-cy : Que personne ne feroit la Medecine à Valence, ny à Grenoble, qu'il ne fut Docteur ou Licentié de ladite Faculté : Et en tout le Dauphiné, ils seroient Bacheliers en Medecine. Deux Medecins Docteurs de Montpelier, l'vn nommé Martin, & l'autre Froger, voulans s'establir à Angers, ont esté empeschez par l'V-niuersité, s'ils n'estoient derechef examinez : apres plusieurs contestations au Parlement de Paris, ils ont esté contrains d'accepter les conditions offertes par l'Vniuersité, y subir l'examen, & soustenir Theses.
units.tr: In our registers we find that on 18 May 1571 the Faculty was assembled to hear a physician of Valence, named Fauchet, who proposed to us articles that the physicians of Valence had drawn up for reforming medicine in Dauphiné. In order to obtain the King's confirmation more easily, they asked for our approval, which was granted after we had examined the proposals; they were signed by Sieur Variquet, then our Dean. Among the articles is this one: that no one should practise medicine at Valence or at Grenoble unless he is a Doctor or Licentiate of that Faculty, and that throughout Dauphiné they should be Bachelors in Medicine. Two doctors of medicine from Montpellier, one named Martin and the other Froger, wishing to settle at Angers, were hindered by the University unless they were examined again; after many disputes in the Parlement of Paris, they were compelled to accept the conditions offered by the University, to undergo the examination there and to maintain theses.

units.la: Hector Boëthius, lib. 2. Historiæ Scoticæ, rapporte, que Reutherus (septiesme Roy d'Escosse, ordonna que nul fust qualifié Medecin, qui ne fust sçauant, & experimenté en la Medecine, & approuvé par les Medecins qui pratiquoient Dogmaticè & Canonicè, feson les preceptes des anciens Medecins.
units.tr: Hector Boece, in book 2 of his History of Scotland, reports that Reuther (the seventh King of Scotland) ordained that no one should be qualified as a physician who was not learned and experienced in medicine and approved by the physicians who practised dogmatically and canonically, according to the precepts of the ancient physicians.

units.la: Vous sçaurez que dans les Pais Bas, qui sont sujets du Roy d'Espagne, par les loix du Prince & du pais, il n'est pas permis de pratiquer la Medecine, si on n'est Docteur des Academies du pais, ou approuvé par icelles, ou par le premier Medecin du Prince. Il est aussi defendu aux villes de donner pensions aux Medecins, s'ils ne sont Docteurs, ou Licentiez des Vniuersitez du pais. En Amsterdam, ils permettent toute sorte de Religion, neantmoins ils n'admettent pas toute sorte de Medecins dans leur ville. Ils veulent qu'ils soient Docteurs du pais, ou Aggregez au College de ladite ville. Pour cet effet ils ont fait bastir vn College de Medecine, où ils font des Anatomies publiques, demonstrations des plantes & aromates, sans faire leçons publiques ordinaires, si ce n'est sur quelque rencontre ou difficulté en Medecine.
units.tr: You will know that in the Low Countries, which are subject to the King of Spain, by the laws of the Prince and of the country, it is not permitted to practise medicine unless one is a Doctor of the academies of the country, or approved by them, or by the Prince's first physician. It is also forbidden for towns to give pensions to physicians unless they are Doctors or Licentiates of the universities of the country. In Amsterdam they allow every kind of religion; nevertheless they do not admit every kind of physician into their city. They require that they be Doctors of the country or aggregated to the College of that city. To this end they have built a College of Medicine, where they hold public anatomies and demonstrations of plants and aromatics, without giving ordinary public lectures, except on some occasion or difficulty in medicine.

units.la: La France sera-t-elle plus malheureuse, & de pire condition que les autres Royaumes, puis que les abus s'y sont glissez aussi bien en la Medecine que dans les autres sciences, en la dispensation des degrez ? Pourquoy les Docteurs de Paris n'auront-ils point droit de chasser les Medecins estrangers, s'ils ne sont par eux examinez & approuvez?
units.tr: Will France be more unfortunate and in worse condition than the other kingdoms, since abuses have crept into medicine as well as into the other sciences, in the granting of degrees? Why should the Doctors of Paris not have the right to drive out foreign physicians if they are not examined and approved by them?

units.la: Il y a 250. ans, que Gabriel Tarrega, Medecin, qui a composé un liure de Medecine, avoit esté choisi & retenu par les Iurats, pour enseigner la Medecine dans la ville de Bordeaux: les Medecins l'empescherent iusques à ce qu'il eut fait paroistre ausdits Medecins sa suffisance, & eust esté approuvé par eux, pour estre Aggregé au College.
units.tr: Two hundred and fifty years ago, Gabriel Tarrega, a physician who had composed a book of medicine, had been chosen and retained by the Jurats to teach medicine in the city of Bordeaux; the physicians prevented him until he had shown them his competence and had been approved by them, so as to be aggregated to the College.

units.la: Au Parlement d'Aix en Provence, a esté donné Arrest le 6. de Septembre 1569. en la Police de la ville, par lequel il est porté en l'article x. que nul Medecin & Chirurgien estranger, pourra pratiquer en ladite ville, qu'il n'ait au preallable licence par escrit des deux Surintendans, y appellez les Gens du Roy, & Consuls de la ville: lesquelles licences seront enregistrées apres que les Medecins l'auront trouvé capable.
units.tr: In the Parlement of Aix in Provence, an Arrest was issued on 6 September 1569 concerning the policing of the city, by which it is provided in article 10 that no foreign physician or surgeon may practise in that city unless he first has a licence in writing from the two superintendents, called "the King's men," and the Consuls of the city; these licences are to be registered after the physicians have found him capable.

units.la: A Montpelier, ils ne veulent pas recevoir un Docteur d'Avignon, s'il ne se fait Docteur de nouveau en ladite Eschole. Louis Saporta venant d'Espagne, d'où il estoit Docteur, & Professeur en l'Université de Lerida, où il avoit enseigné la Medecine l'espace de neuf ans, il fallut pour demeurer en Avignon, qu'il fit tous les actes necessaires pour estre Docteur de ladite Academie. De là, desirant se retirer à Montpelier, il fut obligé de faire tous les actes pour estre Docteur de ladite Vniuersité, au rapport de Laurens Ioubert, Chancelier de Montpelier, que vous ne pouuez honnestement dementir ; de sorte que ledit Saporta a esté trois fois Docteur.
units.tr: At Montpellier they do not want to receive a Doctor from Avignon unless he becomes a Doctor anew in that School. Louis Saporta, coming from Spain, where he had been a Doctor and Professor in the University of Lleida, where he had taught medicine for nine years, was required, in order to remain in Avignon, to perform all the acts necessary to become a Doctor of that Academy. From there, wishing to withdraw to Montpellier, he was obliged to perform all the acts to become a Doctor of that University, according to the report of Laurens Joubert, Chancellor of Montpellier, which you cannot honestly deny; so that the said Saporta has been a Doctor three times.

units.la: Les Sieurs du Laurens & Richer, pour exercer des Lectures Royales qu'ils auoient obtenuës, tous deux estas Docteurs d'Avignon, furent contraints de prendre leurs degrez à Montpelier, comme auoit fait Saporta.
units.tr: Sieurs du Laurens and Richer, to exercise the Royal Lectureships they had obtained, both being Doctors of Avignon, were compelled to take their degrees at Montpellier, as Saporta had done.

units.la: Si les Medecins de Montpelier ont toufiours gardé cette rigueur, & ont titres qu'ils font tant valoir des Papes & des Rois, pourquoy né veulent-ils pas que nous ioüissions des mesmes Priuileges, que les Papes & les Rois nous ont concedez auant l'establissement de l'Vniuersité de Montpelier? Ladite Escole, comme la ville, font du ressort du Parlement de Toulouse, où il y a Vniuersité plus ancienne, que celle de Montpelier, qui a par sa creation, des Priuileges, que n'a pas l'Academie de Montpelier: Neantmoins vn Docteur en Medecine de Montpelier, ne peut demeurer en la ville de Toulouse, s'il n'est Docteur, ou Aggregé en l'Vniuersité: & le pouuoir des Medecins de Montpelier a esté restreint dans leur ressort. Ainsi Monsieur de la Roche-Flauin, en ses Arrests notables du Parlemēt de Toulouse, l'a descrit. Pourquoy voulezvous étendre vostre pouuoir plus auant que vostre Parlement ne vous l'a accordé? Vous voulez que ceux qui prendront le Doctorat à Montpelier, ayét plus de pouuoir que n'ont pas les Professeurs residens en la ville?
units.tr: If the physicians of Montpellier have always kept this strictness, and have the titles from Popes and Kings which they make so much of, why do they not want us to enjoy the same privileges which the Popes and Kings granted us before the establishment of the University of Montpellier? That School, like the city, falls under the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Toulouse, where there is a university older than that of Montpellier, which by its foundation has privileges that the Academy of Montpellier does not have. Nevertheless, a Doctor of Medicine of Montpellier cannot remain in the city of Toulouse unless he is a Doctor or aggregated to the University; and the power of the physicians of Montpellier has been restricted within their jurisdiction. So Monsieur de la Roche-Flavin describes it in his Notable Arrests of the Parlement of Toulouse. Why do you want to extend your power further than your Parlement has granted you? Do you want those who take the Doctorate at Montpellier to have more power than the Professors residing in the city themselves?

units.la: Si on admet les Medecins de Montpelier à pratiquer la Medecine dans Paris, & qu'ils obtiennent ce droict, c'est destruire l'Vniuersité de Paris, composée de quatre Facultez, dautant que celle de la Medecine sera totalement perduë: qui est celuy qui voudra dorefnauant estudier à Paris, employer son temps & son argent dans de longues estudes de six ans, auant qu'estre Docteur, puis qu'en six mois d'estude, à la rigueur, & à meilleur compte, sans estre refusé, on deuient Docteur en Medecine à Montpelier? Ces Docteurs venans de toutes parts, feront corps à Paris, estans assemblez, surmonteront en nombre les Medecins de Paris, & les chasseront de leur Eschole, & de leur ville, ou bien cela produira par enuie vn grand desordre, & confusion dans la Medecine, des querelles continuelles sur les malades, & reduira la Medecine dans vne charlatanerie & brigandage ; chacun fera la Medecine à sa mode, sans regle, discipline, & correction.
units.tr: If the physicians of Montpellier are admitted to practise medicine in Paris, and obtain this right, it would destroy the University of Paris, which is composed of four Faculties, since the Faculty of Medicine would be wholly lost. Who, henceforth, would wish to study at Paris, to spend his time and money on long studies of six years before becoming a Doctor, when in six months of study, strictly speaking, and at less cost, and without being refused, one becomes a Doctor of Medicine at Montpellier? These Doctors, coming from every quarter, would form a body at Paris; gathered together, they would surpass the physicians of Paris in number and drive them from their School and their city, or else this would produce, through envy, great disorder and confusion in medicine, continual quarrels over the sick, and would reduce medicine to quackery and brigandage; each would practise medicine in his own fashion, without rule, discipline or correction.

units.la: De plus, si les Medecins ont droict de s'établir à Paris, & par toutes les villes de France, pour auoir esté receus Docteurs en l'Efchole de Montpelier, les Apothiquaires & Chirurgiens estans receus Maistres de la ville de Montpelier, & approuuez par les Docteurs, peuuent pretendre le mesme droit que les Medecins.
units.tr: Moreover, if the physicians have the right to settle in Paris and throughout all the towns of France, because they have been received as Doctors in the School of Montpellier, then the apothecaries and surgeons, having been received as Masters of the city of Montpellier and approved by the Doctors, may claim the same right as the physicians.

units.la: I'ay descouuert dans Pline, vn secret politique de la Sagesse Romaine, pour refrener la grande auarice des Medecins de Rome, & leur trafic & marchandise, qu'ils faisoient sur les malades, promettans, de retarder la mort par des secrets qu'ils auoiët[?]: Ils ne trouuerent point de moyen plus conuenable, pour remedier à tels inconueniens,que d'ouurir la porte à tous les Charlatans, non pas pour faire honte aux Medecins, mais pour diminuer le prix excessif des guerisons, mettant la ialousie entr'eux.
units.tr: I have discovered in Pliny a political secret of Roman wisdom for restraining the great greed of the physicians of Rome, and their trade and merchandise, which they carried on over the sick, promising to delay death by secrets they possessed. They found no more suitable means of remedying such inconveniences than to open the door to all quacks, not to shame the physicians, but to lower the excessive price of cures by setting them at jealousy with one another.

units.la: Per quæ effectum est, vt nihil magis prodesse videretur, quàm multitudo grassantium, neque enim pudor, sed æmuli precia summittunt.
units.tr: By which it came about that nothing seemed more useful than the multitude of those who swarm about, for it is not shame but rivalry that lowers the prices.
Book 29, chapter 1.

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris font bien esloignez des mœurs de ces Medecins de Rome: Ce que nous remarquōs auiourd'huy en ce peu de Medecins de Montpelier, qui sont icy, ubi hominum animas negotiantur: & partant les Magistrats n'ont point sujet d'accorder cette licence à tous venans, au deshonneur de nostre Medecine, & à la ruine du peuple.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris are far removed from the manners of those physicians of Rome. What we observe today in the few physicians of Montpelier who are here, where they trade in human souls, and therefore the magistrates have no reason to grant this licence to all comers, to the dishonour of our medicine and the ruin of the people.

units.la: Vne grande singularité se remarque en l'Eschole de Montpelier: c'est qu'elle est de fondation Royale, ce qui n'est pas en l'Eschole de Paris. Ie pourrois dire que celle de Paris est de fondation Imperiale, puisque Charlemagne a erigé & formé l'Academie de Paris, & que Henry le Grand a pris le soin de sa reformation & conseruation, apres auoir donné la paix à son Royaume. Mais pour auoir eu des gages octroyez par le Roy Charles VIII. & deliurez par Lettres Patentes par Louys XII. pour entretenir quatre Professeurs, & le bastiment du College, est-elle pour cela Royale? C'est icy où se presente vne belle occasion de vous reprocher vostre ingratitude enuers l'Eschole de Paris, dautant que c'est vn Docteur de Paris, qui vous a procuré ce bien & cet honneur, duquel vous vous glorifiez? Vous ne sçauriez prouuer que Iacques Ponceau ait esté Docteur de Montpelier. Laurens Ioubert, en la Preface d'vn Liure dedié au Duc d'Alençon, frere de Henry III. rapportant tous les Medecins de Montpelier, qui ont seruy les Rois, ne nomme point Iacques Ponceau ; l'inscription du College qui a esté faite en l'honneur de Ponceau, ne me peut persuader qu'il fut Docteur de Montpelier. Les Medecins Professeurs ,soit pour honorer la memoire de leur bienfacteur, l'ont fait Docteur de Montpelier : soit aussi pour cacher l'obligation qu'ils auoient à l'Eschole de Paris, par l'entremise de Iacques Ponceau.
units.tr: A great singularity is noted in the School of Montpelier: it is of royal foundation, which the School of Paris is not. I could say that the School of Paris is of imperial foundation, since Charlemagne erected and formed the Academy of Paris, and Henry the Great took care of its reformation and preservation after giving peace to his kingdom. But because it received stipends granted by King Charles VIII and delivered by letters patent under Louis XII to maintain four professors, and the building of the College, is it for that reason royal? Here presents itself a fine occasion to reproach you for your ingratitude towards the School of Paris, since it was a doctor of Paris who procured for you this benefit and this honour, of which you glory? You could not prove that Jacques Ponceau was a doctor of Montpelier. Laurens Joubert, in the preface to a book dedicated to the Duke of Alençon, brother of Henry III, listing all the physicians of Montpelier who served the kings, does not name Jacques Ponceau; the inscription of the College made in honour of Ponceau cannot persuade me that he was a doctor of Montpelier. The professors, either to honour the memory of their benefactor, made him a doctor of Montpelier, or else to hide the obligation they had to the School of Paris, through the agency of Jacques Ponceau.

units.la: Ie vous prouueray clairement que Iac-ques Ponceau estoit Medecin de Paris , & qu'ayant pitié du miserable estat de vostre Eschole, qui s'en alloit perdue, l'a releuée par les gages qu'il vous a fait auoir du Roy. Iacques des Parts estoit natif de Paris,ses œu-ures ont esté imprimées par le soin de Iacques Ponceau, premier Medecin de Charles VIII. estant reuenu d'Italie, & aux dépens du Roy. Ianus Lascaris, qui a fait la dedicace du liure à Iacques Ponceau, l'appelle Patriotam de Iacques des Parts, & eiusdem artis Professorem : qu'auec le College de ses Confreres , il soustient vn grand fardeau , de conseruer la santé du Roy. Or le Roy ayant tousiours[?] demeuré à Paris depuis son retour d'Italie, & qu'il est mort deux ans après, est-il croyable qu'un Medecin de Montpelier ait eu le soin de faire imprimer trois gros volumes des oeuures de Iacques des Paris[?], Medecin de Paris, & que le College des Medecins de Montpelier, ait esté conuoqué & establý à Paris, pour conseruer la santé du Roy, auec Iacques Ponceau, son premier Medecin? De sorte que ie puis asseurer que ledit Ponceau, Medecin de Paris, est Promoteur de la fondation Royale des Lectures en Medecine dans Montpelier. Cependant ils iniurient & calomnient malicieusemēt ceux qui leur ont fait du bien, & qui leur ont enseigné la Medecine, puisqu'Egidius Corboliensis, Medecin de Paris, est allé à Montpelier faire leçons publiques, au rapport de Baleus. Vousne pouuez nier que vostre Eschole n'ait obligation à Monsieur Bouuart, premier Medecin du Roy Louis XIII. qui vous a assisté, pour oster de vostre ville le Lieutenant du premier Barbier, qui perdoit vostre authorité, & Iurisdiction sur les Chirurgiens.
units.tr: I will clearly prove to you that Jacques Ponceau was a physician of Paris, and that, pitying the miserable state of your School, which was going to ruin, he restored it through the stipends he obtained for you from the King. Jacques des Parts was a native of Paris; his works were printed through the care of Jacques Ponceau, first physician to Charles VIII, on his return from Italy, and at the King's expense. Janus Lascaris, who dedicated the book to Jacques Ponceau, calls him patriot of Jacques des Parts, and professor of the same art, who, together with the College of his colleagues, bears a great burden in preserving the health of the King. Now, since the King had always[?] remained in Paris since his return from Italy, and died two years later, is it credible that a physician of Montpelier took the care to have three large volumes of the works of Jacques des Parts, physician of Paris, printed, and that the College of physicians of Montpelier was summoned and established in Paris to preserve the King's health, together with Jacques Ponceau, his first physician? So I can assure you that the said Ponceau, physician of Paris, is the promoter of the royal foundation of the lectures in medicine in Montpelier. Yet they maliciously insult and slander those who did them good and who taught them medicine, since Giles of Corbeil, physician of Paris, went to Montpelier to give public lectures, according to the report of Bale. You cannot deny that your School is indebted to Monsieur Bouvart, first physician to King Louis XIII, who assisted you in removing from your town the lieutenant of the first barber, who was diminishing your authority and jurisdiction over the surgeons.

units.la: En la forme de proceder à l'élection des Professeurs Royaux, i'y remarque vn grand abus, qui s'y commet auiourd'huy, fondé neantmoins sur le pied de la Lettre de Creation, en laquelle il y a, Qu'aduenant la vacance de quelque Lecture, pour la remplir, il sera pris d'autres notables Regens en ladite Vniuersité. Tellement que si tous les Docteurs de Montpelier sont esgaux pour les droits honorifiques, les Docteurs respandus par toute la France, doiuent estre admis à disputer la Lecture vacante. Or les quatre Professeurs de Montpelier, qui estoiét au temps, qu'ils obtindrent de Charles IX, vne nouuelle forme de proceder à l'élection, & nomination d'vn Professeur à la Lecture vacante, ont fait ordonner que ceux, qui pretendront à la Lecture vacante, seront receus à disputer sur les points donnez par les Professeurs aux Docteurs lisans actuellement en ladite Vniuersité. Or est-il qu'ils font lire deux Aggregez, pour les exercer, qui estans dans l'expectatiue, se preparant à cette dispute, & font aggreer auz Professeurs leurs amis, les points, sur lesquels ils sont desia preparez, par consequent conferent tousiours la Lecture à l'vn des deux Aggregez, à l'exclusion des autres Docteurs plus sçauans, qui n'ont pas leu actuellement dans l'Eschole de Montpelier. Voila comme se forment les Professeurs en Medecine de Montpelier, qui sont les plus sçauans de l'Europe, au dire de Courtaut: Regÿs sedibus vacantibus nobilis prouidendi ratio eorum qui ad disputationes admittuntur, conditiones, & electio: dequoy fait tant d'estat Courtaut.
units.tr: Regarding the manner of proceeding in the election of royal professors, I observe a great abuse which is committed there today, nevertheless based on the wording of the letter of creation, in which it says: That if any lectureship falls vacant, other notable regents of the said University shall be taken to fill it. So that if all the doctors of Montpelier are equal in honorary rights, the doctors scattered throughout France ought to be admitted to dispute for the vacant lectureship. Now the four professors of Montpelier, who at the time when they obtained from Charles IX a new form of proceeding in the election and nomination of a professor to a vacant lectureship, had it ordered that those who aspire to the vacant lectureship shall be received to dispute on the points given by the professors to the doctors actually lecturing in the said University. Now they cause two aggregates to be made to read, to exercise them, who, being in expectation and preparing themselves for this dispute, and have their friend professors approve the points on which they are already prepared; consequently they always confer the lectureship on one of the two aggregates, to the exclusion of the other, more learned doctors, who have not actually lectured in the School of Montpelier. This is how the professors of medicine of Montpelier are formed, who are the most learned in Europe, according to Courtaut: With the seats vacant, the noble method of providing for them, the conditions and the election of those who are admitted to the disputations; of which Courtaut makes so much account.

units.la: Il y a huict ans que deux Lectures estans vacantes, les Professeurs permirent aux Aggregez de les venir demander au Roy. Monsieur Bouuart, pour lors premier Medecin, s'y opposa, en parla au Roy, & les prouisions obtenues par les Aggregez, furent cassées, & renuoyées à la dispute. La corruption s'y estant glissée en la nomination des Aggregez, on y proceda de nouueau plus sincerement, & d'autres que les Aggregez obtindrent les Lectures, par l'entremise de Mosieur l'Euesque de Montpelier, qui prit le soin de cette affaire.
units.tr: Eight years ago, when two lectureships were vacant, the professors allowed the aggregates to go and ask the King for them. Monsieur Bouvart, then first physician, opposed this, spoke to the King, and the provisions obtained by the aggregates were quashed and referred back to the dispute. Corruption having crept into the nomination of the aggregates, the matter was again proceeded with more sincerely, and others than the aggregates obtained the lectureships, through the agency of Monsieur the Bishop of Montpelier, who took care of this affair.

units.la: Courtaut n'est-il pas ridicule de louer l'Eschole de Montpelier, qu'il appelle tousiours Vniuersité, pour estre composée d'vn petit nombre de Docteurs & Professeurs, mais tres-sçauans par dessus tous les Medecins de l'Europe? Quibus Phæbi chorus assurrexerit omnis. Donc quatre Medecins, qui composoient l'Eschole de Montpelier, maintenant accreus de deux, donneront la loy à tous les Medecins de l'Europe? La reformation de la Medecine dependra d'eux? Ils en donneront la tablature, le reglement, & la forme de pratiquer? A ce compte, tous les Medecins des Vniuersitez d'Italie, d'Espagne, d'Allemagne, d'Angleterre, ne sont rien à comparaison de l'Eschole de Montpelier, qui est la mere de toutes les autres, leur ayant donné des Maistres, pour les enseigner & former en la Medecine.
units.tr: Is not Courtaut ridiculous in praising the School of Montpelier, which he always calls a University, for being composed of a small number of doctors and professors, but very learned above all the physicians of Europe? To whom the whole chorus of Phoebus shall rise. So four physicians, who made up the School of Montpelier, now increased by two, will give the law to all the physicians of Europe? The reformation of medicine will depend on them? They will give its tables, its regulation, and the form of practice? At that rate, all the physicians of the universities of Italy, Spain, Germany and England are nothing in comparison with the School of Montpelier, which is the mother of all the others, having given them masters to teach and form them in medicine.

units.la: Ie ne parle point de Paris entre les Escholes de Medecine sçauantes, puis qu'illa qualifie la plus ignorante de la terre habitable, de laquelle les anciens Docteurs estoient des Saltinbancs, qui fautoient par les Carrefours de Paris, lors que l'Eschole de Montpelier estoit florissante: Calomnie horrible, qui meriteroit chastiment. Si ces huict Medecins sont auiourd'huy les plus sçauans, & ont tousiours esté, selon l'estimation de Courtaut, les premiers Medecins de nos derniers Rois, qui ont pris le Doctorat en l'Eschole de Montpelier, ceux de nostre temps, ne sont donc que des ignorans: & cependant le peuple croit que ce sont les plus doctes que l'on prend de l'Eschole de Montpelier. Il adiouste pour faire valoir ce petit nombre de Medecins, anciennement reduit à quatre, depuis [illegible, ~3 letters] ans à fix, ainsi qu'il a esté reglé par le Parlement de Toulouze, & ne peuuent estre dauantage : partant tous ceux qui sont Docteurs à Montpelier, ne peuuent demeurer dans la ville.
units.tr: I do not speak here of Paris among the learned schools of medicine, since it is the most ignorant school on the inhabited earth, whose old teachers were charlatans who performed their tricks at the crossroads of Paris at the time when the school of Montpelier was flourishing. This is a horrible calumny, and it deserves punishment. If these eight physicians are today the most learned, and have always been, according to the estimation of Courtaut, the first physicians of our last Kings, who took the doctorate in the school of Montpelier, then the physicians of our own time are nothing but ignoramuses. Yet the people believe that these are the most learned that one takes from the school of Montpelier. He adds, to make much of this small number of physicians, once reduced to four and now, for [illegible, about 3 letters] years, to six, as was regulated by the Parliament of Toulouse, and they cannot be more than that; therefore all those who are doctors at Montpelier cannot remain in the town.

units.la: Monstrons la folie du personnage. L'accorde qu'ils sont auiourd'huy fix, depuis que les deux Lectures ont esté creées & adioustées par Henry quatriesme, auant les quatre Lectures Royales, ils n'estoient que quatre pauures miserables, qui ont representé aux Roys Charles VIII. & Louis XII. leur pauureté, pour auoir des gages & des robes, autrement leur Eschole s'en alloit perir. Depuis ce temps-là ils n'ont esté que quatre Professeurs, n'ayät[?] aucun Aggregé. Ie le prouue par la Lettre de Charles IX. Les Rois nos predecesseurs ayans estably en nostre ville de Montpelier, Vniuersité de Medecine, composée de quatre Docteurs Regens en icelle. S'ils disent que cela s'entend d. Professeurs seulement, la teneur de la Lettre Patente est toute contraire. De plus, ie leur verifie ce nombre par la Lettre de Monsieur le Marefchal de Danuille, où l'exemption des Soldats est accordée aux quatre Docteurs Regens en la Faculté de Medecine de l'Vniuersité[?] de Montpelier : s'il y eut eu encore deux autres Aggregez, l'exemption euft esté aussi bien donnée pour fix, que pour quatre : ils ne deuoient pas laisser en arriere, & abandonner les deux confreres Regens : ils n'est point dit Professeurs du Roy. Tous les Docteurs de Montpelier, par leurs Lettres sont Regens, puis qu'ils leur donnent le pouuoir de regenter par tout, consequemment à Montpelier. Or auant les quatre Professeurs Royaux, il y a apparence qu'ils estoient en fort petit nombre, & qu'ils couroient la campagne pour voir les malades, & gagner leur vie.
units.tr: Let us show the folly of the man. I grant that they are six today, since the two lectureships were created and added by Henry IV; before the four Royal lectureships, they were only four poor wretches, who represented to the Kings Charles VIII and Louis XII their poverty, in order to have wages and robes, otherwise their school would have perished. From that time they were only four professors, having no aggregated members. I prove this by the letter of Charles IX: "The Kings our predecessors, having established in our town of Montpelier a University of Medicine, composed of four doctors regent in it." If they say that this is to be understood of the professors only, the tenor of the letters patent is entirely contrary. Moreover, I verify this number for them by the letter of Monsieur the Marshal de Danville, where exemption from soldiering is granted to the four doctors regent in the Faculty of Medicine of the University [?] of Montpelier: if there had been two other aggregated members, the exemption would have been given for six as well as for four; they ought not to have left behind and abandoned their two regent colleagues. It is nowhere said "Professors of the King." All the doctors of Montpelier are regents by their letters, since they give them the power to regent everywhere, and consequently at Montpelier. Now, before the four Royal professors, it is likely that they were very few in number, and that they roamed the countryside to visit the sick and earn their living.

units.la: Laurens Ioubert donnant le bonnet Doctoral à Iean Saporta, le prie de s'establir promptement à Montpelier, pour accroistre le nombre des Docteurs, qui leur manque, pour soustenir la dignité de l'Eschole. Vides hanc iusto Doctorum Medicorum numero à multis annis priuatam, miserèque orbatam. Il y a cent cinquante ans que les Docteurs qui enseignoient la Medecine dans Montpelier, estoient presques tous Espagnols, Portugais, Catelans, Arragonois. Ils s'en alloient aux vacances durant trois mois en leur païs, pour reuenir au temps des leçons, ainsi l'Eschole estoit deserte. Ie l'apprens par Ranchin, en son discours de l'Université de Montpelier. Estil croyable que le Parlement ait limité le nombre de quatre en cette fameuse Université? Pourquoy en exclure tous les autres Docteurs? Delà il est aisé de croire qu'il y a deux sortes de Docteurs, les uns pour demeurer, s'ils sont Aggregez, les autres pour sortir de la ville. S'ils estoient douze ou quinze Docteurs composans l'Eschole, elle seroit plus florissante: si six Docteurs sont aussi suffisans, que six vingt, pour terminer les differens de la Medecine, donner les decrets sur la pratique, reformer les abus & erreurs, on s'est fort trompé de faire des Synodes, des Conciles, de grandes assemblées aux Estats, pour decider les differens de la Religion & de l'Estat, & donner authorité aux decisions & resolutions qui s'y prennent.
units.tr: Laurens Joubert, bestowing the doctoral cap on Jean Saporta, asks him to settle promptly at Montpelier, to increase the number of doctors, which they lack in order to uphold the dignity of the school. "You see this, deprived for many years of its due number of doctors of medicine, and sadly orphaned." About one hundred and fifty years ago, the doctors who taught medicine in Montpelier were almost all Spaniards, Portuguese, Catalans, and Aragonese. During the holidays, for three months, they went back to their own countries, returning at the time of the lectures, so that the school was deserted. I learn this from Ranchin, in his discourse on the University of Montpelier. Is it credible that the Parliament limited the number to four in this famous University? Why exclude all the other doctors? From this it is easy to believe that there are two kinds of doctors: some to remain, if they are aggregated, and others to leave the town. If there were twelve or fifteen doctors composing the school, it would be more flourishing; if six doctors are as sufficient as sixty to settle the disputes of medicine, give the decrees on practice, and reform abuses and errors, then one has been greatly mistaken in holding synods, councils, and great assemblies of the Estates, to decide the disputes of religion and of the State, and to give authority to the decisions and resolutions made there.

units.la: J'adiouste que vous trompez vos jeunes Docteurs, quand vous leur donnez Lettres d'exercer la Medecine, hic & ubique terrarum: Puis qu'ils ne peuvent demeurer dans vostre ville, le nombre estant limité à six.
units.tr: I add that you deceive your young doctors when you give them letters to practise medicine "here and everywhere in the world," since they cannot remain in your town, the number being limited to six.

units.la: Le Sieur Ranchin reconnoissant la pauvreté de son Eschole, pour faire valoir le nombre, descrit quantité d'Officiers, qui la composent. Il y a un Chancelier, un Doyen, des Professeurs Royaux, des Docteurs Aggregez, des Procureurs de l'Université, des Licentiez, des Conseillers, des Estudians, des Bacheliers, des Escholiers, le Syndic, le Receueur, le Secretaire, le Bedeau. Voila une belle monstre d'Officiers, & tout cela reduit à quatre ou six Docteurs, dont l'un est Chancelier, l'autre Doyen; les deux autres sont Procureurs; tous quatre sont Professeurs, tellement que quatre tiennent toutes les charges & dignitez: Tout le reste ne sert de rien en la Medecine, pour enseigner & faire de sçauans Medecins; cela depend des quatre ou six Professeurs, qui composent cette fameuse Université.
units.tr: Sieur Ranchin, recognising the poverty of his school, and to make the number count, describes a multitude of officers who compose it. There is a Chancellor, a Dean, Royal Professors, Aggregated Doctors, Procurators of the University, Licentiates, Councillors, Students, Bachelors, Scholars, the Syndic, the Receiver, the Secretary, the Beadle. Here is a fine display of officers, and all of it reduced to four or six doctors, of whom one is Chancellor, another Dean, and the other two are Procurators; all four are Professors, so that four hold all the offices and dignities. All the rest serve nothing in medicine for teaching and producing learned physicians; that depends on the four or six Professors who compose this famous University.

units.la: C'est une vraye mommerie que cette grande liste & longue description d'Officiers de l'Escholle de Medecine de Montpelier, estant reduite à quatre ou six hommes, lesquels sont Examinateurs & Juges de la capacité des aspirans au Doctorat.
units.tr: That long list and lengthy description of officers of the school of medicine at Montpelier is a real farce, since it is reduced to four or six men, who are the examiners and judges of the competence of those seeking the doctorate.

units.la: Courtaut remarque une grande singularité en l'Escholle de Montpelier, c'est; qu'elle ne reçoit point aux degrez de Medecine, les bastards, ny ceux qui sont de mauuaise vie, ny les ignorans, ny ceux qui ont exercé vn art mechanique, comme la Chirurgie, ou Apothiquairerie. Voila une Escholle fort rigoureuse de reietter les bastards, s'ils font sçauans, & ceux qui ont exercé un art mechanique. Quant aux bastards, je sçay que les Jurisconsultes traittent cette question; s'ils doivent estre admis aux dignitez de l'Eglise, aux Offices de Judicature, & s'ils doivent estre receus aux degrez Academiques. Les plus raisonnables Jurisconsultes accordent, que si les bastards sont vertueux & sçauans; ayans effacé le peché originel de leurs parens, qu'ils peuvent estre admis en toutes ces dignitez. Je doute fort que ces Docteurs & Professeurs de Montpelier facent une enqueste de vita & moribus de l'aspirant au Doctorat.
units.tr: Courtaut remarks a great peculiarity in the school of Montpelier: "that it does not admit to the degrees of medicine bastards, nor those of bad life, nor the ignorant, nor those who have practised a mechanical art, such as surgery or apothecary work." This is a school very strict in rejecting bastards, if they are learned, and those who have practised a mechanical art. As for bastards, I know that the jurists treat this question: whether they ought to be admitted to the dignities of the Church, to judicial offices, and whether they ought to be received to academic degrees. The most reasonable jurists agree that if bastards are virtuous and learned, having erased the original sin of their parents, they may be admitted to all these dignities. I strongly doubt that these doctors and professors of Montpelier make an inquiry "concerning the life and morals" of the candidate for the doctorate.

units.la: Pour ce qui est de ceux qui ont exercé un art mechanique; nous voyons souvent de jeunes Barbiers & Chirurgiens de Paris, sachans un peu de Latin, estre receus Docteurs à Montpelier. Ils en font de mesme des Compagnons Apothiquaires. C'est le sujet du refus qu'ont fait les Medecins de Rouen d'un fils d'Apothiquaire, qui avoit durant sept ou huit ans demeuré en la boutique de son pere à Rouen, exerçant l'Apothiquairerie: ayant pris ses degrez à Montpelier, il voulut estre receu dans la ville en montrant ses Bulles Montpelliennes, sans examen: il fit un Factum contre les Medecins de Rouen, qui composerent cette docte response, d'où est tirée la censure de l'Eschole de Montpelier, que i'ay alleguée cy-dessus.
units.tr: As for those who have practised a mechanical art: we often see young barbers and surgeons of Paris, knowing a little Latin, being received as doctors at Montpelier. They do the same with journeyman apothecaries. This is the reason for the refusal by the physicians of Rouen of a son of an apothecary, who had for seven or eight years remained in his father's shop at Rouen, practising apothecary work. Having taken his degrees at Montpelier, he wished to be received in the town by showing his "Montpellier bulls," without examination. He made a memorial against the physicians of Rouen, who composed that learned reply, from which is drawn the censure of the school of Montpelier that I cited above.

units.la: Ie demanderois volontiers à Courtaut, si l'Apothiquairerie est un art mechanique, la Chymie ne l'est-elle pas de mesme, estant plus laborieuse, & plus sordide que l'Apothiquairerie commune? Cela estant posé, comme il est tres-veritable, ceux qui ont exercé cét art mechanique, qui ont vendu des medicamens Chymiques, & qui en vendent encore, ou tiennent ce trafic par d'autres, doivent-ils estre receus au Doctorat? & s'ils sont Docteurs, n'ont-ils pas derogé à la dignité Doctorale; par consequent meritent d'estre degradez. Prenez garde, Monsieur Courtaut, à cét advertissement que ie vous donne, afin de conserver exactement vos belles constitutions, & vos specieux reglemens, desquels nous n'avons encore rien veu d'imprimé & publié, comme nous avôs fait des nostres.
units.tr: I would gladly ask Courtaut: if apothecary-work is a mechanical art, is chemistry not the same, being more laborious and more sordid than ordinary apothecary-work? That granted, as is most true, those who have practised this mechanical art, who have sold chemical medicines, and who still sell them, or carry on this trade through others, ought they to be received into the Doctorate? And if they are Doctors, have they not derogated from the dignity of the Doctorate, and so deserve to be degraded? Take care, Monsieur Courtaut, to heed this warning I give you, so that you may exactly preserve your fine constitutions and your specious regulations, of which we have yet seen nothing printed and published, as we have done with ours.

units.la: Vous n'avez pas pris garde à ce que vous faisiez, quand vous avez donné assistance & adjonction à Renaudot, plaidant contre la Faculté de Medecine de Paris. Il exerçoit dans son Bureau d'Adresse, un mestier infame, qui est l'usure, & autres trafics de toute forte de marchandise, sous pretexte de vente à grace: Ce faisant, il a derogé à la qualité de Docteur en Medecine de Montpelier, & ne la peut retenir legitimement.
units.tr: You did not take care over what you were doing when you gave assistance and support to Renaudot in his suit against the Faculty of Medicine of Paris. In his Bureau d'Adresse he practised an infamous trade, which is usury, and other dealings in every sort of merchandise, under the pretext of sale on credit. In doing so he has derogated from the status of Doctor of Medicine of Montpellier, and cannot lawfully retain it.

units.la: Le Gazettier a reconnu son exercice du Bureau d'Adresse, pour composer & debiter des Gazettes, deroger à l'honneur d'un Medecin, quand il a permis que ses deux enfans ayent renoncé par serment, & par escrit, par deuant Notaires, au mestier du pere, promettant de ne iamais s'en mesler, autrement, qu'ils consentoient d'estre reiettez de l'Eschole. Vous auez emprunté cette Loy de nostre Eschole. Elle est escrite & expliquée en l'article 24. de nos Constitutions. Si quis inter Baccalaureos federit[?], qui Chirurgiam, aut artem manuariam exercuerit, ad Licentias non admittatur, nisi priùs fidem suam adstringat publicis Notariorum instrumentis, se nunquam posthac Chirurgiam, aut aliam artem manuariam exercituram, idque in Collegii Medici commentarios referatur, ordinis enim Medici dignitatem, curam, integramque conseruari par est.
units.tr: The Gazetteer acknowledged that his practice of the Bureau d'Adresse, for composing and selling the Gazettes, derogated from the honour of a physician, when he allowed his two children to renounce, by oath and in writing, before notaries, the father's trade, promising never to meddle in it, on pain of otherwise consenting to be expelled from the School. You have borrowed this law from our School. It is written and explained in article 24 of our Constitutions. If anyone among the Bachelors shall have practised surgery, or a manual art, he shall not be admitted to the licences unless he first bind his faith by public instruments of notaries, that he will never hereafter practise surgery or any other manual art; and this shall be recorded in the commentaries of the College of Medicine, for it is right that the dignity, care and integrity of the medical order be preserved.

units.la: Et de fait, un Docteur en Medecine de Paris, nommé Nicolas, ayant exercé l'Office de Lieutenant Particulier à Beauuais, soustenoit n'auoir point quitté l'estude & l'exercice de la Medecine, voulut apres 40. ans rentrer dans nos Escholes, nous ne l'auons pas voulu receuoir, pour s'estre meslé d'un autre exercice que de celuy de la Medecine.
units.tr: And indeed, a Doctor of Medicine of Paris, named Nicolas, who had held the office of Lieutenant Particulier at Beauvais, maintained that he had never given up the study and practice of medicine, and after forty years wished to re-enter our Schools. We did not wish to receive him, because he had meddled in another occupation than that of medicine.

units.la: Dans les Statuts de l'Universitez de Louvain, il y a un article exprés, qui porte, Doctores, Licentiati, subditi, priuilegiis gaudeant, ea tamen lege, ut quæ litteraria profesioni repugnant nequaquam exercverint, non quæstores aliorum sint toparcharum, non urbium Prætores, non alio sæculari Magistratu fungentes, multo minus mercaturam, aut ullam artem aliquam exercentes.
units.tr: In the Statutes of the Universities of Louvain there is an express article which reads: Doctors and Licentiates, being subject, may enjoy the privileges, but on this condition, that they shall in no way practise what is repugnant to their literary profession: they shall not be tax-farmers of other men's estates, nor governors of cities, nor hold any other secular magistracy, much less engage in trade or practise any other art.

units.la: Il est tres-constant qu'en toutes les Universitez d'Allemagne, les Licentiez ou Docteurs, qui se meslent de marchandise ou d'autres mestiers, que de leur profession, sont privez des Privileges de l'Academie, comme le prouue Bezoldus lib. de privileg. Acad. Cothomannus in responsis Academicis, & VValterus lib. de Statu Doctorum. Rebuffus dit qu'en l'Université de Paris, les Estudians jouïssent des Privileges concedez par les Papes, & les Roys de France, pourveu qu'ils ne s'entremeslent de marchandise : & les Libraires pareillement en jouïssent s'ils ne se meslent que de la Librairie. Nicolaus Florentinus defend aux Medecins de se meslier de la marchandise, qui destourne de l'estude, & de la visite frequente des malades. Hippocrate, qui doit estre le Iuge de cette question, commande, libro, de decenti ornatu, alienationem à mercimoniis, ἀπεμπολησιν[?]. Les Anciens auoient raison d'aduertir, que chacun se meslât de sa profession. Hoc unum age, Spartam quam nactus es orna, Sainct Paul defend de se mesler des affaires qui n'appartiennent pas à sa profession, Ut quisque vocatus est, ita ambulet.
units.tr: It is quite certain that in all the Universities of Germany, Licentiates or Doctors who meddle in merchandise or in occupations other than their profession are deprived of the privileges of the Academy, as Bezoldus proves in his book on the privileges of the Academy, Cothmann in his Academic Responses, and Walther in his book on the State of Doctors. Rebuffus says that in the University of Paris students enjoy the privileges granted by the Popes and the Kings of France, provided they do not engage in trade; and booksellers likewise enjoy them if they meddle only in bookselling. Nicolaus Florentinus forbids physicians to engage in trade, which distracts from study and from frequent visiting of the sick. Hippocrates, who ought to be the judge of this question, commands, in the book On Decent Ornament, abstention from trading, apempolēsin [ἀπεμπολησιν]. The Ancients were right to warn that each man should attend to his own profession. Hoc unum age: "Whatever you have undertaken, adorn Sparta"; Saint Paul forbids meddling in affairs that do not belong to one's profession: Ut quisque vocatus est, ita ambulet: "let each walk as he was called."

units.la: En toutes les Prouinces, où le trafic de marchandise en gros, ou tenir banque ne deroge point à la Noblesse, il n'est pas permis au Medecin de faire le mesme, s'il veut iouir des Priuileges de l'Vniuersité : tant nos Anciens ont esté curieux, & soigneux de recommander aux Medecins d'étudier continuellement, & d'employer tout leur temps en leur vacation & profession. Il ne sert de rien, & n'est pas vne excuse valable, d'alleguer qu'on fait faire ce negoce par des commis, qui fait faire son negoce par autruy en receuant le profit, est reputé le faire soy mesme. Ainsi Bodin l'a iugé en sa Republique, liu. 3. cap. 8. Le trouue que par les Statuts de l'Vniuersité de Tubinge, Vsurarij fœneratores indigni qui Doctoratum ambiant, & si obtinuerint eo priuentur. Petrus Gregerius Tolosanus adioufte, qu'un Docteur qui a negligé sa profession, & n'a pas estudié comme il deuoit, doit estre interrogé derechef pour voir s'il est capable de l'exercer.
units.tr: In all the Provinces where wholesale trade, or keeping a bank, does not derogate from nobility, it is not permitted for a physician to do the same if he wishes to enjoy the privileges of the University: so greatly were our Ancients careful and concerned to exhort physicians to study continually and to spend all their time in their calling and profession. It is of no use, and is no valid excuse, to allege that this business is carried on by clerks; for one who has his business carried on by another, receiving the profit, is reputed to do it himself. So Bodin judged in his Republic, book 3, chapter 8. I find that by the Statutes of the University of Tübingen, "usurers and moneylenders, unworthy, who seek the doctorate, and if they obtain it, shall be deprived of it." Peter Gregory of Toulouse adds that a Doctor who has neglected his profession, and has not studied as he ought, must be examined again to see whether he is capable of practising it.

units.la: Il se remarque vne grande singularité en l'Eschole de Montpelier : c'est qu'elle a fourny beaucoup de Medecins aux Papes, Empereurs, Rois, & grands Princes de la terre : ce quon ne peut prouuer de l'Vniuersité de Paris. C'est la verité que les Papes faisans leur seiour en Avignon, ils ont eu à leur seruice des Medecins de Montpelier. Ioubert en ses Commentaires sur Guy de Cauliac, rapporte que Jan de Alesto, & Guidon, ont esté Chapelains & Medecins du Pape Clement VI. ledit Guidon le tesmoigne, mais je doute fort qu'Arnaud de Ville-neufue ait seruy les Papes, & qu'il fut Docteur de Montpelier ; & partant je soupçonne de fausseté[?], auec grande raison, la Bulle de Clement VI. qui nomme, & ioint Arnaud de Ville-neufue auec Jean de Alesto, comme s'ils eussent esté contemporains, & pris de la ville de Montpelier, comme je feray voir tres-clairement. Symphorianus Campegius, Docteur de Montpelier, Medecin sçauant pour le temps, & homme de bien, qui vivoit du regne de Louis XII. & de François premier, a descrit succinctement la vie des Medecins d'Italie & de France: parlant des François, il a nommé ceux qui estoient de Montpelier, Docteurs, Doyens, & Chanceliers: mais parlant d'Arnaud de Ville neufue, il doute s'il est Provençal, ou Catalan, & ne dit point qu'il fut Docteur de Montpelier. Ledit Campegius a descrit plus amplement la vie d'Arnaud de Ville-neufue, qu'on trouuera au commencement de ses œuures; il ne le qualifie point Docteur de Montpelier, mais qu'il vint à vingt ans à Paris, où il a demeuré iusques à trente, à cause de la celebrité de l'Eschole de Medecine qui estoit florissante. Il auoit son Parent, Oncle, ou Coufin, qui se nommoit, Iean de Ville-neufue, Medecin de Paris, duquel estant Doyen, nous auons vn Decret, que chaque Medecin de Paris, n'aura que deux Escholiers ou Bacheliers à sa suite, allant voir les malades, dautant qu'il faisoit gloire d'en auoir sept ou huict. Ledit Arnaud de Ville-neufue, in suo Breuiario Practica, fait mention des Medecins de Paris, d'vn Campanus, d'vn Vrso, & de Muffandini: Il declare en quoy differoit la pratique des Medecins de Paris, d'auec celle de Montpelier. Campegius adiouste qu'ayant demeuré dix ans à Paris, il s'en alla à Montpelier. Ie trouue dans sa Pratique, qu'il a demeuré à Montpelier, & ne pût guerir un jeune hõme qui avoit un flux de sang, tresgrand, durant trois jours & trois nuicts, qu'une femme guerit avec une herbe. Il parle en son Breuiaire, de Guy de Cauliac, qu'il a connu, & nomme d'autres Medecins de cette Eschole. Delà il s'en alla au Royaume de Naples, où la Medecine estoit celebre, à cause de l'Eschole de Salerne. Il se mit à la suite d'un grand Medecin Praticien, nommé Joannes Casamides, qu'il appelle mille fois son Maistre, qui estoit demeurant à Naples, & l'accompagnoit par tout chez les malades. Il ne parle d'aucune maladie, qu'il ne rapporte la pratique & l'experience de son bon Maistre Casamides. Il a esté à Ferrare, il a pratiqué à Boulogne, il a demeuré à Florence, mais il ne parle point qu'il ait esté à la suite d'aucun Pape, ny d'avoir esté à Rome. Il dit bien avoir assisté un jeune homme neveu d'Alexandre Pape, mais il ne declare point le lieu, où il l'a veu ; il est croyable que ce fut à Naples. Apres la mort de son bon Maistre, il se mit à recueillir tout ce qu'il avoit appris, pratiquant avec luy. S'estant donc retiré dans un Monastere de Religieux de Casa noua, de l'Ordre de Cisteaux, aimé des Religieux, de l'Abbé, & du Prieur, en leur faveur il descriuit comme il falloit rabattre la sensualité de Venus, de sorte que ce n'est point ad instantiam Papæ, qu'il a fait son Breviaire de Pratique : Il est vray qu'il a escrit un Conseil de febre quar-tana ad Clementem Patrem, sans specifier lequel. Il a escrit un Conseil de præseruatione & curatione calculi ad sanctissimum Patrem. Je croy que c'est ou Alexandre IV. ou Urbain V. Il a escrit regimen sanitatis ad inclitum Regem Arragonum, sans declarer le nom & surnom du Roy. Campegius rapporte que le Roy Federic l'ayant envoyé pour visiter le Pape malade, sans dire lequel, qu'il mourut sur la mer, & fut enterré à Genes. Il est croyable que c'estoit pour aller en Avignon, puis qu'il en prenoit le chemin sur les Galeres. Partant je maintiens qu'Arnaud de Ville-neufue n'a pas esté prés des Papes en Avignon, qu'il n'a point esté Docteur de Montpelier, mais sortant de ce lieu, alla estudier à Naples. Quelques Historiens & Annalistes rapportent qu'Arnaud de Ville-neufue a vescu à Paris, faisant profession de la Medecine, Alchymie, & Magie. Il avoit proposé quinze propositions heretiques, qui sont rapportées par Bzouius. Nous trouvons qu'il a esté prisonnier à Paris, dans sainct Denis de la Chartre, pour ses heresies, & s'est sauué de France. Ie croy que ce fut au mesme temps que Petrus Aponensis, son Maistre, Docteur de Paris, soubçonné d'heresie, & de magie, s'enfuit en Italie, & mourut à Padoüe. Voyez Petrus Castellanus, de vitis illustrium Medicorum.
units.tr: There is a remarkable peculiarity in the School of Montpellier: it has supplied many physicians to the Popes, Emperors, Kings and great princes of the earth, which cannot be proved of the University of Paris. It is true that when the Popes were residing at Avignon, they had physicians from Montpellier in their service. Joubert, in his Commentaries on Guy de Chauliac, reports that Jan de Alesto and Guidon were chaplains and physicians to Pope Clement VI. Guidon himself attests this, but I very much doubt that Arnaud de Villeneuve served the Popes, or that he was a Doctor of Montpellier. Accordingly, I suspect with good reason that the Bull of Clement VI, which names Arnaud de Villeneuve together with Jean de Alesto as though they were contemporaries and both came from the city of Montpellier, is false[?], as I shall show very clearly. Symphorianus Campegius, a Doctor of Montpellier, a physician learned for his time and an honest man, who lived under the reigns of Louis XII and Francis I, has described briefly the lives of the physicians of Italy and France. Speaking of the French, he named those who were of Montpellier as Doctors, Deans and Chancellors; but speaking of Arnaud de Villeneuve, he doubts whether he was Provençal or Catalan, and does not say that he was a Doctor of Montpellier. The same Campegius has described the life of Arnaud de Villeneuve more fully, which may be found at the beginning of his works; he does not call him a Doctor of Montpellier, but says that he came to Paris at the age of twenty, where he remained until thirty, on account of the fame of the School of Medicine, which was flourishing. He had a relative, an uncle or cousin, named Jean de Villeneuve, a physician of Paris, and while he was Dean there we have a decree that each physician of Paris should have only two scholars or bachelors following him when he visited the sick, since he took pride in having seven or eight. The same Arnaud de Villeneuve, in his Breviarium Practicae, mentions the physicians of Paris, a Campanus, a Vrso, and Muffandinus; he explains how the practice of the physicians of Paris differed from that of Montpellier. Campegius adds that, having lived ten years in Paris, he went to Montpellier. I find in his Practice that he did live at Montpellier, and that he could not cure a young man who had a very great flow of blood for three days and three nights, which a woman cured with an herb. In his Breviarium he speaks of Guy de Chauliac, whom he knew, and names other physicians of this School. From there he went to the Kingdom of Naples, where medicine was celebrated because of the School of Salerno. He attached himself to a great practising physician named Joannes Casamides, whom he calls his Master a thousand times, who lived at Naples and accompanied him everywhere to the sick. He never speaks of any disease without reporting the practice and experience of his good Master Casamides. He was at Ferrara, he practised at Bologna, he lived at Florence, but he never says that he attended any Pope, or that he was at Rome. He does say that he attended a young man, a nephew of Pope Alexander, but he does not state the place where he saw him; it is credible that it was at Naples. After the death of his good Master, he set himself to gather all that he had learned, practising with him. Having then retired into a monastery of religious de Casanova, of the Order of Cîteaux, beloved by the religious, the Abbot and the Prior, in their favour he described how sensuality of Venus must be curbed; so it is not ad instantiam Papae that he made his Breviarium Practicae. It is true that he wrote a counsel de febre quartana ad Clementem Patrem, without specifying which one. He wrote a counsel de praeservatione et curatione calculi ad sanctissimum Patrem. I believe it was either Alexander IV or Urban V. He wrote regimen sanitatis ad inclitum Regem Arragonum, without stating the king's name and surname. Campegius reports that King Frederick sent him to visit the sick Pope, without saying which, and that he died at sea and was buried at Genoa. It is credible that this was on his way to Avignon, since he was taking that route on the galleys. Therefore I maintain that Arnaud de Villeneuve was not near the Popes at Avignon, that he was not a Doctor of Montpellier, but that, leaving that place, he went to study at Naples. Some historians and annalists report that Arnaud de Villeneuve lived at Paris, professing medicine, alchemy and magic. He had put forward fifteen heretical propositions, which are reported by Bzovius. We find that he was imprisoned at Paris, in the Dungeon of Saint-Denis, for his heresies, and that he escaped from France. I believe it was at the same time that Petrus Aponensis, his Master, a Doctor of Paris, suspected of heresy and magic, fled to Italy and died at Padua. See Petrus Castellanus, de vitis illustrium Medicorum.

units.la: Au lieu d'Arnaud de Villeneufue, que i'ay osté du nombre des Medecins de Montpelier, & de ceux qui ont feruy les Papes, i'en produiray vn autre, inconnu aux Docteurs de Montpelier, qui est Raymundus à Vinario, qui a escrit vn liure de Peste, que Dalechamp a mis en meilleur Latin, le iugeant digne d'estre leu. Il a esté Medecin de trois Papes, qui ont demeuré successiuement en Auignon. Schenckius, en sa Bibliotheque Medicinale, nous aduertit, qu'il a deux exemplaires manuscrits de Raymundus Chalin, de Vinario, Medecin de Montpelier:Il florissoit l'an 1382. Il parle d'Arnaud de Villeneufue en deux ou trois endroits, & de la pratique des Medecins de Montpelier, qui donnoient de la casse à l'entrée de table, pour euiter les inconueniens, qui en pouuoient arriuer, tels qu'il les escrit, n'approuuant pas beaucoup ce remede.
units.tr: Instead of Arnaud de Villeneuve, whom I have removed from the number of the physicians of Montpellier and of those who served the Popes, I will produce another, unknown to the Doctors of Montpellier, who is Raymundus a Vinario, who wrote a book on Plague, which Dalechamp put into better Latin, judging it worthy to be read. He was physician to three Popes who resided at Avignon in succession. Schenckius, in his Bibliotheca Medicinalis, informs us that he has two manuscript copies of Raymundus Chalin, de Vinario, physician of Montpellier; he flourished in the year 1382. He speaks of Arnaud de Villeneuve in two or three places, and of the practice of the physicians of Montpellier, who gave cassia at the beginning of a meal to avoid the inconveniences that might arise from it, such as he describes them; he does not greatly approve of this remedy.

units.la: Voyons maintenant si les Docteurs de Montpelier ont esté Medecins des Empereurs : Je n'en trouve pas un seul, & je voudrois pour leur honneur qu'ils en euffent nommé un, seulement. C'est un erreur de croire que les Medecins de Charlemagne ayent esté Ferragius, Juif, Hali Baha Bengesla, aufquels il commanda de faire le liure des Taquins, ou Tables de Santé, qui sont imprimez à Strasbourg. C'est un Arabe, ou Juif, qui porte un autre nom. Schenckius en sa Bibliotheque, a trompé la posterité, nommant ces Autheurs de la version, qui vivoient du temps de Charlemagne ; mais il ne dit pas qu'ils fussent ses Medecins, encore moins Medecins de Montpelier, qui n'estoit qu'une bourgade du temps de Charlemagne.
units.tr: Let us now see whether the Doctors of Montpellier were physicians to the Emperors. I find not a single one, and I would wish for their honour that they had named at least one. It is an error to believe that the physicians of Charlemagne were Ferragius, a Jew, Hali Baha Bengesla, to whom he commanded that the book of the Taquins, or Tables of Health, which are printed at Strasbourg, should be made. It is an Arab or Jew who bears another name. Schenckius in his Bibliotheca has deceived posterity by naming these authors of the translation, who lived in the time of Charlemagne; but he does not say that they were his physicians, still less physicians of Montpellier, which was only a small market town in the time of Charlemagne.

units.la: Venons aux Medecins de Montpelier : vous n'en produisez aucun, qui ait servy les Rois d'Arragon, durant qu'ils estoient possesseurs de la ville ; ce qui me fait croire qu'ils n'ont pas fait grand estat des Medecins de Montpelier. Ils avoient l'Vniversité de Lerida, tres-ancienne, & tres-celebre du temps des Romains, d'où ils tiroient leurs Medecins. Mais nos Docteurs de Montpelier, font trophée d'avoir servy presque tous les Rois de France, depuis qu'elle est devenuë Françoise.
units.tr: Let us come to the physicians of Montpellier. You produce none who served the kings of Aragon while they held the city, which makes me believe they did not set much store by the physicians of Montpellier. They had the University of Lérida, very ancient and very famous in Roman times, from which they drew their physicians. But our doctors of Montpellier boast of having served almost all the kings of France since the city became French.

units.la: Examinons cét article, & monstrons les fautes qu'a commises le Sieur Ranchin, aux Eloges des Medecins, qu'il a fait graver, & placer dans la Sale du College de Medecine. Il me semble qu'il deuoit commencer la liste des Medecins Royaux par Adam Fumée, qui a esté premier Medecin de Charles VII. On le qualifie de la qualité de Chancelier, mais c'est la verité, qu'estant l'ancien Maistre des Requestes, aduenant la mort du Chancelier Guillaume de Rochefort, il a tenu quelques mois le Seau, iusqu'à l'election du Chancelier du Prat, comme l'a fort bien prouvé Monsieur Naudé, au commencement de son liure des Additions à la vie de Louys XI. Si on se veut preualoir de la qualité de Châcelier: Ie produiray contre luy ce qu'en dit Belleforest, en ses Annales de France, que Louys XI. aduançoit des gens de peu, il a fait son Medecin aussi grand que son Barbier Olivier Dain: Philippe de Comines, ne parle point dans son histoire d'Adam Fumée, pour la Medecine; il nomme seulement deux Medecins du Roy, Angelo Catto, & Iacques Cottier, sur la fin, qui n'a esté que cinq mois auec le Roy: Philippe de Comines parlant de la maladie du Roy, en l'an 1479. au mois de Mars, il ne parle que d'Angelo Catto, & des remedes, qu'il luy fit. Il estoit Neapolitain, & grand Astrologue, & fut Archeuesque de Vienne, grand amy de Comines, lequel certifie qu'Adam Fumée arriua, le Roy se portant mieux, auec Maistre Claude Medecin, & que Adam Fumée estoit Maistre des Requestes, naguères Medecin de Charles VII. Partant il ne se mesloit plus de la Medecine.
units.tr: Let us examine this article and point out the errors committed by Sieur Ranchin in the eulogies of the physicians, which he had engraved and placed in the hall of the College of Medicine. It seems to me he ought to have begun the list of royal physicians with Adam Fumée, who was first physician to Charles VII. He is styled Chancellor, but the truth is that, being the former Master of Requests, when the Chancellor Guillaume de Rochefort died, he held the Seal for some months until the election of Chancellor du Prat, as Monsieur Naudé has very well proved at the beginning of his book on the Additions to the life of Louis XI. If one wishes to rely on the title of Chancellor, I will set against him what Belleforest says in his Annals of France: that Louis XI advanced men of low station, and made his physician as great as his barber Olivier Dain. Philippe de Comines does not mention Adam Fumée in his history as a physician; he names only two royal physicians, Angelo Catto and Jacques Cottier, the latter at the end, who was with the King only five months. Philippe de Comines, speaking of the King's illness in March of the year 1479, mentions only Angelo Catto and the remedies he gave him. He was a Neapolitan and a great astrologer, and was Archbishop of Vienne, a close friend of Comines, who certifies that Adam Fumée arrived, the King being better, together with Master Claude, a physician, and that Adam Fumée was Master of Requests, lately physician to Charles VII. Therefore he no longer meddled with medicine.

units.la: Ie remarque vne grande bevuë arriuée au Sieur Ranchin, quand il escrit qu'Adam Fumée est decedé l'an1400.Commenta-t-il pû estre Medecin de Charles VII. Louis XI. Charles VIII. puis que Charles VII. est decedé l'an 1461.
units.tr: I note a great blunder made by Sieur Ranchin when he writes that Adam Fumée died in the year 1400. Could he have been physician to Charles VII, Louis XI and Charles VIII, since Charles VII died in the year 1461?

units.la: Pour Deodatus Baffolus, n'ayant rien appris de certain de luy, ie doute fort de ses qualitez, il peut auoir esté sçauant Medecin, au moins Monsieur Ranchin le dit, mais ce a esté vne chandelle cachée sous le boisseau, puis qu'il n'a rien escrit. Il est loüé pour auoir affectionné l'Eschole de Montpelier, & auoir fait reuenir vn College qu'on auoit soustrait[?] aux Medecins.
units.tr: As for Deodatus Baffolus, having learned nothing certain about him, I greatly doubt his qualifications. He may have been a learned physician, at least Monsieur Ranchin says so, but it was a candle hidden under a bushel, since he wrote nothing. He is praised for having been devoted to the School of Montpellier and for having restored a college which had been taken away from the physicians.

units.la: Quant à Ioannes Troffeleri, il n'a point esté premier Medecin du Roy Charles VIII. & ne l'a pas suiuy au voyage de Naples, & n'est pas mort à Sienne, comme porte son inscription en l'an 1495. Il y auoit audit voyage avec le Roy pour premier Medecin, Mai-stre Jean Michel, excellent Docteur, qui mourut le douziesme jour d'Aoust, l'an 1491. à Quiers, fort regretté du Roy, comme vous apprendrez par le Journal du voyage fait par saint Gelais, Evesque d'Angoulesme, qui fut de la suite du Roy: & par vn autre Journal d'Antoine de la Vigne, Secretaire de la Reine Anne de Bretagne. Par là vous voyez que l'Inscription de Trosselleri est fausse.
units.tr: As for Ioannes Troffeleri, he was never first physician to King Charles VIII, did not follow him on the voyage to Naples, and did not die at Siena, as his inscription states in the year 1495. On that voyage the first physician with the King was Master Jean Michel, an excellent doctor, who died on the twelfth day of August, 1491, at Quiers, greatly lamented by the King, as you will learn from the Journal of the voyage made by Saint-Gelais, Bishop of Angoulême, who was in the King's retinue, and from another Journal by Antoine de la Vigne, secretary to Queen Anne of Brittany. From this you see that Trosselleri's inscription is false.

units.la: Pour les autres Medecins, qu'il dit avoir suivy Charles VIII. i'en doute fort, si la Lettre Patente du Roy Charles VIII. qui est alleguée, est veritable, où Joannes Martini est nommé: il doit preceder Trosselleri, d'autant qu'il est decedé quatre ans auparavânt. J'ay déja monstré que Jacques Ponceau, n'a point esté Docteur de Montpelier, & partant ie l'oste de la liste.
units.tr: As for the other physicians whom he says followed Charles VIII, I greatly doubt whether the letters patent of King Charles VIII cited for them, in which Joannes Martini is named, are genuine. He must come before Trosselleri, since he died four years earlier. I have already shown that Jacques Ponceau was never a doctor of Montpellier, and therefore I remove him from the list.

units.la: Pour ce qui est de Honoratus Picquetus, & Joannes Graßini, ils sont venus en Cour pour solliciter les gages des quatre Professeurs, ils peuuent avoir eu Lettres de Medecins du Roy, par quartier, ou ad honores, comme plusieurs ont encor aujourd'huy.
units.tr: As for Honoratus Picquetus and Joannes Graßini, they came to Court to solicit the salaries of the four professors. They may have had letters making them physicians to the King by quarter, or ad honores, as many have even today.

units.la: I' accorde que Gabriel Miron a pû estre Medecin du Roy Charles VIII. estant premier Medecin & Chancelier d'Anne de Bretagne, son Espoufe, mais il eft faux qu'il foit mort allant feruir le Roy Charles 8. à Neuers, dautant qu'en l'an 1511. il vint prier les Medecins de Paris, auec Lettres de recommandation de la Reine Anne de Bretagne,sa Maistreffe,pour faire receuoir son fils Bachelier auant l'âge, qui estoit François Miron, pere de Marc Miron, qui a esté premier Medecin de Henry III. partant il estoit en vie durant le regne de Louys XII.
units.tr: I grant that Gabriel Miron may have been physician to King Charles VIII, being first physician and Chancellor to Anne of Brittany, his spouse, but it is false that he died going to serve King Charles VIII at Nevers, since in the year 1511 he came to beg the physicians of Paris, with letters of recommendation from Queen Anne of Brittany, his mistress, to have his son admitted Bachelor before the required age. This son was François Miron, father of Marc Miron, who was first physician to Henry III. Therefore he was alive during the reign of Louis XII.

units.la: Symphorian Champier,sçauant Medecin de Montpelier, qui viuoit du temps de Louys XII. & quia escrit l'histoire de ce Roy, ne parle point de Honoratus Piquetus, en ses lures de Medecine, ny en l'histoire de ce Roy:il en nomme trois, Salomon de Bombellis, Cheualier, Seigneur de Lauaux: Maistre André Briau, & Louys Burgensis: l'Historiographe d'Autun, parlant du voyage de Genes, que fit ce Roy, ne fait mention que de deux Medecins qui le suiuirent, Maistre Salomon, & Maistre André. En l'année 1550. Portasius fit le Paranymphe des Escholes de Medecine; & loüant vn Licentié, nommé Simon Burgensis, qui estoit de race de Medecine, il dit que son grand Pere, Ioannes Burggensis[?], auoit esté Medecin de Charles VIII. puis premier Medecin de Louys XII. & que le Roy voulut estre Parain d'vn sien fils, qu'il nomma de son nom Louys, lequel estant paruenu à l'âge de 22. ans, à la recommandation de son pere ; fut Docteur de l'Eschole de Paris, suiuit la fortune du Roy Francois premier. Durant sa prison en Espagne, il feignit que le Roy estoit malade d'vne langueur, qui l'emporteroit bien tost ; L'Empereur Charles-Quint, qui aimoit mieux l'argent que la personne, accorda la rançon, sur la crainte qu'il auoit de la mort du Roy Francois.
units.tr: Symphorien Champier, a learned physician of Montpellier, who lived in the time of Louis XII and who wrote the history of that King, does not mention Honoratus Piquetus, either in his books of medicine or in the history of this King. He names three: Salomon de Bombellis, knight, Lord of Lavaux; Master André Briau; and Louis Burgensis. The historiographer of Autun, speaking of the voyage to Genoa which this King made, mentions only two physicians who followed him, Master Salomon and Master André. In the year 1550 Portasius delivered the Paranymph of the Schools of Medicine, and in praising a licentiate named Simon Burgensis, who was of a family of physicians, he says that his grandfather, Ioannes Burggensis, had been physician to Charles VIII, then first physician to Louis XII; and that the King wished to be godfather to one of his sons, whom he named Louis after himself. This son, having reached the age of twenty-two, at his father's recommendation, became a Doctor of the School of Paris and followed the fortune of King François I.
