During his imprisonment in Spain, he pretended that the King was suffering from a wasting illness which would soon carry him off. The Emperor Charles V, who loved money more than the person, agreed to the ransom, from fear of the King François' death.

units.la: Quant à Castellan, c'estoit vn bel esprit, grand Courtisan, qui se plaisoit à la Cour, & auoit vn sien parent Euesque de Toulon, en grande reputatiou du temps de Francois I. & Henry II. Il a esté Medecin du Roy par quartier, tenant vne lecture de l'Eschole de Montpelier. Il a esté quelque temps premier Medecin de la Reine Mere Catherine de Medicis ; il est decedé au siege de S. Iean d'Angely. Apres luy a esté Vigoraus, Docteur de Paris, comme vous apprendrez par l'Epistre dedicatoire de Quinquarboreus, en la version des liures d'Aucinne.
units.tr: As for Castellan, he was a man of wit and a great courtier, who took pleasure in the Court, and had a relative, a Bishop of Toulon, in great repute in the time of François I and Henry II. He was physician to the King by quarter, holding a lectureship of the School of Montpellier. For some time he was first physician to the Queen Mother, Catherine de' Medici; he died at the siege of Saint-Jean-d'Angély. After him came Vigoraus, a Doctor of Paris, as you will learn from the dedicatory epistle of Quinquarboreus, in his version of the books of Aucinne.

units.la: Voyant que le Sieur Ranchin, en ses Inscriptions, ne parle point de quelques Medecins, Docteurs de Montpelier, qui ont feruy les Rois en ces derniers temps, comme Ma-zile, qui a esté premier Medecin de Charles IX. Heroard, qui a esté premier Medecin de Louys XIII. & Mayerne-Turquet, qui a esté premier Medecin du Roy d'Angleterre, ny mesme dans son Traité de l'Eschole de Montpelier, ny dans le Catalogue des Medecins illustres de Montpelier, leur baille aucun rang : Ie croy qu'il les a laissez, pour n'auoir pas esté pris des Escholes, comme Regens, & enseignans la Medecine : Peut-estre qu'il n'a pas voulu placer entre les Medecins de Montpelier, le Sieur Maziles[?], pour le malheur qui luy arriua à la mort de Charles IX. accusé de l'auoir maltraité, sans l'auoir fait voir dés les premiers iours aux anciens Medecins de Paris, Simon Pietre, & Louys Duret, qui pour cet effet auoient esté appellez au Bois de Vincennes : la Reine Mere le voulant arrester pour le faire pendre, il se sauua hors de France : sa maison de Paris, & celle des champs en Beauuoisis, furent pillées ; le Sieur Loisel en parle dans son Histoire du Beauuoisis, assez modestement, en plaignant son malheur. Ie confesse que les Medecins de Paris n'ont pas esté Medecins des Papes demeurans en Auignon : Toutefois nous auons eu vn Medecin de Paris, Campanus, Chanoine de Paris, Chapelain du Pape Nicolas Guillelmus Brixiensis, quia fait l'Aggregateur, estoit Medecin de Paris, & a esté Chapelain du Pape. Il estoit Italien, ou s'il est François, il a demeuré en Italie, où sont imprimez ses livres. Nous trouvons dans nos Registres, ce nom de Guillelmus Brixiensis, du mesme temps. Je n'ay pas trouvé des Medecins de Paris, qui ayent esté Medecins de l'Empereur : C'est pourquoy nous ne parlerons que des Medecins, qui ont servy les Rois de France, de la seconde & troisiéme race.
units.tr: Seeing that the Sieur Ranchin, in his Inscriptions, does not mention certain physicians and doctors of Montpellier who served the kings in recent times, such as Mazile, who was first physician to Charles IX; Heroard, who was first physician to Louis XIII; and Mayerne-Turquet, who was first physician to the King of England; nor even in his Treatise on the School of Montpellier, nor in the Catalogue of the illustrious physicians of Montpellier, does he give them any rank. I believe he left them out because they were not taken from the schools as regents teaching medicine. Perhaps he did not wish to place Sieur Mazile among the physicians of Montpellier, because of the misfortune that befell him at the death of Charles IX: he was accused of having mistreated the king without having had him seen from the first days by the old physicians of Paris, Simon Pietre and Louis Duret, who had been summoned for this purpose to the Bois de Vincennes. The Queen Mother, wishing to have him arrested in order to hang him, he escaped out of France; his house in Paris and his country house in the Beauvaisis were plundered. Sieur Loisel speaks of this in his History of the Beauvaisis, quite modestly, lamenting his misfortune. I confess that the physicians of Paris were not physicians to the Popes who lived in Avignon. Nevertheless, we have had a physician of Paris, Campanus, canon of Paris and chaplain to the Pope; Guillelmus Brixiensis, who made the Aggregator, was a physician of Paris and was chaplain to the Pope. He was Italian, or if he was French, he lived in Italy, where his books were printed. We find in our registers this name Guillelmus Brixiensis from the same time. I have not found physicians of Paris who were physicians to the Emperor. That is why we shall speak only of the physicians who served the kings of France of the second and third race.

units.la: Obizo a esté premier Medecin du Roy Louys le Gros. Petrus Lombardus, Chanoine de Chartres, premier Medecin de Louys VII. Petrus Egidius de Corbolio, Chanoine de Paris, & Rigordus, Religieux de S. Denis en France, ont esté premiers Medecins de Philippe second. Roger de Pruvino, Chanoine de Paris, a esté premier Medecin de Louys IX. l'an 1250. Robert de Duaco, Chanoine de Senlis, a esté premier Medecin de Marguerite de Provence, laquelle a esté femme de Louys IX. Henry de Hermondavilla, estoit premier Medecin de Philippe le Bel, cela se prouve parsa Chirurgie. Guido de Cauliaco a estudié sous luy à Paris. Gervais Chrestien, Chanoine de Paris & de Bayeux, premier Medecin de Charles V. qui a fondé le College de Maistre Gervais. Jean de Guisco, Chanoine de Nantes & de Paris, premier Medecin du mesme Roy, qui a fondé le College de Cornouaille. Jacques des Parts, Chanoine de Paris, & Thresorier de l'Eglise de Tournay, a esté premier Medecin du Roy Charles VII. au rapport de Campegius. Le Roy Louys XI. a changé fouvent de Medecins, selon son caprice, & la defiance qu'il avoit d'eux, se resouvenant comme il avoit suborné Adam Fumée, Medecin du Roy Charles VII. son pere. Joannes Burgensis, Medecin de Paris, a esté Medecin de Charles VIII. avec les autres qu'il a eu. Louys Burgensis a esté premier Medecin de Louys XII. Louys Burgensis, son fils, a suivy le Roy François Premier en sa prison d'Espagne. Devant luy Guillelmus Copus, Alleman, Medecin de Paris, avoit esté Medecin du Roy François premier. Fernel estoit premier Medecin de Henry second; Apres luy ce fut Jean Chapelain, par la recommandation qu'en avoit fait Fernel en mourant. Montuus a esté premier Medecin de François second, comme il le tesmoigne en l'Epistre de sa pratique. Mazile, Medecin de Montpelier, demeurant à Beauvais, a esté premier Medecin de Charles
units.tr: Obizo was first physician to King Louis the Fat. Peter Lombard, canon of Chartres, was first physician to Louis VII. Peter Giles of Corbeil, canon of Paris, and Rigordus, a religious of St. Denis in France, were first physicians to Philip II. Roger of Pruvino, canon of Paris, was first physician to Louis IX in the year 1250. Robert of Douai, canon of Senlis, was first physician to Margaret of Provence, who was the wife of Louis IX. Henry of Hermondaville was first physician to Philip the Fair; this is proved by his Surgery. Guy de Chauliac studied under him at Paris. Gervais Chrestien, canon of Paris and of Bayeux, first physician to Charles V, who founded the College of Maistre Gervais. Jean de Guisco, canon of Nantes and of Paris, first physician to the same king, who founded the College of Cornouaille. Jacques des Parts, canon of Paris and treasurer of the Church of Tournai, was first physician to King Charles VII, according to Campegius. King Louis XI often changed his physicians according to his whim and the distrust he had of them, remembering how he had suborned Adam Fumée, physician to King Charles VII, his father. Joannes Burgensis, physician of Paris, was physician to Charles VIII, together with the others he had. Louis Burgensis was first physician to Louis XII. Louis Burgensis, his son, followed King François I into his captivity in Spain. Before him, Guillelmus Copus, a German, physician of Paris, had been physician to King François I. Fernel was first physician to Henry II; after him came Jean Chapelain, on the recommendation that Fernel had made on dying. Montuus was first physician to François II, as he attests in the Epistle of his practice. Mazile, physician of Montpellier, living at Beauvais, was first physician to Charles

units.la: IX. Marc Miron, Medecin de Paris, estoit premier Medecin de Henry Troisiéme. Mais Henry IV. estant Roy de Navarre, & faisant la guerre du costé du Languedoc & Gascogne, a choisi des Medecins de Montpelier. Estant venu à la Couronne de France, il avoit pour Medecin Dortoman, Docteur & Professeur de Montpelier, lequel estant decedé, luy a succedé le Sieur d'Aliboux, & apres luy le Sieur de la Riviere, tous deux Medecins de Basle. Puis le Sieur du Laurent, enfuite les Sieurs Petit, Do-cteur en Medecine d'Orleans, & Milon, Docteur de Poitiers, qui luy avoient esté indiquez & recommandez par la Riviere, comme les plus sçauans de son Royaume.
units.tr: IX. Marc Miron, physician of Paris, was first physician to Henry III. But Henry IV, while he was King of Navarre and waging war on the side of Languedoc and Gascony, chose physicians from Montpellier. On coming to the Crown of France, he had as his physician Dortoman, doctor and professor of Montpellier; when he died, Sieur d'Aliboux succeeded him, and after him Sieur de la Rivière, both physicians of Basel. Then Sieur du Laurent, next the Sieurs Petit, doctor of medicine of Orléans, and Milon, doctor of Poitiers, who had been pointed out and recommended to him by la Rivière as the most learned men of his kingdom.

units.la: Voyez où va la passion d'un homme irrité contre nostre Eschole, de preferer deux hommes qu'il ne connoissoit point particulierement, qui n'avoient jamais veu ny traité le Roy, aux plus sçauans Medecins de l'Europe, qui estoient pour lors à Paris, qui avoient eu l'honneur de traiter le Roy enses maladies. l'entens parler des Sieurs Marefcot, & Martin: & de fait, le plus judicieux Medecin, Monsieur Petit, ne se sentant pas assez fort pour soustenir & exercer cette charge, par l'entremise du Sieur de Pigny, la resigna au Sieur Milon, moyennant que la qualité de premier Medecin luy demeurât, partageans ensemble les gages & emolumens de la charge, esgalement par moitié: Ainsi l'affaire fut triquottée par ledit Sieur Pigny, Medecin de Roüen, amy commun des deux, & leur camarade d'estude. Sans mentir, c'est bien mesprisser la vie du Roy, que de l'exposer & confier à tels Medecins, veu qu'il n'y a rien de plus difficile & hazardeux, que de choisir vn bon Medecin, vertueux, sçauant, fidel, iudicieux pour la personne d'vn Roy. C'est Artaxerxes qui l'a dit, escriuant à Histanides, Gouuerneur de l'Hellespont, pour auoir Hippocrate, prés de sa personne ; il luy recommande d'offrir des richesses tant qu'il voudra, & les honneurs, comme au plus grand Seigneur de Perse. Si vous trouuez encor vn homme de bien dans l'Europe, n'espargnez rien pour le gagner à mon seruice, dautant qu'il est tres-difficile de trouuer des personnes qui soient capables de donner conseil. Mais toutes ces grandes promesses n'ont pû attirer Hippocrate, pour seruir Artaxerxes, Roy des Perses, ny Perdiccas, Roy des Macedoniens, qui tous deux le demandoient: il aima mieux demeurer dans la Grece, pour seruir sa patrie, en assistant les malades, qu'il alloit chercher par toute la Grece, afin d'auoir moyen de composer par ses Obseruations, les liures qu'il nous a laissez: ce qu'il n'eust pû faire estât auprès de l'vn de ces deux Rois, car il eût esté priué d'aller voir toute sorte de malades, crainte d'apporter vn mauuais air, près la personne du Roy. Ioint qu'il sçauoit bien, qu'il n'eust pas eu la liberté de parler au Roy hardiment des remedes, qu'il luy falloit faire en ses maladies, d'autant que sa mere Parisatis, vouloit qu'on parlât à luy, auec des paroles de soye, qui n'est pas le langage des bons & vrais Medecins. Ce n'est pas sans raison que Monsieur le Cardinal d'Offat, escriuant à Monsieur de Villeroy, luy recommande, de prendre garde à la doctrine & fidelité du Medecin qu'on donneroit au Roy Henry le Grand. Ce conseil est louable & digne d'vn bon seruiteur, mais il est tresdifficile à executer. C'est pourquoy quand le Roy est capable de choisir vn Medecin, peu d'hommes sages & prudens osent s'entrementre d'en presenter, non plus qu'vn Cuisinier, & vn Apothiquaire. Dautant qu'vn Medecin dône ce qu'il luy plaist pour medicamens, Huic soli libertas dandi quidquid iubet pro medicamento, atque ut quisque vult facit & medicinam. Ex Plinio & Celso.
units.tr: Look where the passion of a man angry at our School leads him: to prefer two men whom he did not know personally, who had never seen or attended the King, to the most learned physicians of Europe who were then in Paris and had had the honour of attending the King in his illnesses. I mean the Sieurs Marescot and Martin. And indeed, the most judicious physician, Monsieur Petit, not feeling strong enough to sustain and discharge this office, through the intervention of the Sieur de Pigny, resigned it to the Sieur Milon, on condition that the title of first physician remain his, and that they share the salary and emoluments of the office equally between them. So the affair was arranged by the said Sieur Pigny, physician of Rouen, a common friend of the two and their fellow student. Truly, it is to despise the King's life to expose it and entrust it to such physicians, since there is nothing more difficult and hazardous than choosing a good physician, virtuous, learned, faithful and judicious, for the person of a king. It was Artaxerxes who said so, writing to Histanes, governor of the Hellespont, about having Hippocrates near his person; he urges him to offer riches as much as he wishes, and honours, as to the greatest lord of Persia. "If you still find a good man in Europe, spare nothing to win him to my service, since it is very difficult to find persons who are capable of giving counsel." But all these great promises could not draw Hippocrates to serve Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, nor Perdiccas, King of the Macedonians, who both asked for him. He preferred to remain in Greece, to serve his country by assisting the sick, whom he went seeking throughout Greece, so as to have the means of composing from his Observations the books he has left us; this he could not have done at the court of either of those kings, for he would have been deprived of going to see every kind of sick person, for fear of bringing a bad air near the King's person. Moreover, he knew well that he would not have had the liberty to speak frankly to the King about the remedies he had to apply in his illnesses, since his mother Parisatis wanted people to speak to him with words of silk, which is not the language of good and true physicians. It is not without reason that Monsieur the Cardinal d'Ossat, writing to Monsieur de Villeroy, recommends that he take care of the learning and fidelity of the physician who would be given to King Henry the Great. This advice is praiseworthy and worthy of a good servant, but it is very difficult to carry out. That is why, when the King is capable of choosing a physician, few wise and prudent men dare to offer themselves, no more than a cook or an apothecary would. Since a physician gives whatever he pleases as medicine, "To him alone is granted the freedom to give whatever he orders as a medicine, and each does as he wishes both with medicine. From Pliny and Celsus."

units.la: Je confesse que c'estoit anciennement une belle dignité en la Medecine, d'estre premier Medecin des Empereurs, il y a douze cens ans. Il estoit le chef de la Science, toutes les controuerses se rapportoient à luy pour en estre le juge. Il avoit la qualité de Comte, Comes Archiatrorum: Il jouïssoit des droits honorifiques, tels qu'ils sont descrits dans Cassiodore: Mais il falloit que ce premier Medecin fust sçauant, vertueux, & judicieux, puis qu'il y parvenoit par l'âge & le temps de sa reception. Entre dix Archiatres qu'ils estoient, sçauans, & diligemment examinez avant qu'estre receus, le plus ancien portoit la qualité de Comte des Archiatres: Cela se pratique en Espagne, où les Medecins du Roy sont tous sçauans, ayans esté Professeurs en Medecine dans les fameuses Universitez, & selon le temps de leur reception, le plus ancien porte le tiltre de Proto-Medico, lesquels premiers Medecins, tous depuis cent ans, ont escrit tres-doctement en Medecine, comme Valesius, Mercatus, Sanctacrux, La Serna.
units.tr: I confess that it was once a fine dignity in medicine to be first physician to the Emperors, some twelve hundred years ago. He was the head of the profession, and all disputes were referred to him to be decided. He bore the title of Count, Comes Archiatrorum, and enjoyed the honorary rights described by Cassiodorus. But this first physician had to be learned, virtuous and judicious, since he attained the position by age and length of service at his admission. Of the ten Archiatres, all learned and carefully examined before being received, the most senior bore the title of Count of the Archiatres. This custom is observed in Spain, where the king's physicians are all learned, having been professors of medicine in the famous universities; and according to the date of their admission, the most senior holds the title of Proto-Medico. These first physicians, all of them for the last hundred years, have written most learnedly on medicine, such as Valesius, Mercatus, Sanctacrux and La Serna.

units.la: Virgile nous represente en la personne de Japix, Medecin d'Enée, les belles qualitez que doit avoir le Medecin d'un grand Prince: il estoit tres-sçauant Medecin. Phœbo ante alios dilectus Iapix:
units.tr: Virgil presents to us, in the person of Iapis, physician to Aeneas, the fine qualities that the physician of a great prince should have: he was a most learned physician. Iapis, beloved of Phoebus above the others.

units.la: Il avoit une grande connoissance des medicamens pour les maladies.
units.tr: He had a great knowledge of medicines for diseases.

units.la: Scire potestates herbarum, usumque medendi / Maluit & mutas, &c.
units.tr: He preferred to know the powers of herbs and the use of healing, etc.

units.la: Il n'estoit point hableur, exerçoit la Medecine sans vanité & ostentation,
units.tr: He was no boaster; he practised medicine without vanity or ostentation,

units.la: Maluit & mutas agitare inglorius artes.
units.tr: He preferred to practise the silent arts, without glory.

units.la: Aussi avoit-il l'âge de sagesse, & portoit l'habit de Medecin.
units.tr: Moreover he had the age of wisdom, and wore the dress of a physician.

units.la: Pæonium in morem, senior, succinctus amictu,
units.tr: In the manner of the Paeonians, an elder, girded with his cloak,

units.la: Il sçavoit fort bien la Chirurgie pour assister le Prince, s'il estoit blessé dans la guerre, & se servoit de bons & anciens remedes, que Phœbus nous a enseigné.
units.tr: He knew surgery well enough to assist the prince, should he be wounded in war, and he used good and ancient remedies, which Phoebus had taught us.

units.la: Multa manu Medica, Phœbique potentibus herbis.
units.tr: Many things by the healing hand, and by the powerful herbs of Phoebus.

units.la: En son procedé, la fortune n'a point eu de lieu, dautant qu'il n'a rien hazardé.
units.tr: In his method, fortune had no place, since he risked nothing.

units.la: Nulla viam fortuna regit.
units.tr: Fortune governs no path.

units.la: Ayant guery Enée, il luy recommande de reconnoistre, que c'est Dieu qui luy a rendu la vie par son ministere.
units.tr: Having cured Aeneas, he urges him to acknowledge that it is God who restored his life through his ministry.

units.la: Non hæc humanis opibus, non arte Magistra / Prouenient, neque te Ænea mea dextera seruat, / Maior agit Deus :
units.tr: Not by human resources, not by art as mistress, do these things come about, nor does my right hand save you, Aeneas; a greater one, God, acts:

units.la: l'apprens dans Galien, que les premiers Cesars ont eu plusieurs Medecins en leur Cour, entre eux le plus sçauant tenoit le premier rang : c'estoit Andromachus du temps de Neron, lequel a inventé & composé la Theriaque, contre les poisons froids, & les morsures des animaux veneneux.
units.tr: I learn from Galen that the early Caesars had several physicians at their court, and among them the most learned held the first rank: this was Andromachus in the time of Nero, who invented and composed Theriac, against cold poisons and the bites of venomous animals.

units.la: Du temps de Galien, le premier Medecin d'Antonin, estoit Demetrius, son bon amy, qui luy fit voir la composition de la Theriaque. Il loüe Andromachus, de ce qu'il estoit natif de Crete, d'où viennent toutes les bonnes herbes pour la Medecine, & l'air y estant tres pur & excellent : tout cela y auoit seruy pour former vn si excellent Medecin, comme Andromachus.
units.tr: In Galen's time, the first physician of Antoninus was Demetrius, his good friend, who showed him the composition of Theriac. Galen praises Andromachus because he was a native of Crete, whence come all the good herbs for medicine, and whose air is very pure and excellent: all this had served to form so excellent a physician as Andromachus.

units.la: C'est la verité que les Medecins de Paris ont tousiours fort honoré la qualité du premier Medecin, pour le respect qu'ils portent au Roy, leur souuerain Seigneur, mais ils ne l'ont iamais recherchée, se contentans de viure doucement & innocemment, seruant le peuple.
units.tr: It is true that the physicians of Paris have always greatly honoured the rank of first physician, out of the respect they bear to the King, their sovereign lord; but they have never sought it, being content to live gently and innocently, serving the people.

units.la: Curia dat curas, ergo si tu bene curas / Viuere securè, non fit tibi curia cura. / Curia curarum genitrix, nutrixque malorum, / Iustos iniustis, inhonestos aquat honestis.
units.tr: The court gives cares; therefore, if you care well to live securely, the court will not be a care to you. The court, mother of cares and nurse of evils, makes the just equal to the unjust and the dishonourable equal to the honourable.

units.la: Monsieur Marescot disoit souuent à ses confreres, populus Dominus meus nunquam moritur, uno aulso non deficit alter Aureus, & simili frondescit virga metallo. Democedes, Medecin Grec, ayant guery le Roy Darius & sa femme, il receut des presens inestimables, mangeant à la table du Roy: il luy auoit promis de ne iamais quitter son service, neantmoins ayant rencontré l'occasion furtiuement d'eschapper de la Cour, il s'enfuit en Grece, sa patrie, aimant mieux viure auec ses compatriotes, que de seruir ce grand Roy Darius. Le malheur de Mazile premier Medecin du Roy Charles IX. doit faire apprehender aux premiers Medecins telles rencontres. Astragesilde, Reine de France, en mourant pria le Roy Gontran son mary, de faire ietter apres qu'elle seroit morte, ses Medecins par les fenestres, ce qui fut executé; au contraire, Democedes sauua la vie aux Medecins Egyptiens de Darius, qui vouloit les faire pendre pour auoir mal pensé son talon luxé, si Democedes ne les eut hardiment & charitable-ment excusé & conferué. Galien estoit fort bien venu à la Cour de l'Empereur Antonin, & estoit dans les bonnes graces de Pitholaus, gouuerneur de Commodus, qu'il auoit guery d'vne maladie, neantmoins il aima mieux se retirer en son païs, que demeurer à Rome. Il n'y a pas de plaisir, ny d'honneur de faire la Medecine aux grands Seigneurs, qui apportent toufours des contrarietez aux deux remedes, la Saignée & la Purgation, qui leur font plus necessaires qu'aux pauures gens, pour les excez qu'ils font à boire & à manger, & la vie desreglée qu'ils meinent. Ils font plus d'estat d'un bon Cuisinier, qu'ils achepteront au poids de l'or, que d'un sçauant Medecin : Virtutem verba putant, ut lucum ligna, pour avoir leurs bonnes graces, & leurs tables, il faut estre leur esclaue, flateur & complaisant, jusqu'à les laisser mourir faute de les presser à faire les remedes convenables. Ce n'est pas de la sorte que les anciens Medecins conversoient avec les grands Seigneurs, ils obeïssoient aux Medecins, Una artium Medicina Imperatoribus imperat. Iacobus natione Achaius l'a bien monstré aux Courtisans, lors qu'il traitoit l'Empereur Leon.
units.tr: Monsieur Marescot often said to his colleagues, my lord the people never dies; when one golden vessel is broken, another does not fail; and the staff sprouts with a like metal. Democedes, a Greek physician, having cured King Darius and his wife, received priceless gifts, eating at the king's table; he had promised never to leave his service, yet having found an opportunity to slip secretly away from the court, he fled to Greece, his homeland, preferring to live with his compatriots rather than serve the great King Darius. The misfortune of Mazille, first physician to King Charles IX, should make the first physicians fear such encounters. Astragesilde, Queen of France, on dying, asked King Gontran her husband to have her physicians thrown out of the windows after she was dead, which was carried out; on the contrary, Democedes saved the lives of the Egyptian physicians of Darius, who wanted to hang them for having badly treated his dislocated ankle, if Democedes had not boldly and charitably excused and preserved them. Galen was very well received at the court of the Emperor Antoninus, and stood in the good graces of Pitholaus, governor of Commodus, whom he had cured of an illness; nevertheless he preferred to withdraw to his own country rather than remain at Rome. There is no pleasure or honour in practising medicine for great lords, who always bring contrary demands to the two remedies, bloodletting and purging, which are more necessary to them than to poor people, because of the excesses they commit in eating and drinking and the disorderly life they lead. They esteem a good cook, whom they will buy for his weight in gold, more than a learned physician: they think words are virtue, as they think wood is a grove; and to win their favour and their tables, one must be their slave, a flatterer and a complaisant courtier, even to the point of letting them die for want of pressing them to take the proper remedies. It was not in this way that the ancient physicians dealt with great lords; they obeyed their physicians. Medicine alone commands emperors among the arts. Jacobus, an Achaean by birth, showed this well to the courtiers when he treated the Emperor Leo.

units.la: Vne singularité admirable se trouve en l'Eschole de Montpelier, c'est que, les plus sçauàns Medecins de l'Europe, ont tousiours enseigné dans cette Eschole; & aujourd'huy ceux qui y sont demeurans & enseignans, bien qu'ils ne soient que six, sont les plus sçauans & experimentez Medecins de l'Europe.
units.tr: A remarkable singularity is found in the School of Montpellier: the most learned physicians of Europe have always taught in this School; and today those who remain there and teach, although they are only six, are the most learned and experienced physicians of Europe.

units.la: Si c'estoit vn autre que Courtaut qui nous l'asseurât, je le croirois volontiers, mais il m'est fort suspect, connoissant son ignorance. La Grece se vante d'avoir eu sept hommes sages, l'Eschole de Montpelier en a autant aujourd'huy, engendrez & formez dans leur Eschole, non pas choisis par toute l'Europe. Puis que personne n'est juge en sa propre cause, il n'est pas raisonnable de s'en rapporter aux Medecins de Montpelier, qui vivent aujourd'huy, ny à ceux qui ont esté nourrissons de leur Eschole; il faut verifier cela par d'autres tesmoins irreprochables.
units.tr: If it were anyone other than Courtaut who assured us of this, I would gladly believe it, but he is very suspect to me, knowing his ignorance. Greece boasts of having had seven wise men; the School of Montpellier has as many today, born and trained within their own School, not chosen from all of Europe. Since no one is judge in his own cause, it is not reasonable to rely on the physicians of Montpellier who live today, nor on those who were nursed in their School; this must be verified by other unimpeachable witnesses.

units.la: Aristote dit, que les sages femmes sont plus capables de juger de la beauté & deformité des enfans; que les propres meres, & que les Medecins estans malades, ne doivent se fier à leur propre jugement, qu'ils doivent en appeller d'autres, pour se faire traiter; puis que je vois l'esprit de Courtaut malade, & blessé de philautie, i'en appelle au jugement d'autres Medecins: c'est pourquoy je recuse Valeriola, qui se glorifie d'être enfant & nourrisson de Montpelier, bien qu'il n'ait esté Docteur de cette Eschole, que par une Lettre qu'on luy a envoyée.
units.tr: Aristotle says that midwives are better able to judge the beauty and deformity of children than the mothers themselves, and that physicians, when they are ill, should not trust their own judgment but should call in others to treat them. Since I see that the mind of Courtaut is sick and wounded by self-love, I appeal to the judgment of other physicians. That is why I challenge Valeriola, who boasts of being a child and nursling of Montpellier, although he was made a Doctor of that School only by a letter sent to him.

units.la: Pareillement je recuse Laurens Joubert; Docteur; Professeur,& Chancelier de cette Eschole, qui en dit merueilles en l'Epistre presentée à Monsieur le Duc d'Alençon: encore moins au Sieur Ranchin, qui loüé par excez son Eschole, qu'il a restablie à ses dépens. Hors ces trois, je n'en trouve point d'autres, qui l'ayent loüé, par admiration, & par dessus les autres Escholes, & particulierement par dessus celle de Paris.
units.tr: Likewise I challenge Laurens Joubert, Doctor, Professor and Chancellor of that School, who says wonders of it in the Epistle dedicated to Monsieur the Duke of Alençon. Still less do I challenge Sieur Ranchin, who praised his School beyond measure, the School he restored at his own expense. Apart from these three, I find no others who have praised it with admiration, above the other Schools and especially above that of Paris.

units.la: Pour estimer & preferer l'Eschole de Montpelier à toutes les autres, il faut sçavoir, si elle a eu l'entiere possession de la Medecine, pour avoir tourné en langue Latine, les Livres Arabes : puis que les Arabes sont venus enseigner la Medecine à Montpelier : s'ils ont tourné en Latin les Livres Grecs, s'ils ont donné la connoissance des plantes, de la Pharmacie, & de la Chirurgie, & Anatomie: s'ils ont corrigé les erreurs, que les Arabes avoient introduit dans la Medecine: s'ils ont fait reviure la bonne, saine, & salutaire doctrine des Grecs: s'ils ont inventé & introduit quelque chose de nouveau en la Medecine. Je ne trouve rien de tout cela en l'Eschole de Montpelier : j'advoüe qu'il y a eu quelques sçavans hommes Professeurs en cette Eschole, & qu'il en est forty de jeunes Docteurs, lesquels s'estans retirez dans les grandes villes, par l'estude; l'experience, & la conduite, qu'ils ont eu des Anciens Docteurs des lieux, où ils se sont retirez, sont deuenus plus sçauans que les Professeurs de Montpelier.
units.tr: To esteem and prefer the School of Montpellier above all others, one must know whether it has had complete possession of medicine, by having translated the Arabic books into Latin, since the Arabs came to teach medicine at Montpellier; whether they translated the Greek books into Latin; whether they gave knowledge of plants, of pharmacy, of surgery and of anatomy; whether they corrected the errors which the Arabs had introduced into medicine; whether they revived the good, sound and salutary doctrine of the Greeks; and whether they invented or introduced anything new in medicine. I find nothing of all this in the School of Montpellier. I admit that there have been some learned men as Professors in that School, and that young Doctors have come out of it who, having withdrawn to the great cities, through study, experience and the guidance they received from the older Doctors of the places to which they retired, have become more learned than the Professors of Montpellier.

units.la: Ie ne trouue point que les Docteurs de Montpelier ayent tourné les Liures Arabes, que nous auons, qui traittent de la Medecine, il ne s'en trouuerra aucun de leur version, si ce n'est le Commentaire d'Auerroes sur le Cantique d'Auicenne, par Arnegarde Blasii de Montepessulano: Mais ie leur accorde cela, pourueu qu'ils reconnoissent que l'honneur de la version des Liures Arabes appartient aux Venitiens, & Espagnols, Iuifs, & Arabes, de religion, qui estoient à Cordube, & à Complut, Academies d'Espagne.
units.tr: I do not find that the Doctors of Montpellier translated any of the Arabic books on medicine that we have; no translation by them will be found, except the Commentary of Averroes on the Canticle of Avicenna, by Arnegarde Blasii of Montpellier. But I grant them even this, provided they acknowledge that the honour of translating the Arabic books belongs to the Venetians and Spaniards, and to Jews and Arabs by religion, who were at Cordoba and at Complutum, the academies of Spain.

units.la: Quant aux Liures Grecs en Medecine, ie ne trouue point qu'aucun Medecin Professeur de Montpelier ait fait la version d'vn seul Liure d'Hippocrate, ou de Galien, ou d'autres Autheurs Grecs. Ce n'ont point esté les Medecins Professeurs de Montpelier, qui nous ont donné la connoissance des plantes, ny qui en ont escrit les premiers: Nous ne voyons point d'eux vn seul Herbier, ils n'ont pas mesmes descrit les plantes de leurs pais circonuoisins, ny mesme de leur Iardin Royal. Courtaut est si fort ignoignorant, qu'il ne sçait pas qu'il faut escrire Phtora Valdensium & Antiphtora. Pour la Pharmacie, & pour l'Anatomie, ils n'ont rien escrit les premiers, ny pour la Chirurgie, dautant que Lanfranc & Hermondauilla l'auoient enseigné à Paris, auant que Guy de Cauliac la monstât à Montpelier, & pour l'apprendre il vint à Paris.
units.tr: As for the Greek books on medicine, I do not find that any Professor physician of Montpellier has made a translation of a single book of Hippocrates, or of Galen, or of other Greek authors. It was not the Professor physicians of Montpellier who gave us knowledge of plants, nor who first wrote about them. We do not see from them a single herbal; they have not even described the plants of their neighbouring countryside, nor even of their own Royal Garden. Courtaut is so very ignorant that he does not know that one must write "Phtora Valdensium & Antiphtora." As for pharmacy and anatomy, they did not write anything first, nor for surgery, since Lanfranc and Hermondaville had taught it at Paris before Guy de Chauliac displayed it at Montpellier, and to learn it he came to Paris.

units.la: Bref, ie ne trouue point que les Medecins de Montpelier ayent reformé la Medecine, des grands abus & fautes, qui s'y commettoient, & qu'ils ayent inventé quelque chose de nouueau pour l'enrichir & perfectionner.
units.tr: In short, I do not find that the physicians of Montpellier reformed medicine of the great abuses and faults which were committed in it, nor that they invented anything new to enrich and perfect it.

units.la: Toutes ces belles qualitez qui manquent à l'Eschole de Montpelier, se rencontrent à l'Eschole de Paris: toutes fois, ie confesse que durant trois siecles, mil, onze, douze, la Medecine auoit esté par toute l'Europe, grossierement exercée selon la doctrine des Liures Arabes, & que l'Eschole de Paris s'en est ressentie iusques au treiziesme siecle, qu'elle a commencé la premiere, à reconnoistre Hippocrate & Galien, pour les anciens Autheurs de la bonne & vraye Medecine, & a reietté la Medecine Arabique. Campegius Bruyerinus, disciple de Rondelet, en sa Preface sur le Colliget d'Auerroës, qu'il a tourné en meilleur Latin, dit que du regne d'Alphonse Roy d'Espagne, les liures d'Auerroës, & autres Arabes ont esté apportez à Paris, florentibus iam in Lutetia Parisiorum Philosophiæ & Medicinæ studiis: & de fait, nos Anciens auoient en nostre Bibliotheque publique, Opera Auicennæ, Auerrois, & le Continens Rhasis, tous manuscrits. Le Roy Louÿs XI. eut bien de la peine de tirer ce dernier liure par emprunt, la Chambre des Comptes de Paris en respondit, se rendant caution.
units.tr: All these fine qualities which are lacking in the School of Montpellier are found in the School of Paris. Nevertheless, I confess that for three centuries, the tenth, eleventh and twelfth, medicine had been crudely practised throughout all Europe according to the doctrine of the Arabic books, and that the School of Paris felt the effects of this until the thirteenth century, when it was the first to begin acknowledging Hippocrates and Galen as the ancient authors of good and true medicine, and rejected Arabic medicine. Campegius Bruyerinus, a disciple of Rondelet, in his Preface to the Colliget of Averroes, which he translated into better Latin, says that in the reign of Alphonso, King of Spain, the books of Averroes and other Arabs were brought to Paris, "the studies of philosophy and medicine already flourishing in Lutetia of the Parisians." And indeed our forebears had in our public library the Works of Avicenna, of Averroes, and the Continens of Rhazes, all in manuscript. King Louis XI had great difficulty in borrowing this last book; the Chamber of Accounts of Paris answered for it, becoming surety.

units.la: Pour ce qui est de la connoissance des langues Grecques, vn Espagnol sçauant Medecin nommé Huartes, en son Examen des Esprits, vous apprendra que le Turc ayant banny les Lettres, & Sciences de la Grece, a fait passer l'Vniversité d'Athenes à Paris, ville Capitale de la France.
units.tr: As for knowledge of the Greek languages, a learned Spanish physician named Huarte, in his Examination of Wits, will teach you that the Turk, having banished the letters and sciences of Greece, caused the University of Athens to pass to Paris, the capital city of France.

units.la: Il se trouuera depuis deux cens ans vn grand nombre de Medecins de Paris, qui ont trauaillé aux versions d'Hippocrate & de Galien, & autres Autheurs Grecs, qui ont fait des notes & corrections, sur les vieux exemplaires, soit de leur esprit, ou par coniectures, conferans les mots & les sentences ensemblément. Auant Caluus, Italien, Romain, & Cornarius, Alleman, Guillemus Copus, Medecin de Paris, a tourné quelques liures d'Hippocrate en Latin, qui sont les Aphorismes, & le Prognostic: Vassaus, le Prorrhetique, les Epidemies, le livre de victus ratione in acutis. Le mesme Copus, & Guinterius Andernacus, ont tourné beaucoup de livres de Galien, de Grec en Latin: Vous trouverez des versions de Guinterius, une grande liste dans la Bibliotheque imprimée de Schenckius. Cornarius confesse avoir esté grandement assisté d'un vieux exemplaire d'Hippocrate, que Nicolaus Copus, fils de Guillelmus luy avoit presté. Ruellius a tourné Dioscoride en Latin, & a fait de doctes remarques sur Hippocrate, qui sont tombées de main en main aux Docteurs de Pa-ris, & se sont tellement grossies par les additions de Goupil, & d'autres, qu'elles ont fourny ample matiere pour reformer l'Hippocrate de Foësius. Zuingerus en la Preface de son Hippocrate, advoüe que les Medecins de Paris, ont beaucoup travaillé, pour donner Hippocrate en sa perfection, & confesse avoir eu les Notes de Goupil, Medecin de Paris,&Professeur: queDuret, qui a l'esprit & le genie d'Hippocrate, travaille incessamment pour esclaircir Hippocrate: Il ne parle point des Medecins de Montpelier: mais il se plaint du Sieur Dorthoman, Professeur à Montpelier, qui luy promettoit des Notes sur Hippocrate, qui sont encores à venir. Vassaus a trauaillé sur la version de plusieurs liures de Galien. Ces grands personnages ont esté suiuis par Gorrhæus, Hollerius, Lallemantius, Laffleus, Alemanus, Gourmelenus, Duretus, Cordæus, Martinus, qui tous ont fait des Notes & Commentaires sur Hippocrate, mesme Foësius, en l'Epistre dediée aux Medecins de Paris, à l'entrée de son Hippocrate, confesse ingenuëment que la plus grande partie des corrections & remarques sur Hippocrate, viennent des Medecins de Paris. Ioannes Ruellius est le premier Medecin des François, Italiens, & Allemans, qui a escrit si doctement des plantes, qu'il a surmonté Dioscoride & Pline, pour l'vsage & pratique de la Medecine.
units.tr: For the last two hundred years there has been a great number of physicians of Paris who have laboured on the translations of Hippocrates and Galen and other Greek authors, and who have made notes and corrections on the old copies, whether from their own wit or by conjecture, comparing the words and sentences together. Before Caluus, an Italian, Roman, and Cornarius, a German, Guillemus Copus, physician of Paris, translated some books of Hippocrates into Latin: the Aphorisms and the Prognostic; Vassaeus, the Prorrhetic, the Epidemics, and the book On the Regimen in Acute Diseases. The same Copus and Guinterius Andernacus translated many books of Galen from Greek into Latin; you will find a long list of Guinterius's translations in the printed Bibliotheca of Schenckius. Cornarius admits he was greatly helped by an old copy of Hippocrates which Nicolaus Copus, son of Guillelmus, had lent him. Ruellius translated Dioscorides into Latin and made learned remarks on Hippocrates, which passed from hand to hand among the Doctors of Paris and were so enlarged by the additions of Goupil and others that they supplied ample material for reforming the Hippocrates of Foësius. Zwinger, in the Preface to his Hippocrates, admits that the physicians of Paris have worked hard to bring Hippocrates to his perfection, and confesses he had the Notes of Goupil, physician and Professor of Paris. Duret, who has the spirit and genius of Hippocrates, works unceasingly to clarify Hippocrates. He does not speak of the physicians of Montpellier, but he complains of Sieur Dorthoman, Professor at Montpellier, who promised him Notes on Hippocrates, which are still to come. Vassaeus has worked on the translation of several books of Galen. These great men were followed by Gorrhaeus, Hollerius, Lallemantius, Laffleus, Alemanus, Gourmelenus, Duretus, Cordaeus, Martinus, all of whom made Notes and Commentaries on Hippocrates. Even Foësius, in the Epistle dedicated to the physicians of Paris at the beginning of his Hippocrates, ingenuously confesses that the greater part of the corrections and remarks on Hippocrates come from the physicians of Paris. Joannes Ruellius is the first physician of the French, Italians and Germans who wrote so learnedly on plants that he surpassed Dioscorides and Pliny for the use and practice of medicine.

units.la: Dans cette connoissance, il a ouuert & frayé le chemin aux autres, qui ont escrit apres luy, ils n'ont rien adiousté à leurs œuures, que des figures, qui soulagent la memoire & l'imaginatiue, & quelques plantes estrangeres. Pour la Pharmacie, nous auons de vieux liures, qui ont emprunté toutes les compositions de Mesué, mais entre ceux qui ont escrit elegamment de la Pharmacie, Syluius auant Rondelet, & Ioubert, en a traité fort methodiquement en diuers liures, tant pour les Medecins que pour les Apothi-quaires.
units.tr: In this knowledge he opened and cleared the way for those who wrote after him. They added nothing to their works except figures, which ease the memory and the imagination, and some foreign plants. As for Pharmacy, we have old books which borrowed all their compositions from Mesue; but among those who have written elegantly on Pharmacy, Sylvius, before Rondelet and Joubert, treated it very methodically in various books, both for the physicians and for the apothecaries.

units.la: Nous trouvons dans nos vieux Registres, qu'on deputoit tous les ans un Docteur, pour conduire les Escholiers aux herbes à l'entour de Paris : Il nous reste encore de grandes armoires avec quantité de layettes, où estoient reserrées toutes les drogues & aromates, qu'on monstroit aux Escholiers.
units.tr: We find in our old Registers that a Doctor was deputed every year to lead the students to the herbs around Paris. There still remain to us large cupboards with a quantity of drawers, in which were stored all the drugs and aromatics that were shown to the students.

units.la: Pour la Chirurgie avant Guy de Cauliac, qui a escrit methodiquement ce qu'il avoit appris à Paris ; Il y avoit les quatre Maistres Italiens : de plus, Lanfranc avoit enseigné la Chirurgie à Paris : & aussi Hermondaulla. Guy de Cauliac dit l'avoir veu à Paris : Mais dans le 14. siecle, l'Anatomie a commencé d'estre monstrée publiquement dans les Escholes de Paris, avec une grande jalousie des Chirurgiens de robbe longue, qui ne pouvoient souffrir que les Medecins la mõstrassent aux Barbiers : & delà est venu le divorce de cette espece de Chirurgiens de saincte Cosme, d'avec les Medecins, s'estans soustraits de l'obeïssance qu'ils leur devoient. Jean Tagaut, tres-docte Medecin, a amplifié & enrichy la Chirurgie de Guy de Cauliac, puisée des Arabes, de la Chirurgie des Grecs, avec son beau Latin, qui est aussi pur que celuy de Ciceron, combien que la matiere en soit fort differente.
units.tr: As for Surgery before Guy de Chauliac, who wrote methodically what he had learned at Paris: there were the four Italian Masters; moreover, Lanfranc had taught Surgery at Paris, and also Hermondaulla. Guy de Chauliac says he saw him at Paris. But in the 14th century, Anatomy began to be demonstrated publicly in the schools of Paris, with great jealousy from the surgeons of the long robe, who could not bear that the physicians should show it to the barbers; and from this came the divorce of that kind of surgeons of Saint Cosmas from the physicians, they having withdrawn from the obedience they owed them. Jean Tagaut, a most learned physician, enlarged and enriched the Surgery of Guy de Chauliac, drawn from the Arabs and from the surgery of the Greeks, with his fine Latin, which is as pure as that of Cicero, although the subject matter is very different.

units.la: Y a-il eu vn Medecin de Montpelier fi curieux que Belon, Medecin de Paris, qui a voyagé par la Grece, l'Arabie, & autres Prouinces de l'Afrique, & de l'Asie, pour nous donner les connoissances necessaires en Medecine des plantes estrangeres, aromates, & autres raretez, desquelles ledit Belon a escrit des liures admirables: & de plus, il a doctement & curieusement escrit des Oiseaux, & des Poissons. Petrus Brissotus, Medecin de Paris, auoit entrepris le voyage des Indes Orientales; & comme il estoit prest de s'embarquer, il mourut à Lisbonne en Portugal, au rapport d'Amatus Lusitanus, qui regrette la mort de ce Medecin de Paris, duquel il auoit appris beaucoup pour la connoissance des aromates. Fernel auoit conseillé au Roy Henry second, d'enuoyer quelque Medecin sçauant par tout l'Orient, pour en rapporter ce qu'il y auoit de plus rare, & exquis de ces païs, afin de nous apprendre la parfaite connoissance de tous les aromates qui seruent à la Medecine. Auant le Sieur du Laurens, Professeur en Anatomie, & Cabrol, Chirurgien de Montpelier, personne n'auoit rien escrit en l'Anatomie venant de cette Eschole, & ce qu'en a escrit par questions le Sieur du Laurens, est vne Anatomie purement Physiologique. Au fait de l'Anatomie, il a commis de grandes fautes, non pas celles qu'ont remarqué Collado & Laurembergius, qui sont dans les questions, mais je dis dans le texte, du fait & de l'histoire Anatomique ; ce qui est si clairement demonstré, que tout homme un peu versé en l'Anatomie, l'advoüera sans le pouvoir defendre.
units.tr: Has there been any physician of Montpellier as curious as Belon, a physician of Paris, who travelled through Greece, Arabia, and other provinces of Africa and Asia, to give us the knowledge necessary in medicine of foreign plants, aromatics, and other rarities, about which the said Belon wrote admirable books; and moreover, he learnedly and curiously wrote on Birds and on Fishes. Pierre Brissot, a physician of Paris, had undertaken the voyage to the East Indies; and as he was about to embark, he died at Lisbon in Portugal, according to the report of Amatus Lusitanus, who laments the death of this physician of Paris, from whom he had learned much for the knowledge of aromatics. Fernel had advised King Henry the Second to send some learned physician throughout the East, to bring back what was rarest and most exquisite in those countries, so as to teach us the perfect knowledge of all the aromatics that serve medicine. Before Monsieur du Laurens, Professor of Anatomy, and Cabrol, surgeon of Montpellier, no one had written anything on Anatomy coming from that school; and what Monsieur du Laurens has written in the form of questions is an Anatomy that is purely Physiological. In the matter of Anatomy, he has committed great errors, not those which Collado and Laurembergius have noted, which are in the questions, but I say in the text, in the fact and history of Anatomy; which is so clearly demonstrated that every man somewhat versed in Anatomy will admit it without being able to defend him.

units.la: Rondelet a esté fort curieux, & a inventé beaucoup de belles choses en l'Anatomie : on luy attribue l'invention de la Valvule du Colon, les vesicules seminaires, la vraye connoissance du Rein. On voit par son Livre des Poissons, combien il a esté curieux d'en faire la dissection, comme faisoit Aristote. Luy mesme dissequoit les corps humains, au rapport de Joubert, en sa vie, aussi avoit il demeuré quelques annés à Paris pour apprendre l'Anatomie, sous Guinterius & Sylvius ses Maistres, & s'en retourna âgé prés de trente ans, pour se passer Docteur à Montpelier, ville de sa naissance. Il faut confesser qu'il a esté un grand personnage, bien que Monsieur le President de Thou, en son Histoire anno 1566. donne quelque atteinte à sa reputation, disant que son Livre des Poissons a esté basty & formé sur les memoires de Guillelmus Pelisserius, Evesque de Montpelier, tressçauant dans l'histoire naturelle, qui auoit fait vn docte Commentaire, & des corrections sur tous les Liures de Pline, lequel Liure estant venu entre les mains de feu Monsieur le Cardinal de Ioyeuse, il l'a legué aux Reuerends Peres Iesuites, qui en sont possesseurs. Et est à remarquer, que ce tressçauant Euefque, pendant qu'il a vescu, a fait fleurir l'Eschole de Montpelier dans l'étude des Plantes & des Animaux. Rondelet, en son Liure des Poissons, & Pena, in suis Aduersarijs, confesset d'auoir esté grandement assistez de cét Euefque, dans la connoissance des Poissons & des Plantes. Ce mesme Euefque auoit fait vn Commentaire sur Dioscoride, qu'on tient caché. Ioubert fait tort à la memoire de Rondelet, son Maistre: ie pense que c'est pour excuser ses larcins des Liures non imprimez de Rondelet, quand il dit qu'il s'est seruy de Iean du Moulin, sçauant Medecin, pour orner & embellir le Liure des Poissons, que Iacques Brodæus a poly son Liure de ponderibus & mensuris.
units.tr: Rondelet was very curious, and invented many fine things in Anatomy: the invention of the Valve of the Colon, the seminal vesicles, and the true knowledge of the Kidney are attributed to him. One sees from his Book on Fishes how curious he was to make their dissection, as Aristotle did. He himself dissected human bodies, according to the report of Joubert, in his life; he had also stayed some years at Paris to learn Anatomy under Guinterius and Sylvius, his masters, and returned, being nearly thirty years old, to take his doctorate at Montpellier, the town of his birth. It must be admitted that he was a great man, although Monsieur le President de Thou, in his History, year 1566, somewhat injures his reputation, saying that his Book on Fishes was built and formed on the memoirs of Guillaume Pellicier, Bishop of Montpellier, very learned in natural history, who had made a learned Commentary, and corrections, on all the books of Pliny; which book, having come into the hands of the late Monsieur the Cardinal de Joyeuse, he bequeathed to the Reverend Fathers the Jesuits, who are its possessors. And it is to be remarked that this most learned Bishop, while he lived, made the school of Montpellier flourish in the study of Plants and Animals. Rondelet, in his Book on Fishes, and Pena, in his Adversaria, confess to having been greatly assisted by this Bishop in the knowledge of Fishes and Plants. This same Bishop had made a Commentary on Dioscorides, which is kept hidden. Joubert does wrong to the memory of Rondelet, his master: I think it is to excuse his thefts from the unpublished books of Rondelet when he says that he made use of Jean du Moulin, a learned physician, to adorn and embellish the Book on Fishes, and that Jacques Dubois polished his book de ponderibus et mensuris.

units.la: Monsieur de Thou au mesme endroit de sa belle Histoire, se plaint des gausseries qu'a fait ce dangereux Bouffon François Rabelais, de son Maistre Rondelet, qu'il appelle dans son Pantagruelisme, Rondibilis: Blaspheme qui est directement contre le serment d'Hippocrate, qui commande de porter honneur à ses Maistres viuans, & à leur memoire, d'aimer ses enfans comme ses propres freres. Neantmoins, ce Bouffon est mis par le Sieur Ranchin, entre les Medecins illustres de l'Eschole de Montpelier. Il est vray que durant la vie de Rondelet, & quelque temps apres, l'Eschole de Montpelier a eu quelque reputation, & a esté loüée en ce temps là par Gesnerus en ses Epistres, & par Laurentius Grillus, en son Itineraire. Mais il est à remarquer que tous deux en disent encore dauantage de l'Eschole de Paris.
units.tr: Monsieur de Thou, in the same place of his fine History, complains of the jests made by that dangerous buffoon François Rabelais about his master Rondelet, whom he calls Rondibilis in his Pantagruelism: a blasphemy directly against the oath of Hippocrates, which commands us to honour our living masters and their memory, and to love their children as our own brothers. Nevertheless, this buffoon is placed by Monsieur Ranchin among the illustrious physicians of the school of Montpellier. It is true that during the life of Rondelet, and for some time after, the school of Montpellier had some reputation, and was praised at that time by Gesner in his Epistles, and by Laurentius Grillus in his Itinerary. But it is to be remarked that both say even more in praise of the school of Paris.

units.la: Or Rondelet a fait de sçauans Medecins, qui ont honoré sa memoire. Posthius Alleman, en ses Notes sur l'Anatomie de Columbus, se vante d'auoir estudié en Medecine sous Rondelet. Il nomme ses compagnons d'estude Vertunian & Humeau, lequel auoit appris son opinion de Lienis vsu, & toutes ses raisons, de Rondelet: mais sa doctrine vient des Medecins de Paris, ses Maistres, auec les conferences & instructions de ce sçauant Euesque Gulielmus Pelisserius, pour l'histoire naturelle.
units.tr: Now Rondelet produced learned physicians who honoured his memory. Posthius the German, in his Notes on the Anatomy of Columbus, boasts of having studied medicine under Rondelet. He names his fellow students Vertunian and Humeau, the latter of whom had learned from Rondelet his opinion on the use of the spleen, and all his reasons; but his doctrine comes from the physicians of Paris, his masters, together with the conferences and instructions of that learned Bishop Guillaume Pellicier, for natural history.

units.la: Ie ne puis souffrir que Fracastor, Medecin Italien tres-docte, parlant de la fievre pourprée, en son traité de morbis contagiosis, dit qu'elle n'estoit pas connuë en France, l'an 1529. lors que André Naugier, Ambassadeur pour la Republique de Venize, mourut de cette fievre à Blois. Je puis verifier qu'elle est descrite au commencement du siecle 1500. par Sebastianus Montuus en ses Opuscules, & qu'à la fin du 14. siecle, un Medecin de Paris, nommé Jacques des Parts, en a le premier escrit assez clairement & doctement, employant la Saignée pour sa guerison. C'est luy mesme qui dit que de son temps les bains & les estuves estoient si communs à Paris, qu'ayant conseillé au Magistrat deles defendre en temps de peste, les baigneurs estuviers voulurent l'assassiner, s'il ne se fut sauvé. De fait les bains & estuves estoient si communs dans Paris, qu'entre les merveilles de cette ville, un Italien nommé Brixianus la loüe pour les bains & estuves, il y acent cinquante ans.
units.tr: I cannot bear that Fracastor, a very learned Italian physician, speaking of the purple fever in his treatise On Contagious Diseases, says that it was not known in France in 1529, when André Naugier, ambassador for the Republic of Venice, died of this fever at Blois. I can verify that it is described at the beginning of the sixteenth century by Sebastianus Montuus in his Opuscules, and that at the end of the fourteenth century a Paris physician named Jacques des Parts first wrote of it quite clearly and learnedly, employing bloodletting for its cure. He himself says that in his time baths and steam-baths were so common in Paris that, when he advised the magistrate to forbid them in time of plague, the bath-keepers and steam-bath attendants tried to murder him, and he escaped only by flight. Indeed the baths and steam-baths were so common in Paris that, among the marvels of that city, an Italian named Brixianus, writing one hundred and fifty years ago, praises them for their baths and steam-baths.

units.la: Balnea si calidis quaeras sudantia thermis, In claras intrabis aquas, ubi corpus inungitCallidus, & multo medicamine spargit aliptes. Mox ubi membra satis geminis mundata lacertisLaverit, & sparsos crines siccaverit alboMarcida subridens componit corpora lecto.
units.tr: If you seek baths sweating with hot springs, you will enter the bright waters, where the skilful attendant anoints the body and sprinkles it with much ointment. Soon, when the limbs have been cleansed with both arms, and he has dried the scattered hair with white cloth, smiling faintly, he lays the wilted body on the couch.

units.la: Ce que nous voyons avoir esté renouvelé dans ce siecle 1600. qui est une partie de la Medecine des anciens, abolie & perduë, qu'on appelloit iatralepticen, que Prodicus Sylimbrianus, disciple d'Hippocrate avoit cultivé, ayant mis un impost là dessus, au profit des Medecins, & Estuviers, comme il est remarqué dans l'edition de Pline, faite à Mantoüe ; Dalechamp a corrompu ce texte en son edition.
units.tr: What we see having been revived in this sixteenth century, a part of the ancient medicine that had been abolished and lost, which they called iatralepticen (the art of anointing), and which Prodicus of Selymbria, a disciple of Hippocrates, had cultivated, is this: he levied a tax on it for the benefit of physicians and bath-attendants, as is noted in the edition of Pliny printed at Mantua; Dalechamp has corrupted this text in his edition.

units.la: I'ay sujet aussi de reprendre Monsieur Citois, d'avoir dit en son Liure de dolore colico Pictonico, qu'avant le Sieur Milon, premier Medecin & dernier de Henry le Grand, la Colique de Poictou estoit inconnuë aux Medecins de Paris. Fernel l'a descrit sous le nom de Colicus dolor biliosus nothus : comme aussi a fait Hollier en sa Pratique : partant on ne peut proposer aucune maladie, qui n'ait esté premierement connuë par les Medecins de Paris, qui en ont descrit le traitement. Galien, au premier Liure de sa Methode, nous represente qu'il y a eu autres fois dans la Grece trois Escholes en Medecine fort celebres, Coa, Cuidia [?], & Rhodia, laquelle se perdit la premiere, & prit sa place, l'Escholé Italienne au Royaume de Naples, où il y avoit eu des Medecins celebres, Philition[?], Empedocles, Pausanias, & d'autres leurs Sectateurs. Ces trois Escholes debatoient ensemble pour la doctrine, & pour sçauoir laquelle auoit plus contribué pour augmenter, & enrichir la Medecine par leurs estudes & inuentions. Il y auoit une ialousie, & honnefte emulation entre elles, sans disputer de leur ancienneté, & de leurs richesses. Ie voudrois qu'au lieu de rechercher l'antiquité & l'estime qu'on fait les Papes & les Rois des Academies de Paris & de Montpelier, on recherchât en quoy elles ont excellé, ce qu'elles ont produit de leur inuention, quel profit elles ont apporté au public, par les escrits qu'ils nous ont laissé, & par les seruices, qu'ils ont rendu au public. C'est ce que ie pretens monstrer en l'une & l'autre Escole de Medecine.
units.tr: I have also reason to rebuke Monsieur Citois for saying in his book On the Colic of Poitou that before Sieur Milon, first physician and last of Henry the Great, the Colic of Poitou was unknown to the physicians of Paris. Fernel described it under the name colicus dolor biliosus nothus, as Hollier also did in his Practice. Therefore no disease can be put forward that was not first known to the physicians of Paris, who have described its treatment. Galen, in the first book of his Method, tells us that there were formerly in Greece three very celebrated schools of medicine: Coan, Cnidian [?], and Rhodian, of which the last to perish was the first, and in its place rose the Italian school in the kingdom of Naples, where there had been celebrated physicians, Philistion [?], Empedocles, Pausanias, and others, their followers. These three schools contended with one another over doctrine, and over which had contributed more to increase and enrich medicine by their studies and discoveries. There was rivalry and honourable emulation among them, without any dispute over their antiquity and their wealth. I would wish that, instead of seeking the antiquity and the esteem that Popes and Kings place upon the academies of Paris and Montpellier, one would inquire in what they have excelled, what they have produced by their own invention, what profit they have brought to the public through the writings they have left us, and through the services they have rendered to the public. This is what I intend to show in each of the two schools of medicine.

units.la: Les Medecins de Paris ayans les premiers abandonné la Medecine des Arabes, ont corrigé une bonne partie de leurs erreurs, comme ont fait Campegius, & quelques Ita-liens: ayans quitté les Arabes, ils se sont adonnez à la Medecine des Grecs, qui estoit perduë, & l'ont fait reuiure les premiers. Prouuons cela par l'authorité de sçauans Medecins estrangers, dautant que les Medecins de Paris feroient fuspects : neantmoins ie diray que Goupilus, auant qu'estre Bachelier en Medecine, dediant ses Notes sur le texte Grec d'Alexander Trallianus, qu'il auoit fait imprimer, il parle des Medecins de Paris de la sorte. Qui cum squalorem Medicinae, quem ei rude saeculum obduxerat primi, absit dicto inuidia, absterseritis, efficeritisque ut naturalem eius nitorem aliquando intueremur, hoc beneficio plane diuino sic nos vobis deuinxistis, ut hoc nomine tantum vobis, quantum hominem homini debere vix fas sit debiturus sim. Si ce tesmoignage est suspect, dautant que ce grand personnage a depuis esté Docteur de nostre Eschole, Professeur du Roy, & successeur de Sylvius, i'en produiray d'autres.
units.tr: The physicians of Paris, having first abandoned the medicine of the Arabs, have corrected a good part of their errors, as Campegius and some Italians have also done. Having left the Arabs, they devoted themselves to the medicine of the Greeks, which had been lost, and they were the first to revive it. Let us prove this by the authority of learned foreign physicians, since the physicians of Paris would be suspected. Nevertheless I shall say that Goupil, before being Bachelor of Medicine, in dedicating his notes on the Greek text of Alexander of Tralles, which he had had printed, speaks of the physicians of Paris in this manner: Since you have wiped away the squalor of medicine, which the rude age of earlier times had cast over it, let envy be far from my words, and since you have brought it about that we at last behold its natural brightness, you have bound us to you by a benefit truly divine, so that for this alone I shall owe you as much as it is scarcely right for one man to owe another. If this testimony is suspect, because this great man has since become a Doctor of our School, Professor to the King, and successor of Sylvius, I shall produce others.

units.la: Antonius Albus, en l'Epistre sur les Aphorismes d'Hippocrate. Laus prima & praecipua, aliorum pace dixerim, Parisiensis Academiae Medicis, Medicinaeque Professoribus debetur, qui reliquis, abiectisque ex intima barbarie scriptoribus, Veteres illos eloquentissimos, Doctissimosque Medicos, Galenum & Hippocratem quotidie nobis feliciter restituunt, atque in lucem, lectionemque revocant, magno totius Europae applausu & fructu non mediocri. Vn autre Antonius Fortulus, en l'année 1526. en auoit escrit autant en la Preface de la version de quelques Livres de Galien. Hoc autem affirmare verissimè mihi posse videor, in nulla vsquam Academia ita veram vigere Medicinam atque in Parisiensi, à qua longè exulant Sophistice & Barbaries, quæ duæ pestes, sicut in alias omnes egregias disciplinas irruperant, ita in Medicina perditè savicrant[?] apud superioris ætatis homines.
units.tr: Antonius Albus, in the Epistle on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates: The first and chief praise, I would say with the peace of others, is due to the Academy of Paris, to the physicians and professors of medicine, who, having cast aside the other writers, who were sunk in utter barbarism, daily restore to us happily those most eloquent and most learned physicians, Galen and Hippocrates, and recall them to light and to reading, to the great applause and no small profit of all Europe. Another, Antonius Fortulus, in the year 1526, wrote as much in the preface to the translation of some books of Galen: I seem able to affirm most truly that nowhere else in any academy does true medicine flourish as it does in the Parisian, from which sophistry and barbarism are far exiled; these two plagues, which had burst into all other distinguished disciplines, had in medicine raged to ruin among the men of the earlier age.

units.la: Apres le tesmoignage d'vn grand Medecin Professeur de Louuain, il n'y a plus de replique. Hieremias Thriuerius en l'Epistre & au commencement de son Liure de missione sanguinis in pleuritide, parle des Medecins de Paris de la sorte. Per Medicos Parisienses Medicinam plurimùm adiutam negare non possum, plurimáque quæ hactenus latuerant fateri debeo esse inuenta. Et au commencement de son Liure, il employe deux pages à la louange des Medecins de Paris, que ie rapporteray tout au long, pour faire voir que les Medecins de Paris sont les vrais restaurateurs de la Medecine.
units.tr: After the testimony of a great physician, professor at Louvain, there is no further reply. Hieremias Thriverius, in the Epistle and at the beginning of his book On Bloodletting in Pleurisy, speaks of the physicians of Paris in this manner: I cannot deny that medicine has been greatly aided by the Parisian physicians, and I must acknowledge that many things which had hitherto lain hidden have been discovered. And at the beginning of his book he spends two pages in praise of the physicians of Paris, which I shall report in full, to show that the physicians of Paris are the true restorers of medicine.

units.la: VEHEMENTER ego vobis gratulari debeo, viri ornatissimi, vobis plurimum debet studiosa iuuentus, qui nescio an maiori labore, an fructu vberiore, Hippocratem & Galenum, duos Medicina antistites reuocastis. Hoc scio non minori negotio quàm Hercules Cerberum ad superas revulsit auras, antiquam Medicinam in Scholas vestras retraxistis, nec minori invidia. Tantæ molis erat, tanti operis, ex altissima Græcia Romanam quasi postliminio quodam reducere Medicinam, nec victuros tamen diffidite, nam si Hercules nondum Deus immortalis Deæ invidiam laboribus fatigare potuit, vos quorum per omnia fæcula famam, nec poterit ferrum nec edax abolere vetustas, vos dico immortales mortalium contumeliam, injuriam, invidiam superare quare non poteritis? Atque adeo quid jam vicisse dubitatis, qui nedum aliquot in vestri invidiam provocastis, quod faventis, proximæque victoriæ est argumentum, sed propemodum video omnes in inmarcescibilis vestræ gloriæ studium rapitis, non instrenuum in primis Ducem Linacrum sequuti, qui in hanc arenam cum Theodoro Gaza & Georgio Valla felicissimè est ausus primum descendere, cuius gloria non dissimilem in Italia excitauit Leonicenum, virum undecunque doctissimum, in Medicina prosecto Herculem, ut dicere nescias an Herculesque Athlanti, an Athlas Herculi vicem præbuerit. Certè is multo fœcundior, ut qui non unum sed in Italia plurimos Leonicenos, Manardos, in Gallia etiam vestra Copam ad idem certamen provocauit, cuius rursum fructus multo longè uberrimus, ut qui non unum, non duos, sed quemadmodum fœcunda illa, breuisque Iasonis satio armatos plurimos gregatim vos suscitarit, qui antiquam Medicinam tutari certatis, situ squallentem, obscuram, conspurcatam illustratis, & qua oportet genuina, hoc est diuina rursum facie effigiatis. Pergite igitur quando proculdubio eò vocati estis, barbarorum vitiis eam vindicare Medicinam, omnium scientiarum optimam maximam, antiquissimam, difficillimam, cæterarum hactenus artium perditissimam, mendosissimam, obsoletissimam omnibus suis mendis eluere, neque vnquam à tam honesto, tam necessario opere per Deum immortalem cessetis, donec tetricum illum suum vultum deposuerit, & antiquam prorsus alacritatem obtinuerit, id dico quæ clarissima, quæ emendatissima euaserit, nescitis quàm gratam, quàm desideratam Medicis, atque adeo mortalibus omnibus rem facitis, quantam vobis gloriam comparatis, certè maximam, multò tamen apud Deum maiorem ( qui Medicum ob hominum necessitudinem atque ineuitabilem miseriam cæteris Profesforibus præfecit omnibus) habituri, atque eo præterea ampliorem ac ditiorem, quo viri aliquot non modò acceptum beneficium non amant, sed planè centemnunt, quibus vt imprecandum nihil maliest, ita summopere rogandum, vt Dij illis propriam dent mentem aut fortasis meliorem, ita nobilium suorum errorum mallent admoneri, quàm imprudenter posthac hallucinari. Quis enim nescit ignotissima quaedam pro cognitissimis hactenus habita, pro commodis incommoda, & pro salutiferis insalutifera. Praetereo non pauca per saeculi iniuriam litterarum omnium nouercam, non sine magno salutis humanae dispendio peruerse intellecta, quod iam Petrus Brissotus & Leonardus Fuchsius, ac alij de missione sanguinis in pleuritide, atque in omnibus internis phlegmonis ausi sunt dicere.
units.tr: VEHEMENTLY ought I to congratulate you, most distinguished men; studious youth owes you very much, you who (I know not whether with greater labour or more abundant fruit) have recalled Hippocrates and Galen, the two leaders of medicine. I know that it was no less a task than when Hercules dragged Cerberus up into the upper air, that you have drawn ancient medicine back into your schools, and not with less envy. It was of such great effort and such great work to bring medicine back from high Greece, as it were by a kind of right of return, into a Roman form; nor do you doubt that it will live, for if Hercules, not yet a immortal god, could not wear down the envy of the goddess by his labours, can you, whose fame through all ages neither iron nor devouring antiquity can abolish, I say, you immortals, not overcome the insult, injury and envy of mortals? Why then do you doubt that you have already conquered, you who have not only provoked envy against yourselves, which is a sign of a favourable and near victory, but I see almost all of you pursuing eagerly the cause of your unfading glory, having followed especially the not unenergetic leader Linacre, who first dared to descend into this arena with Theodore Gaza and George Valla most happily, whose glory aroused in Italy no unlike Leonicenus, a man most learned in every respect, truly a Hercules in medicine, so that you could not say whether Hercules gave Atlas his place, or Atlas gave his place to Hercules. Certainly that man was much more fruitful, since he challenged to the same contest not one Leonicenus but many in Italy, Manardus, and in your own France Copa; and again the fruit of this is far more abundant, since, as that fertile and brief sowing of Jason raised up armed men in throngs, not one, not two, but many of you have arisen, who strive to defend ancient medicine, and who illumine it, once squalid, obscure and defiled, and restore it to its genuine, that is, its divine, face. Press on, then, since you were without doubt called thither to vindicate this medicine from the faults of barbarians, to cleanse it of all its blemishes, the best and greatest of all sciences, the most ancient, the most difficult, the most ruined of the other arts hitherto, the most faulty and most obsolete; and never, by God immortal, cease from so honourable and so necessary a work, until it has laid aside that gloomy countenance and recovered its former liveliness, I mean becomes most clear and most correct. You do not know how welcome and how desired this will be to physicians, and therefore to all mortals; you win for yourselves a glory that is very great, certainly the greatest, yet to be held far greater with God, who has set the physician over all the other professors because of human need and inescapable misery; and you will have it the more abundantly and richly, since some men not only do not love the benefit received, but plainly despise it. For these, nothing is to be prayed for more than that the gods give them a mind of their own, or perhaps a better one, so that they would rather be warned of their own noble errors than wander in their imprudence hereafter. For who does not know that certain things most unknown have hitherto been held to be most familiar, inconveniences in place of advantages, and things unwholesome in place of healthful? I pass over not a few things, perverted through the injury of the age, the stepmother of all literature, and understood to the great loss of human health, as Petrus Brissotus, Leonardus Fuchsius, and others have already dared to say about bloodletting in pleurisy and in all internal inflammations.

units.la: Quod si tantus in re tam evidenti multis saeculis error trahi potuit nullis animadversis, qui testiores in re obscuriori multis clam insidiatos hactenus latuisse coniecturabimur, certè ab uno omnia facilè erit discere saepissimè hanc neotericorum Medicinam ab eo quae Hippocratis & Galeni est euariasse, & maiori saepe detrimento quàm remedio fuisse; audax aliquis audebit dicere.
units.tr: If such great error could be carried on for many centuries in a matter so evident, with no one noticing it, we may reasonably conjecture that many more errors, in a more obscure matter, have hitherto lain hidden, lying in wait for many people. Surely from one example it will be easy to learn that this modern medicine has very often departed from that of Hippocrates and Galen, and has often done more harm than good; some bold man will dare to say so.

units.la: Non mirum igitur si non ego tantùm, sed plurimi alij antiquae veritatis aemuli, & humanae ut decet salutis studiosi, de recentiorum Medicorum erratis vos disceptantes audiam libenter, & (quod malus aliquis temerarium putet) de sanguinis missione, in his quas diximus inflammationibus cum Petro Brissoto & Leonardo Fuchsio, hominibus profectò litteratissimis digladiari, aut fortasse magis ambigere quàm certare audeamus, vobis dico arbitris, quorum eruditio integrior, ac in commune bonum benevolentia maior, quàm vt in re tam periculosa cum veritatis detrimento alicui haeresi ferat patrocinia.
units.tr: It is therefore no wonder that not only I but many others who are rivals of ancient truth, and who rightly care for human health, will gladly listen to you debating the errors of more recent physicians, and that we will dare, as I say, to contend, or perhaps rather to dispute, with Pierre Brissot and Leonard Fuchs, men truly most learned in letters, about the bloodletting in the inflammations we have mentioned; I speak to you as judges, whose learning is more complete and whose goodwill toward the common good is greater, so that you would not, in a matter so dangerous, lend the protection of any heresy at the expense of the truth.

units.la: Voulez vous encore des preuues pour la restauration d'Hippocrate, faite par les Medecins de Paris, lisez l'Epistre de Foësius, au commencement de son Hippocrate, où vous verrez comme il confesse, que la pluspart de son trauail vient des Medecins de Paris, ausquels il aduoüe d'estre grandement obligé. In Hippocrate si quod spero consequutus sum, id totum vobis acceptum ferent, & gratias habebunt, qui ex nostris laboribus fructum reportabunt, meóque exemplo vestrum amplissimum nomen sæculorum[?] immortalitati consecrabunt, vobis vero vt augustissimis patribus, ex quorum sinu & disciplina hausta sunt & delibata, nostram Hippocratis versionem gratissimi erga vos animi testimonium, perpetua officij observantia denuncio, dedico & offero.
units.tr: Do you want further proof of the restoration of Hippocrates carried out by the physicians of Paris? Read Foësius's dedicatory epistle at the beginning of his Hippocrates, where you will see how he confesses that most of his work comes from the physicians of Paris, to whom he acknowledges that he is greatly indebted. If I have achieved anything in my Hippocrates, you will all receive the credit for it, and those who reap the fruit of our labours will thank you; by my example they will consecrate your illustrious name to the immortality of the centuries[?]. To you, most venerable fathers, from whose bosom and teaching what I have drawn and tasted was drawn, I declare, dedicate and offer our translation of Hippocrates, as a testimony of my most grateful spirit toward you, with unfailing devotion of service.

units.la: Ie finiray cét article par le tesmoignage d'vn sçauant Medecin & Professeur de Montpelier, Honoratus Castellanus, qui a esté oncle maternel de Monsieur André du Laurens. Il a tellement respecté les Medecins de Paris, qu'il confesse en vne oraison qu'il prononça publiquement à Paris, qu'il apprehende paroistre, In ea Ciuitate qua totius orbis[?] praestantissimis ac eruditissimis artis Medica Professoris. est ornata: qu'il a appris la Medecine à Paris, & de là est allé à Montpelier prendre les degrez de Docteur,adioustant à la fin de son Oraison, qu'il n'y a lieu au monde où l'on puisse mieux apprendre toutes les sciences, qu'en l'Universite de Paris, admonestant ses auditeurs de faire profit de cét advertissement. Apres le tesmoignage d'un si grand personnage de l'Eschole de Montpelier, ie produiray l'attestation de deux Medecins de Montpelier, les Sieurs Bompart, & Citois.
