Marcellin Bompart dedie un petit Liure tres-docte, Miser homo, à quatre Medecins de Paris, Docteurs, in omnium antiquissima & nobilissima Medicorum Facultate Parisiensi; dans le corps de l'Epistre, il parle des Medecins de Paris de la sorte, Parisienses Medici puriores & sanctioris Medicinae Athlantes fortissimi, & in bene medendi arte Magistri optimi atque sapientissimi: quis eos dicat χοομωσς[?], cum φιλοσόφοι[?] praluxerint, Hippocratis assertores adamantini. Monsieur Citois, sçavant Medecin, comme ila fait paroistre par ses escrits, ses consultations, & conferences frequentes qu'il a euavec les Medecins de Paris, en l'Epistre liminaire de ses Oeuures, parlant à Monsieur le Cardinal de Richelieu, publie hautement & hardiment, Lutetiana Schola in acutorum morborum curatione, nulla in tota Europa peritior & felicior est. Ce secret est entre les mains des Medecins de Paris, & pour le sçauoir, il faut auoir pratiqué trois ou quatre ans auec eux, pour guerir les maladies aiguës. Ils se seruent de la saignée reiterée selon la grandeur de la maladie & les forces du malade, mesnageans ce remede auec grande discretion : ils ont quitté tous les Cardiaques fort chauds, qui augmentent l'ardeur de la fievre, & se seruent de ceux qui sont mediocrement chauds, spirituels & vaporeux, pour restaurer les esprits, & les forces du corps. Bien souuent ils employent les Cardiaques rafraichissans, acides, & diuretiques, pour purifier le sang, en le rafraichissant ; ils ne font point d'estat d'aucun Cardiaque, s'il n'agit par qualité manifeste, chaude ou froide,& qui soit vaporeuse pour reparer les esprits : ce que ne peuuent faire ny les Perles, ny le Besoart, ny la Licorne, dans vne foiblesse, donnez tous seuls, mais en compagnie d'autres Cardiaques spirituels, on s'en peut seruir pour conteter[?] l'opinion vulgaire. Ils ont aussi reietté les sueurs violentes, & prouoquées par remedes chauds, & quantité de couuertures, qui bruslent davantage les pauvres malades. Ils ont retranché le vin & l'abondance des alimens, & ont donné à boire suffisamment aux malades durant l'ardeur de la fievre, pour l'éteindre. Ils ont aussi diminué la quantité des remedes en diverses façons, qui incommodoient & estouffoient les malades, & se sont contentez de peu, bien choisis, & de grande vertu.
units.tr: I will end this article with the testimony of a learned physician and professor of Montpellier, Honoratus Castellanus, who was the maternal uncle of Monsieur André du Laurens. He so esteemed the physicians of Paris that he confesses, in a speech he delivered publicly at Paris, that he is ashamed to appear, in that city, which is adorned by the most excellent and learned professors of the medical art of the whole world[?]. He learned medicine at Paris and from there went to Montpellier to take his doctorate, adding at the end of his Oration that there is no place in the world where one can better learn all the sciences than at the University of Paris, admonishing his hearers to profit from this advice. After the testimony of so great a man of the school of Montpellier, I will produce the attestation of two physicians of Montpellier, the Messieurs Bompart and Citois. Marcellin Bompart dedicates a very learned little book, Miser homo, to four doctors of Paris, in the most ancient and noble Faculty of Medicine of Paris; in the body of the epistle he speaks of the physicians of Paris in this manner: The Parisian physicians, the most vigorous champions of the purer and more sacred medicine, and the best and wisest masters in the art of healing: who could call them [Greek word unclear], since the philosophers have shone forth, the adamantine defenders of Hippocrates. Monsieur Citois, a learned physician, as he has shown by his writings, his consultations, and the frequent conferences he has held with the physicians of Paris, in the preliminary epistle of his Works, addressing Monsieur le Cardinal de Richelieu, publicly and boldly proclaims: The Lutetian school is, in the treatment of acute diseases, the most skilled and most successful in all of Europe. This secret is in the hands of the physicians of Paris, and to know it one must have practised for three or four years with them, in order to cure acute diseases. They use bloodletting repeated according to the severity of the disease and the strength of the patient, employing this remedy with great discretion. They have abandoned all very hot cardiacs, which increase the heat of the fever, and use those that are moderately warm, spirituous and vaporous, to restore the spirits and the strength of the body. Very often they employ cooling, acidic and diuretic cardiacs, to purify the blood by cooling it; they set no store by any cardiac unless it acts by a manifest quality, hot or cold, and is vaporous so as to repair the spirits. Pearls, bezoar and unicorn horn, given alone in a weakness, cannot do this; but in company with other spiritual cardiacs they may be used to satisfy the common opinion. They have also rejected violent sweats provoked by hot remedies, and the many coverings that scorch the poor patients all the more. They have cut back on wine and the abundance of food, and during the heat of the fever they have given the patients enough to drink to quench it. They have also reduced the quantity of remedies in various ways, which burdened and suffocated the patients, and have been content with few, well chosen, and of great virtue.

units.la: Depuis deux cens ans ils se sont opposez aux Charlatans, Imposteurs, Chymiques, qui promettoient, auec des essences, & or potable, guerir toute sorte de maladies. Auant que Paracelse fut au monde, vn Medecin de Paris, nommé Iean le Brun, faisoit profession de remedes chymiques auec son or potable, & fut condamné comme Imposteur, & chassé des Escholes.
units.tr: For two hundred years they have opposed the charlatans, impostors and chemists who promised, with essences and potable gold, to cure every kind of disease. Before Paracelsus was in the world, a physician of Paris named Jean le Brun made a profession of chemical remedies with his potable gold, and was condemned as an impostor and expelled from the schools.

units.la: En l'an 1560. les Alchymistes s'estans introduits dans Paris, distribuans leurs drogues empoisonnées, & donnans à tout le monde de l'antimoine, qui entroit en vogue, & recommandé par les escrits d'un Medecin de Montpelier, nommé de Launay, ils furent par censure de l'Eschole condamnez, & par Arrest de la Cour l'usage de l'antimoine interdit d'en vendre. En l'an 1580. d'autres Alchymistes, sous la conduite de la Riviere, Docteur de Caën, qui avoit fait des Livres de Chymie, s'estans establis à Paris, en furent chassez par Arrest de la Cour, à la poursuite des Medecins de Paris, qui avoient fait connoistre leur ignorance. L'an 1608. un Medecin de Paris, nommé Pierre Paumier, voulant introduire l'Alchymie, sous pretexte qu'il escrivoit contre Libanius, & monstroit qu'il estoit plus sçauant que luy en Alchymie, qu'il guerissoit les Ladres avec son or potable, & antimoine preparé d'une autre façon que tous les autres Alchymistes, fut condamné avec son Livre, de se dédire, ou sortir de la compagnie. Ce qui fut confirmé par Arrest de la Cour de Parlement. Vous voyez qu'avant Paracelse, l'Alchymie estoit connuë à Paris. Il y a un Medecin de Paris, nommé Guinterius Andernacus, qui a composé deux Tomes de la Medecine Galenique & Chymique, estant Alleman & Lutherien ; il se retira à Strasbourg, durant la perfecution des Lutheriens & Calviniftes, sous Henry second, où il est decedé. Les Medecins de Paris, voyans le tort que faisoient en nostre Religion, & en nostre Medecine, les escrits de Paracelse, ils ont recueilly plus de cent heresies, qu'ils ont presenté à la Sorbonne, qui les a censuré: à l'exemple des Medecins de Paris, le College de Londres a condamné le Livre d'Antonius, Medecin de leur College, de auro potabili, & ont monstré par un docte escrit, la faussetē[?] de son or potable,& là-dessus donnent des loüanges aux Medecins de Paris,restaurateurs & protecteurs de la vraye Medecine, pour s'estre toujours opposez aux remedes Chymiques metalliques pris par la bouche.
units.tr: In the year 1560, the alchemists, having introduced themselves into Paris, distributing their poisonous drugs and giving antimony to everyone, which was coming into vogue and was recommended by the writings of a physician of Montpellier named de Launay, were condemned by censure of the School, and by decree of the Court the use of antimony was forbidden and its sale prohibited. In the year 1580, other alchemists under the leadership of de la Rivière, a Doctor of Caen who had written books on chemistry, established themselves at Paris and were driven out by decree of the Court, at the prosecution of the physicians of Paris, who had made their ignorance known. In the year 1608, a physician of Paris named Pierre Paumier, wishing to introduce alchemy on the pretext that he wrote against Libavius and showed that he was more learned than he in alchemy, and that he cured lepers with his potable gold and antimony prepared in a different way from all other alchemists, was condemned, with his book, either to retract or to leave the company. This was confirmed by decree of the Parliament. You see that before Paracelsus, alchemy was known at Paris. There is a physician of Paris named Guinterius Andernacus, who composed two volumes on Galenic and Chemical Medicine, being a German and a Lutheran; he withdrew to Strasbourg during the persecution of the Lutherans and Calvinists under Henry the Second, and there he died. The physicians of Paris, seeing the harm that the writings of Paracelsus were doing to our religion and to our medicine, collected more than a hundred heresies, which they presented to the Sorbonne, which censured them; following the example of the physicians of Paris, the College of London condemned the book of Antonius, a physician of their College, de auro potabili, and showed by a learned writing the falsity of his potable gold, and on this ground they give praise to the physicians of Paris, restorers and protectors of true medicine, for having always opposed metallic chemical remedies taken by mouth.

units.la: Nous verrons si les Medecins de nostre temps, suivront les traces de leurs anciens Maistres, & s'ils seront assez courageux & vertueux, pour corriger les abus & homicides qui se commettent journellement dans Paris, par l'usage du vin emetique, antimonial, qui en fait vingt fois plus mourir, qu'il n'en guerit, estant donné seul en breuuage. C'est la verité qu'en petite quantité, s'il est mesle avec nos purgatifs violens, ils l'entrainent vistement hors l'estomach dans les boyaux: de la sorte il n'est pas si dangereux: c'est ainsi que des Princesses en ont pris, dont les unes sont mortes, les autres, ont evité le hazard present, non sans crainte de quelque mauvaise impression, que tels remedes laissent ordinairement aux visceres.
units.tr: We shall see whether the physicians of our own time will follow the footsteps of their former masters, and whether they will be brave and virtuous enough to correct the abuses and homicides committed daily in Paris through the use of emetic antimonial wine, which kills twenty times more people than it cures when given alone as a drink. It is true that in small quantity, if it is mixed with our violent purgatives, they carry it quickly out of the stomach into the bowels; in this way it is not so dangerous. Thus some princesses have taken it, of whom some died and others escaped the present danger, not without fear of some bad impression which such remedies ordinarily leave on the viscera.

units.la: Je ne veux pas m'estendre davantage sur cet article, qui a esté tres-doctement & judicieusement expliqué par Monsieur Guillemeau, nostre bon Collegue, en vn discours qu'il en a fait sur ce sujet, dans les Commentaires de sa belle These, Obseruation 2. Puis apres cela, vantez & prisez vostre Antimoine, qu'il est Principium vitæ, balsamum, & medentem mumiam (horrible mot) in se habet. Verum, verum dico, non est sub cælo Medicina sublimior. Il est vray pour estre porté bien-tost au Ciel, & estre deliuré des miseres de ce monde, comme Monsieur d'Auaux, & beaucoup d'autres personnes.
units.tr: I do not wish to dwell further on this point, which has been very learnedly and judiciously explained by Monsieur Guillemeau, our good colleague, in a discourse he made on this subject in the commentaries on his fine thesis, Observation 2. After that, praise and prize your antimony, which has in itself the principle of life, a balsam, and a healing mummy (a horrible word). Verily, verily I say unto you, there is no more sublime medicine under heaven. It is true, for it will soon carry one up to Heaven and deliver one from the miseries of this world, as it did Monsieur d'Auaux and many other persons.

units.la: Pour vous faire connoistre l'excellence & l'vtilité de la pratique des Medecins de Paris, aux maladies, Ie respondray en peu de paroles, à vos obiections iniurieuses, & tresdangereuses pour la vie du public. Ie commenceray par la saignée, bien qu'elle soit auiourd'huy descriée, & pour cela les Medecins de Paris faufsement calomniez & mal voulus. On ne doute point qu'il ne faille saigner: mais les Medecins de Paris ont montré par experience & par escrit, l'vtilité de la frequente saignée, selon la grandeur & la perseuerance de la maladie, qui estoufferoit ou le cerueau, ou le cœur & le poûmon, ou qui feroit inflammation aux visceres; ou pour destourner l'humeur coulant sur la partie affectée, ou évacuer l'humeur attachée à la partie. En faisant ce remede, ils observent soigneusement les forces, & à peu près de ne tirer pas plus de la moitié du sang du corps en toute extremité; & ce, par plusieurs saignées en divers temps. Tellement, puis qu'il y a dans le corps d'une personne bien habitué & formé, environ 24. livres, ou chopines de sang, au rapport d'Avicenne, & qu'on peut perdre en un jour 20. chopines sans mourir, ce qui se voit tous les jours dans les grandes pertes de sang, soit par les hemorrhoides, soit par le nez, soit par la matrice aux femmes: Tirant dix ou douze fois du sang en une maladie violente, furieuse, & tres-dangereuse, les forces estans bonnes, & à chasque fois deux ou trois poilettes durant le temps de six ou sept jours, on ne peut perdre que 26. ou 28. poilettes de sang, qui feront sept chopines, qui est peu à une personne sanguine, qui en un jour en peut perdre 60. poilettes sans mourir.
units.tr: To make you know the excellence and usefulness of the practice of the physicians of Paris in diseases, I shall reply in a few words to your objections, which are injurious and very dangerous to the life of the public. I shall begin with bloodletting, although it is today decried, and for that reason the physicians of Paris are falsely slandered and ill regarded. No one doubts that one must bleed; but the physicians of Paris have shown, by experience and in writing, the usefulness of frequent bleeding, according to the size and persistence of the disease, which would suffocate the brain, the heart and lungs, or which would cause inflammation of the viscera; either to divert the humour flowing to the affected part, or to evacuate the humour attached to the part. In performing this remedy, they carefully observe the strength, and in every extremity they take, as near as possible, no more than half of the blood of the body, and this by several bleedings at different times. Therefore, since in the body of a well-conditioned and well-formed person there are, according to Avicenna, about 24 pounds or pints of blood, and since one can lose 20 pints in a day without dying, as is seen every day in great losses of blood, whether by the haemorrhoids, by the nose, or by the womb in women: drawing blood ten or twelve times in a violent, furious and very dangerous illness, the strength being good, and each time two or three pounds over the space of six or seven days, one can lose only 26 or 28 pounds of blood, which makes seven pints, a small amount for a sanguine person, who in one day can lose 60 pounds without dying.

units.la: Je ne veux point traiter cette question à plain fond, la reservant à un autre lieu, pour l'instruction de ceux qui blasment la saignée des Medecins de Paris. Or pour se fortifier ils alleguent l'authorité de deux celebres Medecins de Paris, Fernel, & Duret. Vous sçaurez que Fernel, auât que venir à la Cour, avoit pour Antagoniste, dans la pratique de Paris, Flesselles, qui avoit esté preferé audit Fernel, en la distribution des lieux de la Licence. Cette jalousie s'estant fort eschauffée dans la pratique sur les malades, Fernel escriuit un petit liuret, De vacuandi ratione, qu'il appella la pratique, & le dedia aux Estudians en Medecine: en cette Epistre, sans nommer de Flesselles, il blasme les frequentes saignées, que faisoit Flesselles, qui avoit la vogue dans Paris, & estoit grand saigneur. Mais ayant reconnu le tort qu'il avoit fait au public, par cette animosité, & escrit dangereux, il l'a tout changé, en supprimât la Preface, & le liure. Et dans un autre liure, il a recommandé la saignée presque en toutes maladies, mesmes aux femmes nouvellement accouchées, faite au bras, plustost qu'au pied. De plus il a advancé d'autres propositions & resolutions encore plus hardies, qu'il a descrit. Vous apprendrez cela dans la vie de Fernel, faite par Plantius, son disciple, Medecin de Paris.
units.tr: I do not wish to treat this question at full depth, reserving it for another place, for the instruction of those who blame the bloodletting of the physicians of Paris. Now, to strengthen themselves, they allege the authority of two celebrated physicians of Paris, Fernel and Duret. You shall know that Fernel, before coming to the Court, had as antagonist in the practice of Paris Flesselles, who had been preferred to the said Fernel in the distribution of the places of the Licence. This jealousy, having grown very heated in the practice upon the sick, led Fernel to write a small book, De vacuandi ratione, which he called the practice, and dedicated it to the students of medicine. In this Epistle, without naming Flesselles, he blames the frequent bleedings which Flesselles made, who was in vogue in Paris and was a great bleeder. But having recognised the wrong he had done the public by this animosity and dangerous writing, he changed it all, suppressing the Preface and the book. And in another book he recommended bleeding in almost all diseases, even in women newly delivered, performed in the arm rather than in the foot. Moreover, he advanced other propositions and resolutions still bolder, which he described. You will learn this in the life of Fernel, written by Plantius, his disciple, physician of Paris.

units.la: Les Medecins uiuans aujourd'huy, le sçavent par traditive de leurs Anciens.
units.tr: The physicians living today know it by the tradition of their Elders.

units.la: * Quant à Monsieur Duret, ils alleguent de luy trois passages tous differens, qu'ils cousent ensemble, pour les faire valoir de suite, lesquels neantmoins sont du tout contraires à leurs intentions. Le premier est couché de la sorte. Vetus quorundam opinio est, nullum dolorem lateris, nedum pleuritidem, nisi unico Phlebotomia alexiterio posse sanari, ac sane operæpretium est nugarum audire garrulitatem, quarum ambagibus ipsorum vanitas solertissima est apud vulgus, omnique potior veritate. C'est la verité que la douleur de costé ne requiert pas la saignée, comme si c'estoit pleurefie, & le Sieur Duret l'explique en suite dans le Commentaire, lequel, si Courtaut l'eust leu, il eust trouvé des armes plus fortes pour nous combattre. Au second passage, faussement allegué, il ne parle pas de la saignée, mais seulement que le foye estant profondement incisé, on perd tout son sang & la vie, qui est attachée au sang ; ce que nous tenons pour veritable. Au 3. passage, Duret defend In torpida refrigeratione, dans une stupeur refroidie, de tirer du sang, selon Hippocrate, d'autant que cet accident vient d'une grande foiblesse, par l'extinction de la chaleur naturelle. Mais si cet accident vient par une inflammation interne, comme il arrive aux fievres ardentes, ce qui se reconnoist par les inquietudes, difficulté de respirer avec vne grande soif, alors, Prodest multum sanguinem detrahere, ut fecimus in Generali Monet, cui refrixerant partes extimæ.
units.tr: * As for Monsieur Duret, they allege from him three passages, all different, which they stitch together so as to make them count as one continuous text, though these are entirely contrary to their intentions. The first is set down thus: It is the old opinion of certain people that no pain of the side, much less pleurisy, can be cured except by bloodletting, a single remedy; and indeed it is worth listening to the chatter of these trifles, whose ambiguities are most cunning in their vanity among the common people, and preferred over all truth. It is true that pain in the side does not require bloodletting, as if it were pleurisy, and Sieur Duret explains this afterwards in the Commentary, which, had Courtaut read it, he would have found stronger weapons to fight us. In the second passage, falsely alleged, he does not speak of bloodletting, but only that when the liver is deeply incised, all its blood and life is lost, which is attached to the blood; this we hold to be true. In the third passage, Duret defends, In torpida refrigeratione, in a cold stupor, drawing blood according to Hippocrates, inasmuch as this accident comes from great weakness, through the extinction of the natural heat. But if this accident comes from an internal inflammation, as happens in burning fevers, which is recognised by restlessness, difficulty of breathing with great thirst, then, it greatly profits to draw off blood, as we did in the General Month, in which the outer parts had grown cold.

units.la: Voila Courtaut, comment vous citez tresmal les textes qu'on vous a donnez pour groffir vos escritures. Puis qu'ils ont faussement allegué Duret, pour improuer la saignée, i'employeray le mesme Autheur, pour monstrer la necessité de la saignée, & comme il l'a recommandé, pag. 329. Nihil æque natiuum calorem extinguit atque febrilis ardor, ac sanè iactura fit maior humidi primigenij septem diebus à febre acuta, quàm à calore insito 70. annis. Septem diebus is vitam finit tabifica vi febris consumptus, qui septuagenarius erat futurus, duce natiuo calore.
units.tr: There you have it, Courtaut, how badly you cite the texts that were given to you in order to swell your writings. Since they have falsely alleged Duret to disapprove of bloodletting, I shall employ the same author to show the necessity of bloodletting, and how he has recommended it, p. 329. Nothing extinguishes the native heat so much as a febrile ardour; and indeed there is a greater loss of the primary moisture in seven days from an acute fever than from the innate heat in seventy years. In seven days he ends his life, consumed by the wasting force of fever, who was going to be a septuagenarian, the native heat leading.

units.la: Là dessus voyons le remede qu'il y apporte: Venæ sectionem qui omittit vbi magnus est morbus, vel à systrophe, vel ab incendio, vel ab oppressione, & virium robur adest, tam est in vitio, quàm si ipse manus inferret agrotanti. pag. 279.
units.tr: Here is the remedy he offers for this: Whoever omits bloodletting when the disease is great, whether from a systrophe, from a fire, or from oppression, and when the strength of the powers is present, is as much at fault as if he himself inflicted it on the sick man. p. 279.

units.la: Ceux qui calomnient malicieusement les Medecins de Paris pour la saignée, se fondent sur vn liure de Botal, de la derniere impression, qui est d'Anuers. Or Botal n'estoit point François, mais Piedmontois, de la ville d'Ast, & Docteur de Pauie, qui ayant reconnu les grands effets de la saignée aux maladies qu'il traitoit, estant fort employé dans Paris, & à la Cour, de la suite du quatriéme fils de Henry II. qui estoit François, Duc d'Alençon; il en fit un livre, contre lequel un Medecin de Paris, nommé Bonaventure Grangier, a escrit, pour apporter une moderation à cette grande licence de tirer du sang, & sçavoir bien user de ce grand remede. Monsieur Citois, Medecin de Montpelier, en a fait un docte livre, & confesse qu'il a fait, à l'exemple des Medecins de Paris, des miracles avec la saignée, par toutes les Provinces du Royaume, suivant son Maistre, le Cardinal de Richelieu, & que faute de ce remede, qu'il meurt dans l'Europe tous les ans plus de cent mil hommes.
units.tr: Those who maliciously slander the physicians of Paris over bloodletting rest their case on a book by Botal, in its latest edition, which is printed at Antwerp. Yet Botal was not French but Piedmontese, from the city of Asti, and a doctor of Pavia. Having recognised the great effects of bloodletting in the diseases he treated, and being much employed in Paris and at Court, in the retinue of the fourth son of Henry II, who was French, the Duke of Alençon, he wrote a book against which a physician of Paris named Bonaventure Grangier wrote, to bring moderation to this great licence to draw blood, and to teach the proper use of this great remedy. Monsieur Citois, a physician of Montpellier, has written a learned book on the subject, and he confesses that, following the example of the physicians of Paris, he has worked miracles with bloodletting throughout all the provinces of the Kingdom, following his master, the Cardinal de Richelieu; and that for want of this remedy more than a hundred thousand men die every year in Europe.

units.la: C'est assez parlé de la Saignée en general, voyons en quelles maladies, & parties affligées du corps, & en quelles personnes, les Medecins de Paris l'employent. Premieremet, pour les maladies du cerveau par repletion, pour les maux de gorge qui estranglent, pour les maladies des yeux avec grande chaleur & inflammation, ou repletion, pour les douleurs d'oreilles insupportables, pour les maladies du cœur, du poumon, de la poitrine, avec fievre, & douleur de costé: pour les inflammations & douleurs des visceres du ventre, pour les maladies de la matrice, auec douleur & chaleur, suppression des mois, pour les dysenteries, flux de ventre, s'il y a de la fievre, pour le rheumatisme ; mais particulierement pour les fievres continuës chaudes, souuent reïterée, & pour les fievres malignes & pourprées. Ils se feruent heureusement de la saignée, pour la rougeole, la petite verole, auec fievre, auant qu'elle paroisse, lors qu'elle sort, & encore mesmes apres qu'elle est sortie, si les accidens requierent ce remede ; ils emploient la saignée aux petits enfans à la mammelle d'vn mois, & de deux, s'ils étoufent ; aux vieilles gens febricitans de 80. & 90. ans, aux femmes enceintes sans maladies, & reïterées souuent quand ils ont la fievre violente, mesme en accouchant, pour faciliter l'accouchement, si la maladie le requiert. C'est vn grand remede aux playes recentes, la saignée auec l'abstinence mesmes aux inflammations externes, & tumeurs chaudes.
units.tr: Enough has been said about bloodletting in general. Let us see in which diseases, and in which afflicted parts of the body, and in which persons, the physicians of Paris employ it. First, for diseases of the brain arising from repletion; for sore throats that threaten strangling; for diseases of the eyes with great heat and inflammation, or repletion; for intolerable earaches; for diseases of the heart, the lungs and the chest with fever and pain in the side; for inflammations and pains of the viscera of the belly; for diseases of the womb with pain and heat, and suppression of the menses; for dysenteries and diarrhoeas, if there is fever; for rheumatism. But particularly for continued hot fevers, repeated often, and for malignant and purple fevers. They use bloodletting successfully for measles and for smallpox with fever, before the eruption appears, while it is coming out, and even after it has come out, if the symptoms call for this remedy. They employ bloodletting for small children at the breast, of one or two months old, if they are suffocating; for old people of eighty or ninety years who have fever; for pregnant women without illness, and repeated often when they have a violent fever, even in childbirth, to facilitate delivery if the illness requires it. It is a great remedy for recent wounds, bloodletting together with abstinence, even for external inflammations and hot tumours.

units.la: Bref, dans vne grande pourriture de sang, il en faut tirer par interualle, pour diminuer la pourriture, & en refaire d'autre meilleur. Or le secret de bien vser de ce remede, qui est commun, & se pratique par le peuple
units.tr: In short, in a great putrefaction of the blood, it must be drawn at intervals, to reduce the putrefaction and to make new, better blood. The secret of using this remedy well, which is common and practised by the people

units.la: fans le conseil du Medecin, il n'y a guere que les Medecins de Paris, qui sçauent iufques à quel point il en faut vser. Puis on dira que les Medecins de Paris font des sangsuës, qui ne viuent que du sang du peuple, qui resemblent à ce serpent Hemorrhoüs, ou Dipsas, qui est friand du sang humain. Bref, qu'ils ont conspiré & coniuré ensemblément la ruine de leurs concitoyens par la saignée : qu'il y a tant de nations, qui guerissent de leurs maladies sans saignées, & qu'il y a beaucoup de personnes trauaillées de mesme maladie en vn mesme temps, qui reschappent sans saignée , cependant que les autres meurent par les saignées.
units.tr: without the advice of a physician, is something only the physicians of Paris know: how far one must go with it. Then it will be said that the physicians of Paris are leeches, living only on the blood of the people, like that serpent Haemorrhous, or Dipsas, which is fond of human blood. In short, that they have conspired and sworn together to ruin their fellow citizens by bloodletting; that there are so many nations which cure their illnesses without bloodletting, and that many people afflicted with the same illness at the same time recover without bloodletting, while others die from it.

units.la: Voila les iniectiues & calomnies, que produisent contre les Medecins de Paris, leurs ennemis, qui sont ces ieunes Medecins, foy disans de Montpelier : Quibus in ore situm bonis & peritis viris maledicere , estans soustenus par vn chef de party , qui leur donne la tablature, qu'ils doiuent chanter. Ce qui apportera dans Paris, & en la Cour, vne grande diuision tres-perilleuse pour les pauures malades, qui en patiront : le malheur ne viendra point de nostre costé ; mais de ces factieux liguez ensemble, pour nous contredire en toute rencontre.
units.tr: These are the invectives and calumnies which their enemies produce against the physicians of Paris: those young physicians, self-styled of Montpellier, who have abuse of good and skilled men on their lips, being supported by a party leader who gives them the score they must sing. This will bring into Paris, and into the Court, a great and very dangerous division, and the poor sick who suffer from it will pay the price. The misfortune will not come from our side, but from these factious men allied together to contradict us on every occasion.

units.la: Pour la defense des Medecins de Paris, je produiray les raisons de Monsieur Citois, Docteur de Montpelier, & de Poitiers, qui pourront avoir plus de force, que si elles venoient d'un Medecin de Paris, qui en est neantmoins tres-croyable, veu qu'il y a demeuré trente ans prés du Cardinal de Richelieu. En une region temperée, comme est celle de la moitié du sixiesme climat, & sous le septiesme tout entier, depuis la hauteur du Pole Arctique, qui s'estend depuis le 45. degré jusqu'à 49. ou 50. les habitans sont à leur aise, oisifs, grands carnassiers, abondans en sang, il leur faut tirer du sang abondamment, c'est pourquoy à Paris, qui a pour hauteur du Ciel 48. degrez & 50. minutes, & en toute cette contrée qui est comprise entre les rivieres de la Seine & Loire, où ils vivent à leur aise, & font bonne chere, ils engendrent beaucoup de sang, & leur en faut tirer bonne quantité, le pouvant mieux supporter, sans affoiblissement, que ceux de Narbonne & Toulouze, & de toute la contrée, qui confine la mer Mediterranée, où ils vivent plus sobrement.
units.tr: For the defence of the physicians of Paris, I will produce the reasons of Monsieur Citois, doctor of Montpellier and of Poitiers, which may carry more weight than if they came from a physician of Paris, though the latter is nonetheless very credible, since he lived there thirty years near the Cardinal de Richelieu. In a temperate region, such as that of half of the sixth climate and the whole of the seventh, from the height of the Arctic Pole, which extends from the 45th degree to 49 or 50, the inhabitants are at their ease, idle, great meat-eaters, abounding in blood; it is necessary to draw blood abundantly from them. That is why at Paris, whose height of the sky is 48 degrees and 50 minutes, and in all this country which lies between the rivers Seine and Loire, where they live at their ease and eat well, they generate much blood, and a good quantity of it must be drawn from them, since they can bear it better, without weakening, than those of Narbonne and Toulouse, and of all the country bordering the Mediterranean Sea, where they live more sparingly.

units.la: De plus, l'air depuis Paris, jusques à la riviere de Loire, est plus grossier & froid; vers la mer Mediterranée, il est plus subtil & chaud, d'où viennent tant de défaillances, jusques aux syncopes convulsives, quand on leur fait tirer du sang, particulierement aux personnes bilieuses. Il se remarque aussi que les personnes de pareille nature, mesme habitude, à mesme temps, qui supportoient alaigrement la saignée de trois ou quatre poilettes au climat de Paris, dans la Provence, & le Languedoc, mesme vers Poictiers, tomber dans des foiblesses par de legeres saignées. Mais ce qui est plus admirable en ces regions, les femmes grosses, qu'on saigne apres le sixiesme mois, bien souvent accouchent avant terme. Tout au contraire à Paris, &dans toute cette contrée, que j'ay designée, les femmes grosses, en tous les mois jusques à l'heure de leur accouchement, supportent la saignée sans faire tort à leur enfant.
units.tr: Moreover, the air from Paris as far as the river Loire is thicker and colder; towards the Mediterranean Sea it is finer and warmer, whence come so many faintings, even convulsive syncopes, when blood is drawn from people, particularly bilious persons. It is also observed that persons of similar nature and the same habit, at the same time, who bore three or four palettes of bloodletting cheerfully in the climate of Paris, in Provence and Languedoc, and even near Poitiers, fall into weakness from slight bloodlettings. But what is more admirable in these regions is that pregnant women, who are bled after the sixth month, very often give birth before term. Quite the contrary at Paris, and in all this country which I have described, pregnant women, in every month up to the hour of their delivery, bear bloodletting without harm to their child.

units.la: Apres toutes ces observations faites par Monsieur Cuiois, blasmerez-vous les saignées des Medecins de Paris? Le mesme prouve tres-clairement comme les Medecins de Paris tirent heureusement du sang aux petits enfans d'un mois, (ce qui pourra servir de leçon au Sieur Riviere Docteur & Professeur de Montpelier, qui ne sçauroit comprendre comment on peut saigner des petits enfans en la verole: ) si la maladie le requiert, & aux vieilles gens de 80. & 90. ans, & qu'au pourpre il n'y a que les Medecins de Paris qui saignent, plustost que de s'amuser aux Cardiaques.
units.tr: After all these observations made by Monsieur Cuiois, will you blame the bleedings of the Physicians of Paris? The same author shows very clearly how the Physicians of Paris happily draw blood from infants of one month old (which may serve as a lesson to Sieur Riviere, Doctor and Professor of Montpellier, who cannot understand how one can bleed small children in smallpox), when the illness requires it, and from old people of 80 and 90 years; and that in purples it is only the Physicians of Paris who bleed, rather than amusing themselves with cardiac remedies.

units.la: Ces ignorans & calomniateurs, quinous reprochent la trop grande saignée, qui est la pierre d'achopement de nos Aduersaires, s'ils sçauoient la generation du sang, & la distribution par tout le corps, ils ne blasmeroient pas la saignée des Medecins de Paris, & encore moins s'ils pouuoient comprendre la Circulation du sang, qui est vne demonstration tres-euidente, de la necessité de tirer du sang d'en haut & d'en bas, pour diminuer sa quantité, & mauuaise qualité, tant en sa putrefactiõ, qu'en sa chaleur excessiue, qui estoufferoit le cœur, le poumon, & le cerueau, & causeroit l'extinction de la chaleur naturelle.
units.tr: These ignorant and slanderous men, who reproach us for excessive bleeding, which is the stumbling block of our adversaries, if they knew the generation of blood and its distribution throughout the whole body, would not blame the bleedings of the Physicians of Paris; and still less if they could understand the circulation of the blood, which is a most evident demonstration of the necessity of drawing blood from above and below, to diminish its quantity and bad quality, both in its putrefaction and in its excessive heat, which would suffocate the heart, the lungs and the brain, and cause the extinction of the natural heat.

units.la: Ie demanderois volontiers à ceux qui nous reprochent les frequentes saignées, s'ils sont plus entendus en la pratique, que les Medecins de Paris, s'ils ont plus grande lumiere en la Medecine par l'estude, & l'exercice, s'ils voyent plus de malades que les Medecins de Paris, si la saignée frequente est vne nouueauté establie depuis peu, par les Medecins de Paris, si elle n'a point d'autre fondement qu'vne coustume & vsage, qu'ils ne peuuent quitter? Quoy? Les
units.tr: I would gladly ask those who reproach us for frequent bleedings whether they are more skilled in practice than the Physicians of Paris; whether they have greater light in Medicine through study and experience; whether they see more patients than the Physicians of Paris; whether frequent bleeding is a novelty recently established by the Physicians of Paris; or whether it has no other foundation than a custom and usage which they cannot give up? What? The

units.la: Medecins de Paris font-ils si cruels & sanguinaires, de vouloir faire mourir leurs parens, amis, concitoyens, & eux-mesmes par la saignée ? Sont-ils si peu curieux de leur honneur, de preferer le blasme qu'ils en peuuent receuoir, au contentement qu'ils donneroient aux malades & assistans, en les laissant mourir auec leur sang, & au lieu faisans d'autres remedes, qui seroient inutils & contraires ? Non, il faut croire des Medecins de Paris tout le contraire, qu'ils possedent la vraye science de Medecine, tant ancienne, que moderne ; qu'ils ont tresbonne conscience, & suffisance, pour bien appliquer leur science sur les particuliers : qu'ils ont acquis cette science par l'estude des bons Liures, & par leur experience iournaliere ; qu'ils ont vne plus grande lecture des bons Liures, que les autres Medecins ; qu'ils sont curieux d'estre sçauans par l'émulation, qu'ils ont entre eux dans les disputes publiques, & les conferences des consultations qu'ils font tous les iours.
units.tr: Physicians of Paris, are they so cruel and bloodthirsty as to want to kill their parents, friends, fellow citizens, and themselves by bleeding? Are they so little concerned for their honour as to prefer the blame they may receive for it to the satisfaction they would give to the sick and their attendants, by letting them die with their blood, and instead of applying other remedies, which would be useless and harmful? No, one must believe the very opposite of the Physicians of Paris: that they possess the true science of Medicine, both ancient and modern; that they have very good conscience and sufficient ability to apply their science well to individuals; that they have acquired this science through the study of good books and through their daily experience; that they read good books more widely than other physicians; and that they are eager to be learned through the emulation they have among themselves in public disputations and in the conferences of the consultations they hold every day.

units.la: Il n'y a lieu au monde, où il se voye plus de rares maladies, & accidens estranges, qu'à Paris, & où ils sont mieux traitez, s'ils sont guerissables. Les malades viennent de tous les endroits de la France, pour recevoir guerison, ou enuoyent consulter leur mal, tellement que ie puis dire de Paris, ce que disoit Galien de Rome, qu'il voyoit en vne seule ruë[?] plus de malades, que ne voyoit Hippocrate, voyageant par toute la Grece, pour rencontrer des malades. Vn seul Medecin de Paris, fort employé, verra en vn iour plus de malades, que ne font les six Medecins, Professeurs de Montpelier en vn mois entier.
units.tr: There is no place in the world where more rare diseases and strange accidents are seen than at Paris, and where they are better treated, if they are curable. Patients come from every part of France to recover their health, or they send to consult about their illness, so that I can say of Paris what Galen said of Rome: that he saw more patients in a single street [?] than Hippocrates saw travelling through all of Greece to meet with patients. A single Physician of Paris, if much employed, will see more patients in one day than six Professors of Montpellier do in a whole month.

units.la: Vn Medecin de Paris faisant six ou sept Conferences, ou Consultations auec ses Colleagues, ou les instruira, ou apprendra quelque chose d'eux, car toute la science n'est pas en la teste d'vn homme seul, c'est en quoy sont vtiles les Consultatiōs, tant pour les malades pour qui l'on consulte, que pour les Medecins qui consultent. Les Medecins de Paris ayans appris par la doctrine d'Hippocrate & de Galien, la necessité de saigner dans les maladies, & par les experiences que leurs ancestres depuis 300. ans ont pratiqué heureusemēt dans ce climat, dont ils voyent tous les iours des effets admirables, ont mieux aimé estre calomniez, que d'estre homicides de leurs malades, les laissans mourir faute de ce remede, ou les laissans mourir par des purgations ; contre leur science & conscience, dequoy ils seroient responsables deuant Dieu.
units.tr: A Physician of Paris, holding six or seven conferences or consultations with his colleagues, will either teach them or learn something from them, for all knowledge is not in the head of one man alone; this is where consultations are useful, both for the patients for whom one consults and for the physicians who consult. The Physicians of Paris, having learned from the teaching of Hippocrates and Galen the necessity of bleeding in diseases, and from the experiences which their ancestors have happily practised in this climate for 300 years, of which they see admirable effects every day, have preferred to be slandered rather than to be murderers of their patients, letting them die for lack of this remedy, or letting them die by purgings, against their science and conscience, for which they would be answerable before God.

units.la: Pour ce qui est de la purgation, les Medecins de Paris l'ordonnent auec vne telle circonspection & moderation, qu'on n'en voit point arriuer de mauuais accidens: ils on tousiours esté loüez pour cela par Symphorianus Campegius, qui blasme les Medecins de Montpelier, pour les rudes & violentes Medecines, dont ils vsent. La pratique des Medecins de Paris, pour les purgatifs, est fondée sur la doctrine d'Hippocrate, qui ne se seruoit ordinairement que de doux medicamens, & ne les employoit q'uapres le septiesme iour passé, aux fieures, & dispositions inflammatoires, la grande chaleur estant diminuée par les saignées, qui precedoient la purgation.
units.tr: As for purging, the Physicians of Paris prescribe it with such caution and moderation that no bad accidents are ever seen from it. They have always been praised for this by Symphorianus Campegius, who blames the Physicians of Montpellier for the harsh and violent medicines they use. The practice of the Physicians of Paris regarding purgatives is founded on the teaching of Hippocrates, who ordinarily used only gentle medicines, and did not employ them in fevers and inflammatory conditions until after the seventh day had passed, once the great heat had been reduced by the bleedings which preceded the purge.

units.la: Platon, qui auoit appris par ses longs voyages, la Medecine des Egyptiens, conseille de n'vser de purgatifs que rarement, encore qu'ils soient benins, d'autant que les violens vsent le corps, gastent les visceres, & abbregent le cours de la vie: c'est ce que font les remedes metalliques, que l'on donne maintenant pour purger, qui est vne pratique toute nouuelle, tres-dangereuse, condamnée par les plus sçauans & experimentez Medecins, auant & depuis la naissance de Paracelse, qui est venuē des Alchymistes Allemans, particulierement des Moines Benedictins, riches & opulens, lesquels s'adonnans à la pierre Philosophale,ont employé les metaux pour la Medecine, ne trouuans pas ce qu'ils cherchoient ; mais c'est vn grand abus, & trespernicieux, de vouloir pratiquer la Medecine sur les François, comme sur les Allemans, qui sont corps robustes, crapuleux, remplis de pituite, lesquels il faut traiter violemment, pour faire vuider par haut & par bas, leur crapule & repletion excessiue: Mais cela se fait auec vne telle violence, qu'il faut qu'ils meurent bien tost, ou qu'ils reschappent auec vn long-temps.
units.tr: Plato, who had learned the medicine of the Egyptians through his long travels, advises using purgatives only rarely, even if they are mild, since violent ones wear out the body, spoil the viscera, and shorten the course of life. This is what the metallic remedies do, which are now given for purging; it is a wholly new practice, very dangerous, condemned by the most learned and experienced physicians, both before and after the birth of Paracelsus, who came from the German alchemists, particularly from the Benedictine monks, rich and wealthy, who, devoting themselves to the philosopher's stone, used metals for medicine, not finding what they were seeking. But it is a great and very pernicious abuse to want to practise medicine on the French as on the Germans, who are robust, gross bodies, full of phlegm, whom one must treat violently in order to purge them above and below of their grossness and excessive fullness. But this is done with such violence that they must die soon, or recover only after a long time.

units.la: De là sont venus les vomitifs metalliques, qui causent vn tel desordre dans le corps, & particulierement dans l'estomach, & aux parties voisines vn tel rauage, que les pauures malades, s'ils n'en meurent, demeurent bien affoiblis, & ont de la peine à se refaire.
units.tr: From this have come the metallic emetics, which cause such disorder in the body, and particularly in the stomach, and such ravage in the neighbouring parts, that the poor patients, if they do not die of it, remain very weakened and have difficulty recovering.

units.la: Ie sçay bien que les anciens vsoient de vomitifs, mais non pas au commencement des maladies aiguës, & ce auec grande circonspection & preparation du corps, pour vomir plus aisément, sans aucune violence : que nous pratiquons, quand nous voyons la nature dispofée, & l'humeur preparé pour le vomissement.
units.tr: I know well that the ancients used emetics, but not at the beginning of acute diseases, and this with great caution and preparation of the body, so that they might vomit more easily and without any violence; which we practise when we see that nature is disposed and the humour prepared for vomiting.

units.la: Ces Medecins de Montpelier, qui pratiquent aujourd'huy, combien qu'en cachette, la Medecine dans Paris, en toute sorte de maladies, aiguës, chroniques, avec fievre, & oppression de poictrine, en tous les temps de la maladie donnent inconsiderément les vomitifs metalliques, pour faire un effort violét à la nature, & au corps, ce qui cause la mort promptement, ou soulage les malades, non sans grandes douleurs, foiblesses, & convulsions durant l'action du remede, & apres l'evacuation des humeurs bons, ou mauvais, ce qui apporte plus de mal au corps que de bien.
units.tr: These Montpellier physicians who now practise medicine in Paris, though in secret, give metallic emetics indiscriminately in every kind of illness, acute and chronic, with fever and oppression of the chest, at every stage of the disease. They make a violent assault on nature and the body, which either brings on death swiftly or relieves the patients, not without great pain, weakness and convulsions while the remedy works, and after the evacuation of humours, whether good or bad. This brings more harm to the body than good.

units.la: Pour condamner cette mauvaise pratique des Medecins de Montpelier, qui sont à Paris, laquelle vient des Alchymistes, ie produiray Courtaut en sa Declamation Satyrique, qui est le seul endroit où il a fait paroistre un peu de jugement, si cela vient de luy.
units.tr: To condemn this bad practice of the Montpellier physicians who are in Paris, which comes from the Alchemists, I will produce Courtaut in his Satirical Declamation, the only place where he has shown a little judgement, if indeed it is his.

units.la: Prompte curare velle morbos per insignes evacuationes furentis Ducis est, per suorum clades victoriam incertam quaerentis, plus enim nocet amico quàm hosti, vel enim sibi lethali vulnere prosternit[?] hostem, aut saltem aequali strage prelium confert, ut uterque aequè victus & ouans inde recedat; Qui per euacuationum excessus precipitanter curare volunt, lentè interficiunt, & dum student ægri palato faucre, cordi nocent, & sic illorum excessu, defectúque deficit æger; Contingit hoc, quia altiora sapientes, nolunt vti natura magistra, quæ omnia paulatim agit.
units.tr: To wish to cure diseases quickly by violent evacuations is the mark of a furious leader, who seeks victory by the slaughter of his own men; for he harms a friend more than an enemy. Either he lays low the enemy with a deadly wound to himself, or at least joins battle with an equal slaughter, so that each withdraws equally defeated and triumphant. Those who wish to cure hastily by excessive evacuations kill slowly, and while they strive to please the patient's palate, they harm the heart; and so, by their excess and exhaustion, the patient fails. This happens because the wise, wishing to use higher things, refuse to use Nature as their teacher, who accomplishes all things gradually.

units.la: Vous blasmez nostre Medecine, ou methode de pratiquer, pour la sterilité & pauvreté des remedes, qui sont reduits à la saignée, le sené, le son, & la reglisse. De plus, que nous ordonnons ces pauvres & miserables remedes en langage François au vulgaire, qui se mocque de nostre art, & façon ridicule de pratiquer, croyant estre aussi sçavans que nous, à conseiller & pratiquer la Medecine, ce qu'ils font bien souvent sans appeller les Medecins.
units.tr: You blame our medicine, or method of practice, for the barrenness and poverty of its remedies, which are reduced to bloodletting, senna, bran and liquorice. Moreover, you say that we prescribe these poor and miserable remedies in French, to the common people, who mock our art and our ridiculous way of practising, believing themselves as learned as we are in advising and practising medicine, which they very often do without calling the physicians.

units.la: Vous adjoustez que nous n'avons point de secrets en la Medecine comme les Medecins de Montpelier, qui en sont tout farcis. Que nous profanons la Medecine, la rendant si vulgaire & communeau peuple, ce que nos Anciens cachoient, crainte qu'il n'enabusât. Que nous reiettons tous les remedes topiques, confortatifs & cordiaux, qui sont les plus grandes richesses de la Medecine. Bref, qu'on peut faire un Medecin de Paris, pratiquant de la sorte, en huict jours.
units.tr: You add that we have no secrets in medicine, as the Montpellier physicians do, who are stuffed full of them. You say that we profane medicine by making it so common and open to the people, whereas our ancestors kept it hidden for fear that it would be abused. You say that we reject all topical, comforting and cordial remedies, which are the greatest riches of medicine. In short, you say that one can make a Paris physician, practising in this way, in eight days.

units.la: Nous respondrons en peu de paroles à toutes ces reproches ridicules. Vous sçauez que Dieu par sa bonté & misericorde a creé toutes les choses de l'Univers pour l'usage de l'homme, afin qu'il s'en seruit pour alimens & medicamens, & autres commoditez; Par toute la terre habitable, dedans & dehors, dans la mer, & dans l'air, il a dispersé selon la difference des lieux, les alimens & medicamens, afin que chacun choisit ce qui luy estoit utile & convenable. Il a donné à chasque Province ses alimens & medicamens qui luy sont propres, pour sa nourriture, & pour la Medecine, sans en aller mandier ailleurs: c'est nostre paresse de ne les pas rechercher & employer: il semble que tout ce qui vient de loing est meilleur, que ce qui croist en nostre pays: Campegius, Medecin de Montpelier s'en plaint, & en a composé le Jardin de la France, pour y cueillir tous les medicamens necessaires à la Medecine, quittant les medicamens des pays estrangers. Fernel avoit eu un pareil dessein, qu'il eut executé s'il n'eust esté preuenu par la mort, au rapport de Plantius. Un autre Medecin de Montpelier, nommé Antoine Constantin, a escrit la Medecine Provinciale, du pais où l'on est. Posans ce fondement,
units.tr: We shall answer these ridiculous reproaches in a few words. You know that God, by his goodness and mercy, created all the things of the universe for the use of man, so that he might use them for food, medicine and other conveniences. Throughout the habitable earth, within and without, in the sea and in the air, he has scattered foods and medicines according to the difference of places, so that each person might choose what was useful and suitable for him. He has given each province its own foods and medicines, proper to it, for its nourishment and for its medicine, without going to beg them elsewhere. It is our laziness not to seek them out and use them; it seems that whatever comes from far away is better than what grows in our own country. Campegius, a physician of Montpellier, complains of this, and has composed the Garden of France, in order to gather there all the medicines necessary to medicine, giving up the medicines of foreign countries. Fernel had a similar plan, which he would have carried out had he not been prevented by death, according to the report of Plantius. Another physician of Montpellier, named Antoine Constantin, has written Provincial Medicine, concerning the country in which one lives. Laying this foundation,

units.la: Nous pouuons facilement nous passer de medicamens estrangers, & pour cela nostre Medecine n'en sera pas plus pauure & miserable. L'excellence & la richesse de la Medecine ne dépend pas de la grande multitude & varieté des remedes, mais de peu & de bons, bien choisis & approuuez, car les remedes ne sont rien, & sont quelque chose. Ils sont quelquefois les mains des Dieux, quelquefois des poisons, selon qu'ils sont bien ou mal ordonnez & appliquez, à ce que disoit Herophile, dans Galien: tellement que pour s'en seruir comme il faut, il conuient estre sçauant Medecin en toutes les parties de la Medecine: de plus, il faut auoir vne parfaite connoissance oculaire de la nature des plantes, & rationelle des facultez, pour en vser seuls ou meslez auec d'autres, selon nos intentions, pour produire diuers effets: C'est vn axiome de Philosophie & d'Oeconomie, Frustra fit per plura, quod æquè commodè fieri potest per pauciora. Le Medecin est vn trompeur & malicieux, qui peut guerir vn malade auec des medicamens simples, s'il se fert de composez, disoit Arnaud de Villeneufue. Langius, en ses Epistres, prouue cela doctement: il nous faut tenir au iugement qu'en donne Hipp. lib. 4. de articulis. Puis qu'on peut rendre la santé en plusieurs manieres, il faut toufiours choisir celle qui est la plus simple, & plus aisée à executer: en cela paroist la probité d'vn Medecin, & son industrie, si ce n'est qu'il veüille faire le Charlatan. Le mesme, au liure de Dieta acutorum: vn seul, ou peu de remedes qui soient propres aux malades, sont plus à estimer que plusieurs, dautant qu'auec peu de remedes, on peut guerir les malades.
units.tr: We can easily do without foreign medicines, and for that reason our medicine will be no poorer or more miserable. The excellence and richness of medicine does not depend on a great multitude and variety of remedies, but on a few good ones, well chosen and approved. For remedies are nothing and are something: they are sometimes the hands of the gods, sometimes poisons, according as they are rightly or wrongly prescribed and applied, as Herophilus said, in Galen. So that to use them as they should be used, it is necessary to be a learned physician in all parts of medicine. Furthermore, one must have a perfect knowledge of the nature of plants by sight, and a rational knowledge of their faculties, in order to use them alone or mixed with others, according to our intentions, to produce various effects. It is an axiom of philosophy and economy: What can be done equally conveniently by fewer things is done in vain by more. The physician is a deceiver and a cunning fellow who can cure a patient with simple remedies, yet uses compound ones, said Arnald of Villanova. Langius, in his Epistles, proves this learnedly. We must hold to the judgement given on it by Hippocrates, book 4, On the Articles. Since health can be restored in several ways, one should always choose the simplest and easiest to carry out; in this the probity and skill of a physician appear, unless he wishes to play the charlatan. The same author, in the book On the Diet of Acute Diseases: one or a few remedies that are suited to the patients are to be valued more than many, since with few remedies the patients can be cured.

units.la: Nous n'improuuons pas la varieté des remedes, mais nous preferons les bons & vsitez en petit nõbre, & croyons que les moins compofez sont les meilleurs, dautant que dans vn grand meslange, ils se destruisent l'vn l'autre, & faut qu'il s'en forme vne qualité toute autre, que celle des medicamens simples donnez separément. C'est vne calomnie & imposture de dire, que nostre Medecine soit reduite à la saignée, sené, son, & reglisse: c'est là verité que nous reconnoissons par la doctrine d'Hippocrate, & par l'experience iournaliere, que la saignée est le principal remede au traitement des maladies chaudes, quelquefois froides, quand il y a plenitude d'humeurs dans les veines: que la purgation tient le second rang d'ordinaire, quelquefois nous luy donnons le premier lieu, la faisant marcher deuant la faignée. Nous nous seruons aussi de remedes topiques, & confortatifs,alteratifs,tant internes, qu'externes.
units.tr: We do not disapprove of a variety of remedies, but we prefer good and well-tried ones in small number, and we believe that the least compounded are the best, since in a great mixture they destroy one another, and a quality quite different from that of the simple remedies given separately must be formed. It is a calumny and an imposture to say that our medicine is reduced to bloodletting, senna, bran and liquorice. This is the truth, which we recognise from the teaching of Hippocrates and from daily experience: that bloodletting is the principal remedy in the treatment of hot diseases, and sometimes of cold ones, when there is fullness of humours in the veins; that purging ordinarily holds the second place, though sometimes we give it the first place, putting it before bloodletting. We also make use of topical, comforting and alterative remedies, both internal and external.

units.la: Pour dementir Courtaut, ie luy produiray vn article de nos Statuts imprimez, qui portent, Remediorum tum confortantium, tum alterantium, tum purgantium, tam internorum, quàm externorum formula, præscribentium chirographis obsignentur, anno & die adscriptis. Ie puis dire auec verité, que la Medecine de Montpelier est reduite dans vne plus grande pauureté si elle est racourcie à vn Laudanum pour endormir, à vn purgatif d'Antimoine, pour vuider auec violence par haut & par bas. Nous voyons à Paris ces nouueaux Medecins qui se disent Docteurs de Montpelier, pratiquer la Medecine de la sorte; Ils portent toute leur science & marchandise en vne boëtte enfermée dans leur pochette, ils n'ont pas besoin d'Apothiquaires pour preparer & administrer leurs drogues, qui consistent en vne poudre dite cordiale, qu'ils deguisent de la sorte, & en des grains benits: Voila comme ils cachent leur science mysterieuse, se vantans d'auoir des secrets admirables, & infaillibles pour la guerison de toutes les maladies, qu'on tient incurables, blasmans les Medecins de Paris en tous les lieux où ils sont appellez.
units.tr: To refute Courtaut, I will produce for him an article from our printed Statutes, which read: The formula of remedies, whether comforting, alterative or purging, internal or external, prescribed, shall be sealed with the prescriber's signature, with the year and day added. I can say with truth that the medicine of Montpellier is reduced to a greater poverty if it is cut down to a Laudanum to send one to sleep, and a purgative of Antimony, to empty the body violently from above and below. We see in Paris these new physicians, who call themselves Doctors of Montpellier, practising medicine in this way. They carry all their learning and merchandise in a little box shut up in their pocket; they have no need of apothecaries to prepare and administer their drugs, which consist of a powder called cordial, which they disguise in this way, and of blessed pills. Thus they hide their mysterious science, boasting of having admirable and infallible secrets for curing all diseases that are held to be incurable, and blaming the physicians of Paris in every place where they are called.

units.la: Courtaut, vous blasmez les Consultations & conferences des Medecins de Paris, qui sont si bien ordonnées, & si profitables pour les malades, & utiles pour l'instruction des jeunes Medecins. Personne ne les peut improuver, s'il n'est ennemy du genre humain. Il n'y a que les ignorans qui les condamnent & mesprisent, pour ne point descouvrir leur ignorance. Les consultations en toutes choses sont recommandées. Dans l'Ecclesiaste : Sine consilio nihil facias, & post finem non pœnitebit, melius est esse duos, quàm unum. Et cap. 4. Erit salus ubi multa sunt consilia. Aristote lib. 3. Ethic ad Nicomachum, cap. 7. loüe grandement les consultations faites par les hommes sages, il les appelle resolutions sages & divines. Hippocrate, sur la fin des Epidem. nous advertit par son exemple, d'appeller d'autres Medecins en consultations sur les malades : ce qu'il repete in præceptionibus : dans les difficultez, qui se rencontrent dans la curation des maladies, on doit y appeller d'autres pour consulter, ensemblément, afin qu'ils soient coadjuteurs dans le traitement de la maladie, d'autant que si dans la violence du mal, un Medecin ordinaire se trouuoit empesché, & qu'il oubliât quelquechose, vn autre l'en aduertisse; Mais cela se doit faire, dit Hippocrate, amiablement, sans contestation & médisance : Voila comme les Consultations sont profitables pour les malades; mais elles sont aussi vtiles pour les Medecins aux Conferences, chacun tasche de bien faire pour le profit du malade, & rapporte ce qu'il sçait modestement, sans vanité : Telles Conferences bien souuent donnent grandes lumières à la connoissance des maladies, & de leur guerison.
units.tr: Courtaut, you blame the consultations and conferences of the Paris physicians, which are so well ordered and so profitable for the sick, and useful for the instruction of young physicians. No one can disapprove of them unless he is an enemy of the human race. Only the ignorant condemn and despise them, so that they do not have to reveal their ignorance. Consultations are recommended in all matters. In Ecclesiastes: "Do nothing without counsel, and you will not repent afterwards; it is better that two be together than one." And in chapter 4: "There is safety where there are many counsels." Aristotle, in book 3 of the Ethics to Nicomachus, chapter 7, greatly praises the consultations made by wise men; he calls them wise and divine resolutions. Hippocrates, at the end of the Epidemics, warns us by his example to call other physicians into consultation about the sick; he repeats this in the Precepts: in the difficulties that arise in the cure of diseases, one should call in others to consult together, so that they may be helpers in the treatment of the disease, since if in the violence of the illness an ordinary physician were hindered and forgot something, another would remind him of it. But this must be done, says Hippocrates, amicably, without contention and slander. Thus consultations are profitable for the sick; but they are also useful to physicians in the conferences, where each strives to do well for the profit of the patient, and reports what he knows modestly, without vanity. Such conferences very often give great light to the knowledge of diseases and their cure.

units.la: L'ordre de nos Consultations est si bien ordonné, & reglé par nós Anciens, qu'il n'y a rien à redire. Dans nos Constitutions imprimées, il y a vn article exprés. In Consultationibus Iuniores primi pro more sententiam dicant, & eo ordine quo quisque ad doctoratum promotus fuerit, quod in eiusmodi Consultationibus à maiore parte probatum fuerit, id ægro, vel parentibus ægri, vel assidentibus, qui ægri curam habent, à seniore de Collegarum consensu prudenter referatur.
units.tr: The order of our consultations is so well arranged and regulated by our Ancients that there is nothing to object to. In our printed Constitutions there is a specific article: "In consultations, the junior men shall give their opinion first, according to custom, and in the order in which each was promoted to the doctorate; and whatever has been approved by the greater part in such consultations shall be prudently reported to the patient, or to the patient's relatives, or to those attending who have charge of the patient, by the senior, with the agreement of the colleagues."

units.la: L'vnion de nos Consultations est admirable, chacun est libre de dire son aduis, il est permis à celuy qui parle apres, de corriger modestement, sans passion & animosité, l'advis precedent, à la façon de Seneque, Regatus in senatu dicere sententiam ridebor, si non examinem; nam semper unam illius sententiam sequi, non id curia sed factionis est. Le dernier, qui est le plus ancien, doit recueillir les opinions, pacifier doucement les differens, pour en former le resultat & conclusion de la Consultation. Galien n'approuue point les altercatiōs sur les malades, qui ne sont bonnes qu'en l'Eschole de Medecine, Medicorum controuersia (disoit Hipp. lib. 1. de diæt. acut.) iustam ignorantia suspicionem ostendunt, concordia inter eos magnam cognitionis spem demonstrat. C'est pourquoy nous fuyons tant que nous pouvons chez les malades, Altercationes Medicorum, nullo idem sentiente, ne videatur accessio alterius, dans Pline.
units.tr: The unity of our consultations is admirable: each is free to state his opinion, and it is permitted to the one who speaks after to correct the preceding opinion modestly, without passion and animosity, in the manner of Seneca: "If I did not examine it, I would be laughed at for giving my opinion in the senate; for to always follow one and the same opinion belongs not to the council but to a faction." The last, who is the most senior, ought to gather the opinions and gently calm the disagreements, in order to form the result and conclusion of the consultation. Galen does not approve of altercations over the sick, which are good only in the school of medicine: "Disputes among physicians" (said Hippocrates, book 1 of the Acute Diseases) "show a just suspicion of ignorance; agreement among them shows a great hope of knowledge." This is why we avoid, as far as we can, disputes among physicians in the presence of the sick: "Altercations among physicians, when no one agrees with the other, lest the case seem to be the addition of another," in Pliny.

units.la: Haud quaquam vel concionos, vel curia dictis Audivit pugnare, animo sed semper eodem Et sentire eadem, atque etiam decernere vidit.
units.tr: "Never did they hear in the sermon or the senate speeches contending in spirit, but always the same, and they saw them agreeing and even deciding alike."

units.la: Les ignorans ne peuvent gouster les Consultations & Conferences, & maintiennent qu'un Medecin ne peut bien juger de la maladie sur le champ, ny ordonner les remedes convenables, qu'il doit plustoft consulter ses maistres muets, qui sont les liures, pour en mieux juger, & trouver les remedes propres : Ainsi se gouvernoit le Sieur Turquet, dit Mayerne, comme il confesse ingenuëment en son liure diffamatoire contre les Medecins de Paris. La façon des brauës Medecins de Montpelier est, après auoir veu le malade, de rapporter le lendemain vn escrit, remply de quantité de remedes superflus, sans ordre & iugement. Galien a escrit sa methode pour instruire les Medecins, à bien iuger de la maladie sur le champ, en presence du malade, & des assistans, après l'auoir bien examiné & consideré. Il a escrit des Liures de la compofition des medicamens, & de leurs facultez, pour monstrer la methode de trouuer les remedes conuenables, sans les chercher dans les Liures: car ayant la connoissance parfaite des medicamens, & sçachant sa methode, on peut à l'instant prescrire les medicamens aux malades, sans consulter les Liures. Il veut quand on auroit perdu tous les Liures, qu'on en puisse faire d'autres, afin de ne point tomber dans l'inconuenient & malheur, qui arriua à deux Medecins, lesquels ayans perdu leurs Liures de Medecine, n'estans sçauans que par Liures, l'vn quitta la Medecine, l'autre se pendit de regret d'auoir perdu sa science.
units.tr: The ignorant cannot taste consultations and conferences, and they maintain that a physician cannot judge a disease well on the spot, nor prescribe suitable remedies, and that he ought instead to consult his silent masters, which are books, in order to judge better and find the proper remedies. Thus the Sieur Turquet, called Mayerne, governed himself, as he openly confesses in his defamatory book against the physicians of Paris. The practice of the brave physicians of Montpellier is, after seeing the patient, to bring the next day a written paper full of many superfluous remedies, without order or judgment. Galen wrote his method for teaching physicians to judge a disease well on the spot, in the presence of the patient and of those assisting, after having examined and considered it carefully. He wrote books on the composition of medicines and their faculties, to show the method of finding suitable remedies without seeking them in books; for, having a perfect knowledge of medicines and knowing his method, one can at once prescribe medicines to the sick without consulting books. He wished that, if all books were lost, one could make others, so as not to fall into the inconvenience and misfortune that befell two physicians who, having lost their medical books, and being learned only from books, one gave up medicine and the other hanged himself out of regret at having lost his learning.

units.la: Vous estes mal instruit & informé des affaires de nostre Vniuersité ; Si vous sçauiez l'institution du College des Professeurs Royaux , vous ne nous reprocheriez pas l'heredité & succession dans les Lectures Royalles. Le College Royal ne dépend point des Medecins de Paris,& consequemment les Lectures en Medecine ne sont pas en leur disposition;cela est affecté à la charge de Monsieur le Grand Aumosnier de France ; s'il n'obserue les Ordonnances & Reglemens du Roy François premier, Fondateur, de Charles I X. Reformateur de l'institution, ce n'est pas à nous de le corriger, nous n'auons connoissance que sur nos Professeurs , que l'Eschole de Medecine tous les deux ans eslit & establit, pour enseigner la Medecine. Il y en a trois qui sont obligez d'enseigner assiduément, ce qu'ils font courageusement,plûtost par honneur,que pour les gages , qui sont fort petits, selon le reuenu de nostre Eschole.
units.tr: You are badly instructed and misinformed about the affairs of our University. If you knew the institution of the College of the Royal Professors, you would not reproach us with hereditary succession and inheritance in the Royal Lectureships. The Royal College does not depend on the physicians of Paris, and consequently the lectures in medicine are not at their disposal; this is entrusted to the charge of the Grand Almoner of France. If he does not observe the Ordinances and Regulations of King Francis I, the founder, and of Charles IX, the reformer of the institution, it is not for us to correct him; we have knowledge only of our Professors, whom the School of Medicine elects and appoints every two years to teach medicine. There are three who are bound to teach assiduously, which they do courageously, rather for honour than for the wages, which are very small according to the revenue of our School.

units.la: En contre-eschange de cette fausse accusation, nous vous reprocherons l'inobseruance de vos Statuts en l'élection du Chancelier, & des Professeurs en Medecine. Vostre Chancelier n'est plus esleu par les Docteurs, le Roy y pourvoit , & auez toleré cela depuis soixante ans , pour dire que vostre Eschole est Royale. Ce n'a pas esté l'intention des Fondateurs, Rondelet a esté esleu par les Professeurs, & Joubert de mesme façon. Depuis dix ans, les lectures ont esté demandées au Roy, & les brevets ont esté obtenus pour deux lectures vaquantes, que Mosieur Bouuard, pour lors premier Medecin du Roy Louys XIII. a fait revoquer, pour les mettre à la dispute, à l'ordinaire, contre vos deliberations qui favorisoient les deux Aspirans, qui avoient obtenu brevet du Roy: Ce qui est une honte à vostre Eschole, & une tache ignominieuse, qu'il ait fallu qu'un Docteur de Paris, premier Medecin du Roy, vous ait contraint d'observer la fondation de vos Lectures Royalles.
units.tr: In return for this false accusation, we shall reproach you with the non-observance of your Statutes in the election of the Chancellor and of the Professors of Medicine. Your Chancellor is no longer elected by the Doctors; the King provides for it, and you have tolerated this for sixty years, so that your school may be called Royal. This was not the intention of the Founders: Rondelet was elected by the Professors, and Joubert likewise. For ten years the lectureships have been requested from the King, and the warrants have been obtained for two vacant lectureships, which Monsieur Bouvard, then First Physician to King Louis XIII, had revoked, in order to put them to the usual dispute, against your deliberations, which favoured the two candidates who had obtained the King's warrant. This is a shame to your School and an ignominious stain, that a Doctor of Paris, First Physician to the King, had to compel you to observe the foundation of your Royal Lectureships.

units.la: Pour vous faire connoistre le soing que Monsieur Bouuard a eu de vostre Eschole, il vous a osté la jurisdiction du Lieutenant du premier Medecin, qui vous bravoit dans vostre ville: Il vous a conservé le Privilege du Chancelier de vostre Eschole, que Monsieur l'Evesque vouloit oster, desirant reformer l'Universitè de Montpelier, sur le modele de Paris, comme elle l'a esté par la fondation. Et afin que vous ne pensiez pas que j'allegue des faussetez à vostre mode, je produiray les Lettres que les Professeurs de Montpelier, ont escrit à Monsieur Bouvard, & celle du Sieur Ranchin, Chancelier, audit Sieur Bouvard.
units.tr: To show you the care that Monsieur Bouvard has taken for your School, he has removed from you the jurisdiction of the Lieutenant of the First Physician, who defied you in your own city. He has preserved the privilege of the Chancellor of your School, which Monsieur the Bishop wished to remove, wanting to reform the University of Montpellier on the model of Paris, as it was established by its foundation. And so that you do not think I allege falsehoods in your manner, I will produce the letters which the Professors of Montpellier wrote to Monsieur Bouvard, and that of Sieur Ranchin, Chancellor, to the said Sieur Bouvard.

units.la: Voila la lettre des Professeurs.
units.tr: Here is the letter of the Professors.

units.la: MONSIEVR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: L'asseurance que nostre Faculté a receu de vos bons mouvemens au restablissement, & reformation des abus, & desordres, qui se commettent journellement en toutes les parties de la Medecine, luy donne le courage d'implorer vostre faveur & assistance, au dessein qu'elle a fait, de poursuivre la suppression de la charge de Lieutenant de premier Barbier du Roy en cette ville, le possesseur de laquelle a tellement entrepris sur l'authorité que nous avions, en la reception des Maistres en Chirurgie par nos anciens Statuts, & tellement renversé l'ordre qui avoit esté gardé durant plusieurs siecles, aux examens des aspirans à ladite Maistrise; que sans nous appeller, avec trois ou quatre des autres Maistres, qui sont de sa cabale, il reçoit indifferemment tous ceux qui se presentent, sans y apporter autre soing que d'espuiser leurs bourses. De sorte que nous voyons tous les jours paroistre de nouvelles boutiques de Chirurgiens, dressées par des personnes, de qui nous ne connoissons ny les noms, ny les visages. Et ainsi il a remply cette ville d'un nombre exorbitant de Chirurgiens ignorans, au grand prejudice, & scandale de nostre profession. Nous vous supplions donc, Monsieur, d'assister nos bonnes intentions du pouvoir que vous y avez, lequel nous estimons estre tel, que la chose sera purement decidée, suivant vos sentimens. Et ainsi nous vous aurons toute l'obligation du bon succez qui en arrivera ; Et prians Dieu pour vostre conservation, & prosperité, nous demeurerons à jamais,
units.tr: The assurance which our Faculty has received of your good intentions towards the restoration and reform of the abuses and disorders that are daily committed in every part of Medicine gives it the courage to implore your favour and assistance in the design it has formed of pursuing the suppression of the office of Lieutenant of the King's First Barber in this city. The holder of that office has so encroached upon the authority we had, under our ancient statutes, in the admission of Masters in Surgery, and has so overturned the order observed for several centuries in the examinations of candidates for that mastership, that without calling us, together with three or four of the other Masters who are of his faction, he admits indifferently all who present themselves, taking no other care than to drain their purses.
