As a result, we see new surgeons' shops opening every day, set up by persons whose names and faces we do not know. Thus he has filled this city with an exorbitant number of ignorant surgeons, to the great prejudice and scandal of our profession. We therefore beseech you, Sir, to support our good intentions with the power you have in this matter, which we believe to be such that the affair will be decided purely according to your judgment. And so we shall owe you the whole obligation for the good outcome that comes of it; and praying God for your preservation and prosperity, we remain for ever,

units.la: MONSIEVR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: Vos tres-humbles, & tres-obeïssans serviteurs, Les Professeurs, & Docteurs Regens en Medecine de l'Vniversité de Montpelier.
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servants, the Professors and Regent Doctors of Medicine of the University of Montpellier.

units.la: DE LORT. SCHARPE. COVRTAVT. RIVIERE. I. DVRANC.
units.tr: DE LORT. SCHARPE. COVRTAVT. RIVIERE. I. DURANC.

units.la: A Montpelier, le 29. Aoust 1633.
units.tr: At Montpellier, 29 August 1633.

units.la: Voicy la Lettre du Sieur Ranchin.
units.tr: Here is the letter of Sieur Ranchin.

units.la: MONSIEVR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: Vous reconnoissant comme le General de l'Ordre de toutes les Vniuersitez de France de la Profession, I'ay eu charge de nostre Compagnie de vous instruire de ce qui s'est passé au differend que nous auons eu auec Monsieur l'Euesque de Montpelier, assisté des Sieurs de Scharpe Professeur, & Durand, Docteur Aggregé, deserteurs de la liberté, & de l'honneur de la Faculté. Ledit Scharpe ne se contente pas de nous auoir troublé, & empesché nos Actes de l'Eschole, durant huict mois, sous l'authorité de Monsieur l'Euesque, qui nous refusoit à sa persuasion, de donner la Licence aux Bacheliers, qui auoient esté examinez, & approuuez, pour establir une Iustice extraordinaire, au preiudice de la Royale, & pour supprimer les fonctions de nos charges, du Chancelier de l'Vniversité. Mais Dieu nous a fait la grace de sortir de cette tyrannie. L'en nous menace du Conseil par euocation ; en ce cas i'ay desia la botte pour aller soustenir nostre Arrest. Ie vous supplie tres-humblement Monsieur, au nom de nostre Compagnie, attendant l'evenement de nos miseres & l'honneur de vostre bien-veillance, & de me croire en particulier,
units.tr: Recognising you as the General of the Order of all the Universities of France in the Profession, I have been charged by our Company to inform you of what has passed in the dispute we have had with Monsieur the Bishop of Montpellier, assisted by Sieurs de Scharpe, Professor, and Durand, Aggregate Doctor, deserters of the liberty and honour of the Faculty. The said Scharpe is not content to have troubled us and prevented our Acts of the School for eight months, under the authority of Monsieur the Bishop, who, at his persuasion, refused us to grant the Licence to the Bachelors who had been examined and approved, in order to establish an extraordinary court to the prejudice of the Royal one, and to suppress the functions of our offices, of the Chancellor of the University. But God has granted us the grace to escape this tyranny. They threaten us with the Council by evocation; in that case I already have my boots on to go and uphold our Decree. I beseech you most humbly, Sir, in the name of our Company, awaiting the outcome of our miseries and the honour of your goodwill, and to believe me in particular,

units.la: MONSIEUR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tresobeïssant serviteur, RANCHIN.
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant, RANCHIN.

units.la: A Montpelier ce 8. d'Aoust, 1634.
units.tr: At Montpellier, this 8th of August 1634.

units.la: Vous nous reprochez la composition des Theses, que soustiennent les Bacheliers, faites par les Docteurs : il est vray, que si les Docteurs Presidens de l'Acte font disputer quelque belle question nouvelle, qu'ils auront estudiée, ils donnent le point ou tiltre au Bachelier pour faire sa These, le Docteur de son costé, qui sçait l'explication de ce tiltre, en fait une autre. Si le Docteur President ne trouve la These de son Escholier assez bien faite, selon son sens, il fait soustenir la sienne, qui est une besogne plus difficile que si le Bachelier l'avoit composée, d'autant qu'il ne rempliroit sa These de questions, qu'autant qu'il luy plairoit, & sur quoy il seroit tres-bien preparé. Or les Bacheliers de Montpelier, qui ont la plus part estudié quelque temps à Paris, remportent avec eux les Theses de l'Eschole tant vieilles, que nouvelles, & ne se servent que des vieilles, qu'ils font imprimer à Montpelier, pour les soustenir. Quant au point de la These, le Docteur & le Bachelier s'entendent bien ensemble, & laisse cela à la disposition du Bachelier, comme il a esté prouvé cy-dessus. Je puis asseurer sans vanité, que les Theses des disputes en Medecine de Paris, sont si excellentes, & si doctes, si bien expliquées & suivies, qu'elles meriteroient d'estre assemblées dans un volume, pour faire honte à ces rhapsodies & confusion de Theses des Allemans.
units.tr: You reproach us with the composition of the Theses which the Bachelors defend, said to be made by the Doctors. It is true that if the Doctors presiding over the Act have some fine new question debated, which they have studied, they give the point or title to the Bachelor to make his Thesis, and the Doctor on his side, who knows the explanation of this title, makes another. If the presiding Doctor does not find his pupil's Thesis well enough made according to his own sense, he has his own defended, which is a more difficult task than if the Bachelor had composed it, since he would not fill his Thesis with questions except as much as pleased him, and on which he would be very well prepared. Now the Bachelors of Montpellier, most of whom have studied for some time at Paris, carry back with them the Theses of the School, both old and new, and use only the old ones, which they have printed at Montpellier to defend. As for the point of the Thesis, the Doctor and the Bachelor understand each other well, and leave that to the Bachelor's choice, as has been proved above. I can assure you without vanity that the Theses of the medical disputations at Paris are so excellent, so learned, so well explained and sustained, that they deserve to be gathered into one volume, to shame those rhapsodies and the confusion of the Theses of the Germans.

units.la: Vous vous plaignez de nostre Advocat, qui vous a fait une injure notable, disant qu'on donne à Montpelier assez facilement & favorablement les Lettres de Doctorat, à ceux qui les demandent. Là-dessus vous asseurez que c'est une fausseté tres-malicieuse, veu qu'en ce temps-cy malheureux, où l'Academie a esté forcée de payer le tributà Mars, elle ne s'est pas emancipée jusques là, de donner des lettres à tous venans, pour avoir de l'argent, afin de payer les taxes; Que sont devenus vos beaux Privileges; que ne les avez vous fait valoir, s'ils sont si authentiques? Je m'estonne comme la ville, le Parlement, les Estats de la Province, ne vous ont exemptez, si vous estes l'ornement & la santé de la ville, & de la Province: par là vous faites connoistre qu'on ne fait pas grand estat de vostre Eschole. Tacité remarque, que les Empereurs Romains ont exemté la ville de Coos de tributs pour avoir donné naissance à ce grand Hippocrate, Medecin. Nous sçauons, que vous avez donné des lettres Doctorales à quelques-vns qui n'ont jamais esté à Montpelier, quand ils sont parvenus aux dignitez prés des grands Princes, Rois, & Reines, pour les obliger d'assister & favoriser vostre Eschole en Cour aux occasions. Pour preuue que vous donnez des Lettres du Doctorat aux absens, comme aux presens, je vous produiray Valeriola, à qui on a envoyé la Lettre de Docteur de Montpelier, pour honorer sa grande doctrine, par le conseil de Rondelet, comme rapporte Joubert en sa vie. Si cela s'est fait de ce tempslà, où les Statuts de l'Eschole estoient fort rigoureusement observez, de là on jugera, ce que peuvent faire les Professeurs de ce siecle corrompu, pour avoir la faveur d'un Medecin avancé dans la Cour, prés du Roy, ou de la Reine.
units.tr: You complain of our Advocate, who has done you a notable injury by saying that at Montpellier the Letters of Doctorate are granted rather easily and favourably to those who ask for them. On this you assert that it is a most malicious falsehood, since in these unhappy times, when the Academy has been forced to pay tribute to Mars, it has not gone so far as to give letters to all comers in order to get money to pay the taxes. What has become of your fine Privileges? Why have you not made them count, if they are so authentic? I am astonished that the city, the Parlement, and the Estates of the Province have not exempted you, if you are the ornament and health of the city and of the Province; by this you make known that not much account is taken of your School. Tacitus remarks that the Roman Emperors exempted the city of Cos from tributes for having given birth to the great Hippocrates, the physician. We know that you have given Doctoral letters to some who have never been at Montpellier, when they have risen to dignities near great Princes, Kings and Queens, in order to oblige them to assist and favour your School at Court on occasion. As proof that you give Letters of Doctorate to the absent as to the present, I will produce Valeriola, to whom the Letter of Doctor of Montpellier was sent, to honour his great learning, on the advice of Rondelet, as Joubert reports in his life. If this was done in those days, when the statutes of the School were very rigorously observed, one may judge from this what the Professors of this corrupt age can do to win the favour of a physician advanced at Court, near the King or the Queen.

units.la: Vous nous reprochez le prix d'argent excessif qu'il faut donner pour obtenir le Doctorat à Paris, qu'on l'acquiert à meilleur marché à Montpelier ; vous mettez toute sorte de marchandise à mesme prix, sans discerner l'estoffe à la valeur. Anciennement en Grece, on faisoit plus d'estat de ceux qui avoient emporté le prix aux jeux Olympiques, chez les Eliens, qu'en d'autres villes. De mesme est-il des Universitez. Ceux qui prennent leurs degrez à une fameuse Université, remplie de plusieurs sçauans hommes, sont obligez à une plus grande depense, qu'en des petites Academies, où ils ne sont que six ou sept, comme à Montpelier. Neantmoins la somme que les aspirans au Doctorat donnent pour la distribution de six ou sept, est douze fois plus grande pour chacun Docteur, que ne reçoit un Docteur de Paris d'un aspirant au Doctorat. Et quand ces jeunes gens ont donné leur argent aux Docteurs de Montpelier, ils les chassent de leur Eschole, & de leur ville, & ne participent point aux emolumens qui en prouiennent. Tant qu'ils vivent, ne viennent point aux charges & dignitez de l'Eschole ; Ils ne les reçoiuent point aux Conferences & assemblées de l'Eschole, n'ont aucun suffrage, ny droit. Au contraire à Paris, nos ieunes Docteurs, dés lors qu'ils sont receus en la Compagnie, commencent de recevoir quelque profit de leur argent, ils sont esgaux en suffrages comme le plus ancien, & jouissent des mesmes Privileges. Si vous sçaviez l'honneur, & le merite d'un Docteur en une fameuse & celebre Université, vous ne plaindriez pas l'argent pour obtenir le Doctorat, & estre aggregé-en la Compagnie, jouissant esgallement des mesmes droits, Privileges, & emolumens.
units.tr: You reproach us for the excessive sum of money one must pay to obtain the Doctorate at Paris, saying that it is acquired more cheaply at Montpellier. You put every sort of merchandise at the same price, without distinguishing the value of the material. In ancient Greece, people set greater store by those who had carried off the prize at the Olympic Games among the Eleans than by those in other cities. The same is true of universities. Those who take their degrees at a famous university, full of many learned men, are obliged to a greater expense than in small academies, where there are only six or seven of them, as at Montpellier. Nevertheless, the sum that candidates for the Doctorate give for the admission of six or seven is twelve times greater for each Doctor than what a Doctor of Paris receives from a candidate for the Doctorate. And when these young men have given their money to the Doctors of Montpellier, those Doctors drive them out of their School and their city, and they do not share in the emoluments that come from it. As long as they live, they do not attain to the offices and dignities of the School; they are not admitted to the conferences and assemblies of the School, and have no vote or right. On the contrary, at Paris, our young Doctors, as soon as they are received into the Company, begin to receive some profit from their money; they are equal in votes to the most senior, and enjoy the same privileges. If you knew the honour and the merit of a Doctor in a famous and celebrated University, you would not begrudge the money to obtain the Doctorate and to be admitted into the Company, enjoying equally the same rights, privileges and emoluments.

units.la: Un Docteur de Paris de quelque Faculté qu'il soit, peut obtenir benefice au mois des graduez, plaider au Chastelet de Paris, contre l'Indult des Cardinaux, qui ont leurs causes commises au Grand Conseil ; ainsi at-il esté jugé au Conseil du Roy, en faveur d'un gradué, contre Monsieur le Cardinal de Gondy, qui vouloit le traduire au Grand Conseil, en vertu de son Indult. En Allemagne, le Doctorat des fameuses Universitez Catholiques, est d'un grand prix. C'est pour[?]voy la plus part ne sont que Licentiez, & demeurent là. Mais ceux qui veulent [?]arvenir aux Canonicats des grands Euefchez, parmy les Nobles, qui sont obligez de recevoir en leurs compagnies six Docteurs, soit en Theologie, Jurisprudence, ou Medecine, ou aspirent aux dignitez Ecclesiastiques & Politiques, ils se font Docteurs, & la despense d'un seul Doctorat monte à plus de mil escus: la magnificence, qui s'observe en cette solemnité, est fort belle en Allemagne, principalement à Cologne. Le Pape Clement in Concilio Viennensi, voulant moderer les despenses, qui se faisoient aux promotions du Doctorat, il a obligé par serment les Facultez de ne prendre, & aux aspirans de ne donner que trois mil tournois d'argent pour le Doctorat. Voyez Pasquier, livre 2. Chapitre 4. Si vous aviez leu les Constitutions imprimées de l'Vniversité de Bologne, les frais qu'il falloit faire il y a six vingt ans, pour estre Docteur en Droit, & en Medecine, residens en ladite Vniversité, sont plus grands que ceux qui se font à Paris. Je sçay que Ramus, par une haine, qu'il portoit à l'Vniversité, avoit tasché de moderer toutes les despenses en toutes les Facultez, comme il se voit par vne fienne Oraison, mais il y a perdù son temps, & cela auec son herefie, luy ont causé la mort, au carnage de la sainct Barthelemy. I'apprens par Ioubert, que les fraiz pour le Doctorat à Montpelier, du temps de Rondelet, estoient fort grands, & furent moderez par Arrest de la Cour de Parlement de Toulouse. Ie doute qu'ils soient auiourd'huy dans cette moderation reglée par le Parlement.
units.tr: A Doctor of Paris, of whatever Faculty he may be, can obtain a benefice in the month reserved for graduates, and plead at the Châtelet of Paris against the indult of the Cardinals, whose causes are committed to the Grand Conseil; thus it was judged by the King's Council in favour of a graduate against Monsieur the Cardinal de Gondy, who wished to summon him before the Grand Conseil by virtue of his indult. In Germany, the Doctorate of the famous Catholic universities is of great value. Most of them are only Licentiates and remain there. But those who wish to reach the canonries of the great bishoprics, among the Nobles, who are obliged to receive six Doctors into their companies, whether in Theology, Jurisprudence or Medicine, or who aspire to ecclesiastical and political dignities, make themselves Doctors, and the expense of a single Doctorate amounts to more than a thousand crowns; the magnificence observed in this solemnity is very fine in Germany, principally at Cologne. Pope Clement at the Council of Vienne, wishing to moderate the expenses made at the promotions to the Doctorate, obliged the Faculties by oath to take, and the candidates to give, only three thousand tournois of silver for the Doctorate. See Pasquier, book 2, chapter 4. If you had read the printed Constitutions of the University of Bologna, you would see that the costs one had to incur sixty years ago to become a Doctor of Law and of Medicine, resident in the said University, are greater than those incurred at Paris. I know that Ramus, out of a hatred he bore the University, had tried to moderate all the expenses in all the Faculties, as is seen in one of his orations, but he wasted his time there, and that, together with his heresy, caused his death in the massacre of St Bartholomew. I learn from Joubert that the fees for the Doctorate at Montpellier, in the time of Rondelet, were very great, and were moderated by decree of the Parlement of Toulouse. I doubt whether they are today within the moderation regulated by the Parlement.

units.la: Nous auons cét aduátage d'honneur sur les Med. de Montpelier, que nous donnons gratis aux pauures Escholiers qui sont sçauans, les fraiz de Licence,& du Doctorat ; ce que ne sont pas les Medecins de Montpelier. Nos Registres sont pleins de telles gratifications que nous auons fait aux François , & aux étrangers ; comme à Guinterius ; qui estoit Alleman , de la ville d'Andernac sur le Rhin ; on luy donna les fraiz du Doctorat pour sa doctrine. Depuis 48. ans, vn nommé Rabeux, du Cours des Sieurs Riolan & Guerin, ne paya rien pour sa Licence. Le Sieur Frey, Suisse, sçauant Philosophe, ne paya rien , ny vn Polonois nommé Golemoski, n'a rien donné pour la Licence & le Doctorat. Nous auons dans nos Constitutions imprimées, vn article qui porte en termes exprez, Ne pau-peribus ad Medicinæ gradus aditus intercludatur:
units.tr: We have this advantage of honour over the Doctors of Montpellier, that we give gratis to poor scholars who are learned the fees for the Licence and the Doctorate; which the Doctors of Montpellier do not. Our registers are full of such favours that we have granted to the French and to foreigners, as to Guinterius, who was German, from the city of Andernach on the Rhine; the fees of the Doctorate were given to him for his learning. For 48 years, a man named Rabeux, of the course of the Sieurs Riolan and Guérin, paid nothing for his Licence. Sieur Frey, a Swiss, a learned philosopher, paid nothing, nor did a Pole named Golemoski give anything for the Licence and the Doctorate. We have in our printed Constitutions an article which states in express terms: Let no access to the degrees of Medicine be closed to the poor.

units.la: [?]arse pro Licentiis & Doctoratu Facultati de[?]ite remittantur iis qui manifeste pauperes erunt, alioquin constet eos doctos & probos esse.
units.tr: Fees for Licences and the Doctorate shall be remitted by the Faculty to those who are manifestly poor, provided that they are known to be learned and upright.

units.la: Pour ce qui est de la facilité d'obtenir les degrez du Doctorat, qu'on nous reproche, ceux qui ont esté refusez pour Bacheliers, incontinent apres receus Docteurs à Montpelier, le sçauent bien. Nous en refusons tous les deux ans aux examens, qui se font, pour recevoir des Bacheliers ; & quand ils reviennent au bout de deux ans ou quatre ans, on les examine derechef, & s'ils ne sont plus avancez on les renvoye estudier. Les enfans de Maistres s'ils ne sont capables, on les reiette, toute la grace qu'on leur fait, c'est d'estre dispensez de l'âge de 25 ans, qu'il faut avoir pour estre Bacheliers, pourvu qu'ils ayent pere, ou proche parent, qui aye soin de leur conduite. Cela s'est pratiqué de tout temps, l'Ordonnance y est formelle, approuvée par le Roy, & par Arrest de la Cour de Parlement, en la reformation de l'Université, qui est imprimé.
units.tr: As for the ease of obtaining the degrees of the Doctorate, of which we are accused, those who have been refused for Bachelors, and were received Doctors at Montpellier straight afterwards, know this well. We refuse some of them every two years at the examinations held to receive Bachelors; and when they return after two or four years, they are examined again, and if they are not further advanced they are sent back to study. The sons of Masters, if they are not capable, are rejected; the only favour shown them is that they are exempted from the age of 25 years, which one must have to be a Bachelor, provided they have a father or a close relative who takes care of their conduct. This has been the practice from all time; the Ordinance is explicit on it, approved by the King, and by decree of the Parlement, in the reform of the University, which is printed.

units.la: Mais pour estre Bachelier on n'est pas asseuré de la Licence ; avant ce temps-là il faut estre deux ans dans un exercice perpetuel des disputes durant deux hyvers ; & devant qu'estre Licentié, on doit estre interrogépar tous les Docteurs, sur la pratique, lesquels assemblez, jugent de la capacité ou incapacité des Bacheliers aspirans à la Licence, & bien souuent quelques vns sont refusez & renuoyez estudier pour vne autre Licence, où, deuant qu'estre admis, il faut derechef estre interrogé, pour sçauoir s'il ont profité en la Medecine. Partant vous estes vn grand imposteur, de soustenir que ceux qui sont refusez à Montpelier, sont receus à Paris Docteurs en Medecine.
units.tr: But to be a Bachelor one is not assured of the Licence; before that time one must spend two years in a perpetual exercise of disputations, over two winters; and before being admitted to the Licence, one must be examined by all the Doctors on practice, who, assembled, judge the capacity or incapacity of the Bachelors aspiring to the Licence; and very often some are refused and sent back to study for another Licence, where, before being admitted, they must again be examined to know whether they have made progress in Medicine. Therefore you are a great impostor in maintaining that those who are refused at Montpellier are received Doctors of Medicine at Paris.

units.la: Apres nous auoir reproché le prix excessif d'argent pour acquerir le Doctorat, vous venez à la longueur du temps d'estude dequatre ans, & deux années qu'il faut estre en perpetuelles disputes publiques, auant qu'estre Licentié: & nonobstant tout cela, les ignorans Escholiers de Montpelier, qui sont refusez, viennent prendre leurs degrez en l'Eschole de Paris, & sont receus n'ayans que le rebut de Montpelier. Ce qui est tresfaux, & ne merite point de response.
units.tr: After reproaching us for the excessive price of money to acquire the doctorate, you come to the length of study, four years, and the two years during which one must be in constant public disputations before being licensed. And notwithstanding all this, the ignorant scholars of Montpellier who are refused come to take their degrees at the School of Paris, and are received having only the leftovers of Montpellier. This is quite false, and does not deserve any reply.

units.la: En suitte de ce discours, Courtaut se met sur les louanges de l'Eschole de Montpelier, qu'il pretend auoir deliurée des griffes de la calomnie, qu'il a terrassé & accablé les Autheurs, qui lefchent maintenant la terre comme des serpens. Voila de grandes rodomontades de ce braue Courtaut, triomphant couronné de lauriers, pour avoir remporté la victoire sur l'Eschole de Paris. Attendez que l'Eschole de Montpelier vous aye promené par la ville, à la façon des Empiriques, qui vont là debiter leur marchandise, c'est le triomphe, qui vous appartient justement.
units.tr: Following this speech, Courtaut sets himself to praise the School of Montpellier, which he claims to have delivered from the claws of calumny, and to have struck down and crushed the authors who now lick the earth like serpents. Those are grand boasts from this brave Courtaut, triumphant and crowned with laurels, for having won the victory over the School of Paris. Wait until the School of Montpellier has paraded you through the city in the manner of the Empirics, who go there to peddle their wares; that is the triumph which rightfully belongs to you.

units.la: Il maintient, que nostre Eschole est si chetive & miserable, qu'elle n'a point d'honneur, de pouvoir, de science, si elle ne luy vient de l'Eschole de Montpelier, sa bonne mere, cependant elle ne reconnoist pas en ses enfans, qu'elle envoye à Paris, tant elle est ingrate: toutes les Escholes en Medecine de l'Europe sans l'Eschole de Montpelier, ne seroient pas au monde, d'autant qu'elle a instruit tous ceux qui ont erigé lesdites Escholes, & successivement leur a fourny des Docteurs pour leur instruction: ce petit vaisseau du Soleil, qui a porté Hippocrate par toute la Grece dans ses voyages, c'estoit Montpelier. Il ne reste plus qu'à conclure, qu'Hippocrate a puisé sa doctrine de l'Eschole de Montpelier, qu'il l'a visitée, quand il est venu à Marseille cueillir le seeli [?] Masiliense, duquel il parle souvent en ses Livres, que Crinias & Charmis, natifs de Marseille, qui estoient Medecins à Rome, en grand vogue, durant les premiers Cesars, estoientMedecins de Montpelier.Ie croy que tous ceux qui auront leu nostre responfe iusques à ce lieu, des louanges de l'Eschole de Montpelier, perdront la bonne opinion qu'ils en pourroient auoir, & iugeront que tout ce discours vient d'vne ceruelle mal timbrée, & trop passionnée pour son Eschole. Si Courtaut ne nous eut provoqué, & deffié de monstrer les déformitez, & imperfections de son Eschole, iamais nous n'eussions éuenté ses ordures, que nous auons tousiours cachées.
units.tr: He maintains that our School is so wretched and miserable that it has no honour, power or learning unless these come to it from the School of Montpellier, its good mother; yet it does not acknowledge in its children, whom it sends to Paris, how ungrateful it is. All the Schools of Medicine in Europe, without the School of Montpellier, would not exist in the world, inasmuch as it has taught all those who founded the said Schools, and successively furnished them with teachers for their instruction. That little vessel of the Sun which carried Hippocrates through all Greece on his travels was Montpellier. It only remains to conclude that Hippocrates drew his doctrine from the School of Montpellier, that he visited it when he came to Marseilles to gather the seeli [?] Masiliense, which he often mentions in his books; that Crinas and Charmis, natives of Marseilles, who were physicians at Rome in great vogue during the first Caesars, were physicians of Montpellier. I believe that all those who have read our response up to this point, concerning the praises of the School of Montpellier, will lose the good opinion they might have of it, and will judge that this whole discourse comes from a badly constructed brain, too passionate for its own School. If Courtaut had not provoked us and challenged us to show the deformities and imperfections of his School, we would never have exposed its filth, which we have always kept hidden.

units.la: Pour faire plus grand dépit à Courtaut, en contrechange, ie luy representeray en peu de mots les singularitez de l'Eschole de Paris, qui ont déja esté prouvées. L'Eschole de Medecine est aussi ancienne que l'Vniversité, sa naissance est de plus de sept cens ans, qu'elle a enseigné la Medecine publiquement, avec celebrité; toutes les nations estrangeres venoient apprendre la Medecine à Paris, elle a excellé en pieté, n'ayant iamais changé de Religion, en charité enuers les pauures, & les pestiferez, en doctrine qu'elle a donnée à la posterité, & par la version des bons Liures Grecs & Latins, & autres œuures; elle a suiuy la premiere, la doctrine des Grecs, reformé les erreurs des Arabes Medecins, & les abus, qui s'estoient glissez dans la Medecine, elle a eu des Medecins qui ont voyagé dans l'Afrique, dans l'Asie, pour auoir vne parfaite connoissance des Arabes, & des Grecs, elle a fourny les Medecins aux Roys depuis huict cens ans, & les Priuileges de l'Vniversité donnez par les Papes & les Roys, estans communs aux Facultez, l'Eschole de Medecine en a de plus excellens que l'Eschole de Montpelier, & toutes les autres de l'Europe. Ie diray librement que dans l'Eschole de Montpelier, il ne se rencontre point ce que l'on trouue dans l'Eschole de Paris, ce qui a esté verifié. Monstrez nous des Medecins Docteurs de Paris, qui ayent esté à Montpelier se faire receuoir Bacheliers, comme nous auons veu Sylvius & Bouguier, Docteurs de Montpelier, se faire Bacheliers de nostre Eschole. Monstrez nous des Medecins de Paris, qui soient allez à Montpelier se faire aggreger, comme nous auons eu les Sieurs Chapelain, & Pidou, Docteurs de Montpelier? Monstrez nous des Docteurs de Paris, qui ayent enuoyé leurs enfans prendre le degré de Docteur, comme nous auons veu le Sieur Gabriel Miron, Docteur de Montpelier, premier Medecin d'Anne de Bretagne, venir supplier, auec Lettres de la Reine, pour faire receuoir son fils François Miron, Bachelier en nostre Eschole. Monstrez nous des Lettres des Rois, des Reines, des Princes du sang escrites à l'Eschole de Mõpelier, comme nous en monstrons escrites à l'Eschole de Paris, pour des affaires? Monstrez-nous un Empereur, venir & assister à un acte celebre, qu'on nomrie[?] le Paranymphe, comme nous avons veu à nostre Eschole, l'Empereur Sigismond, en sortir fort satisfait, publiant des louanges de nostre Eschole? Monstrez nous un Pape sorty de vostre Eschole, & qui ait enseigné la Medecine, comme nous monstrons le Pape Jean vingtdeuxiesme, dit auparavant Joannes Petrus Hispanus, qui est venu d'Espagne pour estudier à Paris? Monstrez nous une Bulle d'un Pape, qui porte, que les Medecins de Montpelier seront receus dans toutes les autres Universitez, pour enseigner & pratiquer la Medecine, avec droit de Docteur en ladite Eschole, & ce sans examen, comme nous monstrons une Bulle du Pape Nicolas, 3. qui nous donne pouvoir d'aller enseigner, & demeurer en vostre ville, malgré vous, & sans examen, & y enseigner la Medecine?
units.tr: To cause Courtaut greater spite, in return, I will set out in a few words the singularities of the School of Paris, which have already been proved. The School of Medicine is as old as the University; its origin is more than seven hundred years old; it has taught medicine publicly, with renown; all foreign nations came to Paris to learn medicine; it has excelled in piety, never having changed its religion; in charity towards the poor and the plague-stricken; in the doctrine it has handed down to posterity, both through the translation of good Greek and Latin books and other works; it has followed first the doctrine of the Greeks, and corrected the errors of the Arabian physicians and the abuses which had crept into medicine; it has had physicians who travelled through Africa and Asia in order to have a perfect knowledge of the Arabs and the Greeks; it has furnished physicians to the Kings for eight hundred years; and since the privileges of the University, granted by the Popes and Kings, are common to all the Faculties, the School of Medicine has more excellent ones than the School of Montpellier and all the other schools of Europe. I will say freely that in the School of Montpellier one does not find what is found in the School of Paris, as has been verified. Show us doctors of Paris who have gone to Montpellier to be received as bachelors, as we have seen Sylvius and Bouguier, doctors of Montpellier, become bachelors of our School. Show us physicians of Paris who have gone to Montpellier to be aggregated, as we have had the Sieurs Chapelain and Pidou, doctors of Montpellier? Show us doctors of Paris who have sent their children to take the doctorate, as we have seen Sieur Gabriel Miron, doctor of Montpellier, first physician to Anne of Brittany, come to beg, with letters from the Queen, that his son François Miron be received as a bachelor in our School. Show us letters from Kings, Queens and princes of the blood written to the School of Montpellier, as we show letters written to the School of Paris on affairs? Show us an Emperor coming to attend a celebrated act, which they call the Paranymph, as we have seen the Emperor Sigismund at our School, leaving it very satisfied and publicly praising our School? Show us a Pope who came out of your School and taught medicine, as we show Pope John XXI, previously called Joannes Petrus Hispanus, who came from Spain to study at Paris? Show us a Bull of a Pope stating that the physicians of Montpellier will be received in all other universities to teach and practise medicine, with the right of doctor in the said School, and this without examination, as we show a Bull of Pope Nicholas III, who gave us power to go and teach and reside in your city, despite you, and without examination, and there to teach medicine?

units.la: Courtaut, apres avoir loüé son Eschole par des excez ridicules, il s'adresse à Monsieur de la Vigne, pour lors nostre Doyen, lequel pendant son Decanat a gouverné l'Eschole auec vne grande prudence, & a courageusement entrepris Renaudot, & ses associez.
units.tr: Courtaut, after praising his School with ridiculous excesses, addresses Monsieur de la Vigne, then our Dean, who during his deanship governed the School with great prudence, and courageously took on Renaudot and his associates.

units.la: Ignauum fucos pecus, à præsepibus arcet.
units.tr: The idle drones he keeps away from the mangers.

units.la: Il a maintenu les droits & Priuileges de l'Eschole, pour cela nos ennemis le haissent, & Courtaut par tout son infame liure vomit des iniures horribles, contre son honneur: Mais tant que l'Eschole de Medecine subsistera, nous tesmoignerons luy auoir tresgrande obligation ; Nous souhaitons, qu'il ait beaucoup de successeurs semblables à luy, il s'est acquis vne gloire immortelle, pour auoir conserué la bonne Medecine, que Renaudot alloit destruire, à la ruine de nos Concitoyens.
units.tr: He has maintained the rights and privileges of the School, and for this our enemies hate him; and Courtaut, through his whole infamous book, vomits horrible insults against his honour. But so long as the School of Medicine endures, we will bear witness that we owe him very great thanks. We wish that he may have many successors like himself. He has acquired immortal glory for having preserved sound medicine, which Renaudot was about to destroy, to the ruin of our fellow citizens.

units.la: Courtaut, deschirez tant que vous voudrez la Vigne ; elle ne manquera pas de fournir le farment au sacrifice de Vulcain, quand on fera brusler voftre liure diffamatoire par les mains du Boureau.
units.tr: Courtaut, tear the Vine to pieces as much as you like; it will not fail to furnish the vine-shoot for the sacrifice to Vulcan, when your defamatory book is burned by the hands of the hangman.

units.la: Rode caper vitem, tamen hàc cum stabis ad aram, In tua quod spargi cornua possit, erit.
units.tr: Gnaw at the vine, goat, as much as you like; yet when you stand at the altar, there will be a way for your horns to be sprinkled.

units.la: Pourquoy en voulez-vous si furieusement à Monsieur Patin, qui est auiourd'huy nostre Doyen, & tres-sçauant Docteur de l'Eschole de Paris ? Prenez garde à vous, Maistre Courtaut ; ce braue Docteur a fait teste, & a puissamment rembarré vn vieux Docteur de Montpelier en plein Auditoire, lors que plaidant luy-mesme sa cause, sans employer d'Aduocat, il le menaça & le terrassa de ce beau passage de S. Hierofme ; Epistola centesima: en ces termes: Dispessi fœtentem secare nasum, timeat qui stumosus est. Momus, au rapport de Pline le Grand, ne trouuoit rien à redire au portrait de Venus, sinon qu'elle auoit des patins qui faisoient trop de bruit: quod sandalias crepitantes haberet: Pareillement, entre les Medecins de Paris, qui vous ont courageusement refisté, en defendant nostre Eschole, vous taxez particulierement ledit Sieur Patin, pource qu'il est fort genereux, & qu'il a defendu tres-courageusement, les droits & les prerogatiues de nostre Faculté, au procez que nous auons eu par cy-deuant auec le Gazettier Renaudot, & contre les pretensions de vos Medecins de Montpelier, qui estoient interuenus au procez.
units.tr: Why do you rage so furiously against Monsieur Patin, who is today our Dean and a most learned teacher of the School of Paris? Take care, Master Courtaut; this brave doctor has stood his ground and has powerfully driven back an old doctor of Montpellier in full hall, when, pleading his own cause without an advocate, he threatened and overthrew him with that fine passage of St Jerome, from his Epistle one hundred: in these words: Dispessi fœtentem secare nasum, timeat qui stumosus est. Momus, according to Pliny the Elder, found nothing to criticise in the portrait of Venus except that she had sandals that made too much noise: quod sandalias crepitantes haberet. Likewise, among the physicians of Paris who have bravely resisted you in defending our School, you particularly attack the said Sieur Patin, because he is very generous and has very courageously defended the rights and prerogatives of our Faculty in the lawsuit we had previously with the gazetteer Renaudot, and against the claims of your physicians of Montpellier, who had intervened in the suit.

units.la: Courtaut aduertit nostre Doyen d'alors, (c'est l'an 1644.) Maistre Michel de la Vigne, que d'vne cause d'vn particulier, il n'en fa-ce point vne generale. C'est là où ie vous attends & arreste, & vous reproche vostre imprudence & temerité: d'vne cause particuliere que nous auions auec Renaudot, vous en auez fait vne generale: Nostre querelle estoit auec luy & ses associez, pourquoy l'Eschole de Montpelier est-elle interuenuë en cause pour assister Renaudot? Il nous attaque en nostre honneur, il veut destruire nos Priuileges, pour introduire cent fripons dans Paris, soy disans Medecins de Montpelier: Et nous n'oserons pas nous defendre, pource que l'Eschole de Montpelier le protege, & ses associez? Quelle iniustice & inhumanité, & plustost brutalité, d'attaquer l'Eschole de Medecine de Paris par escrits diffamatoires, laquelle n'a iamais rien dit, ny escrit dans les responses faites aux libelles diffama-toires de Renaudot, qui pût offenser l'Eschole de Montpelier.
units.tr: Courtaut warned our Dean of that time (this was the year 1644), Master Michel de la Vigne, that he should not make a general matter out of a particular person's cause. Here is where I await you and stop you, and I reproach you for your imprudence and rashness: out of a particular cause that we had with Renaudot, you have made a general one. Our quarrel was with him and his associates; why has the School of Montpellier intervened in the case to support Renaudot? He attacks us in our honour, he wants to destroy our privileges, in order to introduce a hundred rogues into Paris, calling themselves physicians of Montpellier; and we are not to dare defend ourselves, because the School of Montpellier protects him and his associates? What injustice and inhumanity, or rather brutality, to attack the School of Medicine of Paris with defamatory writings, a School which has never said or written anything in its replies to the defamatory libels of Renaudot that could offend the School of Montpellier.

units.la: Mais bien esloignez de cela, Monsieur Mo-reau, tres-docte Medecin de Paris, & Professeur du Roy, a donné aux Imprimeurs de Lyon, la Pratique de Franciscus Feineus, Docteur & Professeur du Roy à Montpelier, pour faire valoir cette Eschole en cõtre-eschãge[?].
units.tr: But far removed from this, Monsieur Moreau, a most learned physician of Paris and royal professor, has given to the printers of Lyon the Practice of Franciscus Feineus, doctor and royal professor at Montpellier, to enhance that School in return.

units.la: Ie veux croire que le Sieur Riuiere nous a voulu rendre la pareille, quand à la fin de son liure des Obseruations, il a appellé vn Medecin de Paris, depuis peu decedé, nommé Harduyn de S. Iacques, Illustrissimum, & le premier Medecin du Roy, Docteur de Montpelier, il le nomme seulement Illustrem. Ie ne sçay comme ce pauure malade a pû guerir, dautant qu'il escrit en son beau Latin, Medico ordinario inuisus est, pour dire qu'il a esté visité par le Medecin ordinaire de la Charité.
units.tr: I am willing to believe that Sieur Riviere wanted to repay us in kind when, at the end of his book of Observations, he called a physician of Paris, recently deceased, named Harduyn de Saint-Jacques, Illustrissimus, and the first physician of the King, a doctor of Montpellier, he calls him only Illustris. I do not know how this poor sick man could recover, since he writes in his fine Latin, Medico ordinario inuisus est, to say that he was visited by the ordinary physician of the Charité.

units.la: Renaudot nous reproche, que nous sommes si simples & peu aduisez, d'auoir loüé l'Eschole de Montpelier, que nous deuions blasmer, & reprocher. Courtaut & les Medecins de Montpelier veulent que nous endurions toutes les calomnies, medisances, injures, & reproches que Renaudot publie dans ses escrits diffamatoires, contre l'Eschole de Paris: Qu'elle est de nouuelle erection, longtemps apres celle de Montpelier: qu'elle n'est pas establie par les Papes & les Rois: qu'elle n'a aucun Priuilege, comme celle de Montpelier: qu'elle n'a point de pouuoir ny faculté de donner la Licence de pratiquer la Me-decine, hîc & vbique Terrarum: Qu'elle n'a iamais eu, & n'a pas encore de sçauans Medecins: Que la source de la vraye Medecine est à Montpelier, l'ignorance en celle de Paris: qu'elle n'a point fourny de Medecins aux Papes, Empereurs, Rois de France, & autres estrangers, comme l'Eschole de Montpelier. Partant les Medecins de ladite Eschole de Montpelier, sont les premiers de l'Europe, qui doiuent estre receus par tout le monde, dans la France, & à Paris, pour pratiquer la Medecine, estans les Aisnez sur les Medecins de Paris, qui ne sont que leurs cadets, & par consequent qu'ils doiuent auoir la prefeance en tous lieux, dautant qu'vn Docteur de Montpelier, vaut plus que six vingt Medecins de Paris, fussent-ils encor vne fois autant.
units.tr: Renaudot reproaches us for being so simple and ill-advised as to have praised the School of Montpellier, which we ought to have blamed and reproached. Courtaut and the physicians of Montpellier want us to endure all the calumnies, slanders, insults and reproaches that Renaudot publishes in his defamatory writings against the School of Paris: that it is of recent foundation, long after that of Montpellier; that it was not established by the Popes and the Kings; that it has no privilege, as that of Montpellier has; that it has no power or faculty to grant the licence to practise medicine, hîc & vbique Terrarum; that it has never had, and does not yet have, learned physicians; that the source of true medicine is at Montpellier, and ignorance in that of Paris; that it has not supplied physicians to the Popes, Emperors, Kings of France and other foreigners, as the School of Montpellier has. Therefore the physicians of the said School of Montpellier are the first in Europe, who ought to be received everywhere in the whole world, in France and at Paris, to practise medicine, being the elder brothers over the physicians of Paris, who are merely their younger brothers, and consequently they ought to have precedence in every place, since one doctor of Montpellier is worth more than six score physicians of Paris, even were they twice as many again.

units.la: Toutes ces iniures & calomnies, qui ne sont point inconnuës aux Docteurs & Professeurs de Montpelier, veulent-ils que nous les endurions par humilité Chrestienne, sans rien repartir ; Ce seroit nous declarer tels que nous depeint le Gazettier, & meriterions d'estre chassez de la ville. Ie laisse à iuger laquelle des deux Escholes, d'vne cause particuliere, en a fait vne generale, & si nous n'auons pas esté forcez de nous opposer aux Docteurs de Montpelier, interuenans & assistans, & mesmes à Renaudot. Auant cette interuention, nous n'auions rien dit & escrit, qui pût offenser l'Eschole de Montpelier, & en fussions demeuré là, si Courtaut, par son escrit diffamatoire, ne nous eust derechef attaqué plus furieusement que le Gazettier, sans aucune preuue de ce qu'il allegue contre l'Eschole de Paris.
units.tr: Are they willing that we should endure all these insults and calumnies, which are not unknown to the doctors and professors of Montpellier, out of Christian humility, without answering a word? That would declare us to be such as the gazetteer depicts us, and we would deserve to be chased out of the city. I leave it to be judged which of the two Schools has made a general matter out of a particular cause, and whether we were not forced to oppose the doctors of Montpellier, who intervened and gave their support, and even Renaudot. Before this intervention, we had said and written nothing that could offend the School of Montpellier, and we would have remained there, if Courtaut, by his defamatory writing, had not attacked us again more furiously than the gazetteer, without any proof of what he alleges against the School of Paris.

units.la: Courtaut croit auoir bien adoucy les affaires, quand il loüe les anciens Medecins de Paris pour leur modestie, doctrine, & douceur, estant bien adverty qu'ils n'ont point consenty au plaidoyer qu'on a fait contre l'Eschole de Montpelier, ny aux deux harangues Latines du Doyen. Il est tresmal adverty de ce qui se passe en nos Escholes. Aux affaires importantes, il ne se prend aucune resolution que tous les Docteurs ne soient assemblez, par un billet envoyé exprés à chasque Docteur, pour se trouver à l'assemblée. La resolution estant prise, elle est reduite en decret, par le Doyen, que personne ne peut contredire ny rejetter, de sorte que rien ne s'est fait contre Renaudet, & l'Eschole de Montpelier, que par l'advis des Anciens, & personne n'osé[?] aller à l'encontre.
units.tr: Courtaut believes he has softened matters well when he praises the ancient physicians of Paris for their modesty, learning and gentleness, being well informed that they did not consent to the pleading that was made against the School of Montpellier, nor to the two Latin harangues of the Dean. He is very badly informed about what goes on in our Schools. In important affairs no resolution is taken unless all the doctors have been assembled, by a note sent expressly to each doctor, to attend the assembly. The resolution having been taken, it is drawn up as a decree by the Dean, which no one can contradict or reject, so that nothing has been done against Renaudot and the School of Montpellier except by the advice of the elders, and no one has dared to act against it.

units.la: Courtant nous advertit, qu'il est tres-mal seant & deshonneste à un Medecin, de se mocquer des imperfections du corps, desquels un homme de bien doit avoir compassion, & un Medecin charitable y remedier ou donner conseil, & luy par une malice premeditée, a declaré, que par les constitutions d'Vrbain V. ceux qui seront chosis pour estudier en Medecine à Montpelier, ne seront point boiteux, ny bossus, ny epileptiques, ny galeux, ny atteints de quelque infirmité notable, ny impuissance de marcher, ny deformité de visage. Voila le Gazetier bien dépeint auec son nez, que ie voudrois qu'il eust fait racoustrer par l'artifice de Taliacotius, selon qu'il est enseigné en son Liure de curtorum Chirurgia. C'est vn conseil que ie luy donne charitablement. Là dessus ie prēds occasion d'expliquer cét article. En l'Vniuersité de Louuain, ils nē reçoiuent point au Doctorat en Medecine, ny à l'exercice, vn homme qui a quelque déformité au visage. Lanfranc veut qu'vn Chirurgien ne soit point difforme au visage. Hippocrate desire qu'vn Medecin soit vn homme bien sain & bien formé.
units.tr: Courtaut warns us that it is most unbecoming and dishonourable for a physician to mock the bodily imperfections which a good man ought to pity, and which a charitable physician ought to remedy or give counsel about; and he, by a premeditated malice, has declared that by the constitutions of Urban V, those who are chosen to study medicine at Montpellier shall not be lame, hunchbacked, epileptic, scabby, or afflicted with any notable infirmity, nor incapable of walking, nor deformed in face. There is the gazetteer well portrayed with his nose, which I would wish he had had repaired by the art of Taliacotius, as taught in his book De curtorum chirurgia. It is a piece of advice I give him charitably. On this point I take the occasion to explain this article. In the University of Louvain they do not admit to the doctorate in medicine, nor to the practice, a man who has some deformity of the face. Lanfranc wants a surgeon not to be deformed in face. Hippocrates desires that a physician be a man who is sound and well formed.

units.la: Distortum vultum sequitur distortio morum.
units.tr: Distorted face, distorted morals.

units.la: Vn homme difforme ne doit point estre admis à l'exercice de la Medecine, dautant qu'il peut troubler l'imagination des femmes enceintes, qui pourroient faire des monstres semblables à ces Medecins difformes. Ioint qu'vn tel visage fait peur aux malades, ce qui leur pourroit causer la mort, comme à Phaillus, dans Pausanias, lequel pour auoir regardé attentiuement le scelet d'airain, qu'Hippocrate auoit consacré au temple d'Esculape, par apprehension, songeant à la laideur du scelet, il deuint en peu de temps malade, & en mourut.
units.tr: A man with a deformed appearance ought not to be admitted to the practice of medicine, since he may disturb the imagination of pregnant women, who might then produce monsters resembling these deformed physicians. Moreover, such a face frightens the sick, which could cause their death, as happened to Phaillus in Pausanias, who, having looked intently at the bronze skeleton that Hippocrates had dedicated in the temple of Aesculapius, fell ill within a short time out of apprehension, brooding on the ugliness of the skeleton, and died of it.

units.la: Ceux qui avoient le nez coupé, n'estoient point admis au Sacerdoce, dans le Levitique, afin de ne point espouvanter les femmes, lesquelles regardans à l'Autel cét homme sacrifiant, pouvoient en retenir l'idée, & faire des monstres semblables.
units.tr: Those whose noses had been cut off were not admitted to the priesthood, according to Leviticus, so that they would not frighten women, who, looking at this man as he sacrificed at the altar, might retain the image and produce similar monsters.

units.la: Ayât suiuy pas à pas Courtaut, en sa Declamation Satyrique, qui ressemble plutost à vn Roman fabuleux en Medecine, qu'à vne histoire veritable ; nous voila paruenus à la fin où il implore l'assistance de Monsieur de Fenoüillet, Euesque de Montpelier, pour donner son iugement, & son tesmoignage sur l'excellence de l'Eschole de Montpelier, en tous les points qu'il a prononcé en sa presence. Il demeure d'accord d'en passer par son iugement, puis qu'il est l'Oracle de verité, & qu'il ne peut mentir. L'ay vne Lettre dudit Sieur Evefque, qui est vn original, escrit de sa propre main, Olographe, qui fera connoistre à tout le monde, son iugement sur l'Eschole de Montpelier ; elle est adressée à Monsieur Beuuart, Ancien Docteur de Paris, qui estoit pour lors premier Medecin de Louis XIII. de glorieuse memoire, qui destruit absolument, tout ce que Courtaut a publié en la louange de son Eschole. Elle est suffisante pour le faire declarer le plus grand menteur & imposteur de la terre.
units.tr: Having followed Courtaut step by step in his Satirical Declamation, which resembles a fabulous romance of medicine rather than a true history, we have now arrived at the end, where he begs the assistance of Monsieur de Fenouillet, Bishop of Montpellier, to give his judgment and testimony on the excellence of the school of Montpellier, on all the points he has pronounced in his presence. He agrees to abide by his judgment, since he is the oracle of truth and cannot lie. I have a letter from the said Lord Bishop, which is an original, written in his own hand, autograph, and which will make known to everyone his judgment on the school of Montpellier; it is addressed to Monsieur Beuvart, former Doctor of Paris, who was at that time first physician to Louis XIII, of glorious memory, and it completely destroys everything that Courtaut has published in praise of his school. It is sufficient to have him declared the greatest liar and impostor on earth.

units.la: MONSIEVR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: J'avois bien desiré que cette premiere lettre, outre l'asseurance qu'elle vous porte de mon tres-humble service, & de l'estime que je fais avec toute la France de vos merites, fust encore chargée de quelque nouvelle, qui vous fust agreable; mais je suis contraint de vous escrire une chose, laquelle sans doute vous fera prendre part à nostre déplaisir, pour l'esperance que j'ay, que par vostre entremise & recommandation, on y pourra trouver quelque remede. Elle consiste en grand desordre, qui se trouve à present dans la Faculté de la Medecine, tant à cause des contentions, jalousies, & inimitiez counertes, qui sont entre les Professeurs, que de l'infraction des Statuts anciens, de la cessation des leçons ordinaires, & de plusieurs nouveautez introduites durant le temps que ceux de la Religion pretendue reformée ont esté les Maistres de cette ville, contraires aux formes, & à la discipline de toutes les Universitez du Royaume. Je vous en cotteray icy sommairement quelques-unes, qui font connoistre la necessité qu'il y a d'y remedier, si on veut empescher la perte entiere de l'honneur ancien de cette Faculté. Premierement: Elle se comporte comme toute separée des autres deux, ne reconnoissant point le Recteur de l'Vniversité, faisant corps à part, & prenant pour elle seule le nom d'Vniversité. Ce seul point est la source de plusieurs desordres, premierement de la jalousie des deux autres Facultez contre cette troisieme, & cela produit souvent de mauvais effets. Car encore qu'à faute de gages, il n'y ait point icy de leçons publiques en la Theologie, comme il y en a pour le Droit Canon, & le Ciuil, Il y a toutefois des Docteurs matriculez & Aggregez, qui examinent, & approuvent les presentez pour recevoir les degrez en ladite Faculté. Outre que le corps de l'Vniversité en reçoit un grand affoiblissement, puis que ses membres ne conspirent point par une bonne union à sa subsistance. Et de plus, il arrive que cette separation, est cause que les differens, qui naissent dans l'Eschole, ou les combats entre lesdits Professeurs en la Medecine, qui sont tres-frequents, demeureront sans remede: Car de six qu'ils sont en nombre, avec un Docteur Aggregé (ils sont deux par l'institution, mais le deuxiesme a quitté ce pais depuis plusieurs années,) il y en a toufjours vn, ou deux absens ; Et arriuant que les autres se querellent, le plus grand nombre d'vne seule voix l'emporte; & se rend Iuge des autres en son fait propre, ce qui ne seroit pas si ceux-cy vouloient s'assembler avec les Professeurs, & Docteurs Aggregez des autres Facultez, qui pourroient les mettre d'accord, ou vuider sur le champ tels differens sans passion. Aufsi ce desordre est la cause que Monsieur Scharpe, que ie puis appeller veritablement, l'honneur de cette Faculté, ayant ordinairement 50. ou 60. Escholiers pour ses Auditeurs, quand les autres en ont huict ou dix, lassé de diuerses attaques qu'on luy a fait par enuie, s'est en fin resolu de nous quitter non seulement avec nostre regret, mais nostre honte, de ne sçauoir conseruer ce que les Estrangers estiment, & viennent chercher au milieu de nous. Secondement: Cette Faculté n'a point de Statuts certains, desquels les Professeurs soient d'accord; Car le Sieur Ranchin les ayant en son pouvoir, tantost il dit qu'ils ont esté égarez, ou perdus durant les guerres, tantost il en produit piece à piece quelquesuns, qui servent selon ses desirs, au suiet de quelque contention entre eux. Et quoy que le Sieur Scharpe, & quelques autres, ayent souuent requis d'en faire des nouueaux, en renouuellant les anciens, qui restoient, & que tous ensemble l'ayent resolu en ma presence, & confirmé plusieurs fois leur deliberation; neantmoins, la brigue des quatre preualant contre les deux autres Professeurs, & le Docteur Aggregé, on n'y a point satisfait; & de plus, on se plaint que le Sieur Ranchin, apres auoir ioüy des reuenus de plusieurs benefices Ecclesiastiques, durant enuiron trente ans, s'estant marié auec vne femme de la Religion pretendue reformée, laquelle feignit de se faire Catholique pour l'espouser, & depuis fait profession ouuerte de l'heresie, garde neantmoins tous les titres de ladite Faculté, lesquels apres sa mort peuuent tomber entre les mains de sa femme, auec de grands perils d'estre égarez, ou communiquez à des personnes suspectes.
units.tr: I had very much desired that this first letter, besides the assurance it brings you of my most humble service, and of the esteem that I, together with all France, hold for your merits, should also be filled with some news that would be agreeable to you; but I am constrained to write you a matter which, no doubt, will make you share in our displeasure, in the hope I have that, through your intervention and recommendation, some remedy may be found for it. It consists in the great disorder that now prevails in the Faculty of Medicine, both because of the contentions, jealousies and secret enmities that exist among the Professors, and because of the infringement of the ancient Statutes, the cessation of the ordinary lectures, and several novelties introduced during the time when those of the so-called Reformed Religion were the masters of this city, contrary to the forms and discipline of all the Universities of the Kingdom. I will here summarily set down some of them, which make clear the necessity of remedying them, if we wish to prevent the total loss of the ancient honour of this Faculty. First: it conducts itself as though entirely separate from the other two, not recognising the Rector of the University, forming a separate body, and taking for itself alone the name of University. This single point is the source of several disorders; first, the jealousy of the other two Faculties against this third, which often produces bad effects. For although, for lack of funds, there are here no public lectures in Theology, as there are for Canon and Civil Law, there are nevertheless matriculated and affiliated Doctors who examine and approve those presented to receive degrees in the said Faculty. Besides, the body of the University receives great weakening from this, since its members do not conspire by good union for its support. Furthermore, it happens that this separation is the cause that the disputes which arise in the School, or the quarrels among the said Professors of Medicine, which are very frequent, remain without remedy. For of the six who are in number, together with one affiliated Doctor (there are two by institution, but the second has left this country several years ago), there is always one or two absent; and when the others quarrel, the greater number carries the day by a single vote, and makes itself judge of the others in its own cause, which would not be so if these men would meet with the Professors and affiliated Doctors of the other Faculties, who could reconcile them or settle such disputes on the spot without passion. Likewise, this disorder is the cause that Monsieur Scharpe, whom I may truly call the honour of this Faculty, who ordinarily has 50 or 60 students as his hearers, when the others have eight or ten, wearied by various attacks made on him out of envy, has at last resolved to leave us, not only with our regret but with our shame, at not being able to preserve what foreigners esteem and come to seek in our midst. Second: this Faculty has no fixed Statutes on which the Professors agree; for Sieur Ranchin, having them in his power, sometimes says they were mislaid or lost during the wars, and sometimes he produces some of them piece by piece, which serve according to his wishes in some dispute among them. And although Sieur Scharpe and some others have often requested that new ones be made by renewing the old ones which remained, and they have all together resolved this in my presence and confirmed their deliberation several times; nevertheless, the cabal of the four prevailing against the two other Professors and the affiliated Doctor, nothing has been done about it; and moreover, complaint is made that Sieur Ranchin, after having enjoyed the revenues of several ecclesiastical benefices for about thirty years, having married a woman of the so-called Reformed Religion, who pretended to become a Catholic in order to marry her, and afterwards made open profession of heresy, nevertheless keeps all the records of the said Faculty, which after his death may fall into the hands of his wife, with great danger of being lost or communicated to suspect persons.

units.la: Troisiesmement, l'intention des Regences Royales, sur tout des deux dernieres, n'est point gardée, par lesquels les Professeurs, qui en sont pourueus, sont obligez de lire, l'vn aux Apothiquaires, l'autre aux Chirurgiens: & de fait, ces derniers se sont plaints à moy, & depuis au Parlement, du Sieur Riuiere, de ce qu'il ne leur faisoit point de leçons, qu'il deuoit faire par l'institution de la Regence, qui luy a esté conferée.
units.tr: Thirdly, the intention of the Royal Regencies, especially of the last two, is not observed, by which the Professors who hold them are obliged to lecture, one to the apothecaries, the other to the surgeons; and indeed, these last have complained to me, and afterwards to Parliament, about Sieur Rivière, because he did not give them the lectures which he was bound to give by the institution of the Regency conferred on him.

units.la: Quatriesmement: Les autres Professeurs, excepté le Sieur Scharpe, se dispensent aussi fort librement de lire aux temps ordonnez, par les anciens Statuts, & reglemens de l'Eschole. Le Sieur Ranchin est souuent absent, le Sieur Riuiere aussi, à cause des procez qui le diuertissent ordinairement: le Sieur Courtaut lit fort rarement, le Sieur de Lort, outre la foiblesse de son âge, s'amuse à la pierre Philosophale, & neantmoins par un abus, qu'on ne doit plus souffrir, exigeans & recevans aisément les tesmoignages de quelques Escholiers, qu'ils se sont bien acquittez de leurs charges; la Cour des Comptes leur a passé leurs gages, au preiudice du public, & contre l'intention de sa Maiesté, qui a fondé & dotté les six Regences.
units.tr: Fourthly: The other Professors, except Monsieur Scharpe, also dispense themselves quite freely from lecturing at the times fixed by the old statutes and regulations of the School. Monsieur Ranchin is often absent, and so is Monsieur Riviere, because of the lawsuits that usually distract him. Monsieur Courtaut lectures very rarely. Monsieur de Lort, besides the weakness of his age, amuses himself with the Philosopher's Stone, and yet, by an abuse which must no longer be tolerated, they readily demand and accept the testimonies of some students that they have discharged their duties well; the Chamber of Accounts has passed their salaries, to the prejudice of the public and contrary to the intention of His Majesty, who founded and endowed the six Regencies.

units.la: Cinquiesmement: On a souuent aduerty le Sieur Riuiere, qu'il contreuenoit aux reglemens de l'Eschole, se meslant de donner en cachette dans la ville, & à decouuert, quand il estoit appellé à la campagne, pour visiter quelques malades, des poudres camens me-talliques: il l'a tesmoigné assez en ses Observations, où il parle souuent du Ca-lomelanos de Turquet, duquel il donne de quatre à six grains qui est l'Antimoine, puis sa poudre cephalique, le Bezoard mineral, Aqua benedi-ctia[?], & autres remedes trespernicieux.
units.tr: Fifthly: Monsieur Riviere has often been warned that he is contravening the regulations of the School, by secretly and openly dispensing metallic powders and remedies in the town, and when he is called into the countryside to visit some sick people. He has amply testified to this in his Observations, where he often speaks of the Calomelanos of Turquet, of which he gives four to six grains, which is antimony; then his cephalic powder, the mineral Bezoar, Aqua benedicta[?], and other very pernicious remedies.

units.la: La Cour de Parlement veut connoistre des Vniuersitez, craignant que les Euesques n'én chassent les Religionnaires.
units.tr: The Parliament wishes to take cognizance of the Universities, fearing that the bishops will drive the Religionists out of them.

units.la: & certaines essences, au lieu de pratiquer la Medecine selon les loix anciennes de la Faculté. A quoy il n'y a point de remede, pource que le Sieur Riuiere s'est vny & ligué avec le Sieur Ranchin, De Lort, & Courtaut, qui dissimulent cette permicicieuse[?] nouveauté en faveur de leur cabale ; contre les autres.
units.tr: & certain essences, instead of practising medicine according to the ancient laws of the Faculty. There is no remedy for this, because Monsieur Riviere has united and allied himself with Monsieur Ranchin, De Lort and Courtaut, who conceal this pernicious novelty in favour of their clique; against the others.

units.la: Ie puis compter pour un sixiesme desordre, le peu ou point d'esperance qu'il y a de trouver le remede dans le Parlement de Toulouse, auquel nous avons eu recours, & Monsieur Scharpe aussi, mais luy a esté renvoyé à ses propres parties. Et pour mon regard, tous mes advis, & toutes mes requestes en cette matiere sont[?] devenuës fort suspectes, & ont esté mal receuës, depuis que Messieurs du Parlement ont eu dispute avec Monsieur l'Archevesque, touchant l'Université de Tolose, s'estans assez expliquez, qu'ils ne veulent point prononcer en faveur des authoritez Episcopales establies ailleurs, pour ne faire point de prejudice à leurs Professeurs, contre Monsieur l'Archevesque. La chose donc est reduite au desespoir, s'il ne plaist à Monsieur le Garde des Seaux, d'en avoir compassion, & receuoir une Requeste, qui luy sera presentée en mon nom, pour en retenir la connoissance: A quoy vostre credit, & recommandation pourroit grandement aider, comme i'ose esperer, que vous ne la refuserez pas, à la tres-humble priere que ie vous en fais, estant d'ailleurs asseuré du zele & affection, que vous auez, pour conseruer & faire fleurir auec honneur, cette belle, & precieuse science de la Medecine, auec laquelle vous obligez si heureusement toute la France, & toute l'Eglise de Dieu, par la conseruation de la santé du Roy. Cependant ie demeure,
units.tr: I may count as a sixth disorder the little or no hope there is of finding a remedy in the Parliament of Toulouse, to which we have had recourse, and Monsieur Scharpe too, but he has been sent back to his own parties. And as for me, all my advice and all my petitions in this matter have become very suspect and have been badly received, since the gentlemen of Parliament had a dispute with Monsieur the Archbishop concerning the University of Toulouse, having made it sufficiently clear that they do not wish to pronounce in favour of episcopal authorities established elsewhere, so as not to cause any prejudice to their Professors, against Monsieur the Archbishop. The matter is therefore reduced to despair, unless it pleases Monsieur the Keeper of the Seals to take pity on it and receive a petition, which will be presented to him in my name, in order to take cognizance of it. In this your credit and recommendation could greatly help, as I dare hope you will not refuse it, at my most humble request, being moreover assured of the zeal and affection you have for preserving and making flourish with honour this fine and precious science of medicine, by which you so happily oblige all France and the whole Church of God, through the preservation of the King's health. Meanwhile I remain,

units.la: MONSIEVR,
units.tr: SIR,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble, & tresaffectionné seruiteur, PIERRE E. de Montpelier;
units.tr: Your most humble and most affectionate servant, PIERRE E., of Montpellier;

units.la: A Montpelier, ce 6. d'Aoust, 1634. Apres ce tesmoignage de Monsieur l'Euesque, sur l'Eschole de Montpelier, ie n'ay plus rien à repartir à Courtaut, sinon de luy dire,
units.tr: At Montpellier, 6 August 1634. After this testimony of Monsieur the Bishop concerning the School of Montpellier, I have nothing more to reply to Courtaut, except to say to him,

units.la: Quò moriturus ruis, maioráque viribus audes, Fallit te incautum pietas tua, nec minùs ille Exultat.
units.tr: Where are you rushing to your death, daring things beyond your strength? Your piety deceives you, unwary as you are, and that one exults no less.

units.la: Pour conclusion de ce discours, Ie supplie Messieurs les Professeurs de l'Eschole de Montpelier, de considerer le tort qu'ils se sont procurez, d'estre intervenus au procez de Renaudot, d'avoir permis que cette Declamation satyrique de Courtaut fût imprimée dans leur ville, d'y avoir laissé tous les solecismes & barbarismes qui s'y rencontrent, lesquels devoient estre corrigez, avant que ce Roman fabuleux en Medecine fut publié.
units.tr: To conclude this discourse, I beg the Gentlemen Professors of the School of Montpellier to consider the wrong they have brought upon themselves: to have intervened in the lawsuit of Renaudot, to have allowed this satirical Declamation of Courtaut to be printed in their town, and to have left in it all the solecisms and barbarisms that are found there, which ought to have been corrected before this fabulous novel in medicine was published.

units.la: De plus, que vous avez un Professeur en Medecine, qui se mesle d'escrire des Observations, remplies de paradoxes tres-pernicieux en la Medecine, contenant aussi des secrets qu'il a particulierement, comme Aqua benedicta, sa poudre Cephalique, le Calomelanos Turqueti, qui se donne par grains de cinq à six, qui est l'Antimoine. Si vous ne corrigez ces abus, en conservant la bonne & ancienne Medecine d'Hippocrate & Galien, nous aurons sujet de nous plaindre de vous, avec Symphorianus Campegius, sans toutesfoit vous donner aucune imprecation, comme il a fait, libro de clysteribus. Nostris temporibus hæreses in Medicina, quas non parum multas fuisse accepimus apud Papienses, & Montispessulanos. Id omne ex Arabum ac Iudæorum dogmatum fontibus nascitur; Quare non possum me continere, quin male precer illis, qui in culpa sunt. Dij itaque vobis malefaciant, Papienses, & Montispessulani, Neoterici iniustissimi, qui in hominum perniciem Arabes, Persas, Iudæosque, in ciuitatibus ac Gymnasiis vestris introire permisistis.
units.tr: Moreover, you have a Professor of medicine who busies himself with writing Observations, filled with very pernicious paradoxes in medicine, also containing secrets which he keeps to himself, such as Aqua benedicta, his cephalic powder, the Calomelanos of Turquet, which is given in doses of five to six grains, and which is antimony. If you do not correct these abuses, preserving the good and ancient medicine of Hippocrates and Galen, we shall have cause to complain of you, with Symphorianus Campegius, though without giving you any curse, as he did, in the book on clysters. In our times there have arisen heresies in medicine, which we have learned were not a few among the people of Pavia and Montpellier. All this springs from the fountains of the doctrines of the Arabs and Jews; wherefore I cannot restrain myself from cursing those who are at fault. May the gods therefore do you harm, people of Pavia and Montpellier, most unjust moderns, who in the destruction of men have permitted Arabs, Persians and Jews to enter your cities and schools.

units.la: Ie ne puis finir ce Discours, sans aduertir mon Lecteur, que Monsieur Naudé, tressçauant en toutes les Sciences, & Docteur en Medecine, comme il a tesmoigné par diuers liures tres-doctes, qu'il a mis en lumiere, a fait vn discours Latin ; De Antiquitate & dignitate Scholæ Medicæ Parisiensis, qu'il a prononcé publiquement dans les Escholes de Medecine, en vn Paranymphe celebre, & depuis imprimé, duquel ie me suis seruy, ayant le premier par son industrie & grand trauail, defriché & dechifré cette matiere assez obscure, à cause de la perte de nos cinq anciens Registres de deux cens ans, dequoy nostre Eschole, & moy particulierement luy sommes tres-obligez.
units.tr: I cannot end this discourse without advising my reader that Monsieur Naudé, most learned in all the sciences and Doctor of Medicine, as he has shown by various very learned books which he has published, has made a Latin discourse, On the Antiquity and Dignity of the Parisian School of Medicine, which he delivered publicly in the schools of medicine, in a famous Paranymph, and afterwards printed. I have used it, having been the first, through his industry and great labour, to clear and decipher this matter, which is rather obscure because of the loss of our five ancient registers of two hundred years, for which our School, and I in particular, are very much indebted to him.

units.la: F I N.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: ADDITIONS AU DISCOURS precedent.
units.tr: ADDITIONS TO THE PRECEDING DISCOURSE

units.la: DEPUIS peu quelque bonne personne voyant approcher le grand Jubilé de cinquante ans, a fait restitution à l'Eschole d'un vieux Registre des affaires de nostre Faculté, qui commencé en l'année 1395. & va jusques en l'année 1430. qui m'a esté communiqué par Maistre Guy Patin, nostre Doyen: en feuilletant ledit Registre, i'apprens, que le Doyen esleu le Samedy apres laToussaint, donnoit à son Devancier un Recepissé, comme il avoit receu de luy Bona Facultatis, qui estoient le Seau attaché à une chaine d'argent, un Livre des principaux Statuts, avec la figure d'un Crucifix de Nostre Seigneur, sur lequel il juroit d'estre fidele observateur des Statuts, & de procurer le bien de l'Eschole. De plus, qu'il rendroit à son successeur, les cinq Registres, qui contiennent nos Statuts, Privileges ,& autres affaires de l'Eschole. Puis il declare les Manuscrits en Medecine, qu'on luy livroit. Mais il y en a un specifié ,qui est le Livre de Galien , de vitilitate membrorum, legué à la Faculté l'an 1090. Qui fait paroistre l'antiquité de nostre Eschole. En suite les autres Doyens ont fait les mesmes fermens, faisans toufjours mention des cinq Registres, lesquels ont esté dérobez par les Anglois, qui s'estoient introduits par force, & jussions du Roy d'Angleterre dans nos Escholes, pendant qu'ils possedoient la ville de Paris.
units.tr: Not long ago, some good person, seeing the great Jubilee of fifty years approaching, returned to the School an old register of the business of our Faculty, begun in the year 1395 and running to the year 1430. It was lent to me by Master Guy Patin, our Dean. In leafing through this register, I learn that the Dean elected on the Saturday after All Saints' Day gave his predecessor a receipt, acknowledging that he had received from him the Bona Facultatis: these were the seal attached to a silver chain, a book of the principal statutes, and the figure of a crucifix of Our Lord, on which he swore to be a faithful observer of the statutes and to promote the good of the School. Moreover, he would hand over to his successor the five registers that contain our statutes, privileges and other affairs of the School. Then he lists the medical manuscripts that were handed to him. Among them one is specified: the book of Galen de utilitate membrorum, bequeathed to the Faculty in the year 1090, which shows the antiquity of our School. Afterwards the other Deans made the same oaths, always mentioning the five registers, which were stolen by the English, who had forced their way into our Schools by force and by command of the King of England while they held the city of Paris.

units.la: Nous apprenōs par ledit Registre, que les Medecins estoiēt dās l'ordre Ecclesiastique sans estre mariez, pour pratiquer la Medecine, & que ceux qui se faisoiētPrestres, estoiēt interdits de pratiquer, s'ils n'auoient Bulle expresse du Pape, pour en auoir la Licence.
units.tr: We learn from this register that physicians were in holy orders without being married in order to practise medicine, and that those who became priests were forbidden to practise unless they had an express bull from the Pope to grant them the licence.

units.la: Que tous ceux, qui se passoient Licentiez, juroient qu'ils n'estoient pas mariez, & qu'ils n'exerceroiēt jamais les operations manuelles de la Chirurgie, & les Maistres Regens, qui s'en mesloient, estoient chassez du corps. Ceux qui favorisoient Extraneos, & Cabusatores, estoient bannis de l'Eschole.
units.tr: All who were licensed swore that they were not married and that they would never perform the manual operations of surgery; and the regent masters who meddled in them were expelled from the body. Those who favoured Extraneos and Cabusatores were banished from the School.

units.la: Le Doyen estoit esleu par quatre Docteurs, un de chaque Nation, & s'ils ne se trouvoient que deux Nations, ils faisoient le Doyen, qui n'estoit que pour un an ; neantmoins il pouvoit estre continué.
units.tr: The Dean was elected by four teachers, one from each nation; and if only two nations were found, they made as Dean the one who served for a single year; nevertheless he could be continued in office.

units.la: La Licence se donnoit avec grande celebrité dans la grande Sale de l'Euesché, & qu'un Reginaldus, Professeur en Theologie, Confesseur du Roy, en l'absence du Chancelier de l'Université, qui estoit Jean Gerson, deputé par l'Université au Concile de Constance, fist des merveilles avec admiration en sa Harangue.
units.tr: The licence was conferred with great solemnity in the great hall of the Bishop's palace, and Reginaldus, professor of theology and confessor of the King, in the absence of the Chancellor of the University, who was Jean Gerson, deputed by the University to the Council of Constance, performed wonders with admiration in his oration.

units.la: Les Medecins du Roy, & de la Reine, du Duc de Bourgogne, & du Duc d'Orleans, supplioient pour estre dispensez de la Leçture, & Regence, qui estoit de presider, & disputer à leur rāg aux actes des Bachéliers.
units.tr: The physicians of the King, of the Queen, of the Duke of Burgundy and of the Duke of Orléans begged to be excused from the lecturing and regency, which consisted in presiding and disputing in their turn at the acts of the bachelors.

units.la: De ce temps là il n'y avoit point de Doctorat, mais apres la Licence obtenuë, on presidoit à un acte cum Pastillaria, sive resupta, apres la Presidence on estoit declaré Magister actu Regens, & Aggregé au corps.
units.tr: In those days there was no doctorate; but after the licence had been obtained, one presided at an act cum Pastillaria, sive resupta, and after the presidency one was declared Magister actu Regens and admitted into the body.

units.la: Au Concile de Constance, on voulut priver les Maistres és Arts, & les Medecins de l'Indult, pour obtenir, & posseder de grands benefices. Ils s'opposerent genereusement au Decret, & fut accordé & arresté, que les Privileges de l'Université seroient communs à toutes les quatre Facultez.
